N is countable (@fd2:thm-product-countable). The map a \mapsto [a], from 
N 	imes 
N to 
Z = (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim}, is surjective, since every class is the class of each of its elements (@fd2:def-quotient-set). By @fd2:prp-countable-image, 
Z is countable. 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} is countable. 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
Z is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-subset, and the product of two countable sets is countable (@fd2:cor-product-countable (a)). 
Q is countable. The map (p, q) \mapsto [(p, q)], from 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} to 
Q, is surjective (@fd2:def-quotient-set), so 
Q is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-image. (Section 1.7 lets a review exercise cite @fd2:thm-product-countable and @fd2:cor-product-countable (a), which run on \omega through @prp-omega-powers-parity.) The conclusion is @fd2:thm-integers-rationals-countable for the constructed 
Q; that theorem, about the school rationals, is not used. [R3] Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} and s \in 
Q. Write “s is a supremum of A in 
Q” in symbols, with bounded quantifiers. Then write its negation, moving 
eg inward as far as it goes and naming the law used at each step. The proof that A has no supremum in 
Q has two cases; which half of the negation does each case establish, and with which witness? By @fd2:def-order-supremum, “s is a supremum of A” is the conjunction of (S1) and (S2):  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \wedge \  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . Its negation is, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d), 
eg  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \vee \ 
eg  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), the first disjunct becomes \exists x \in A \ 
eg(x \le s), that is, \exists x \in A \ \ s < x (totality of \le, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a) and then @fd1:prp-negated-implication, the second becomes \exists v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) \wedge 
eg(s \le v)  igr) , that is, there is an upper bound v of A with v < s. In words: s fails to be the supremum when some element of A lies above s, or some upper bound lies below s. In the proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2, Case 1 (s^2 < 2) establishes the first disjunct, with witness x = u(s) = 4s/(s^2 + 2). Case 2 (s^2 > 2) establishes the second, with witness v = t(s) = (s^2 + 2)/(2s). (The proof itself needs no negation law: it derives a contradiction from (S1) in Case 1 and from (S2) in Case 2.) [R4] Is there a rational number x with x^3 = 2, where x^3 \coloneqq x^2 \cdot x? Prove your answer. No. The tool is descent on the denominator, as in @thm-no-rational-square-two, but run with parity, which @prp-rational-integer-part supplies. Parity. For every a \in 
Z there is m \in 
Z with a = 2m or a = 2m + 1, and not both forms occur. Indeed, let m \coloneqq  loor{a/2} (@prp-rational-integer-part): m \le a/2 < m + 1, so 2m \le a < 2m + 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). The integer r \coloneqq a - 2m has 0 \le r < 2; if r > 0, then r \ge 1, and if r > 1, then r \ge 2, by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); so r = 0 or r = 1. If 2m = 2m' + 1, then d \coloneqq m - m' has 2d = 1; but d \le 0 gives 2d \le 0, and d \ge 1 gives 2d \ge 2, and by discreteness one of these holds. Moreover an odd cube is odd: (2m + 1)^3 = 2(4m^3 + 6m^2 + 3m) + 1 . Descent. Suppose x \in 
Q and x^3 = 2. Then x > 0: x = 0 gives x^3 = 0, and x < 0 gives x^2 > 0 and x^3 = x^2 \cdot x < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c)). So x = p/q with p, q \in 
Z_{>0} and p^3 = 2q^3 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), @def-rational-operations). Take q least among such denominators (@prp-integer-least-element), with its p. Since p^3 = 2q^3 has the even form, p is not odd (its cube would be odd), so p = 2m with m \in 
Z, and m > 0 because p > 0 (m \le 0 would give 2m \le 0). Then 2q^3 = 8m^3, and canceling the non-zero factor 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), q^3 = 2(2m^3). So q is not odd either: q = 2l with l \in 
Z_{>0}. Then 8m^3 = 2 \cdot 8l^3, so m^3 = 2l^3, and l < l + l = q. So l is a smaller admissible denominator, with m \in 
Z_{>0}: a contradiction. Why the look-alike fails. The substitution p' \coloneqq 2q - p, q' \coloneqq p - q of the square-root proof came from x = (2 - x)/(x - 1), which used x^2 = 2. For cubes the same algebra fails: expanding, (2q - p)^3 - 2(p - q)^3 = -3p^3 + 12p^2 q - 18pq^2 + 10q^3 , which is not a constant multiple of p^3 - 2q^3 (it has a p^2 q term), so this identity gives no way to derive p'^3 = 2q'^3 from p^3 = 2q^3, and the descent has no smaller pair to move to. Parity, by contrast, works for every power: “even cube, so even base” is the same argument for squares and cubes.

title: Divisibility, Division with Remainder, and Modular Arithmetic
content:
Divisibility, Division with Remainder, and Modular Arithmetic Chapter 2 built 
Z out of pairs of natural numbers and proved it an ordered ring, but it said nothing about which integers divide which. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 did, for the school integers: it proved division with remainder, showed that every integer from 2 on has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of prime factorization aside as a fact it neither proved nor used. This chapter proves that arithmetic again for the constructed 
Z, and goes further, using the ordered-ring axioms and two properties of the order of 
Z: there is no integer strictly between 0 and 1 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), and a non-empty set of integers with a lower bound has a least element (@prp-integer-least-element); the field 
Q enters chiefly for the integer part  loor{a/n} and for lowest terms. The second property gives division with remainder at once. Then one move does most of the work. In a set of integers closed under sums and under multiplication by any integer, the least positive element divides every element, and dividing by it with remainder is how one sees this. Applied to the combinations ax + by, it makes the greatest common divisor a combination of a and b (Bézout’s theorem), and the Euclidean algorithm computes it. Multiplying that combination by a third integer gives Euclid’s lemma, that a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors, and with it the uniqueness of prime factorization and the lowest terms of a rational number. The second half returns to the clock of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5. There, and again for 
Z and 
Q in Chapter 2, each sum and product of classes was checked separately to be well defined. Section 3.4 makes the check once, for the quotient of any commutative ring by an ideal, and 
Z/n
Z becomes a commutative ring with n elements on which, for n \ge 2, no order fits. In it the classes that can be divided by are exactly the classes of the integers coprime to n. So 
Z/p
Z is a field with p elements for every prime p, and two congruences with coprime moduli have exactly one class of solutions modulo the product of the moduli, the Chinese remainder theorem. Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, as classes of rational Cauchy sequences whose difference is null (the null sequences play the part of the ideal), though it checks its operations directly; Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Two integers, one theory. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 proved its facts about divisibility for the school integers, from school facts such as the closure of 
Z under +, - and \cdot (@fd2:prp-integers-closed). This chapter keeps their definitions of divisibility, prime and congruence (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime, @fd2:def-congruence), read word for word on the ring of Chapter 2, and proves the results again; no proof in it cites a result of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality about integers. Each such result has a twin here, named in the section that proves it: division with remainder (@fd2:thm-division-algorithm) and the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N (@fd2:prp-divides-partial-order) in Section 3.1; a prime factor of every n \ge 2 (@fd2:thm-prime-factor) and lowest terms (@fd2:lem-lowest-terms) in Section 3.3; and the arithmetic of congruence classes (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) in Section 3.4. Nothing earlier was circular: the earlier chapters used these facts about the school integers as stated facts, and this chapter proves them for the constructed ones. What you need. Chapters 1 and 2, chiefly Section 2.3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Sections 2.2 and 2.5. From Chapter 2: the commutative ring 
Z and its algebra (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @thm-integers-commutative-ring, @prp-ring-algebra), its order, its positive elements, the rules for inequalities and discreteness (@prp-order-from-positives, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @thm-integers-ordered-ring), the least element of a set of integers bounded below (@prp-integer-least-element), the copy of 
N inside 
Z (@prp-naturals-embed-integers), the lemma that a rule on classes is a function when equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs (@thm-well-defined-on-classes), the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), and the field 
Q with 
Z inside it, its order, reciprocals and integer part (@def-rational-operations, @thm-rationals-field, @prp-integers-embed-rationals, @thm-rationals-ordered-field, @prp-reciprocal-order, @prp-rational-integer-part). From Chapter 1, the citing rule of Section 1.7 (@cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; and powers and parity on 
N (@prp-omega-powers-parity), compared with in Section 3.1 and used in review exercise R2. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, the definitions of divisibility and prime (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime); from its Section 2.3, finite products (@fd2:def-sum-product), used in Section 3.3 as a pattern for products of lists; from its Section 2.5, equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition) and congruence (@fd2:def-congruence); from its Section 2.6, suprema and the divisibility order (@fd2:def-order-supremum, @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm), in a remark of Section 3.2 and in Section 3.3’s B2. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1: products, equality of functions and bijections (@fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-bijective); and from its Section 3.1, finite sets and equinumerous sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-equinumerous-properties), to count 
Z/n
Z, with more on finite sets (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, @fd2:exr-finite-sets-c2, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) in Section 3.5’s B3 and C2. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for Section 3.3’s B1 and C2 and Section 3.5’s C2. A few results are compared with and not used: the twins listed above; the even square of Logic and Proof, Section 2.1 (@fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even) in Section 3.1; Euclid’s argument in Logic and Proof, Section 5.1’s C1 (@fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1) in Section 3.3’s C3; a rule on classes that is not a function (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map) in Section 3.4’s C1; lowest terms in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2’s C2 (@fd2:exr-induction-in-practice-c2) in Section 3.3; and, in the review exercises, the countable product of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 3.2 (@fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2, @fd2:thm-product-countable) in R2, the two proofs that \sqrt 2 is not rational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, @thm-no-rational-square-two) in R3. Review exercise R1 also returns to the integers as classes of pairs (@def-integers-as-classes). Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - Divisibility and Division with Remainder. Divisibility and primes read on the constructed 
Z, the rules for divisibility proved from the ring and its order, division with a unique quotient and remainder from a least element, the quotient as the integer part  loor{a/n}, even and odd integers, and the small-primes remark that 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime. - The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The combinations a
Z + b
Z and the multiples n
Z, the greatest common divisor with \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0, Bézout’s theorem (the least positive combination is the gcd, and every combination is a multiple of it), coprime integers, and the Euclidean algorithm as a recursion that keeps the set of combinations fixed, with back-substitution for the coefficients. - Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Euclid’s lemma from the Bézout identity, a prime dividing a product of primes equal to one of them, coprime divisors, the least divisor above 1 as a prime, existence and uniqueness of non-decreasing prime factorizations by comparing the largest primes, a monoid in which factorization is not unique, and lowest terms in 
Q. - Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n. Ideals as the subsets that a quotient needs, the quotient ring R/I of a commutative ring by an ideal, the failure for 
Z \subseteq 
Q, the ideals of 
Z as the sets n
Z, and 
Z/n
Z as a commutative ring with n elements that no order fits when n \ge 2. - Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Units of a commutative ring, the units of 
Z/n
Z as the classes coprime to n with inverses from back-substitution, 
Z/n
Z a field exactly when n is prime, and the Chinese remainder theorem for two coprime moduli, with the failures when the moduli share a factor; the review exercises reach back to Chapters 1 and 2, Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3. Named moves - Least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set of integers closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. This proves Bézout’s theorem in Section 3.2 and the description of the ideals of 
Z in Section 3.4, and Section 3.3’s B2 and Section 3.4’s C2 use it for common multiples and for sets closed under subtraction. - Multiply the Bézout identity. From 1 = ax + by, multiply by c: c = acx + bcy, and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about common divisors into an equation, and it gives Euclid’s lemma in Section 3.3; in Section 3.5 the same identity, read modulo n, gives inverses, and read modulo m and modulo n at once, the Chinese remainder theorem. - Compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. An operation on classes a + I is well defined because a change of representative is an element of I, and multiplying it by the other argument keeps it in I. This is Chapter 2’s check one argument at a time, now made once for every commutative ring and every ideal.

title: 3.1 Divisibility and Division with Remainder
content:
Divisibility and Division with Remainder Chapter 2 built 
Z as an ordered commutative ring, and a Quick check in Section 2.3 showed that it is not a field: 2x = 1 has no solution in 
Z. So “a/b” is not available among the integers. What remains is a relation, “b is a multiple of a”, and the next best thing to division: dividing with a quotient and a remainder. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 defined the relation and proved division with remainder for the school integers. This section does both again for the integers of Chapter 2, where every step must come from the ordered-ring axioms and from the least-element property of 
Z. Throughout, 
Z is the ordered ring of @thm-integers-ordered-ring, with 
N \subseteq 
Z and 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). Numerals 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 3 \coloneqq 2 + 1, and so on, are the natural numbers of those names, as in Section 2.6; a sum or product of numerals may be computed in 
N, because the embedding of @prp-naturals-embed-integers preserves + and \cdot, and a sign is moved by @prp-ring-algebra (c), as in (-4) \cdot 5 = -(4 \cdot 5) = -20. Divisibility on the constructed integers The definition of divisibility needs nothing that the ring 
Z lacks. We restate it, and the definition of a prime, from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, with 
Z now the ring of Chapter 2. Divisibility (@fd2:def-divides). Let a, b \in 
Z. Then a divides b, written a \mid b, if there exists k \in 
Z with b = ka. Then a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. We write a 
mid b when a does not divide b. Prime (@fd2:def-prime). An integer p is prime if p \ge 2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p. A prime factor of an integer n is a prime p with p \mid n. Both definitions use only the multiplication of 
Z, its order \le, and the set 
Z_{>0}, and Chapter 2 provides all three. They are the same definitions as before; what changes is that every fact about them must now be proved from Chapter 2. Divisibility is a question about existence: is b some integer times a? Some instances. 3 \mid -12, since -12 = (-4) \cdot 3. -4 \mid 0, since 0 = 0 \cdot (-4). Even 0 \mid 0 holds, since 0 = 1 \cdot 0: the definition asks for some k, and here every k works. On the other hand 5 
mid 12. That is a statement that no k \in 
Z has 12 = 5k, and to prove it we need the theorem on division with remainder below. The relation “a \mid b” is not a fraction. It is a statement, true or false, about two integers. The expression b/a, for a 
e 0, is a rational number, and this chapter does not use it to decide divisibility. Here are the rules for divisibility that the rest of the chapter uses. Each is a short consequence of the ring laws or of the order. [Rules for Divisibility in 
Z] Let a, b, c, x, y \in 
Z. 1. a \mid 0, 1 \mid a and a \mid a. If 0 \mid a, then a = 0. 2. If a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c. 3. If a \mid b and a \mid c, then a \mid bx + cy. 4. If a \mid b, then (-a) \mid b and a \mid (-b). 5. If a \mid b, a > 0 and b > 0, then a \le b. 6. If a, b \in 
N, a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. 7. If a \mid 1, then a = 1 or a = -1. 8. If a 
e 0, then exactly one of a, -a lies in 
Z_{>0}. Parts (a)–(d) are identities in the commutative ring 
Z: write each hypothesis as an equation b = ka and rearrange. Part (e) is the one that needs the order. If b = ka with a, b > 0, the factor k cannot be zero or negative, so by discreteness it is at least 1, and multiplying a by something at least 1 cannot make it smaller. Parts (f) and (g) then follow from (e), and (h) is (P2) for the positives of 
Z. We use the ring laws (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring) without further mention. (a) 0 = a \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot a by @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6), so a \mid 0 with k = 0. Also a = a \cdot 1 by (F7), so 1 \mid a with k = a; and a = 1 \cdot a, so a \mid a with k = 1. If 0 \mid a, then a = k \cdot 0 = 0 for some k \in 
Z, by @prp-ring-algebra (b). (b) Let b = ka and c = lb with k, l \in 
Z. Then c = l(ka) = (lk)a by (F5), so a \mid c. (c) Let b = ka and c = la. Then bx + cy = (ka)x + (la)y = (kx)a + (ly)a = (kx + ly)a by (F5), (F6) and (F9), and kx + ly \in 
Z. So a \mid bx + cy. (d) Let b = ka. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), (-k)(-a) = ka = b, so (-a) \mid b; and (-k)a = -(ka) = -b, so a \mid (-b). (e) Let a 
e 0. By the converse part of @prp-order-from-positives, applied to the ordered ring 
Z, the set \{ x \in 
Z : x > 0 \} satisfies (P2), so exactly one of a > 0, -a > 0 holds. That set is 
Z_{>0} by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). (f) Let b = ka with k \in 
Z, a > 0 and b > 0. We show first that k > 0. If k = 0, then b = 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), against b > 0. If k < 0, then ka < 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (multiplying k < 0 by a > 0), again against b > 0. So k > 0, and by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c), with 0 < k) 1 \le k. If k = 1, then b = a. If 1 < k, then k - 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so (k - 1)a > 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), that is, b - a = ka + (-1)a = (k - 1)a > 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (c), (F7) and (F9)), and a < b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). In both cases a \le b. (g) Let a, b \in 
N with a \mid b and b \mid a. If a = 0, then 0 \mid b, so b = 0 = a by (a). If b = 0, then a = 0 in the same way. Otherwise a, b \in 
N are non-zero, hence positive (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and (e) gives a \le b and b \le a. Since \le is a total order (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), it is antisymmetric, and a = b. (h) Let a \mid 1, say 1 = ka. Then a 
e 0: otherwise 1 = k \cdot 0 = 0, against 1 
e 0 in 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring). By (h), one of a, -a is positive; call it e. Then e \mid 1, by (d) if e = -a. Since 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), part (e) gives e \le 1; and e > 0 gives 1 \le e by discreteness. So e = 1. If e = a, then a = 1; if e = -a, then a = -(-a) = -1 by @prp-ring-algebra (a). This proves the proposition. Part (f) is the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N, @fd2:prp-divides-partial-order of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.4, now proved on 
N \subseteq 
Z for the constructed integers. On all of 
Z it fails: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, by (d), yet 2 
e -2. That is why (f) is stated for a, b \in 
N, and why (e) needs b > 0: 3 \mid -3, but 3 > -3. (The hypothesis a > 0 is a convenience for the proof: a = 0 cannot divide b > 0, by (a), and if a < 0 < b, then a \le b holds anyway.) Which hypothesis of (e) fails for a = 3, b = 0, and is the conclusion a \le b true there? 3 \mid 0 by (a), and a = 3 > 0, but b = 0 is not positive. The conclusion 3 \le 0 is false. Every integer divides 0, so no bound of the form a \le b can hold for b = 0; that is the reason for the hypothesis b > 0. Division with remainder Now the substitute for division. Given a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, we want to write a as a multiple of n plus something small, and we want “small” to make the answer unique. The obvious attempt subtracts n from a until what is left lies in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}, adding n instead when a is negative. That is a process; the theorem replaces it by a least element. [Division with Remainder in 
Z] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. 1. There are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . 2. Moreover q =  loor{a/n}, the integer part of the rational number a/n (@prp-rational-integer-part), so r = a - n  loor{a/n}. The integers q and r are the quotient and the remainder of a on division by n. Among the integers a - kn, k \in 
Z, look at the non-negative ones. If there is at least one, @prp-integer-least-element hands us the least, r. It must be below n: otherwise r - n would be a smaller non-negative one of the same form. Finding a non-negative a - kn is easy for a \ge 0 (take k = 0) and needs one inequality for a < 0 (take k = a). For uniqueness, two remainders differ by a multiple of n and yet by less than n, and (e) of the rules above forbids a positive multiple of n below n. Part (b) moves the inequalities qn \le a < qn + n into 
Q and divides by n. (a) Existence. Let R \coloneqq \{ a - kn : k \in 
Z \} \cap \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} . We show R 
e \emptyset. If a \ge 0, take k = 0: a - 0 \cdot n = a - 0 = a \ge 0, by (F6), @prp-ring-algebra (b) and -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and @prp-ring-algebra (a)). If a < 0, take k = a: then a - an = a + a(-n) = a(1 - n) by @prp-ring-algebra (c), (F7) and (F9). Since n > 0, discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) gives 1 \le n. If n = 1, then a(1 - n) = a \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). If 1 < n, then -n < -1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so 1 - n < 0 by (O3); multiplying a < 0 by 1 - n < 0 reverses the inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), so a(1 - n) > 0 \cdot (1 - n) = 0. In every case R has an element. The set R \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and has the lower bound 0, so by @prp-integer-least-element it has a least element r. Write r = a - qn with q \in 
Z. Then a = qn + r and r \ge 0. Suppose r \ge n. Then r - n \ge 0: if r = n, then r - n = 0 by (F4); if r > n, then r - n > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). Also r - n = a - qn - n = a + (-1)(qn) + (-1)n = a + (-1) igl((q + 1)n igr) = a - (q + 1)n, since -x = (-1)x for every x (@prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7)) and by (F9), so r - n \in R. But -n < -0 = 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), since n > 0), so r - n < r by (O3). This contradicts the choice of r as least. Hence r < n. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with q, q', r, r' \in 
Z, 0 \le r < n and 0 \le r' < n. Suppose r 
e r'. Exchanging (q, r) and (q', r') changes neither the hypotheses nor the goal, so we may suppose r' < r. Then r - r' = (q' - q)n , so n \mid r - r'. Here r - r' > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), and n > 0, so @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) gives n \le r - r'. But adding r - r' to 0 \le r' gives r - r' \le (r - r') + r' = r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), and r < n; so r - r' < n, a contradiction. Hence r = r'. Then qn = q'n, so (q - q')n = 0, and since n 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f) gives q - q' = 0, that is, q = q'. (b) From (a), 0 \le r < n; adding qn (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)) gives qn \le a < qn + n . These are inequalities between integers, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) and @prp-integers-embed-rationals they hold in 
Q as well, with the same sums and products. In 
Q, n > 0, so n^{-1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Multiplying by n^{-1} preserves strict inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and equalities, so q = qn \cdot n^{-1} \le a \cdot n^{-1} < (qn + n) \cdot n^{-1} = q + 1 . That is, q \le a/n < q + 1, with q \in 
Z. By the uniqueness in @prp-rational-integer-part, q =  loor{a/n}, and then r = a - qn = a - n  loor{a/n}. This proves the theorem. The hypothesis n > 0 is used four times in (a): to find an element of R when a < 0 (through 1 - n \le 0), to see that r - n < r, and in the uniqueness both to apply @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) and, as n 
e 0, to cancel n from (q - q')n = 0. For n = 0 the statement fails outright: no r satisfies 0 \le r < 0. Exercise B1 handles n < 0. Uniqueness is what turns the theorem into a test for divisibility: n \mid a if and only if the remainder of a on division by n is 0. Indeed, if a = kn, then a = kn + 0 is a division with remainder, and by uniqueness it is the only one; conversely a = qn + 0 says n \mid a. For instance 12 = 2 \cdot 5 + 2 with 0 \le 2 < 5, so the remainder is 2 
e 0, and 5 
mid 12. The statement of (a) is @fd2:thm-division-algorithm of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, which was proved there for the school integers. The existence proof above follows the same route, with each school fact replaced by a result of Chapter 2: the closure of 
Z under +, -, \cdot by @thm-integers-commutative-ring; “a positive integer is at least 1” by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b), (c); and the least element of a set of integers bounded below by @prp-integer-least-element. The uniqueness argument there is the one packaged here as @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). For n = 2 and a \in 
N, (a) is @prp-omega-powers-parity (d) of Section 1.6, which we compare with but do not use. Part (b) pays a debt of Section 2.5. There, after @prp-rational-integer-part, the integer part  loor{p/q} was announced as a quotient; (b) says exactly that, and it gives a second way to compute q and r. Exercise C1 turns (b) around and proves the existence half of (a) from the integer part. Find the quotient and the remainder of a = -17 on division by n = 5, and check them against (b). q = -4 and r = 3: (-4) \cdot 5 + 3 = -20 + 3 = -17, and 0 \le 3 < 5. For (b), -4 \le -17/5 < -3, since (-4) \cdot 5 = -20 \le -17 and -17 < -15 = (-3) \cdot 5 (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)); so  loor{-17/5} = -4. “The remainder” means the r with 0 \le r < n. The equation -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 - 2 is true, but -2 is not the remainder of -17 on division by 5; the remainder is 3. If negative “remainders” were allowed, uniqueness would fail at once: -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 + (-2) = (-4) \cdot 5 + 3. For negative a, the quotient is not “a/n with the fraction dropped”: that would give -3 here, while  loor{-17/5} = -4. Even and odd Recall that an integer a is even if a = 2k for some k \in 
Z, that is, 2 \mid a, and odd if a = 2k + 1 for some k \in 
Z. These are the words Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 used, now read on the constructed 
Z. Section 2.6 had parity for natural numbers from @prp-omega-powers-parity (d). With n = 2, the theorem gives it for every integer, negative ones included, with one citation. [Even and Odd Integers] 1. Every a \in 
Z is even or odd, and not both. More precisely, either a = 2q for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k + 1, or a = 2q + 1 for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k. 2. If a \in 
Z and a^2 is even, then a is even. Divide by 2. The remainder lies in \{0, 1\}, by discreteness, and it is unique, so each integer has exactly one of the two forms. For (b), square the odd form and read off the remainder. (a) Since 2 = 1 + 1 > 0, the theorem with n = 2 gives unique q, r \in 
Z with a = 2q + r and 0 \le r < 2. Then r \in \{0, 1\}: if r 
e 0, then 0 < r, so 1 \le r by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); and if moreover 1 < r, then 2 = 1 + 1 \le r by discreteness again, against r < 2. If a = 2k and a = 2k' + 1 for some k, k' \in 
Z, then (k, 0) and (k', 1) would be two pairs as in the theorem, and 0 
e 1 contradicts its uniqueness. The same uniqueness shows that q is the only integer with a = 2q + r. (b) Suppose a is not even. By (a), a = 2q + 1 with q \in 
Z. Then a^2 = (2q + 1)^2 = 4q^2 + 4q + 1 = 2(2q^2 + 2q) + 1 , by @prp-ring-algebra (d) and (F5), (F6), (F9), so a^2 is odd, and by (a) it is not even. This proves (b) by contraposition. Part (b) is @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even of Logic and Proof, Section 2.1, proved there from the school facts (E1)–(E3) about the integers. Part (a) proves (E1) and (E2) for the constructed 
Z, and the computation in (b) is (E3). We compare with that proof and do not use it. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 proved (E1) and (E2) for the school integers right after @fd2:thm-division-algorithm. Section 2.6 proved that no rational squares to 2 by a descent on denominators (@thm-no-rational-square-two), a route that needs only the order and the least-element property of 
Z and adapts to other non-squares. With (b), and with lowest terms from Section 3.3, the classical parity proof of Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 can also be run on the constructed 
Q, every step citable; one of the review exercises at the end of this chapter does so. Small primes Later sections need to know that a few small integers are prime in the constructed 
Z. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 checked some of these after @fd2:def-prime, for the school integers; that check is not a proof about the ring of Chapter 2, so we redo it here. The small-primes remark. The integers 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime in 
Z. Let p \in \{2, 3, 5, 7\}. Then p \ge 2. Let d be a positive divisor of p. Then 1 \le d by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) and d \le p by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), so d is one of 1, 2, \dots, p: applying discreteness repeatedly (if d 
e 1 then 2 \le d; if d 
e 2 then 3 \le d; and so on up to p) leaves no other value. Each d with 1 < d < p leaves a non-zero remainder:  egin{aligned} 3 &= 1 \cdot 2 + 1, \qquad 5 = 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 1 \cdot 3 + 2 = 1 \cdot 4 + 1, \ 7 &= 3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1 = 1 \cdot 4 + 3 = 1 \cdot 5 + 2 = 1 \cdot 6 + 1 . \end{aligned} (For p = 2 there is no such d.) So d 
mid p for these d, by the divisibility test after @thm-integers-division-remainder: p = kd would give p = kd + 0, a second division of p by d, with remainder 0, against the uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a). Hence the positive divisors of p are 1 and p, and p is prime. The later sections of this chapter cite this paragraph as “the small-primes remark”. The same procedure decides, for any given p \ge 2, whether p is prime; Section 3.3 shortens it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Find the quotient and the remainder on division by n = 6 of a = 47, of a = -47 and of a = 0. 2. Where is n > 0 used in the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a)? 3. True or false, with a reason: 0 \mid 0. 4. True or false, with a reason: for all a, b \in 
Z, if a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. (a) 47 = 7 \cdot 6 + 5, so (q, r) = (7, 5). -47 = (-8) \cdot 6 + 1, since -48 + 1 = -47, so (q, r) = (-8, 1). 0 = 0 \cdot 6 + 0, so (q, r) = (0, 0). In each case 0 \le r < 6, so by uniqueness these are the quotient and remainder. Note (-8, 1), not (-7, -5). (b) Twice. For a < 0, the element a - an = a(1 - n) of R is non-negative because 1 - n \le 0, which comes from n \ge 1, that is, from n > 0 and discreteness. And the contradiction “r - n < r” needs -n < 0, that is, n > 0. (c) True: 0 = 1 \cdot 0, so k = 1 witnesses 0 \mid 0 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). (d) False: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d)), but 2 
e -2. The statement is true for a, b \in 
N (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (f)). B. Practice [B1: Negative divisors] Let a, n \in 
Z with n < 0. Prove that there are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r and 0 \le r < -n. Since n < 0, -n > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so -n \in 
Z_{>0}. Existence. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) applied to a and -n, there are q_0, r \in 
Z with a = q_0(-n) + r and 0 \le r < -n. Let q \coloneqq -q_0. Then q_0(-n) = (-q_0)n = qn by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so a = qn + r. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with 0 \le r, r' < -n. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), qn = (-q)(-n) and q'n = (-q')(-n), so a = (-q)(-n) + r = (-q')(-n) + r' are two divisions of a by -n. The uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) gives r = r' and -q = -q', hence q = -(-q) = -(-q') = q' by @prp-ring-algebra (a). [B2: Three in a row] Let a \in 
Z. Prove that exactly one of a, a + 1, a + 2 is divisible by 3. At least one. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), a = 3q + r with 0 \le r < 3, and r \in \{0, 1, 2\} by discreteness, as in the proof of @cor-integers-even-odd. If r = 0, then 3 \mid a. If r = 1, then a + 2 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). If r = 2, then a + 1 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). At most one. Suppose 3 \mid a + i and 3 \mid a + j with 0 \le i < j \le 2. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c) (with x = 1, y = -1), 3 \mid (a + j) - (a + i) = j - i, and j - i \in \{1, 2\} is positive. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), 3 \le j - i \le 2, which is false. So no two of the three are divisible by 3. (Equivalently: the remainders of a, a + 1, a + 2 on division by 3 are r, and then the other two of 0, 1, 2, and uniqueness of remainders allows only one of them to be 0.) C. Going deeper [C1: Division from the integer part] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) directly from @prp-rational-integer-part, without the set R: put q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} and r \coloneqq a - qn, and show that 0 \le r < n. Say where n > 0 is used. By @prp-rational-integer-part, q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} \in 
Z satisfies q \le a/n < q + 1 in 
Q, where a/n = a \cdot n^{-1} and n 
e 0 in 
Q. Since n > 0, multiplying by n preserves the strict inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and the equality case, so qn \le (a \cdot n^{-1}) \cdot n = a < (q + 1)n = qn + n . Subtracting qn (that is, adding -qn, (O3)) gives 0 \le a - qn < n. Here r \coloneqq a - qn is an integer, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) the inequalities 0 \le r < n, proved in 
Q, hold in 
Z. So a = qn + r with 0 \le r < n. The hypothesis n > 0 is used when multiplying by n: for n < 0, multiplication reverses inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), and the same q would give qn \ge a > qn + n, so n < r \le 0 instead. (This exercise is practice with a result already proved; nothing later rests on it.)

title: 3.2 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm

The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm Section 3.1 gave the constructed integers a relation a \mid b and a division with remainder (@thm-integers-division-remainder). This section asks what two integers have in common. Here is a concrete version. A machine accepts only coins worth 12 and 42 units, and gives change in the same coins. Which amounts can be paid exactly? Paying x coins of the first kind and y of the second, with negative numbers for coins received as change, pays 12x + 42y. So 42 - 3 \cdot 12 = 6 can be paid, and hence every multiple of 6; and since 6 divides both 12 and 42, nothing else can. Why 6, and why exactly the multiples of 6? The answer is a theorem about every pair of integers, and its proof is the main move of this chapter. Integer combinations The amounts 12x + 42y form a set that deserves a name. For the coins, 6 is a common divisor of 12 and 42, and the question was why it is the one that matters. The greatest common divisor is the largest integer that divides both. In words: among all integers dividing both a and b, take the largest. The definition says “the greatest element”, so it owes us a proof that there is one. Well-definedness. Let (a, b)

Every d \in D satisfies d \le c: if d > 0, then d \mid c by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d), and d \le c by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e); if d \le 0, then d \le 0 < c. So D is bounded above, and by @prp-integer-least-element it has a greatest element. Since 1 \in D, that element is at least 1. Hence \gcd(a, b) \ge 1 whenever (a, b)

A positive common divisor d satisfies d \le 4, by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), and d \ge 1, so d \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), as in the small-primes remark of Section 3.1. Every integer divides 0, so 0 and 0 have no greatest common divisor for \le, and some value has to be chosen. The value 0 is the one that keeps clauses (c) and (e) of the theorem below true for (0, 0), as the remark after it shows. It also matches @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6, where 0 is the top of (

The Euclidean algorithm below replaces the list by one division per step, and Bézout’s theorem is what makes it work. It stalls: the definition of \gcd(a, b) says nothing about combinations, so there is nothing to build x and y from. The attempt on 12 and 42 suggests starting at the other end. The positive combinations 12, 42, 30, 18, 6, \dots have a least element, and it was found as a combination. Why should it divide 12? Divide 12 by it. Once the least positive combination d is known to divide a and b, the rest is bookkeeping: every common divisor divides the combination d, so none exceeds it. The procedure only computes; nothing rests on it. That some x, y exist is @thm-integers-bezout (d), and the final multiplication checks the particular x, y found. [Two runs of the algorithm] Compute \gcd(252, 198) and \gcd(-35, 15), and write each as a combination of the two numbers. The pair (252, 198). The chain of divisions is  egin{aligned} 252 &= 1 \cdot 198 + 54, \ 198 &= 3 \cdot 54 + 36, \ 54 &= 1 \cdot 36 + 18, \ 36 &= 2 \cdot 18 + 0 . \end{aligned} In the notation of the theorem, (x_k, y_k) runs through (252, 198), (198, 54), (54, 36), (36, 18), (18, 0), so K = 4 and \gcd(252, 198) = x_4 = 18. Back-substitution, from the third division up:  egin{aligned} 18 &= 54 - 1 \cdot 36 = 54 - (198 - 3 \cdot 54) = 4 \cdot 54 - 198 \ &= 4 \cdot (252 - 198) - 198 = 4 \cdot 252 - 5 \cdot 198 . \end{aligned} Check: 4 \cdot 252 = 1008, 5 \cdot 198 = 990, and 1008 - 990 = 18. The pair (-35, 15). The first entry may be negative; only the second must be positive. The remainder of -35 on division by 15 is 10, not -5:  egin{aligned} -35 &= (-3) \cdot 15 + 10, \ 15 &= 1 \cdot 10 + 5, \ 10 &= 2 \cdot 5 + 0 . \end{aligned} So \gcd(-35, 15) = 5, and 5 = 15 - 10 = 15 -  igl( -35 + 3 \cdot 15  igr) = (-1) \cdot (-35) + (-2) \cdot 15 . Check: (-1) \cdot (-35) = 35, (-2) \cdot 15 = -30, and 35 - 30 = 5. Bézout coefficients are not unique. From 18 = 4 \cdot 252 - 5 \cdot 198 and 11 \cdot 252 = 2772 = 14 \cdot 198, 18 = (4 - 11) \cdot 252 + (-5 + 14) \cdot 198 = (-7) \cdot 252 + 9 \cdot 198 . So “the” coefficients of \gcd(a, b) means nothing by itself; when a computation needs particular ones, they are those produced by back-substitution, and any other pair works as well. Compute \gcd(0, -6) and \gcd(84, 35). \gcd(0, -6) = 6. Every integer divides 0, so the common divisors of 0 and -6 are the divisors of -6, which are those of 6 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d) and @prp-ring-algebra (a)). The positive ones are at most 6 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)), and 6 is one of them. (The theorem does not apply directly to (0, -6), since its second entry is negative; it does apply to (0, 6), with the one division 0 = 0 \cdot 6 + 0.) \gcd(84, 35) = 7, by the chain 84 = 2 \cdot 35 + 14, 35 = 2 \cdot 14 + 7, 14 = 2 \cdot 7 + 0. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-integers-bezout. 1. Where is the minimality of d used? 2. Run the proof on (a, b) = (12, 42): find d, x_0, y_0, and the divisions of (b). 3. Which step fails for (a, b) = (0, 0)? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) Once, in (b): the remainder r of a on division by d is a combination of a and b, and if it were positive it would be an element of S smaller than d. Minimality forces r = 0. (b) The set S contains 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1. Every element of 12
Z + 42

Hence d = 6, with x_0 = -3 and y_0 = 1. The divisions of (b) are 12 = 2 \cdot 6 + 0 and 42 = 7 \cdot 6 + 0: both remainders are 0, as the proof predicts. (c) Step (a): 0

title: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic Section 3.2 gave every pair of integers, not both zero, a greatest common divisor, and wrote it as a combination ax + by (@thm-integers-bezout). This section spends that identity. Take 60. It splits as 2 \cdot 30, as 6 \cdot 10, as 4 \cdot 15, and every way of splitting it further, until no factor splits again, ends with the same primes 2, 2, 3, 5. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 proved, for the school integers, that every integer at least 2 has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of the full splitting aside. Here we prove both, for the integers of Chapter 2. The key is a property of primes that the definition (“no positive divisors except 1 and itself”) does not obviously give: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. As in Section 3.1, numerals are the natural numbers of those names, and their sums and products may be computed in 
N (@prp-naturals-embed-integers (a)). Euclid’s lemma The definition of a prime p speaks about the divisors of p. The property we want speaks about the numbers that p divides. Something has to connect the two, and the connection is the Bézout identity of Section 3.2. We first prove a version for any divisor that shares no factor with one of the two numbers multiplied. Euclid’s Lemma Let a, b, c \in 
Z. If a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1, then a \mid c. The hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1 is a statement about common divisors, which is hard to use directly. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination it is the same as an equation 1 = ax + by, and an equation can be multiplied. Multiplying it by c writes c as acx + bcy. The first term is a multiple of a on sight, and the second is one because bc is. Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1. Since a \mid bc, there is k \in 
Z with bc = ka (@fd2:def-divides). Multiplying the identity by c, with (F7), (F9), (F5) and (F6), c = c(ax + by) = a(cx) + (bc)y = a(cx) + a(ky) = a(cx + ky) . Since cx + ky \in 
Z, this shows a \mid c. We call the move of this proof multiply the Bézout identity: from 1 = ax + by, multiply by c and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about divisors into an equation, which is where the work can be done. Each hypothesis has a job. Without \gcd(a, b) = 1 the conclusion fails: 4 \mid 2 \cdot 6 = 12, but 4 
mid 6, since 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 leaves a non-zero remainder (uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a)); here \gcd(4, 2) = 2. The common factor 2 of 4 and 2 let 4 divide the product without dividing 6. Lists, products and prime factorizations To say that a factorization is unique, we must first say what a factorization is. The products 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 and 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 are equal and use the same primes, and we want to count them as one. We do so by writing the primes in order, smallest first. A factorization also has a length, and the length may be 0: the number 1 is the product of no primes at all. Products of lists are defined by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product. That definition was made for sequences of real numbers, and we use it as a pattern, as group (iii) of the citing rule of Section 1.7 allows, with the ordered field 
Q (@thm-rationals-ordered-field) in place of 
R. A product of integers is an integer (@prp-integers-embed-rationals), so the products of lists below lie in 
Z; the paragraph “Why the product exists” below checks directly that the recursion runs in 
Z. [List, Product of a List, Prime Factorization] Let k \in 
N. A list of length k in 
Z is a function p \colon \{1, \dots, k\} 	o 
Z, written (p_1, \dots, p_k) with p_i \coloneqq p(i); for k = 0 it is the empty list. Its product \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i \in 
Z is given by the recursion \prod_{i=1}^{0} p_i = 1 , \qquad \prod_{i=1}^{j+1} p_i = \Bigl( \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i \Bigr) p_{j+1} \quad 	ext{for } j < k , where \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i is the product of the shortened list (p_1, \dots, p_j). A prime factorization of n \in 
Z_{>0} is a list (p_1, \dots, p_k) such that every entry p_i is prime (@fd2:def-prime), the list is non-decreasing (i \le j implies p_i \le p_j), and \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i = n. In words: a list is a finite sequence of integers, possibly empty; its product starts at 1 and multiplies by one more entry at each stage; and a prime factorization lists primes in non-decreasing order with the right product. Why the product exists. Extend the list to a sequence  ar p on 
Z_{>0} by  ar p_i \coloneqq p_i for i \le k and  ar p_i \coloneqq 1 for i > k. Then @fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b), with X = 
Z, starting value 1 and step g(j, x) \coloneqq x  ar p_{j+1}, gives exactly one function P \colon 
N 	o 
Z with P_0 = 1 and P_{j+1} = P_j  ar p_{j+1}; we set \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i \coloneqq P_j for j \le k. The “Finite lists” remark after @fd2:def-sum-product shows that P_j depends only on p_1, \dots, p_j, not on how the list was extended. Its proof is an induction on j that uses only the recursion and the multiplication of the target set, so it runs unchanged in 
Q, and, since 
Z is closed under multiplication, with target set 
Z. In particular P_j is also the product of the shortened list (p_1, \dots, p_j), which is the displayed recursion. We cite it as the recursion of @def-prime-factorization: it peels the last entry off a product. Examples. - (2, 2, 3, 5) is a prime factorization of 60. Its entries are prime by the small-primes remark of Section 3.1; it is non-decreasing; and the recursion gives the products 1, 2, 4, 12, 60. - (5) is a prime factorization of 5, with products 1, 5. A prime p has the one-entry factorization (p). - The degenerate case: the empty list is a prime factorization of 1. Its product is 1 by the first clause of the recursion, and the conditions “every entry is prime” and “non-decreasing” hold vacuously. Without this case the number 1 would have no factorization, and the theorem below would fail for n = 1; its existence proof uses this case to rule out n = 1. Non-examples by minimal change. Exchange two entries of the first example: (2, 3, 2, 5) has prime entries and product 60, but it is not non-decreasing, since positions 2 \le 3 carry 3 > 2. Merge two entries: (2, 2, 15) is non-decreasing with product 60, but 15 = 3 \cdot 5 is not prime. Why these clauses. Without “non-decreasing”, 60 would have twelve factorizations, its four primes in every order, and uniqueness could only be stated up to rearrangement, which needs a theory of permutations. Without “prime”, splitting would stop anywhere. And the requirement p \ge 2 in @fd2:def-prime is what keeps (1, 2, 2, 3, 5) out: if 1 counted as a prime, every factorization could be padded with as many 1s as we like. Find the prime factorization of 360, and check each clause of @def-prime-factorization. (2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5). Its entries are prime by the small-primes remark of Section 3.1. It is non-decreasing. Its products, by the recursion, are 1, 2, 4, 8, 24, 72, 360. By the theorem below there is no other. Primes dividing products For a prime, the coprimality that Euclid’s lemma asks for comes almost free: a prime shares no factor with a number unless it divides that number. [A Prime Dividing a Product] Let p be prime. 1. For every a \in 
Z: p \mid a or \gcd(p, a) = 1. 2. For all b, c \in 
Z: if p \mid bc, then p \mid b or p \mid c. 3. If (q_1, \dots, q_l) is a list of primes, with l \in 
N, and p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, then p = q_j for some j \in \{1, \dots, l\}. For (a), the gcd of p and a is a positive divisor of p, so it is 1 or p, and the second case says p \mid a. Then (b) is Euclid’s lemma in the case \gcd(p, b) = 1 of (a). For (c), peel the last prime off the product and apply (b) to the two factors; an induction on the length handles the rest, and a prime that divides a prime is equal to it. (a) Since p \ge 2, (p, a) 
e (0, 0), so g \coloneqq \gcd(p, a) \ge 1 (@def-integer-gcd). As a common divisor, g \mid p and g \mid a. So g is a positive divisor of the prime p, and g = 1 or g = p (@fd2:def-prime). If g = p, then p \mid a. (b) Let p \mid bc. By (a), p \mid b or \gcd(p, b) = 1. In the second case @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, with a = p, gives p \mid c. (c) We use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on l, for P(l): “for every list of primes (q_1, \dots, q_l), if p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, then p = q_j for some j \le l”. Base case P(0). The empty product is 1 (the recursion of @def-prime-factorization). If p \mid 1, then p = 1 or p = -1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), and both contradict p \ge 2. So the hypothesis of P(0) never holds, and P(0) is true. Step. Assume P(l), and let (q_1, \dots, q_{l+1}) be a list of primes with p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j. By the recursion of @def-prime-factorization, \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j = \Bigl( \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j \Bigr) q_{l+1} , where the first factor is the product of the list of primes (q_1, \dots, q_l). By (b), p divides that first factor or p \mid q_{l+1}. In the first case P(l) gives j \le l with p = q_j. In the second, p \ge 2 > 0 is a positive divisor of the prime q_{l+1}, so p \in \{1, q_{l+1}\}, and p 
e 1; hence p = q_{l+1}. This proves P(l + 1), and with it the corollary. Part (b) is the property promised at the start of the section, and it is what makes primes the right atoms for multiplication. It fails for 6, which is not prime: 6 \mid 2 \cdot 3, but 6 
mid 2 and 6 
mid 3, since 0 < 2 < 6 and 0 < 3 < 6 rule both out by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). The second application of Euclid’s lemma combines two coprime divisors into one. [Coprime Divisors of a Number] Let m, n, c \in 
Z with m \mid c, n \mid c and \gcd(m, n) = 1. Then mn \mid c. Write c = km with k \in 
Z. Then n \mid km, and \gcd(n, m) = \gcd(m, n) = 1 (@def-integer-gcd), so @thm-euclid-lemma-integers gives n \mid k, say k = ln with l \in 
Z. Hence c = (ln)m = l(mn), by (F5) and (F6), and mn \mid c. The coprimality is needed: 4 \mid 12 and 6 \mid 12, but 24 
mid 12, since a positive divisor of 12 is at most 12 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)); here \gcd(4, 6) = 2. The least divisor is prime The existence half of unique factorization needs a supply of primes: every integer n \ge 2 must have a prime factor. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 proved this for the school integers by strong induction (@fd2:thm-prime-factor). On the constructed 
Z the least-element property gives a shorter route: the least divisor bigger than 1 is already prime. The Least Divisor Is Prime Let n \in 
Z with n \ge 2. The set D \coloneqq \{ d \in 
Z : d \ge 2 	ext{ and } d \mid n \} has a least element, and that element is prime. In particular, n has a prime factor. Since n \ge 2 and n \mid n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)), n \in D, so D is non-empty; and 2 is a lower bound of D by its definition. By @prp-integer-least-element, D has a least element p. Suppose p were not prime. Since p \ge 2, the clause of @fd2:def-prime that fails is the one about divisors: p has a positive divisor e with e 
e 1 and e 
e p. Then e \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), and e \le p by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). So 1 < e < p, and e \ge 2 by discreteness again. Also e \mid p and p \mid n give e \mid n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)). So e \in D and e < p, against the choice of p. Hence p is prime, and p \mid n because p \in D. This is @fd2:thm-prime-factor on the constructed 
Z, proved by a least element instead of strong induction. It also shortens the primality test of Section 3.1’s small-primes remark. If p \ge 2 is not prime, its least divisor e \ge 2 is prime by the lemma, so it is not p itself, and p = ef with f \in 
Z; then f > 0 (as e, p > 0), f 
e 1, so f \ge 2 and f \mid p, and therefore e \le f by the choice of e. Multiplying by e > 0 gives e \cdot e \le ef = p (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality if e = f). So to prove p \ge 2 prime it is enough to check that no d with d \ge 2 and d \cdot d \le p divides p. For 11 only d = 2, 3 need checking, since 4 \cdot 4 = 16 > 11. The fundamental theorem Everything is now in place for the main result of the chapter’s first half. [Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic] Every n \in

The proof promises a new prime factor of N, not that N itself is prime. This is the direct proof asked for in part (c) of @fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1, now on the constructed 
Z and including the empty list. Its two school facts are replaced by @lem-least-divisor-prime and @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines N as the product plus 1 and shows N \ge 2, with a reason that the product is positive. - 2: shows that each p_i divides the product, by an induction or a cited result. - 2: produces a prime factor q of N, citing @lem-least-divisor-prime or an equivalent. - 3: shows q is not any p_i, since it would divide 1. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in order: for every list there is a prime outside it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that N is prime; assuming “the set of primes is finite” and taking its product without a list (no list, no product).

Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 turned the school integers into a clock, 
Z/n, and checked by hand that its sum and product are well defined (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic). Chapter 2 made the same kind of check twice more, for 
Z and for 
Q, each time through @thm-well-defined-on-classes and a computation special to the formula. This section makes the check once, for every commutative ring and every subset of the right kind, called an ideal. The integers modulo n, now a ring, are the first example. Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, from classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals that differ by a null sequence, and checks its operations there directly; Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What a quotient needs Let I \subseteq R, and call a and b related when they differ by an element of I: a \sim_I b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a - b \in I . For R = 
Z and I the multiples of n, this is congruence modulo n. We want two things: \sim_I should be an equivalence relation, and the sum and product of classes should be computable on representatives. Each wish makes a demand on I. - Reflexivity, a - a \in I, needs 0 \in I. - Symmetry: b - a = -(a - b), so it needs I to be closed under negatives. - Transitivity: a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), so it needs I to be closed under sums. - The sum on classes. Changing a to a' changes a + b to a' + b, and the difference is a - a' again: no new demand. - The product on classes. Changing a to a' changes ab to a'b, and the difference is (a - a')b: an element of I multiplied by an arbitrary element of R. So I must swallow such products. The last demand contains the second: -x = (-1)x. Three clauses remain, and they get a name. An ideal is a set of allowed errors: it contains 0, it is closed under adding errors, and an error multiplied by anything is still an error. [Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring. A subset I \subseteq R is an ideal of R if 1. 0 \in I; 2. for all a, b \in I, a + b \in I; 3. for all a \in I and all r \in R, ra \in I. In words: (I1) and (I2) say that I contains 0 and is closed under addition; (I3), absorption, says that multiplying an element of I by any element of the ring, inside I or not, lands in I. The ring element r in (I3) ranges over all of R, and that is what separates (I3) from mere closure under multiplication, where r would have to lie in I. Two consequences are used constantly. First, an ideal is closed under negatives and differences: for a \in I, -a = (-1)a \in I by (I3), since (-1)a = -(1 \cdot a) = -a by @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7) with (F6); then a - b = a + (-b) \in I for a, b \in I, by (I2). Second, if 1 \in I, then I = R, since every r = r \cdot 1 \in I by (I3). Examples. - The degenerate cases: \{0\} and R itself are ideals of R. For \{0\}: 0 + 0 = 0 and r \cdot 0 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)). For R, every clause asks for an element of R. They are the two extremes: “no error allowed” and “everything allowed”. - For n \in 
Z, the multiples n
Z = \{ kn : k \in 
Z \} form an ideal of 
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations): 0 = 0 \cdot n; kn + ln = (k + l)n; r(kn) = (rk)n. In particular the even integers 2
Z form an ideal. - For a, b \in 
Z, the combinations a
Z + b

otin

Z : x \ge 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). And

Q satisfies (I1), (I2) and is even closed under negatives and products, but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = 1/2: (1/2) \cdot 1 = 1/2 
otin

Z, then 2m = 1, but 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd and so not of the form 2m, by @cor-integers-even-odd (a).) In both cases the ring element r comes from outside the subset, which is exactly what (I3) allows. Why these clauses. Each clause was forced by one of the five wishes above, and dropping one loses its wish: without (I1) or (I2), \sim_I is not reflexive or not transitive; without (I3), the product on classes can fail, as the warning after the next theorem shows for 
Z \subseteq 
Q. The quotient ring The payoff is a single theorem that builds a ring of classes from any ideal. We write [a], or [a]_I when the ideal must be named, for the class of a under \sim_I, and R/I for the quotient set R/{\sim_I} (@fd2:def-quotient-set). [Quotient Ring by an Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring and I an ideal of R. 1. Setting a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I defines an equivalence relation \sim_I on R, and the class of a is [a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}. 2. The rules [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], [a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab] and -[a] \coloneqq [-a] are well defined on R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}. 3. R/I, with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The quotient map \pi \colon R 	o R/I, \pi(a) \coloneqq [a], satisfies \pi(a + b) = \pi(a) + \pi(b), \pi(ab) = \pi(a) \pi(b) and \pi(1) = [1]. 4. [a] = [0] if and only if a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] if and only if I = R. In words: (a) and (b) say that classes modulo an ideal can be added, multiplied and negated through any representatives; (c) says that the result obeys every ring law, and that passing to classes respects the operations; (d) says that the elements of I are exactly those that become 0, and that the quotient collapses to the zero ring exactly when I is everything. A change of representative is an element of I. The equivalence-relation clauses ask that such changes can be reversed and chained, which is closure under negatives and sums. The operations ask that a change in one argument produce a change in the output: for the sum the change is the same element of I, and for the product it is that element multiplied by the other argument, which (I3) keeps in I. The ring laws are then laws of R read on classes. Before reading on: where is “ra \in I for every r \in R” used, and why does closure under + not suffice for the product? (a) Let a, b, c \in R. (Eq1): a - a = 0 \in I, by (F4) and (I1). (Eq2): if a - b \in I, then b - a = -(a - b) \in I, since I is closed under negatives; here (a - b) + (b - a) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), so b - a = -(a - b) by the uniqueness of negatives (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). (Eq3): if a - b \in I and b - c \in I, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) \in I, by (F2)–(F4) and (I2). So \sim_I is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). For the class: if x \sim_I a, then x - a \in I and x = a + (x - a) \in a + I; conversely, for y \in I, (a + y) - a = y \in I, so a + y \sim_I a. Hence [a] = a + I. (b) We check the hypotheses of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), with X = R and the relation \sim_I, for the maps (a, b) \mapsto a + b and (a, b) \mapsto ab. Let a \sim_I a', so a - a' \in I, and let b \in R. Then  egin{aligned} (a + b) - (a' + b) &= a - a' \in I , \ ab - a'b &= (a - a')b = b(a - a') \in I , \end{aligned} by (F1)–(F4) in the first line, and by (F9), (F6) and @prp-ring-algebra (c) in the second, where the membership is (I3) with r = b: the ideal absorbs b. This is the first hypothesis. Since a + b = b + a and ab = ba ((F1), (F6)), the second hypothesis is the first with the two arguments exchanged. For the negative we check the hypothesis of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) for a \mapsto -a: (-a) - (-a') = -(a - a') \in I, by @prp-ring-algebra (a) and closure under negatives. Hence the three rules define functions. (c) Every element of R/I is a class [a] (@fd2:def-quotient-set). Each axiom of @def-commutative-ring-and-field other than (F8) is an equation, and by (b) both of its sides, read on classes, are the classes of the two sides of the same equation in R. For example, for (F9), [a] igl([b] + [c] igr) = [a][b + c] = [a(b + c)] = [ab + ac] = [ab] + [ac] = [a][b] + [a][c] , using (F9) in R in the middle; for (F3), [a] + [0] = [a + 0] = [a]; for (F4), [a] + (-[a]) = [a] + [-a] = [a + (-a)] = [0]; for (F7), [a][1] = [a \cdot 1] = [a]. The laws (F1), (F2), (F5) and (F6) go the same way. So R/I is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The equations for \pi are the definitions in (b) read from right to left, and \pi(1) = [1] by definition of \pi. (d) [a] = [0] holds if and only if a \sim_I 0 (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)), that is, a - 0 \in I; and a - 0 = a + 0 = a, since -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and @prp-ring-algebra (a)). So [a] = [0] \iff a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] \iff 1 \in I. If 1 \in I, then I = R, since r = r \cdot 1 \in I for every r \in R by (I3); and if I = R, then 1 \in I. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Absorption with an arbitrary r \in R, the full force of (I3), is used exactly once in the proof of (a) and (b): in the product, at ab - a'b = (a - a')b, where the change of representative a - a' \in I is multiplied by an arbitrary b \in R. Elsewhere (I3) enters only with r = -1, through closure under negatives (-x = (-1)x), and otherwise the proof uses (I1) and (I2). Closure under + does not suffice for the product because b need not lie in I: the product changes by a multiple of the error, not by a sum of errors. We call this move compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. It is the move of Chapter 2’s “one argument at a time”, now with the change of representative recorded as one element of I. Closure under + and - is not enough for the product.

A unit is an element that has a multiplicative inverse in the ring itself. [Unit of a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring (@def-commutative-ring-and-field). An element u \in R is a unit of R if there exists v \in R with uv = 1. The set of units of R is written R^{	imes}. For a unit u, the element v is unique; it is written u^{-1} and called the inverse of u. In words: u is a unit when the equation ux = 1 can be solved inside R. The definition asks for one solution; it does not ask u to be non-zero. Well-definedness of u^{-1}. Let uv = 1 and uv' = 1. Then, by (F7), (F5) and (F6), v = v \cdot 1 = v(uv') = (vu)v' = (uv)v' = 1 \cdot v' = v' . So the inverse is unique, and the notation u^{-1} names one element. Closure. The element 1 is a unit, since 1 \cdot 1 = 1. If u is a unit, so is u^{-1}, with (u^{-1})^{-1} = u, because u^{-1} u = u u^{-1} = 1 by (F6). If u and w are units, then (uw)(u^{-1} w^{-1}) = (u u^{-1})(w w^{-1}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 , reordering the four factors by (F5) and (F6); so uw is a unit and (uw)^{-1} = u^{-1} w^{-1}, by uniqueness. A unit is not a zero divisor. If u is a unit and ux = 0, then x = (u^{-1} u) x = u^{-1}(ux) = u^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 , by u^{-1} u = 1 (above) and 1 \cdot x = x \cdot 1 = x ((F6), (F7)) in the first equality, (F5) in the second, and @prp-ring-algebra (b) in the third.
