title: Ordered Fields and Sequences in an Ordered Field
content:
Ordered Fields and Sequences in an Ordered Field In 
Q the numbers 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots crowd together, and their squares crowd toward 2; yet Chapter 2 proved that no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). Chapter 5 will make the missing number out of sequences like this one. Before it can, we must say what “crowd together” means when the only yardsticks are rationals, and prove the rules for such sequences without presupposing the number they are aiming at. This chapter does that once, for an arbitrary ordered field F, with every tolerance \varepsilon taken from F itself. It adds to the inequality rules of Chapter 2 what limits need (halving, fractions, the absolute value and the triangle inequality), places a copy of 
N and of 
Q inside every ordered field, and names the Archimedean property, which 
Q has and an ordered field need not have. Then come limits (uniqueness, boundedness, the limit laws, limits and order) and Cauchy sequences (convergent implies Cauchy, Cauchy implies bounded, sums and products, and the sign of a Cauchy sequence that is not null). Chapter 5 applies all of it with F = 
Q. The chapter ends at the gap it was written for. The sequence above is Cauchy in 
Q and has no limit in 
Q, so in 
Q “Cauchy” does not imply “convergent”. If you have met limits in a course on 
R, most statements here will look familiar. What is new is that they are proved in any ordered field, from the axioms alone. Watch where the Archimedean property is needed (each use names it), and note that completeness never appears: no supremum, no monotone convergence theorem and no Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem is used, as Section 4.6 checks. What you need. Chapters 1 and 2, chiefly Sections 2.3, 2.5 and 2.6, and Section 3.4 for review exercise R1 only; Logic and Proof, Chapters 2–5, chiefly Chapter 4; and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 and 2, with Chapter 3 for one exercise. From Chapter 2, Section 2.3: commutative rings and fields, ordered rings and fields and the rules for inequalities (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-order-from-positives), the integers as an ordered ring with least elements of sets bounded below (@thm-integers-commutative-ring, @thm-integers-ordered-ring, @prp-integer-least-element), and the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@exm-finite-ring-not-orderable). From Sections 2.2, 2.4 and 2.5: the copies of 
N in 
Z and of 
Z in 
Q (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals), 
Q as an ordered field with reciprocals reversing order (@thm-rationals-ordered-field, @def-rational-order, @prp-reciprocal-order), and the Archimedean property of 
Q, its form 1/N < \varepsilon, and the integer part (@thm-rationals-archimedean, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon, @prp-rational-integer-part). From Section 2.6: no rational squares to 2, and the Newton sequence with the term-wise facts proved there (@thm-no-rational-square-two, @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2), which Sections 4.3, 4.5 and 4.6 use. From Chapter 1: the citing rule of Section 1.7 (@cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; the arithmetic and order of 
N (@def-omega-arithmetic, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, @thm-omega-order, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic); and the powers of Section 1.6 (@prp-omega-powers-parity), which Section 4.2 compares with powers in F and Exercise B2 of Section 4.6 uses as indices. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: the negation laws (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication), used to negate the definitions of limit, Cauchy sequence and Archimedean field, and the statement “eventually keeps one sign” in review exercise R3; the translation of a limit statement and the bounded quantifier rules (@fd1:exm-translate-limit, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules) in Section 4.3; and the argument that numbers arbitrarily close are equal (@fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal), which Section 4.3 reruns in F. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, the rule ulename{RAA} (@fd1:def-rule-raa), and De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan), which R3 also uses; from its Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for the find-the-error exercises C2 of Section 4.3 and C3 of Section 4.5. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality: sequences as functions (@fd2:def-function), from Chapter 1; total orders (@fd2:def-partial-order) and finite maxima (@fd2:prp-finite-max), from Sections 2.6 and 2.3. A few items reach further. Exercise C1 of Section 4.2 uses finite and infinite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 3.1. Review exercise R1 uses Chapter 3’s ideals and quotient ring (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal), from Section 3.4: the null sequences form an ideal of the ring of Cauchy sequences in 
Q, and the quotient by it, which Chapter 3 built with Chapter 2’s lemma on operations on classes (@thm-well-defined-on-classes), gives the classes and their sum. Nothing else from Chapter 3 is used. Section 4.6 names suprema (@fd2:def-order-supremum) without using them. One example, the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Section 4.2, uses school algebra of polynomials, which Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 4 builds; it appears only in examples, remarks, warnings and exercises, and no proof of a numbered result cites it. Nothing from Analysis on the Real Line is used, and no fact about 
R. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 40 hours for everything. Roadmap - Working in an Ordered Field. The standing setup of an arbitrary ordered field F, the fraction rules of a field and the absence of zero divisors, halving a tolerance and the midpoint, comparing reciprocals and multiplying non-negative inequalities, and the absolute value with the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities, ending in the form \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < x < a + \varepsilon that the rest of the chapter uses. - The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property. The elements n \cdot 1_F and powers in F, which add, multiply and compare as in 
N; the unique embedding \iota_F of 
Q into every ordered field, strictly increasing and order-reflecting; the Archimedean property as a property of F, with its reciprocal form 1/(n \cdot 1_F) < \varepsilon; the integer part and the density of the rationals in an Archimedean field; and 
Q(t), an ordered field that is not Archimedean. - Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field. Sequences indexed from 0 and “eventually”, the limit with tolerances from F and its negation, first limits in 
Q and the divergence of ((-1)^n) in every ordered field, null and bounded sequences, 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 as a restatement of the Archimedean property, changing finitely many terms, uniqueness of limits, and the boundedness of convergent sequences. - The Algebra and Order of Limits. Null times bounded is null, terms near a non-zero limit stay away from 0, the limit laws for sums, multiples, products and quotients, and weak inequalities passing to the limit, with the squeeze; no result of the section uses the Archimedean property. - Cauchy Sequences. Terms close to one another instead of to a point, convergent sequences Cauchy and Cauchy sequences bounded, sums and products of Cauchy sequences, the sign theorem (a Cauchy sequence that is not null eventually stays at least some c > 0 above 0, or at least c below it), sign stability under null differences, reciprocals, and a sequence of rationals whose steps shrink to 0 and which is not Cauchy. - A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit. The Newton sequence for \sqrt 2 is decreasing with overshoot e_n \le 1/(4n), Cauchy in 
Q, and convergent to no rational, since a limit L would satisfy L^2 = 2; the section then lists what the chapter did not prove (suprema, monotone convergence, Bolzano–Weierstrass), each of which fails in 
Q, and the review exercises return to Chapter 3’s quotient by an ideal, to induction, and to the negation laws of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4. Named moves - Split \varepsilon. To make a sum of k small terms smaller than \varepsilon, give each term the tolerance \varepsilon/k, and combine the finitely many thresholds by a maximum. It proves the sum law in Section 4.4 and the sum of two Cauchy sequences in Section 4.5; Exercise B3 of Section 4.4 and Exercise C1 of Section 4.5 leave part of it to you. - Bound, then shrink. In a product, replace the factor you cannot control by a bound fixed in advance, then make the other factor small enough to absorb the bound. The bound comes from the whole sequence, before \varepsilon is named. It proves the product law in Section 4.4 and the product of two Cauchy sequences in Section 4.5. - Fix the bad \varepsilon. “Not null” says: some \varepsilon is missed beyond every threshold. It hands you one \varepsilon, to keep for the rest of the proof; ask the Cauchy condition for a threshold with \varepsilon/2 first, and only then take a term beyond it that misses \varepsilon. This is the sign theorem of Section 4.5. - Locate the missing limit. Suppose a limit L exists, and use the limit laws and uniqueness to find an equation that L must satisfy; if the field has no solution, there is no limit. In Section 4.6 the equation is L^2 = 2.

title: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content:
Working in an Ordered Field Section 2.3 proved the rules for inequalities from the order axioms, and Section 2.5 added the one rule that needs division: reciprocals reverse order. A limit argument asks for a few more. It halves a tolerance, so it needs 0 < \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon; it subtracts fractions, so it needs 1/b - 1/d = (d - b)/(bd); and above all it measures how far apart two numbers are, so it needs the absolute value and the triangle inequality. Each of these is a few lines from the rules we have. This section proves them once, in an arbitrary ordered field, and the rest of the chapter uses them on nearly every page. The standing setup Throughout this chapter, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field): a field with a relation < satisfying (O1)–(O4). The rationals are one, by @thm-rationals-ordered-field, and for most of the chapter they are the one that matters: the next chapter applies these results first with F = 
Q, to build the real numbers from Cauchy sequences of rationals, and then again with F = 
R, once 
R is shown to be an ordered field. We state results for a general F because the proofs never use anything about 
Q beyond (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4), and saying so on the page makes it checkable. We use the results of Sections 2.3 and 2.5 by their letters, without restating them: the algebra of a commutative ring (@prp-ring-algebra), the rules for inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)–(i)), and the reversal of order by reciprocals (@prp-reciprocal-order). In a field 1 
e 0, so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) gives 1 > 0 in every ordered field. We write F_{>0} \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x > 0 \} , \qquad F_{\ge 0} \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x \ge 0 \} , so that 
Q_{>0} of Section 2.5 is the case F = 
Q. Recall that a/b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0, so 1/b = b^{-1}, and that 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 and x^2 \coloneqq x x (@prp-ring-algebra (d)). Fractions School algebra adds fractions by cross-multiplying and subtracts reciprocals by a common denominator. Both are identities in any field, and the second is how we will compare 1/b_n with 1/b in Section 4.4. The only point needing care is that a product of non-zero elements is non-zero, so that bd may stand in a denominator. [Fraction Rules in a Field] Let F be a field (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), and let a, b, c, d \in F with b 
e 0 and d 
e 0. 1. b^{-1} is the only element y with b y = 1, and (b^{-1})^{-1} = b. Moreover bd 
e 0 and (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}. 2. \dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad + bc}{bd} and \dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}. 3. \dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{d - b}{bd}. 4. For all x, y \in F: if xy = 0, then x = 0 or y = 0. Everything rests on one move from Section 2.3: to identify an element, show it satisfies the defining equation of the element you want and let uniqueness finish. The product b^{-1} d^{-1} satisfies the defining equation of (bd)^{-1}; once bd is known to be a legal denominator, (b) and (c) are bookkeeping with (F5), (F6) and (F9). (a) Suppose by = 1. Then y = 1 \cdot y = (b^{-1} b) y = b^{-1} (b y) = b^{-1} \cdot 1 = b^{-1} , by (F7), (F8) with (F6), (F5), the hypothesis, and (F7); this is the uniqueness argument of @prp-ring-algebra (a), run with multiplication. Next, b^{-1} 
e 0: otherwise 1 = b b^{-1} = b \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), against 1 
e 0. So (b^{-1})^{-1} exists, and since b^{-1} b = b b^{-1} = 1 by (F6), the element b satisfies its defining equation; uniqueness gives (b^{-1})^{-1} = b. Now, by (F5) and (F6), (bd)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) = (b b^{-1})(d d^{-1}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 . If bd = 0, the left side would be 0 \cdot (b^{-1} d^{-1}) = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6), so 1 = 0, which is false in a field. Hence bd 
e 0, and the display says that b^{-1} d^{-1} satisfies the defining equation of (bd)^{-1}; by uniqueness, (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}. (b) By (a), bd 
e 0, so both right-hand sides are defined. For the product, by (F5), (F6) and (a),  egin{aligned}  rac{a}{b} \cdot  rac{c}{d} &= (a b^{-1})(c d^{-1}) = (ac)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) \ &= (ac)(bd)^{-1} =  rac{ac}{bd} . \end{aligned} For the sum, first \dfrac{ad}{bd} = (ad)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) = (a b^{-1})(d d^{-1}) = \dfrac{a}{b}, and likewise \dfrac{bc}{bd} = \dfrac{c}{d}. Then (F9) with (F6) gives  egin{aligned}  rac{a}{b} +  rac{c}{d} &= (ad)(bd)^{-1} + (bc)(bd)^{-1} \ &= (ad + bc)(bd)^{-1} =  rac{ad + bc}{bd} . \end{aligned} (c) Apply the sum rule of (b) with a = 1 and c = -1. Since (-1) d^{-1} = -(d^{-1}) by @prp-ring-algebra (c), the left side is 1/b + (-1)/d = 1/b - 1/d, and the numerator on the right is 1 \cdot d + b(-1) = d - b, again by @prp-ring-algebra (c). (d) Let xy = 0, and suppose x 
e 0. Then y = 1 \cdot y = (x^{-1} x) y = x^{-1} (xy) = x^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0, by (F7), (F8), (F5) and @prp-ring-algebra (b). So x = 0 or y = 0. This proves the lemma. In an ordered field, (d) is also @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f). The point of (d) here is that it needs no order: a field has no zero divisors. The commutative ring of integers modulo 6, in the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field, has them ([2][3] = [0] with [2] 
e [0] 
e [3]), so by (d) it is not a field. Halving and comparing The commonest move in a limit proof is to give each of two terms half the tolerance. That needs \varepsilon/2 to be positive, smaller than \varepsilon, and to add up to \varepsilon with itself. The next proposition collects these facts with two comparisons we will need as often. [Halves and Comparisons in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field. 1. \le is a total order on F (@fd2:def-partial-order), and its strict part is <. 2. 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 > 0. For every \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, 0 <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . For all a, b \in F with a < b, a < \dfrac{a + b}{2} < b. 3. For a, b \in F_{>0}: if a \le b, then \dfrac{1}{b} \le \dfrac{1}{a}. 4. For a, b, c, d \in F: if 0 \le a \le b and 0 \le c \le d, then ac \le bd. Nothing new happens: each part is one or two of the rules of Sections 2.3 and 2.5 in sequence. The only care needed is with \le, which hides an “or”: each non-strict hypothesis splits into an equality case and a strict case, and the strict rules apply only to the second. (a) This is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i). (b) Since 1 > 0, (O3) gives 2 = 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1, and 2 > 0 by (O2). So 2 
e 0, and 2^{-1} > 0 by @prp-reciprocal-order (a). For \varepsilon > 0, \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} > 0 by (O4). By (F9) and (F7),  egin{aligned}  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} &= \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} \cdot 1 + \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} \cdot 1 \ &= (\varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1})(1 + 1) = \varepsilon (2^{-1} \cdot 2) = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} the third equality by (F5) and (F6). Adding \varepsilon/2 to 0 < \varepsilon/2 by (O3) gives \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. For the midpoint, let a < b. By (O3), a + a < a + b and a + b < b + b, and a + a = a(1 + 1) = 2a, b + b = 2b by (F7), (F9), (F6). Multiplying by 2^{-1} > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives a < (a + b)/2 < b, since (2a) 2^{-1} = a (2 \cdot 2^{-1}) = a. (c) If a = b, then 1/b = 1/a. Otherwise 0 < a < b, and 1/b < 1/a by @prp-reciprocal-order (b). In both cases 1/b \le 1/a. (d) First, ac \le bc: if a = b or c = 0, the two sides are equal (for c = 0 both are 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b)); otherwise a < b and c > 0, and ac < bc by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). Next, bc \le bd, by the same argument with the roles of the factors exchanged by (F6): c \le d, and b \ge 0 since 0 \le a \le b (transitivity, part (a)). By transitivity of \le (part (a)), ac \le bd. Part (b) is used whenever a proof splits a tolerance: the sum of two quantities, each below \varepsilon/2, is below \varepsilon, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). The midpoint is the same fact read for two points: between any two elements of F lies a third. Part (d) is how a product of two small, or two bounded, quantities is estimated. The non-negativity in (d) cannot be dropped. In 
Q, take a = c = -2 and b = d = 0: then a \le b and c \le d, but ac = 4 and bd = 0, and 4 \le 0 is false. Section 2.3 gave a strict version of the same trap (the warning after @prp-ordered-ring-rules). Before multiplying two inequalities, check that both sides are non-negative. Absolute value To say that x is close to a, we want one element of F measuring the gap between them, whichever of the two is larger. In school this is \abs{x - a}, and \abs{x} is sometimes written \sqrt{x^2}. That formula needs a square-root function, and an ordered field has none in general: no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). The square x^2 does have the two square roots x and -x, and picking the non-negative one is already a definition by cases. So we define the absolute value by cases, using only the order. The absolute value of x is x with its sign made non-negative. [Absolute Value in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field. For x \in F, the absolute value of x is \abs{x} \coloneqq  egin{cases} x & 	ext{if } x \ge 0 , \ -x & 	ext{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} For x, y \in F, the element \abs{x - y} is the distance from x to y. The two cases do not overlap and cover F, by trichotomy (O1), so \abs{x} is a well-defined element of F. The map x \mapsto \abs{x} is a function F 	o F. Examples. In 
Q, \abs{3/4} = 3/4 and \abs{-3/4} = 3/4, the second because -3/4 < 0 (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a): (-3) \cdot 1 < 0 \cdot 4) and -(-3/4) = 3/4 (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). The distance from 1/3 to 1/2 is \abs{1/3 - 1/2} = \abs{-1/6} = 1/6. The degenerate case is \abs{0} = 0, from the first clause. Part (a) below shows that 0 is the only element with absolute value 0, so the distance from x to y is 0 exactly when x = y. A non-example by minimal change. Replace the definition by x \mapsto x^2. This map is also non-negative, zero only at 0, and multiplicative, so it passes (a) and the product rule of (b) below. It fails the triangle inequality (e): in 
Q, with x = y = 1, the “size” of x + y would be 2^2 = 4, while the sizes of x and y add up to 1 + 1 = 2. A measure of size must not grow faster than its argument, and that is the clause the square breaks. [Rules for the Absolute Value] Let F be an ordered field, and let x, y, z, r \in F. 1. \abs{x} \ge 0, and \abs{x} = 0 if and only if x = 0. 2. \abs{-x} = \abs{x}, \abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y} and \abs{x}^2 = x^2; if x 
e 0, then \abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}. 3. -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}. 4. \abs{x} \le r if and only if -r \le x \le r; and \abs{x} < r if and only if -r < x < r. 5. (Triangle inequality.) \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, and \abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}. 6. (Reverse triangle inequality.)  igl| \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr| \le \abs{x - y}. Parts (a)–(d) are case checks on the sign of x (and of y). The triangle inequality then needs no cases: by (c), x and y are each trapped between \pm their absolute values; adding the two traps traps x + y between \pm (\abs{x} + \abs{y}), and (d) reads that as the inequality. The reverse triangle inequality is the triangle inequality applied to x = (x - y) + y and to y = (y - x) + x. (a) If x \ge 0, then \abs{x} = x \ge 0. If x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), since -0 = 0. So \abs{x} \ge 0 always, and \abs{x} = 0 only in the first case with x = 0; conversely \abs{0} = 0. (b) Negation. If x > 0, then -x < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so \abs{-x} = -(-x) = x = \abs{x} (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). If x = 0, both sides are 0. If x < 0, then -x > 0, so \abs{-x} = -x = \abs{x}. Product. If x \ge 0 and y \ge 0, then xy \ge 0 (by (O4), or @prp-ring-algebra (b) if a factor is 0), so \abs{xy} = xy = \abs{x}\abs{y}. If x \ge 0 and y < 0, then -y > 0, and x(-y) = -(xy) by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so \abs{x}\abs{y} = x(-y) = -(xy); and -(xy) \ge 0 by the first case, so xy \le 0 and \abs{xy} = -(xy) (if xy = 0, both readings give 0). The case x < 0 \le y is the same with the roles exchanged. If x < 0 and y < 0, then xy = (-x)(-y) > 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (O4), so \abs{xy} = xy = (-x)(-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Square. \abs{x}^2 is x x or (-x)(-x), and both are x^2 by @prp-ring-algebra (c). Reciprocal. Let x 
e 0. By the product rule, \abs{x} \, \abs{1/x} = \abs{x \cdot x^{-1}} = \abs{1} = 1, and \abs{x} 
e 0 by (a). So \abs{1/x} satisfies the defining equation of \abs{x}^{-1}, and @lem-field-fraction-rules (a) gives \abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}. (c) If x \ge 0, then -\abs{x} = -x \le 0 \le x = \abs{x}, using @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) for -x \le 0. If x < 0, then -\abs{x} = -(-x) = x, and x < 0 < -x = \abs{x}. In both cases -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}, by transitivity (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). (d) (\Rightarrow) Let \abs{x} \le r. By (c), x \le \abs{x} \le r. By (c) and (b) applied to -x, -x \le \abs{-x} = \abs{x} \le r, and negating reverses the inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or equality), so -r \le x. (\Leftarrow) Let -r \le x \le r. If x \ge 0, then \abs{x} = x \le r. If x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x \le r, by negating -r \le x. The strict version is the same argument with < in place of \le at the steps that involve r: for instance x \le \abs{x} < r gives x < r by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i). (e) By (c), -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} and -\abs{y} \le y \le \abs{y}. Adding (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), - igl(\abs{x} + \abs{y} igr) \le x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} , where (-\abs{x}) + (-\abs{y}) = -(\abs{x} + \abs{y}) by uniqueness of negatives (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). By (d) with r \coloneqq \abs{x} + \abs{y}, \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. For the second form, apply the first to x - z = (x - y) + (y - z). (f) By (e), \abs{x} = \abs{(x - y) + y} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y}, so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y} by (O3). Exchanging x and y, and using \abs{y - x} = \abs{-(x - y)} = \abs{x - y} from (b), gives \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{x - y}. So -\abs{x - y} \le -(\abs{y} - \abs{x}) by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) (or equality), and -(\abs{y} - \abs{x}) = \abs{x} - \abs{y} by uniqueness of negatives (@prp-ring-algebra (a)), since (\abs{y} - \abs{x}) + (\abs{x} - \abs{y}) = 0; that is, -\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} - \abs{y}. By (d),  igl| \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr| \le \abs{x - y}. This proves the proposition. The form of (d) that the rest of the chapter uses is about a distance. Apply the strict half of (d) to x - a with r = \varepsilon, and add a throughout by (O3); the step is reversible, since adding -a (by (O3) again) goes back, and (x - a) + a = x: \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < x < a + \varepsilon . In words: x lies within \varepsilon of a exactly when it lies strictly between a - \varepsilon and a + \varepsilon. In Section 4.3 the role of x is played by the terms a_n of a sequence and a is a candidate limit. Example. In 
Q, which x satisfy \abs{x - 1/2} < 1/4? By the display above, exactly those with 1/2 - 1/4 < x < 1/2 + 1/4, that is, 1/4 < x < 3/4. So 2/3 qualifies (1 \cdot 3 = 3 < 8 = 2 \cdot 4 and 2 \cdot 4 = 8 < 9 = 3 \cdot 3, by the comparison formula of @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)) and 3/4 does not: the inequality is strict, and \abs{3/4 - 1/2} = 1/4. Is \abs{a} - \abs{b} \le \abs{a - b} for all a, b \in F? Is \abs{a - b} \le \abs{a} - \abs{b} for all a, b \in F? The first: yes. By (f) and (c), \abs{a} - \abs{b} \le  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{b}  igr| \le \abs{a - b}. The second: no. In 
Q, take a = 0 and b = 1: then \abs{a - b} = \abs{-1} = 1, while \abs{a} - \abs{b} = -1, and 1 \le -1 is false. The triangle inequality is the tool of the whole chapter. In its second form it says that a detour through a third point y cannot shorten the way from x to z. Run backwards, it turns two small distances, from x to y and from y to z, into one small distance from x to z. That is the move of almost every proof in Sections 4.3–4.5. The same two-case formula appears in Logic and Proof, Chapter 1, for the school numbers, and in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, for 
R. Here it is defined, and its rules are proved, for an arbitrary ordered field, from (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4) alone. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let F be an ordered field. 1. Here is a proof that 0 < 1/2 < 1 in F: (1) 1 > 0; (2) 2 = 1 + 1 > 1 > 0; (3) 0 < 1/2 < 1/1 = 1. Name the rule behind each of the three steps. 2. True or false in every ordered field: “if a < b, then a^2 < b^2”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. 3. True or false in every ordered field: “if \abs{a} < \abs{b}, then a < b”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. 4. True or false in every ordered field: “x^2 + 1 > 0 for every x”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. (a) (1) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), since 1 
e 0 in a field. (2) 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1 by (O3) (or @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict), then 2 > 0 by (O2). (3) @prp-reciprocal-order (b), applied to 0 < 1 < 2; and 1/1 = 1 \cdot 1^{-1} = 1, since 1 is its own inverse (1 \cdot 1 = 1, and @lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). (b) False. In 
Q, -2 < 1, but (-2)^2 = 4 > 1 = 1^2. The true statement needs a, b \ge 0: @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). (c) False. In 
Q, a = 1 and b = -2 give \abs{a} = 1 < 2 = \abs{b}, but a = 1 > -2 = b. (d) True. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), x^2 > 0 if x 
e 0, and x^2 = 0 if x = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)); so x^2 \ge 0. Also 1 > 0. Hence x^2 + 1 > 0 + 0 = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict in the second summand. B. Practice [B1: Two companions of (c) and (d)] Let F be an ordered field. 1. Prove that if 0 \le a < b and 0 < c \le d, then ac < bd. 2. Prove that for a, b \in F_{>0}, a \le b if and only if 1/b \le 1/a. Name the rule behind each step. (a) Since 0 \le a < b, b > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i). First, ac < bc: a < b and c > 0, so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) applies. Next, bc \le bd: if c = d the two sides are equal; otherwise c < d and b > 0, so cb < db by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), that is, bc < bd by (F6). Combining ac < bc \le bd by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i) gives ac < bd. (b) (\Rightarrow) is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c). (\Leftarrow) Let 1/b \le 1/a. Both are positive, by @prp-reciprocal-order (a). Applying @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) to the positive elements 1/b \le 1/a gives 1/(1/a) \le 1/(1/b), and 1/(1/a) = (a^{-1})^{-1} = a, 1/(1/b) = b by @lem-field-fraction-rules (a). So a \le b. [B2: Solving an inequality] In an ordered field F, find all x with \abs{2x - 3} < 5, naming the rule behind each step. Here 3, 5, 8 and so on denote the multiples 3 \cdot 1, 5 \cdot 1, 8 \cdot 1, … of Section 2.3 (defined before @prp-ordered-ring-rules), and 2 = 1 + 1 = 2 \cdot 1. We use the sum law of @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), (m + k) \cdot 1 = m \cdot 1 + k \cdot 1; in particular 5 + 3 = 8, 2 + 3 = 5 and 4 + 4 = 8 hold in F because they hold in 
N. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), strict form, \abs{2x - 3} < 5 if and only if -5 < 2x - 3 < 5 . Adding 3 throughout is reversible (add -3 to go back), so by (O3) this holds if and only if -5 + 3 < 2x < 5 + 3. Here 5 + 3 = 8, and -5 + 3 = -(2 + 3) + 3 = -2, using -(2 + 3) = (-2) + (-3) (uniqueness of negatives, @prp-ring-algebra (a)). So the condition is -2 < 2x < 8. Multiplying by 1/2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)) is reversible too (multiply by 2 > 0 to go back), so by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) the condition is equivalent to (-2)/2 < x < 8/2. Now 2/2 = 1, so (-2)/2 = -(2/2) = -1 by @prp-ring-algebra (c). And 8 = 4 + 4 = 4(1 + 1) by (F7) and (F9), the field product of the elements 4 and 2, so 8/2 = 4 (2/2) = 4 by (F5). Hence \abs{2x - 3} < 5 \iff -1 < x < 4 . Check at an endpoint: x = 4 gives \abs{8 - 3} = 5, not < 5, as the strict inequality predicts. [B3: Two more triangle inequalities] Prove that for all a, b, c in an ordered field, 1. \abs{a + b + c} \le \abs{a} + \abs{b} + \abs{c}; 2.  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{b}  igr| \le \abs{a + b}. (a) By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e) twice, \abs{(a + b) + c} \le \abs{a + b} + \abs{c} \le (\abs{a} + \abs{b}) + \abs{c}, the second step by adding \abs{c} to \abs{a + b} \le \abs{a} + \abs{b} (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). Conclude by transitivity (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). (b) Apply @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f) to a and -b:  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{-b}  igr| \le \abs{a - (-b)}. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{-b} = \abs{b}, and a - (-b) = a + b by @prp-ring-algebra (a). This is the claim. C. Going deeper [C1: A field that cannot be ordered] 1. Prove that in an ordered field no x satisfies x^2 = -1. 2. Deduce that if a field contains an element i with i^2 = -1, then no relation < makes it an ordered field. [Hint 1] Which sign does a square have, and which sign does -1 have? [Hint 2] Show first that x^2 \ge 0 for every x, splitting on whether x = 0. (a) Let F be an ordered field and x \in F. If x = 0, then x^2 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)); if x 
e 0, then x^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So x^2 \ge 0. On the other hand 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in a field), so -1 < 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). If x^2 = -1, then 0 \le x^2 = -1 < 0, so 0 < 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i), against (O1). (b) If some relation < made the field an ordered field, then (a), applied to that ordered field, would forbid i^2 = -1. So no such relation exists. The complex numbers of Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 contain such an i, so they form a field that cannot be ordered. Compare @exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, where the obstacle was 1 + 1 = 0; here it is that -1 is a square. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: shows x^2 \ge 0 for every x (cases x = 0, x 
e 0), or rules out x = 0 for the x with x^2 = -1 and then shows x^2 > 0, giving the rule for each step. - 2: shows -1 < 0 from 1 > 0 (justified by 1 
e 0 and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), or by citing the standing remark of Section 4.1) and from negation reversing order. - 2: derives the contradiction with trichotomy (O1) or irreflexivity. - 2: (b) states that any order would make (a) apply, so none exists. Fatal errors (0 for the step): asserting x^2 > 0 for all x (false at 0) and then using strictness; asserting 1 > 0 with no justification (accept 1 
e 0 with @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), or the standing remark of Section 4.1); using properties of 
R or of \sqrt{\ }. [C2: Maximum and minimum through the absolute value] For a, b in an ordered field F, let \max\{a, b\} be b if a \le b and a otherwise, and \min\{a, b\} be a if a \le b and b otherwise. 1. Prove that \max\{a, b\} =  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} , \qquad \min\{a, b\} =  rac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2} . 2. Deduce that \abs{x} = \max\{x, -x\} for every x \in F. (a) Case a \le b. Then a - b \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or equality), so \abs{a - b} = b - a: by the second clause of @def-absolute-value-ordered-field if a - b < 0, and because both sides are 0 if a = b. Hence  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} =  rac{a + b + b - a}{2} =  rac{2b}{2} = b = \max\{a, b\} , and likewise \dfrac{a + b - (b - a)}{2} = \dfrac{2a}{2} = a = \min\{a, b\}, using b + b = 2b and (2b) 2^{-1} = b as in the proof of @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). Case b < a. Then a - b > 0, so \abs{a - b} = a - b, and the two formulas give (2a)/2 = a = \max\{a, b\} and (2b)/2 = b = \min\{a, b\}. (b) By (a) with a = x and b = -x: \max\{x, -x\} =  igl(x + (-x) + \abs{2x} igr)/2 = \abs{2x}/2. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{2x} = \abs{2}\abs{x} = 2\abs{x}, since 2 > 0. So \max\{x, -x\} = \abs{x}.

title: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property In an ordered field F we can form 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, and so on. They look like the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, \dots, but they are elements of F, and two questions need answers before the next section can use them as thresholds. Do they behave like natural numbers, adding, multiplying and comparing as 
N does? And does every element of F lie below one of them? For 
Q, Section 2.5 answered the second question with yes (@thm-rationals-archimedean). This section answers the first for every ordered field, and goes further: a whole copy of 
Q sits inside F, in exactly one way. The second question has the answer no in general. Fields where the answer is yes are called Archimedean, and in them every element has an integer part and the rationals are dense. The natural numbers in an ordered field Section 2.3 defined, in any commutative ring R and for any a \in R, the multiples n \cdot a for n \in 
N (just before @prp-ordered-ring-rules): 0 \cdot a = 0 and (n + 1) \cdot a = n \cdot a + a. With a = 1 they are the elements 0, 1, 1 + 1, \dots of the opening paragraph. We give them a name, together with powers, which this chapter needs for estimates such as 2^k \ge k + 1. [Natural Numbers and Powers in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field, with unit element 1_F. 1. For n \in 
N, n \cdot 1_F \in F is the multiple of 1_F of Section 2.3: the map 
N 	o F, n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F, is the unique function with 0 \cdot 1_F = 0 , \qquad (n + 1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F \quad 	ext{for every } n \in 
N . 2. For x \in F, the powers x^k (k \in 
N) are given by @fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b), with X = F, starting value 1_F and step (k, y) \mapsto y x: x^0 \coloneqq 1_F , \qquad x^{k+1} \coloneqq x^k x \quad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . The subscript in 1_F is there because two fields will often be in play, F and 
Q, each with its own 1; where only one field is in play the subscript is dropped. For natural numbers n, k, the power n^k \in 
N is the one of Section 1.6, defined (just before @prp-omega-powers-parity) by the same recursion with X = 
N: n^0 = 1 and n^{k+1} = n^k n. So 2^k may mean a natural number or an element of F; part (c) of the next proposition says the two readings match. Examples. 1 \cdot 1_F = 0 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 0 + 1_F = 1_F, and 2 \cdot 1_F = 1_F + 1_F, the element written 2 in Section 4.1. Also x^1 = 1_F x = x and x^2 = x x, which is the square of @prp-ring-algebra (d). The degenerate case: 0 \cdot 1_F = 0, and 0^0 = 1_F by the first equation, a convention the recursion imposes and nothing below questions. A non-example by minimal change. Keep the field axioms and drop the order. In the two-element field of @exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, the same recursion gives 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 = 0 \cdot 1. So the map n \mapsto n \cdot 1 is not injective there, and the elements 0 \cdot 1, 1 \cdot 1, 2 \cdot 1, \dots are not a copy of 
N. The next proposition shows that the order axioms prevent this. [The Natural Numbers inside an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field, and let m, n, k \in 
N. 1. (m + n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F and (mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F). 2. If m < n, then m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F. Hence n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F is injective, and n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0 whenever n \ge 1. 3. (n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k. In particular (2^k) \cdot 1_F = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k, the k-th power in F of 2 = 1 + 1. 4. In 
Q, n \cdot 1_{
Q} = j(\iota(n)), the image of n under the embeddings @prp-naturals-embed-integers and @prp-integers-embed-rationals. With the identifications 
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q, this says n \cdot 1_{
Q} = n. The sum law in (a) and part (b) are rules for multiples (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)); the product law and (c) are inductions following the recursion defining the left side. The product law is the only step with content: multiplying by n + 1 is multiplying by n and adding one more copy, and the sum law and distributivity turn that into the same step on the right. Part (d) compares two functions on 
N that satisfy the same recursion, and the uniqueness half of the recursion theorem makes them equal. (a) The sum law is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) with R = F and a = 1_F. For the product law, fix m and use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on n, for P(n): “(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)”. Base: m \cdot 0 = 0 by @def-omega-arithmetic (b), so the left side is 0 \cdot 1_F = 0, and the right side is (m \cdot 1_F) \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). Step: assume P(n). By @def-omega-arithmetic (b) and (c), m(n + 1) = mn + m. Hence  egin{aligned}  igl(m(n + 1) igr) \cdot 1_F &= (mn) \cdot 1_F + m \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F) + (m \cdot 1_F) 1_F \ &= (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F + 1_F) = (m \cdot 1_F) igl((n + 1) \cdot 1_F igr) , \end{aligned} by the sum law, P(n) with (F7), (F9), and the recursion of (a) in @def-naturals-in-ordered-field. So P(n + 1) holds, and P(n) holds for every n. (b) Since 1_F 
e 0 in a field, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) gives m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F whenever m < n. If m 
e n, then m < n or n < m by trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)), so m \cdot 1_F 
e n \cdot 1_F by (O1): the map is injective. Finally 1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F (the examples above), and for n > 1, 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F; so n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F for every n \ge 1, and 1_F > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). (c) Fix n and induct on k. Base: n^0 = 1, so (n^0) \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^0. Step: if (n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k, then, since n^{k+1} = n^k n, (n^{k+1}) \cdot 1_F =  igl((n^k) \cdot 1_F igr)(n \cdot 1_F) = (n \cdot 1_F)^k (n \cdot 1_F) = (n \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} , by the product law of (a), the hypothesis, and @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). The special case is n = 2, with 2 \cdot 1_F = 1_F + 1_F. (d) Let f(n) \coloneqq j(\iota(n)) \in 
Q. The zero and one of 
Z are \iota(0) and \iota(1) (@thm-integers-commutative-ring), and j sends them to the zero and one of 
Q (@prp-integers-embed-rationals). So f(0) = 0, and, since \iota and j preserve sums (@prp-naturals-embed-integers (a), @prp-integers-embed-rationals), f(n + 1) = j igl(\iota(n) + \iota(1) igr) = j(\iota(n)) + j(\iota(1)) = f(n) + 1_{
Q} . So f and n \mapsto n \cdot 1_{
Q} both satisfy the recursion of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a) with F = 
Q, and by the uniqueness in @fd2:thm-recursion (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) they are equal. This proves the proposition. So the order axioms do what the non-example above lacked: by (b), the elements n \cdot 1_F are all different and increase with n, and by (a) they add and multiply as natural numbers do. In 
Q, (d) says that nothing new has happened: n \cdot 1_{
Q} is n. When only one field is in play, we will sometimes write n for n \cdot 1_F in a general ordered field too; the statements of this section keep n \cdot 1_F, because there the difference between n \in 
N and its image in F is the point. A copy of the rationals in every ordered field The copy of 
N extends. Negatives exist in F, so the integers have images too, and inverses of non-zero elements exist, so fractions have images. The next theorem says that the result is a copy of 
Q, compatible with +, \cdot and <, and that there is no other way to place 
Q inside F. Later chapters of this volume use this map to compare an arbitrary ordered field with the rationals. Every ordered field contains a copy of 
Q, and only one. [The Rationals Embed in Every Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field. There is exactly one map \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F such that, for all x, y \in 
Q,  egin{gathered} \iota_F(1) = 1_F , \ \iota_F(x + y) = \iota_F(x) + \iota_F(y) , \qquad \iota_F(xy) = \iota_F(x)\, \iota_F(y) . \end{gathered} It satisfies \iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F for every n \in 
N. It is injective and strictly increasing (x < y implies \iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y)), and it reflects order: \iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y) implies x < y. Uniqueness tells us how to build \iota_F. A map respecting 1 and + must send n = 1 + \dots + 1 to n \cdot 1_F; respecting negatives, it must send -n to -(n \cdot 1_F); and respecting products, it must send p/q to (p \cdot 1_F)(q \cdot 1_F)^{-1}. So we take that formula as the definition, and the work is to check it. Step roadmap. ① Extend n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F to 
Z and check that it respects +, \cdot and negation. ② Define \iota_F on fractions and check that the value does not depend on the fraction chosen. ③ Check + and \cdot with the fraction rules. ④ Check the order. ⑤ Uniqueness: run the opening argument as a proof. Step 1: the integers. By @prp-naturals-embed-integers (c), read through the identification 
N \subseteq 
Z, every m \in 
Z is n or -n for some n \in 
N. Define m \cdot 1_F \coloneqq  egin{cases} n \cdot 1_F & 	ext{if } m = n 	ext{ with } n \in 
N , \ -(n \cdot 1_F) & 	ext{if } m = -n 	ext{ with } n \in 
N . \end{cases} This is well defined. Within one case, n is determined by m: directly in the first case, and in the second because -n = -n' gives n = n' by @prp-ring-algebra (a). The cases overlap only at 0: if n = -n' with n, n' \in 
N, then n + n' = 0, and n, n' \ge 0 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)); if n' > 0, then n + n' > n + 0 \ge 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), against n + n' = 0, so n' = 0 and then n = 0. At m = 0 both cases give 0, since -0 = 0. We check three rules, for m, m' \in 
Z. Negation: (-m) \cdot 1_F = -(m \cdot 1_F). If m = n \in 
N, this is the second case of the definition. If m = -n, then -m = n by @prp-ring-algebra (a), and (-m) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F = - igl(-(n \cdot 1_F) igr) = -(m \cdot 1_F). Sums: (m + m') \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + m' \cdot 1_F. If m, m' \in 
N, this is @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). We write out the mixed case m = n, m' = -n' with n, n' \in 
N. If n' \le n, then n = n' + k for some k \in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)), so m + m' = (n' + k) - n' = k in 
Z, and  egin{aligned} m \cdot 1_F + m' \cdot 1_F &= (n' + k) \cdot 1_F - n' \cdot 1_F \ &= n' \cdot 1_F + k \cdot 1_F - n' \cdot 1_F = k \cdot 1_F , \end{aligned} by @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). If n < n', then n' = n + k, m + m' = -k, and the same computation gives n \cdot 1_F - (n + k) \cdot 1_F = -(k \cdot 1_F) = (-k) \cdot 1_F. The case m = -n, m' = n' follows by (F1). If m = -n and m' = -n', then m + m' = -(n + n'), and - igl((n + n') \cdot 1_F igr) = -(n \cdot 1_F) - (n' \cdot 1_F), by the sum law and uniqueness of negatives. Products: (m m') \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(m' \cdot 1_F). If m, m' \in 
N, this is @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). We write out m = -n, m' = n': then mm' = -(nn') by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so  egin{aligned} (mm') \cdot 1_F &= - igl((nn') \cdot 1_F igr) = - igl((n \cdot 1_F)(n' \cdot 1_F) igr) \ &=  igl(-(n \cdot 1_F) igr)(n' \cdot 1_F) = (m \cdot 1_F)(m' \cdot 1_F) , \end{aligned} by negation, @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a), and @prp-ring-algebra (c) in F. The two remaining sign patterns are the same with signs: (-n)(-n') = nn' in 
Z and  igl(-(n \cdot 1_F) igr) igl(-(n' \cdot 1_F) igr) = (n \cdot 1_F)(n' \cdot 1_F) in F, both by @prp-ring-algebra (c), and m = n, m' = -n' follows from the case written out by (F6). Step 2: the definition on 
Q. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), every x \in 
Q is p/q for some p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. Since q \in 
Z_{>0}, that is, q \in 
N and q 
e 0, we have q \ge 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)), and @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) gives q \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0, so q \cdot 1_F 
e 0. Define \iota_F\Bigl( rac{p}{q}\Bigr) \coloneqq (p \cdot 1_F)(q \cdot 1_F)^{-1} =  rac{p \cdot 1_F}{q \cdot 1_F} . The value does not depend on the fraction chosen: if p/q = r/s with r \in 
Z and s \in 
Z_{>0}, then ps = rq (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)), so (p \cdot 1_F)(s \cdot 1_F) = (r \cdot 1_F)(q \cdot 1_F) by the product rule of Step 1. Multiplying both sides by (q \cdot 1_F)^{-1} (s \cdot 1_F)^{-1} and using (F5), (F6), (F8) gives (p \cdot 1_F)(q \cdot 1_F)^{-1} = (r \cdot 1_F)(s \cdot 1_F)^{-1}. So \iota_F is a function 
Q 	o F. For m \in 
Z, m = m/1, so \iota_F(m) = (m \cdot 1_F)(1_F)^{-1} = m \cdot 1_F; in particular \iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F for n \in 
N, and \iota_F(1) = 1_F. Step 3: sums and products. Let x = p/q and y = r/s as in Step 2. In the field 
Q, @lem-field-fraction-rules (b) gives x + y =  rac{ps + rq}{qs} , \qquad xy =  rac{pr}{qs} , with qs \in

Q(t). - 3: (b) names the representation x = p/q with integers p, q as the step that fails. - 4: (b) proves that t is not \iota_{
Q(t)}(r) for any rational r, using the Archimedean property of 
Q and that \iota_{
Q(t)} is strictly increasing. Fatal errors (0 for the step): naming the comparison formula or discreteness as the failing step (both hold for images of rationals); asserting that t “is not a fraction” without proof. [C3: The order of the rationals is the only one] Prove that the usual order of 
Q (@def-rational-order) is the only relation < on 
Q that makes 
Q, with its usual operations, an ordered field. [Hint 1] Which elements must be positive in any such order? Start with 1, then n \cdot 1, then p/q. [Hint 2] By @prp-order-from-positives, an order on a commutative ring is determined by its set of positive elements. Let P be the positive set of an order \prec making 
Q an ordered field; show P = 
Q_{>0}. Let \prec be a relation making 
Q an ordered field, and P \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : 0 \prec x \}. By @prp-order-from-positives, P satisfies (P1) and (P2), and x \prec y holds if and only if y - x \in P. The usual order has positive set 
Q_{>0} (@thm-rationals-ordered-field) and is described by 
Q_{>0} in the same way. So it suffices to prove P = 
Q_{>0}. The multiples n \cdot 1_{
Q} are defined by the recursion of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a), which uses only addition, so they do not depend on the order; by @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (d), n \cdot 1_{
Q} = n. Applying @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) to the ordered field (
Q, \prec), in which 1 
e 0, gives 0 \prec n for every n \in 
Z_{>0}: so 
Z_{>0} \subseteq P. Let x \in 
Q_{>0}. Then x = p/q with p, q \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b) and the comparison formula, @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)), so x = p \cdot q^{-1}. Here p, q \in P, so q^{-1} \in P by @prp-reciprocal-order (a) applied in (
Q, \prec), and x \in P by (P1). Hence 
Q_{>0} \subseteq P. Conversely, let x \in P. Then x 
e 0 by (P2). If x 
otin 
Q_{>0}, then x < 0 in the usual order, so -x \in 
Q_{>0} \subseteq P; but then both x and -x lie in P, against (P2). So x \in 
Q_{>0}, and P = 
Q_{>0}. Hence \prec is the usual order. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: reduces the claim to the positive sets, citing @prp-order-from-positives. - 2: shows every positive integer is positive for the new order, noting that n \cdot 1 does not depend on the order. - 3: shows every usual-positive p/q is in P, via inverses and products. - 3: shows P \subseteq 
Q_{>0} by (P2). - Route through @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field for F = (
Q, \prec), same 10 points: 4 for \iota_F = \mathrm{id} by uniqueness (the equations ignore the order), 6 for reading off the order. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming 1 \succ 0 without 1 
e 0 or a rule; using the usual order’s comparison formula to compare elements in the new order.

title: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field In 
Q the fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, \dots “tend to 1”. Sections 4.1 and 4.2 supplied the tools to say what that means without leaving 
Q: an absolute value to measure distance, and the Archimedean property to make 1/(n + 1) small. This section defines the limit of a sequence in an arbitrary ordered field, with tolerances taken from that field. It then proves that a sequence has at most one limit, and that a convergent sequence is bounded. Chapter 5 applies these results with F = 
Q, at a stage when no other number system is available. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), and F_{>0} = \{ x \in F : x > 0 \} is its set of positive elements, as in Section 4.1; for F = 
Q this is 
Q_{>0}. As agreed after @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field, we write n for n \cdot 1_F where no confusion arises. So 1/(n + 1) in F means 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F), which exists and is positive, since (n + 1) \cdot 1_F \ge 1 > 0 by @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) and reciprocals of positive elements are positive (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Sequences A list 1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots is a rule that assigns a term to each position, and a rule of that kind already has a name: a function on 
N. [Sequence; Eventually] A sequence in F is a function a \colon 
N 	o F (@fd2:def-function). Its value at n is written a_n and called the n-th term; the sequence is written (a_n)_{n \in 
N}, or (a_n), and \{ a_n : n \in 
N \} is its set of values. A property P(n) of natural numbers holds eventually if there is N_0 \in 
N such that P(n) holds for every n \in 
N with n \ge N_0. Examples. - In 
Q: a_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1), with terms 1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots. - In any F: a_n \coloneqq n, that is, n \cdot 1_F, with terms 0, 1, 2, \dots; and a_n \coloneqq (-1)^n, with the powers of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field, with terms 1, -1, 1, \dots. The second sequence has infinitely many terms but only two values: its set of values is \{ 1, -1 \}. A sequence is ordered and may repeat; its set of values forgets both. - The degenerate case: a constant sequence a_n \coloneqq c for a fixed c \in F. It matters because every definition below must give the expected answer on it. - A sequence may be defined by recursion (@fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega as @thm-omega-recursion through @cor-omega-identification (b)). The Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, x_0 = 2 and x_{n+1} = (x_n^2 + 2)/(2x_n), is a sequence in 
Q; Section 4.6 studies it. Non-example by minimal change. The formula n \mapsto 1/n defines no sequence: at n = 0 it asks for 1/0, and 0 has no inverse. Everything else about the first example survives the change, and only “a function on all of 
N” fails. This is why the book’s sequences start at n = 0 and why we write 1/(n + 1). “Eventually” absorbs any finite beginning. In 
Q, “1/(n + 1) < 1/10” holds eventually, from N_0 = 10 on, although it fails for n \le 9; “(-1)^n = 1” does not hold eventually, since it fails at every odd n. Two eventual properties hold together eventually: if P(n) holds for n \ge N_0 and Q(n) for n \ge N_1, then both hold for n \ge \max\{N_0, N_1\}, the larger of the two numbers, which exists by trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)). The same goes for any finite number of properties, taking the larger number one comparison at a time. For infinitely many properties it fails: “1/(n + 1) < 1/(k + 1)” holds eventually for each k \in 
N, from N_0 = k + 1 on, but no single N_0 serves every k, since k = N_0 fails at n = N_0. The limit of a sequence We want a precise sense in which 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, \dots “tends to 1” in 
Q. The first idea is “the terms get closer and closer to 1”. Here is why it fails. With a_n \coloneqq (n + 1)/(n + 2), 1 - a_n =  rac{1}{n + 2} , \qquad 2 - a_n =  rac{n + 3}{n + 2} = 1 +  rac{1}{n + 2} . Both distances shrink at every step, so the terms get “closer and closer” to 2 as well. What singles out 1 is that the distance to 1 falls below any tolerance we name, and stays below it, while the distance to 2 never falls below 1. The tolerances must come from F itself, since in 
Q there is nothing else to measure with. Every tolerance in F is eventually met. [Limit of a Sequence in an Ordered Field] Let (a_n) be a sequence in F and a \in F. The sequence converges to a in F, written a_n 	o a, if for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there exists N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. In symbols,  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) . Then a is a limit of (a_n). The sequence is convergent if it converges to some a \in F, and divergent otherwise. In words: the first clause hands us an arbitrary tolerance \varepsilon, a positive element of F. The second says that some index N can be found, and it may depend on \varepsilon. The third says that from N on, every term lies within \varepsilon of a: the inequality holds eventually. The absolute value is that of @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, and by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d) the condition on each term reads \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < a_n < a + \varepsilon . The domain of \varepsilon is part of the definition. For F = 
Q, \varepsilon is a rational number, and “a_n 	o a in 
Q” mentions nothing outside 
Q. The formula is the one translated in @fd1:exm-translate-limit (a), where it was read in the school real numbers. Here it is read in F, and every fact used about it will be proved from the ordered-field axioms. Well-definedness. Nothing needs checking for “converges to a”. We say “a limit” for now, because a sequence might have two; @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field below rules that out. Negating the definition, quantifier by quantifier (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation for the bounded quantifiers, @fd1:prp-negated-implication for the implication), and using that 
eg(x < \varepsilon) means x \ge \varepsilon in the totally ordered F (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)): a_n 
ot	o a means \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . One bad tolerance, and beyond every threshold a term that misses it. A sequence is divergent when this holds for every a \in F. [First Limits] Decide, from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, which of these converge, and to what. 1. A constant sequence a_n = c in any ordered field F. 2. a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. 3. a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2) in 
Q. 4. a_n = (-1)^n in any ordered field F. (a) a_n 	o c. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0} and take N \coloneqq 0. For every n, \abs{a_n - c} = \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon. Here N does not depend on \varepsilon at all: the degenerate case. (b) a_n 	o 0. The field 
Q is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, by @thm-rationals-archimedean). Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. For n \ge N also n + 1 \ge N, so \abs{a_n - 0} = 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon, where the absolute value drops because 1/(n + 1) > 0. The N depends on \varepsilon, and Archimedes is what supplies it. (c) a_n 	o 1. By the computation above the definition, \abs{a_n - 1} = 1/(n + 2). Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, take the N of (b). For n \ge N, n + 2 > n + 1 \ge N, so 1/(n + 2) < \varepsilon. (d) Divergent, in every ordered field. By the recursion for powers, (-1)^{n+1} = (-1)^n (-1) = -(-1)^n (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), and \abs{(-1)^n} = 1 for every n, by induction with @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b). Hence \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} = \abs{-2 a_n} = 2 \abs{a_n} = 2 for every n. Suppose a_n 	o a for some a \in F. Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 and its N, and let n \coloneqq N, so that n and n + 1 are both \ge N. The three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) gives 2 = \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} \le \abs{a_{n+1} - a} + \abs{a - a_n} < 1 + 1 = 2 , so 2 < 2, against (O1). So no a \in F is a limit. The bad tolerance is \varepsilon = 1: two consecutive terms are 2 apart and cannot both lie within 1 of one point. For a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q and \varepsilon = 1/100, which N \in 
N satisfy “\abs{a_n} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N”? Exactly the N \ge 100. By the comparison formula (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)), 1/(n + 1) < 1/100 if and only if 100 < n + 1, that is, n \ge 100. So every N \ge 100 works, and an N \le 99 fails at n = N itself, where 1/(N + 1) \ge 1/100. The definition asks only for some working N; any larger one works too. Non-example by minimal change. Keep the sequence a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2) and change the candidate limit from 1 to 2. The distance \abs{a_n - 2} = 1 + 1/(n + 2) still shrinks at every step, and still the definition fails, at its first clause: for \varepsilon \coloneqq 1, every term has \abs{a_n - 2} > 1, so no N exists. This is the negation displayed above, with \varepsilon = 1 and n = N for every N. Why this definition. - Strict or not. Replacing \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon by \abs{a_n - a} \le \varepsilon gives the same notion: given \varepsilon, apply the weak form to \varepsilon/2, and \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). - Every n \ge N, not some. With “some n \ge N” the sequence (-1)^n would “converge” both to 1 and to -1: beyond any N there are terms equal to each. - The order of the quantifiers. With \exists N before  orall \varepsilon, the condition says that a_n = a for every n \ge N: for each such n, \abs{a_n - a} lies below every element of F_{>0}, so it is not itself positive, and it is 0 by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a). (Exercise A1 (b) asks for the details.) Then 1/(n + 1) would have no limit in 
Q. - Tolerances from F. In a field with more elements than 
Q, “every rational tolerance is eventually met” can be strictly weaker than “every tolerance in F is eventually met”. The remark after @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean shows this happen. a_n 	o a does not say that some term equals a: 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), and no term is 0. Nor does it say that \abs{a_n - a} decreases: a_n \coloneqq (1 + (-1)^n)/(n + 1) in 
Q has 0 \le a_n \le 2/(n + 1), so \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon as soon as 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon/2, and it tends to 0; yet its terms run 2, 0, 2/3, 0, 2/5, \dots, up and down, hitting 0 at n = 1, 3, 5, \dots. Two kinds of sequence get their own names, because they recur throughout the rest of the chapter. [Null Sequence] A sequence (a_n) in F is null if a_n 	o 0. [Bounded Sequence] A sequence (a_n) in F is bounded if there exists M \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N. Such an M is a bound for (a_n). Examples. In 
Q, (1/(n + 1)) is null and bounded by 1; in every F, ((-1)^n) is bounded by 1 and not null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)); a constant sequence c is bounded by \abs{c} + 1, which is positive even when c = 0. Non-example. In 
Q the sequence (n) is not bounded: for any M \in 
Q_{>0}, Archimedes (@thm-rationals-archimedean) gives n \in 
N with M < n = \abs{n}. The bound is required to be positive only for convenience, so that we may divide by it; any M \ge 0 that works can be replaced by M + 1. Archimedes and the sequence 1/(n + 1) In 
Q, 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 came straight from Archimedes. In a general ordered field, the two statements turn out to be the same. [Archimedes as a Null Sequence] The sequence  igl( 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F)  igr)_{n \in 
N} is null in F if and only if F is Archimedean. One direction is @prp-archimedean-reciprocal read as a limit. For the other, a field that is not Archimedean has an element x above every n \cdot 1_F; then every 1/(n + 1) is at least 1/x, and 1/x is a tolerance that is never met. (\Leftarrow) Let F be Archimedean and \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is N \in 
Z_{>0} (depending on \varepsilon) with 1/(m \cdot 1_F) < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. For n \ge N also n + 1 \ge N, so \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} - 0 \Bigrvert =  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon , where the absolute value drops because the term is positive. So the sequence is null. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose F is not Archimedean. Negating @def-archimedean-ordered-field (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, and @prp-ordered-field-halves (a) for 
eg(x < n \cdot 1_F) \iff x \ge n \cdot 1_F), there is x \in F with x \ge n \cdot 1_F for every n \in 
N. In particular x \ge 1 \cdot 1_F = 1 > 0, so \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/x \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). For every n \in 
N, 0 < (n + 1) \cdot 1_F \le x (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} - 0 \Bigrvert =  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} \ge  rac{1}{x} = \varepsilon . So for this \varepsilon no N works, even with n = N, and the sequence is not null. So in 
Q(t), the field of @exm-rational-function-field, which is not Archimedean, 1/(n + 1) does not tend to 0: the tolerance 1/t is never met. In 
Q, 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 is @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b), which rests on the Archimedean property; every result proved without the Archimedean property holds in 
Q(t) as well. The same example shows why tolerances must come from F. In 
Q(t), every rational tolerance is eventually met by 1/(n + 1). Write \iota for the embedding \iota_F of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field. Since \iota respects products, \iota(1) = 1 and \iota(n + 1) = (n + 1) \cdot 1, we have ((n + 1) \cdot 1) \cdot \iota(1/(n + 1)) = \iota(1) = 1, so the term 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1) is \iota(1/(n + 1)). Given q \in 
Q_{>0}, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b) gives N with 1/(n + 1) < q in 
Q for every n \ge N, and \iota, being strictly increasing, carries this to \iota(1/(n + 1)) < \iota(q). Yet the sequence is not null in 
Q(t). For F = 
Q the two readings coincide, because there every tolerance is rational. Changing finitely many terms Whether a sequence converges, and to what, depends only on its terms from some point on. Two forms of this are used constantly: altering finitely many terms, and dropping the first k. [Only the Tail Matters] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be sequences in F, and a \in F. 1. If there is N_0 \in 
N with a_n = b_n for every n \ge N_0, then a_n 	o a if and only if b_n 	o a; in particular (a_n) is null if and only if (b_n) is; and (a_n) is bounded if and only if (b_n) is. 2. For k \in 
N, the shifted sequence (a_{n+k})_{n \in 
N} converges to a if and only if (a_n) does. For limits, a threshold for one sequence becomes a threshold for the other once it is pushed past N_0, or moved by k. For bounds, the finitely many terms before N_0 are absorbed by a finite maximum. (a) Limits. Suppose a_n 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N, and let N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N_0\}. For n \ge N', b_n = a_n and \abs{b_n - a} = \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon. So b_n 	o a. The hypothesis is symmetric in the two sequences, so the converse follows by exchanging them. The case a = 0 is the statement about null sequences. Bounds. Suppose \abs{a_n} \le M for every n, with M \in F_{>0}. If N_0 = 0, the two sequences are equal. Otherwise let M' \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{b_0}, \dots, \abs{b_{N_0 - 1}}, M \} , the maximum of finitely many elements of F, which exists by @fd2:prp-finite-max (its proof works in any ordered field, as Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 remarks). Then M' \ge M > 0. For n < N_0, \abs{b_n} \le M' because \abs{b_n} is one of the listed elements; for n \ge N_0, \abs{b_n} = \abs{a_n} \le M \le M'. So M' bounds (b_n). The converse is the same with the sequences exchanged. (b) Suppose a_n 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, with N as in the definition. For n \ge N, also n + k \ge N, so \abs{a_{n+k} - a} < \varepsilon. Hence (a_{n+k})_n converges to a, with the same N. Conversely, suppose a_{n+k} 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, with N such that \abs{a_{m+k} - a} < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. Let n \ge N + k. Then n = m + k for the natural number m \coloneqq n - k, and m \ge N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), (c)). So \abs{a_n - a} = \abs{a_{m+k} - a} < \varepsilon, and N + k is a threshold for (a_n). This proves the proposition. The shift clause is about convergence only; it is used to start a sequence later, for instance to read a formula such as 1/n, which needs n \ge 1, as the shift by 1 of a sequence indexed from 0. Section 4.5 adds the Cauchy property to clause (a). One more reformulation moves every limit to 0. [Limits Through Null Sequences] For a sequence (a_n) in F and a \in F: a_n 	o a if and only if the sequence (a_n - a) is null. For every n, \abs{(a_n - a) - 0} = \abs{a_n - a}. So the two conditions of @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, for (a_n) with limit a and for (a_n - a) with limit 0, say word for word the same thing, with the same N for each \varepsilon. A sequence has at most one limit If “the terms are eventually within every tolerance of a” is to name the number the sequence tends to, it must single out one a. It does. [Uniqueness of Limits] Let (a_n) be a sequence in F and a, b \in F. If a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b, then a = b. Try it first (ten minutes): suppose a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b with a 
e b. Which \varepsilon makes the two tails collide? The natural first choice is \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a - b}, positive because a 
e b; it is the choice that worked in @fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal. Beyond both thresholds a term a_n is within \abs{a - b} of a and of b, and the triangle inequality through a_n yields only \abs{a - b} < 2\abs{a - b}: true, and no contradiction. The two tolerances add. So give each half: with \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a - b}/2, the same chain ends in \abs{a - b} < \abs{a - b}. Let a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b, and suppose, for a contradiction, that a 
e b. Then a - b 
e 0, so \abs{a - b} > 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), and \varepsilon \coloneqq  rac{\abs{a - b}}{2} \in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b); it depends only on a and b. Since a_n 	o a, there is N_1 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1; since a_n 	o b, there is N_2 with \abs{a_n - b} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_2. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. Then both inequalities hold at this n, and the three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), with \abs{a - a_n} = \abs{a_n - a} by part (b) of the same proposition, gives \abs{a - b} \le \abs{a - a_n} + \abs{a_n - b} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon = \abs{a - b} , where the strict inequality is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) and the last equality is @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). So \abs{a - b} < \abs{a - b}, against (O1). Hence the assumption a 
e b is refuted, and a = b (@fd1:def-rule-raa). This is the argument of @fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal, rerun in F. There a hypothesis valid for every \varepsilon was fed the one \varepsilon that makes the numbers collide. Here the two hypotheses give \abs{a - b} < 2\varepsilon for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, and the colliding choice is \abs{a - b}/2. The facts about the absolute value that the old argument took from school are now @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field, valid in every ordered field. Since a convergent sequence has exactly one limit, we may speak of the limit and write it \lim a_n, or \lim_{n 	o \infty} a_n. So \lim a_n = a means the same as a_n 	o a. In 
Q, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field gives \lim 1/(n + 1) = 0 and \lim (n + 1)/(n + 2) = 1, while \lim (-1)^n names nothing. Convergent sequences are bounded A convergent sequence cannot run off: from some index on, its terms are trapped near the limit, and only finitely many terms come before that index. Convergent Sequences Are Bounded Every convergent sequence in F is bounded. Use the definition once, with the tolerance 1: from some N on, \abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}. The terms before N are finitely many, so one of them, or \abs{a} + 1, is the largest absolute value in sight. Let a_n 	o a. Applying @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field with \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 \in F_{>0} gives N \in 
N with \abs{a_n - a} < 1 for every n \ge N. For such n, the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), with x = a_n - a and y = a) gives \abs{a_n} = \abs{(a_n - a) + a} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a} . If N = 0, let M \coloneqq \abs{a} + 1. Otherwise let M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{a} + 1 \} , which exists by @fd2:prp-finite-max in the totally ordered F (as in the proof of @prp-tail-change-ordered-field). In both cases M \ge \abs{a} + 1 \ge 1 > 0, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), so M \in F_{>0}. For n < N, \abs{a_n} \le M because \abs{a_n} is one of the listed elements; for n \ge N, \abs{a_n} < \abs{a} + 1 \le M. So M bounds (a_n). The bound M depends on the whole sequence, through a, N and the first N terms, but on no tolerance: it is one element of F, fixed once. Section 4.4 uses exactly that, in the product of two limits. The converse fails: ((-1)^n) is bounded by 1 and divergent (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write “a_n 
ot	o a” in symbols, and name the law used at each step. 2. What does \exists N \in 
N \  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \  orall n \in 
N \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) say about (a_n)? Does (1/(n + 1)) satisfy it in 
Q, with a = 0? 3. For a_n = (2n + 1)/(n + 1) in 
Q, find the least N that works in @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field for the limit 2 and \varepsilon = 1/50. (a) Start from 
eg  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon). The bounded negation laws (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), then (b), then (a)) move
