eg(n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon), which is n \ge N \wedge 
eg(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon) by @fd1:prp-negated-implication. Finally 
eg(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon) is \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon, by trichotomy in F (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). The result: \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . (b) It says that a_n = a for every n \ge N: the sequence is eventually constant, equal to a. Indeed, fix n \ge N. Then \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. If a_n 
e a, then \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a_n - a} is in F_{>0} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)) and gives \abs{a_n - a} < \abs{a_n - a}, against (O1); so a_n = a. This is the argument of @fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal, rerun in F for one n at a time (no halving is needed: only one tolerance is in play). Conversely, an eventually constant sequence satisfies the formula, since \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) does not satisfy it: no term equals 0. It converges to 0, but its N must depend on \varepsilon. The quantifier order is the whole difference. (c) a_n - 2 =  igl( 2n + 1 - 2(n + 1)  igr)/(n + 1) = -1/(n + 1), so \abs{a_n - 2} = 1/(n + 1). By the comparison formula, 1/(n + 1) < 1/50 if and only if n + 1 > 50, that is, n \ge 50. So N = 50 works, and every N \le 49 fails at n = 49 (which is \ge N), where \abs{a_{49} - 2} = 1/50. The least N is 50. B. Practice [B1] Prove from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field that, in 
Q,  rac{2n + 1}{n + 1} 	o 2 \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad  rac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 + 3} 	o  rac{1}{2} . Say exactly where the Archimedean property is used. First limit. As in A1 (c), \abs{(2n + 1)/(n + 1) - 2} = 1/(n + 1). Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. Since 
Q is Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean), @prp-archimedean-reciprocal gives N \in 
Z_{>0}, depending on \varepsilon, with 1/m < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. For n \ge N, n + 1 \ge N, so the distance 1/(n + 1) is < \varepsilon. Second limit. Bring the difference to one fraction:  rac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 + 3} -  rac{1}{2} =  rac{2(n^2 + 1) - (2n^2 + 3)}{2(2n^2 + 3)} =  rac{-1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} , so the distance is 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)). We bound it by 1/(n + 1). For n \ge 1, n^2 = n \cdot n \ge n \cdot 1 = n (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), applied to 0 \le 1 \le n and 0 \le n \le n), so 2(2n^2 + 3) - (n + 1) = 4n^2 - n + 5 \ge 3n + 5 > 0 ; for n = 0 the left side is 5 > 0. So 0 < n + 1 < 2(2n^2 + 3), and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)) \le 1/(n + 1). With the N of the first part, every n \ge N has distance \le 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon. Where Archimedes is used. Only in obtaining N from \varepsilon, through @prp-archimedean-reciprocal. The algebra of the distances holds in any ordered field. In 
Q(t) the same algebra gives the same distances, and the proofs fail exactly there: both take N from 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon, and by the proof of @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean with x = t (@exm-rational-function-field) no N makes 1/(n + 1) < 1/t for all n \ge N. [B2] Prove that if a_n 	o a in F, then \abs{a_n} 	o \abs{a}. Show by an example that the converse fails, and prove that it holds when a = 0. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, and choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for n \ge N. By the reverse triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)), for n \ge N,  igl\lvert \abs{a_n} - \abs{a}  igrvert \le \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon . So \abs{a_n} 	o \abs{a}, with the same N. The converse fails for a_n = (-1)^n and a = 1: \abs{a_n} = 1 for every n, a constant sequence, so \abs{a_n} 	o 1 = \abs{1} (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)); but (a_n) converges to nothing (part (d) of that example). For a = 0 the converse holds:  igl\lvert \abs{a_n} - \abs{0}  igrvert =  igl\lvert \abs{a_n}  igrvert = \abs{a_n} = \abs{a_n - 0}, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), since \abs{a_n} \ge 0. So the two conditions coincide: a sequence is null if and only if its absolute values form a null sequence. [B3: Bounded but not convergent, in 
Q(t)] In the field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field, show that the sequence (n \cdot 1)_{n \in 
N} is bounded and does not converge. Is (n) bounded in 
Q? Bounded. By @exm-rational-function-field, t > n \cdot 1 for every n \in 
N. Also n \cdot 1 \ge 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), and 0 \cdot 1 = 0), so \abs{n \cdot 1} = n \cdot 1 < t. And t > 1 \cdot 1 = 1 > 0, so M \coloneqq t \in 
Q(t)_{>0} is a bound. Not convergent. Suppose n \cdot 1 	o a for some a \in 
Q(t). Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/2, which is positive (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), and its N. With n \coloneqq N, both n and n + 1 are \ge N, and (n + 1) \cdot 1 - n \cdot 1 = 1 by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). The three-point triangle inequality gives 1 = \abs{(n + 1) \cdot 1 - n \cdot 1} \le \abs{(n + 1) \cdot 1 - a} + \abs{a - n \cdot 1} < 	frac12 + 	frac12 = 1 , against (O1). So the sequence diverges. In 
Q. No: by the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field, Archimedes puts some n above any proposed bound. The same sequence is bounded in one field and unbounded in another. Boundedness is a property of the sequence in F, like convergence. C. Going deeper [C1: A positive limit keeps the terms positive] 1. Prove that if a_n 	o a in F and a > 0, then a_n > a/2 eventually; in particular a_n > 0 eventually. 2. Give a sequence in 
Q with a_n > 0 for every n whose limit is not positive. What does this say about the converse of (a)? (a) Let \varepsilon \coloneqq a/2, which lies in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b), since a > 0. Choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < a/2 for every n \ge N. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), for such n, a_n > a -  rac{a}{2} =  rac{a}{2} > 0 , where a - a/2 = a/2 because a/2 + a/2 = a (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). So a_n > a/2 for every n \ge N. (b) a_n = 1/(n + 1): every term is positive, and the limit is 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). So “every term positive” does not give “limit positive”: the strict inequality is lost in the limit. What survives is the weak inequality a \ge 0, proved in Section 4.4. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument for @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. Then repair the argument. (1) Let a_n 	o a. (2) Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 in the definition of the limit, and let N be the index it provides. (3) Then for every n \in 
N, \abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}. (4) So M \coloneqq 1 + \abs{a} is a bound for (a_n). The conclusion is true: it is @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. The argument is not correct. The failing line is (3). The first inequality is the triangle inequality and is fine. The second uses \abs{a_n - a} < 1 “for every n \in 
N”. Line (2) supplies it only for n \ge N: it is the bounded universal  orall n \in 
N \, (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < 1). Instantiating it at n needs the line n \ge N (bounded ulename{ orall E}, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and for n < N no such line is available. Line (3) cites a line that is not there: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Counterexample to the step. In 
Q, let a_0 \coloneqq 5 and a_n \coloneqq 0 for n \ge 1, with a = 0. Then a_n 	o 0, and N = 1 is a legitimate choice in line (2) for \varepsilon = 1, since \abs{a_n - 0} = 0 < 1 for n \ge 1. At n = 0, line (3) claims \abs{a_0} < 1 + \abs{0} = 1, but \abs{a_0} = 5; and the M = 1 of line (4) is not a bound. No counterexample to the conclusion exists: 5 is a bound. Repair. Keep line (3) for n \ge N only, and take M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{a} + 1 \}, the finite maximum of the proof of @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and the argument is not correct. - 3: names line (3) and the use of \abs{a_n - a} < 1 for n < N, where the hypothesis does not apply (bounded  orall used outside its range; entry (N9)). - 3: gives a convergent sequence and a legitimate N for which the step’s inequality fails at some n < N, and checks it. - 2: repairs the argument with a finite maximum over the terms before N. Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; offering a counterexample to the conclusion; blaming the triangle inequality.

title: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content:
The Algebra and Order of Limits So far every limit has been found by hand: we computed the distance from a_n to the candidate limit and bounded it, as in @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field and Exercise B1 of Section 4.3. This section proves the rules that make most such work unnecessary. Sums, multiples, products and quotients of convergent sequences converge to the sum, multiple, product and quotient of the limits; limits respect \le; and a sequence trapped between two sequences with a common limit has that limit too. Everything holds in an arbitrary ordered field F. No result of this section uses the Archimedean property; only the examples and exercises set in 
Q do, each time through @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b) or the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field. Throughout, F is an ordered field and F_{>0} its set of positive elements, as in Section 4.3. Two tools The first tool says that a small factor wins against a factor that merely stays bounded. [Null Times Bounded Is Null] Let (a_n) be a null sequence in F, and let (b_n) be a sequence with \abs{b_n} \le M for every n, where M \in F_{>0}. Then (a_n b_n) is null. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/M \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a) and (O4)). Since (a_n) is null, there is N (depending on \varepsilon and M) with \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon/M for every n \ge N. For such n, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{a_n b_n - 0} = \abs{a_n} \abs{b_n} \le \abs{a_n} M <  rac{\varepsilon}{M} \, M = \varepsilon , where the first inequality multiplies \abs{b_n} \le M by \abs{a_n} \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)), and the second multiplies \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon/M by M > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). For instance,  igl( (-1)^n/(n + 1)  igr) is null in 
Q: it is 1/(n + 1), null by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b), times (-1)^n, bounded by 1. The bound M is fixed before \varepsilon and enters the tolerance \varepsilon/M. That is the pattern of the product law below. The second tool is the fact behind every division by b_n: if b_n 	o b 
e 0, the terms eventually stay away from 0, by a margin we can name. [Terms Near a Non-zero Limit] Let b_n 	o b in F with b 
e 0. Then there is N_0 \in 
N with \abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2 for every n \ge N_0. If b > 0, then moreover b_n > b/2 for every n \ge N_0. Since b 
e 0, \abs{b} > 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), so \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{b}/2 \in F_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). Choose N_0 (depending on (b_n) and b) with \abs{b_n - b} < \abs{b}/2 for every n \ge N_0. For such n, the reverse triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)), together with x \le \abs{x} and \abs{-x} = \abs{x} (parts (c), (b)), gives \abs{b} - \abs{b_n} \le  igl\lvert \abs{b} - \abs{b_n}  igrvert \le \abs{b - b_n} = \abs{b_n - b} <  rac{\abs{b}}{2} , so \abs{b_n} > \abs{b} - \abs{b}/2 = \abs{b}/2, adding \abs{b_n} - \abs{b}/2 to both sides (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). If b > 0, then \abs{b} = b, and @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d) turns \abs{b_n - b} < b/2 into b - b/2 < b_n, that is, b_n > b/2. In particular b_n 
e 0 for every n \ge N_0, since \abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2 > 0. The lemma needs b 
e 0. In 
Q, b_n \coloneqq (1 + (-1)^n)/(n + 1) tends to 0 (the warning after @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field in Section 4.3: 0 \le b_n \le 2/(n + 1), and 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b), which uses Archimedes), yet b_n = 0 at every odd n, so for b = 0 no N_0 has \abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2 = 0 for every n \ge N_0. Even 1/(n + 1), which tends to 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)) and is never 0, is bounded away from 0 by no positive margin. The limit laws [Limit Laws] Let a_n 	o a and b_n 	o b in F, and let c \in F. Then: 1. a_n + b_n 	o a + b; 2. c a_n 	o c a; in particular -a_n 	o -a and a_n - b_n 	o a - b; 3. a_n b_n 	o a b; 4. if b 
e 0 and b_n 
e 0 for every n, then a_n / b_n 	o a / b. Work backwards from each target distance. For (a), \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (a + b)} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{b_n - b}: a sum of two terms, each of which we can make small, so we give each half the tolerance. For (c), write a_n b_n - ab = a_n (b_n - b) + b (a_n - a) . The factors b_n - b and a_n - a can be made small, but a_n cannot. It is, however, bounded (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field), so we replace \abs{a_n} by a bound M and ask \abs{b_n - b} to be smaller than \varepsilon/(2M). For (d), it is enough to treat 1/b_n and then use (c). Before reading on: why must M be fixed before \varepsilon? (a) Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). Since a_n 	o a, choose N_1 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1; since b_n 	o b, choose N_2 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. For n \ge N, both estimates hold, and the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) gives  egin{aligned} \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (a + b)} &= \abs{(a_n - a) + (b_n - b)} \ &\le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{b_n - b} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the strict inequality is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) and the last equality @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). (b) If c = 0, then c a_n = 0 = c a for every n (@prp-ring-algebra (b)), a constant sequence, which converges to 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)). Let c 
e 0, so \abs{c} > 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/\abs{c} \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a) and (O4)). Choose N (depending on \varepsilon and c) with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/\abs{c} for every n \ge N. For such n, by distributivity and @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{c a_n - c a} = \abs{c (a_n - a)} = \abs{c} \abs{a_n - a} < \abs{c} \,  rac{\varepsilon}{\abs{c}} = \varepsilon , multiplying by \abs{c} > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). With c = -1, and (-1) x = -x (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), this gives -a_n 	o -a. Then (a), applied to (a_n) and (-b_n), gives a_n - b_n = a_n + (-b_n) 	o a + (-b) = a - b. (c) By @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field there is M \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N. We fix this M now; it depends on the sequence (a_n) only. Now let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since \abs{b} \ge 0, the element \abs{b} + 1 is \ge 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (e)). Since 2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), 2M > 0 and 2(\abs{b} + 1) > 0 by (O4), so @prp-reciprocal-order (a) and (O4) give  rac{\varepsilon}{2M} \in F_{>0} \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad  rac{\varepsilon}{2(\abs{b} + 1)} \in F_{>0} . Since b_n 	o b, choose N_1 with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon/(2M) for every n \ge N_1. Since a_n 	o a, choose N_2 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) for every n \ge N_2. Both depend only on \varepsilon, M and b. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, and let n \ge N. Using the identity of the Idea, the triangle inequality and the product rule (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), (b)),  egin{aligned} \abs{a_n b_n - ab} &\le \abs{a_n} \abs{b_n - b} + \abs{b} \abs{a_n - a} \ &\le M \abs{b_n - b} + (\abs{b} + 1) \abs{a_n - a} \ &< M \,  rac{\varepsilon}{2M} + (\abs{b} + 1) \,  rac{\varepsilon}{2(\abs{b} + 1)} =  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . \end{aligned} The second line uses @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) twice, with 0 \le \abs{a_n} \le M and 0 \le \abs{b} \le \abs{b} + 1, and adds the two estimates (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). The third multiplies the two estimates by the positive elements M and \abs{b} + 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and adds them (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)); the last equality is @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). So a_n b_n 	o ab. (d) First we show 1/b_n 	o 1/b. By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field there is N_0 (depending on (b_n) and b) with \abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2 for every n \ge N_0. For such n, @lem-field-fraction-rules (c) and @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) give \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{b_n} -  rac{1}{b} \Bigrvert = \Bigl\lvert  rac{b - b_n}{b_n b} \Bigrvert =  rac{\abs{b_n - b}}{\abs{b_n} \abs{b}} . Multiplying \abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2 by \abs{b} > 0 gives \abs{b_n}\abs{b} > \abs{b}^2/2 > 0, so 1/(\abs{b_n}\abs{b}) < 2/\abs{b}^2 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Multiplying by \abs{b_n - b} \ge 0, \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{b_n} -  rac{1}{b} \Bigrvert \le  rac{2}{\abs{b}^2} \, \abs{b_n - b} \qquad (n \ge N_0) . Now let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon \abs{b}^2/2 \in F_{>0} ((O4), @prp-ordered-field-halves (b)); choose N_1 (depending on \varepsilon and b) with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon \abs{b}^2/2 for every n \ge N_1, and let N \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1\}. For n \ge N, the last display and multiplication of \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon \abs{b}^2/2 by 2/\abs{b}^2 > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4); @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) give \abs{1/b_n - 1/b} < (2/\abs{b}^2)(\varepsilon \abs{b}^2/2) = \varepsilon. So 1/b_n 	o 1/b. Finally a_n/b_n = a_n \cdot (1/b_n), and (c) gives a_n/b_n 	o a \cdot (1/b) = a/b. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: the tolerance \varepsilon/(2M) contains M, so M must exist before that tolerance is written down. And M must not depend on n: it has to bound \abs{a_n} for every n \ge N at once, including indices not yet chosen. That is why it comes from @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field, a single bound for the whole sequence, and not from “\abs{a_n} is some element of F”. The + 1 in \abs{b} + 1 is there because b may be 0, and \varepsilon/(2\abs{b}) would then mean nothing. Part (a) is the move we call split \varepsilon: to make a sum of k small terms smaller than \varepsilon, give each term the tolerance \varepsilon/k, and combine the finitely many thresholds by a maximum. Part (c) is bound, then shrink: replace the factor you cannot control by a bound fixed in advance, then make the other factor small. Alternatively, (c) follows from the earlier tools without new estimates. By @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field, (b_n - b) and (a_n - a) are null; a_n (b_n - b) is null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, with the bound M; b (a_n - a) is null by (b); so their sum a_n b_n - ab is null by (a), and @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field again gives a_n b_n 	o ab. The bound M is still fixed first: it is the hypothesis of @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field. In (d), the hypothesis “b_n 
e 0 for every n” is there only so that a_n / b_n is defined for every n. By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field, b_n 
e 0 holds eventually anyway once b 
e 0. If some early b_n vanish, the quotient is a sequence from some N_0 on, and @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b) applies the law to the shifted sequences (a_{n+N_0}) and (b_{n+N_0}). Part (d) needs b 
e 0, even when every b_n 
e 0. In 
Q, a_n = 1/(n + 1) and b_n = 1/(n + 1)^2 are both null (the first by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b), the second by (c), since b_n = a_n a_n), with every b_n 
e 0, and a_n / b_n = n + 1. Since n + 1 > n, the sequence (n + 1) is not bounded (the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field), and so has no limit (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field). The “law” \lim (a_n/b_n) = 0/0 names nothing. Find \lim (3n^2 - n)/(n^2 + 5) in 
Q, citing a law, or another result, for each step. The limit is 3. Let u_0 \coloneqq 0 and u_n \coloneqq 1/n for n \ge 1. The shifted sequence (u_{n+1})_n = (1/(n + 1))_n is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b); this is where Archimedes enters), so (u_n) is null by @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b). By @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field: 3 - u_n 	o 3 - 0 = 3 (the constant 3 converges to 3 by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a); then (b) and (a)); u_n^2 	o 0 ((c)); 1 + 5u_n^2 	o 1 ((b), (a)). Every 1 + 5u_n^2 \ge 1 > 0: u_n^2 \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) if u_n 
e 0, and u_0^2 = 0), so 5u_n^2 \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)), and 1 + 5u_n^2 \ge 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). Also the limit 1 
e 0, so (d) gives c_n \coloneqq  rac{3 - u_n}{1 + 5u_n^2} 	o  rac{3}{1} = 3 . For n \ge 1, multiplying numerator and denominator by n^2 shows c_n = (3n^2 - n)/(n^2 + 5). The two sequences agree from N_0 = 1 on (at n = 0 they differ: 3 versus 0), so @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (a) gives the limit 3. Limits and order Inequalities between terms pass to the limits, provided we accept that a strict inequality may become an equality. [Limits Preserve Weak Inequalities] Let a_n 	o a and b_n 	o b in F, and let N_0 \in 
N. 1. If a_n \le b_n for every n \ge N_0, then a \le b. 2. In particular, for c \in F: if a_n \le c for every n \ge N_0, then a \le c; and if a_n \ge c for every n \ge N_0, then a \ge c. 3. (Squeeze.) Let (c_n) be a sequence in F. If a = b and a_n \le c_n \le b_n for every n \ge N_0, then c_n 	o a. For (a), suppose instead that b < a. The midpoint (a + b)/2 separates them, and from some index on a_n lies above it and b_n below it, contradicting a_n \le b_n. The tolerance that achieves this is half the gap, (a - b)/2. For (c), from some index on a_n and b_n both lie in the window (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon), and c_n is trapped between them. (a) Suppose, for a contradiction, that b < a. Let \varepsilon \coloneqq  rac{a - b}{2} , which lies in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) and @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). Choose N_1 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1, and N_2 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_2. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1, N_2\}. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), at this n, a_n > a - \varepsilon =  rac{a + b}{2} = b + \varepsilon > b_n . This contradicts a_n \le b_n, which holds because n \ge N_0. So b < a is false, and a \le b by trichotomy (O1). (b) A constant sequence c converges to c (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)). Apply (a) to (a_n) and the constant sequence c for the first claim, and to the constant sequence c and (a_n) for the second. (c) Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Choose N_1 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for n \ge N_1 and N_2 (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{b_n - a} < \varepsilon for n \ge N_2 (recall b = a), and let N \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1, N_2\}. For n \ge N, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d) gives a - \varepsilon < a_n \le c_n \le b_n < a + \varepsilon , so \abs{c_n - a} < \varepsilon by the same part (d). Hence c_n 	o a. The two midpoint equalities in (a) are field algebra: a - (a - b)/2 = (2a - a + b)/2 = (a + b)/2, and likewise b + (a - b)/2 = (a + b)/2. Chapter 5 uses the squeeze (c) repeatedly, mostly with F = 
Q to show that a sequence is null. In the squeeze (c), the middle sequence is not assumed to converge: its convergence is the conclusion. Strict inequalities do not pass to the limit. In 
Q, 1/(n + 1) > 0 for every n, and the limit is 0, not positive (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). From a_n < b_n for every n, (a) gives only a \le b. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of the product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c). 1. Why is M fixed before \varepsilon, and what does it depend on? 2. Which hypothesis supplies N_1, which supplies N_2, and which supplies M? 3. Why does the proof use \abs{b} + 1 rather than \abs{b}? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 5. Run the proof in 
Q on a_n = 1 + 1/(n + 1), b_n = 2 and \varepsilon = 1/10: give a valid M, the least N_1, the least N_2, and N. (a) The tolerance \varepsilon/(2M) is built from M, so M must be available first. It depends only on the sequence (a_n): it bounds \abs{a_n} for every n, independently of \varepsilon and of n. A “bound” depending on n would be useless, since the tolerance for \abs{b_n - b} must be named before n is. (b) N_1 comes from b_n 	o b, applied with the tolerance \varepsilon/(2M); N_2 from a_n 	o a, with the tolerance \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)); M also from a_n 	o a, through @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. (c) b may be 0, and then \varepsilon/(2\abs{b}) is undefined. Since \abs{b} + 1 \ge 1 > 0, the tolerance \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) always exists, and \abs{b} \le \abs{b} + 1 keeps the estimate valid. (d) Write a_n b_n - ab = a_n(b_n - b) + b(a_n - a), so that each term has a factor tending to 0. The other factor of the first term is not small, but it is bounded by a constant M fixed in advance, so making \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon/(2M) and \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) makes each term smaller than \varepsilon/2. (e) Here a = 1 and b = 2. Since 0 < 1/(n + 1) \le 1, \abs{a_n} \le 2 for every n, so M = 2 is valid. Then \varepsilon/(2M) = 1/40, and \abs{b_n - b} = 0 < 1/40 for every n: the least N_1 is 0. Next \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) = (1/10)/6 = 1/60, and \abs{a_n - a} = 1/(n + 1) < 1/60 if and only if n + 1 > 60, that is, n \ge 60: the least N_2 is 60. So N = \max\{0, 60\} = 60. Check at n = 60: a_{60} b_{60} - ab = 2(1 + 1/61) - 2 = 2/61 < 1/10. B. Practice [B1] Find the following limits in 
Q by the limit laws, naming the result used at each step. 1. \dfrac{n + 2}{3n + 1}. 2. \dfrac{n^2 + 1}{(n + 1)^2}. 3. \Bigl( \dfrac{1}{n + 1} - 2 \Bigr) \Bigl( 3 + \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} \Bigr). Hint: write each term through u_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1). Let u_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1), so u_n 	o 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), and constant sequences converge to their value (part (a) of that example). All laws cited are parts of @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field. (a) With m \coloneqq n + 1 \ge 1: (n + 2)/(3n + 1) = (m + 1)/(3m - 2) = (1 + u_n)/(3 - 2u_n), dividing numerator and denominator by m. Now 1 + u_n 	o 1 by (a), and 3 - 2u_n 	o 3 by (b) and (a). Since 0 < u_n \le 1, 3 - 2u_n \ge 1 > 0 for every n, and the limit 3 
e 0, so (d) gives the limit 1/3. (b) With m = n + 1: (n^2 + 1)/(n + 1)^2 = ((m - 1)^2 + 1)/m^2 = 1 - 2u_n + 2u_n^2. By (c), u_n^2 	o 0; by (b) and (a), 1 - 2u_n + 2u_n^2 	o 1 - 0 + 0 = 1. No quotient law is needed. (c) u_n - 2 	o -2 by (b) and (a). The sequence (-1)^n u_n is null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, since u_n is null and \abs{(-1)^n} = 1 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)); so 3 + (-1)^n u_n 	o 3 by (a). By (c), the product tends to (-2) \cdot 3 = -6. In each part Archimedes enters once, through u_n 	o 0; every other step is a law valid in any ordered field. [B2: Put the proof in order] Here are lines of the proof of @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (a), shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Recall the hypotheses: a_n 	o a, b_n 	o b, and a_n \le b_n for every n \ge N_0. Write the seven lines of a correct proof in a correct order, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. 1. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1, N_2\}. 2. Let \varepsilon \coloneqq a - b, which lies in F_{>0}. 3. Choose N_2 with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_2. 4. Suppose, for a contradiction, that b < a. 5. This contradicts a_n \le b_n; so b < a is false, and a \le b by trichotomy. 6. Let \varepsilon \coloneqq (a - b)/2, which lies in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-field-halves. 7. Let n \coloneqq N_1. 8. Then a_n > a - \varepsilon = (a + b)/2 = b + \varepsilon > b_n. 9. Choose N_1 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1. An admissible order is 	ext{(iv)}, \ 	ext{(vi)}, \ 	ext{(ix)}, \ 	ext{(iii)}, \ 	ext{(i)}, \ 	ext{(viii)}, \ 	ext{(v)} . The only other admissible order exchanges (ix) and (iii), which use only \varepsilon and one hypothesis each. Nothing else moves: (vi) uses the assumption b < a of (iv) to make \varepsilon positive; (ix) and (iii) use \varepsilon; (i) uses N_1 and N_2; (viii) uses the two estimates at this n, and needs n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2; (v) uses (viii) and n \ge N_0, and closes the assumption of (iv). Line (ii) is an \varepsilon of the wrong size. It is positive, but with it (viii) becomes a_n > a - (a - b) = b and b_n < b + (a - b) = a, and “a_n > b and b_n < a” is no contradiction with a_n \le b_n: for instance a_n = b_n = (a + b)/2 satisfies all three at once. The two windows of half-width a - b around a and b overlap; half-width (a - b)/2 makes them touch only at the midpoint, which neither open window contains. Line (vii) chooses an index that depends on the wrong thing. With n \coloneqq N_1, the estimate for a_n holds, but nothing makes n \ge N_2 or n \ge N_0: the estimate for b_n and the hypothesis a_n \le b_n may both fail at this n. The index must lie beyond all three thresholds, which the maximum in (i) ensures. [B3: Close to a convergent sequence] Let a_n 	o a in F, and let (b_n) be a sequence in F such that (b_n - a_n) is null. Prove that b_n 	o a. Here is the start of a proof. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0}. Since a_n 	o a, choose N_1 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1. Since (b_n - a_n) is null, choose N_2 with \abs{b_n - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. … Name the move, then complete it. The move is split \varepsilon, with two terms: each gets \varepsilon/2, and the two thresholds are combined by a maximum. Completion. Let n \ge N. Then n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2, and the three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) gives \abs{b_n - a} \le \abs{b_n - a_n} + \abs{a_n - a} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . Since \varepsilon \in F_{>0} was arbitrary, b_n 	o a. (The same result also follows from the laws: b_n = (b_n - a_n) + a_n 	o 0 + a by @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a). The exercise is the law’s proof, run once more.) C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the product law] Prove, from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, that if a_n 	o a and b_n 	o b in an ordered field F, then a_n b_n 	o ab. You may use that convergent sequences are bounded (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field), the rules for the absolute value (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field and @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, but not @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field. By @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field there is M \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N. It depends only on (a_n), and we fix it before any tolerance is named. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since \abs{b} + 1 \ge 1 > 0, both \varepsilon/(2M) and \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) lie in F_{>0}. By b_n 	o b there is N_1 with \abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon/(2M) for every n \ge N_1; by a_n 	o a there is N_2 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/(2(\abs{b} + 1)) for every n \ge N_2. These depend only on \varepsilon, M and b. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. Let n \ge N. Since a_n b_n - ab = a_n (b_n - b) + b (a_n - a) , the triangle inequality and \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y} give  egin{aligned} \abs{a_n b_n - ab} &\le \abs{a_n}\abs{b_n - b} + \abs{b}\abs{a_n - a} \ &\le M \abs{b_n - b} + (\abs{b} + 1)\abs{a_n - a} \ &<  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the second line uses 0 \le \abs{a_n} \le M and 0 \le \abs{b} \le \abs{b} + 1 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)), and the third multiplies the two estimates by M > 0 and \abs{b} + 1 > 0. So for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_n b_n - ab} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N: a_n b_n 	o ab. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: fixes a bound M \in F_{>0} for (\abs{a_n}), justified (convergent sequences are bounded), before \varepsilon. - 2: writes a_n b_n - ab as a sum of two terms, each with a factor tending to 0. - 3: chooses N_1, N_2 depending only on \varepsilon, M and b, with the case b = 0 handled, and N as their maximum. - 2: carries out the estimate with the triangle inequality and the product rule for \abs{\cdot}. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in the order  orall \varepsilon \, \exists N \,  orall n \ge N. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a threshold or tolerance that depends on n; the bound “\abs{a_n} \le \abs{a} + 1 for every n” without the finite part for n < N; dividing by \abs{b} without b 
e 0. A route through null sequences ((b_n - b) and (a_n - a) are null by @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field; a_n(b_n - b) and b(a_n - a) are null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, with bounds M and \abs{b} + 1; the sum of two null sequences is null, proved from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field by splitting \varepsilon) earns the same points: decomposition 2, the bound 2, the two null products and the proved sum 5, conclusion 1. Citing @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field for the sum or for b(a_n - a) gets 0 for that step. A three-term route (a_n b_n - ab = (a_n - a)(b_n - b) + a(b_n - b) + b(a_n - a), with a tolerance such as \delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/(1 + \abs{a} + \abs{b})\} chosen from \varepsilon, a and b only) earns the same points: decomposition 2; the choice of \delta, independent of n and with \delta \le 1 controlling the product term (in place of the bound M), 2; a threshold N for both sequences at tolerance \delta (the case a = 0 or b = 0 covered by the 1 in the denominator) 3; the estimate 2; conclusion 1. [C2: Non-negative terms and reciprocals] Let a_n 	o a in F, with a_n \ge 0 for every n. 1. Prove that a \ge 0. 2. Suppose moreover a > 0. Prove that there is N_0 \in 
N with a_n > 0 for every n \ge N_0, and that the sequence (1/a_{n+N_0})_{n \in 
N} converges to 1/a. 3. Give an example in 
Q where a_n > 0 for every n and (1/a_n) does not converge. [Hint 1] For (a), compare with a constant sequence. For (b), which result keeps terms away from a non-zero limit? [Hint 2] For (b), start: “By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field, since a > 0, there is N_0 with a_n > a/2 for every n \ge N_0.” (a) Since a_n \ge 0 for every n \ge 0, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (b) with c = 0 gives a \ge 0. (b) Since a > 0, @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field gives N_0 with a_n > a/2 > 0 for every n \ge N_0. The shifted sequence (a_{n+N_0})_n converges to a by @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b), and each of its terms is non-zero. By @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (d), applied to the constant sequence 1 and to (a_{n+N_0})_n, whose limit a is non-zero, 1/a_{n+N_0} 	o 1/a. (c) a_n = 1/(n + 1): every term is positive, and 1/a_n = n + 1 is not bounded in 
Q: for any M \in 
Q_{>0}, the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field gives n with M < n < n + 1 = \abs{1/a_n}. So it does not converge (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field). The hypothesis a > 0 of (b) fails here: a = 0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), by comparison with the constant sequence 0 (or by contradiction with \varepsilon = -a/2). - 3: (b), an index N_0 beyond which a_n is bounded away from 0, from a > 0. - 2: (b), 1/a_{n+N_0} 	o 1/a, either by the quotient law (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (d)) applied to the shift, with its convergence to a and a 
e 0 checked, or directly from \abs{1/a_{n+N_0} - 1/a} \le (2/a^2)\abs{a_{n+N_0} - a}, which uses a_{n+N_0} > a/2. - 2: (c), an example with the failure of convergence justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): concluding a > 0 in (a) from a_n > 0; applying the quotient law without checking that the limit is non-zero.

title: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content:
Cauchy Sequences Every convergence proof so far began with the limit in hand: to show a_n 	o a we estimated \abs{a_n - a}, and the limit laws of Section 4.4 compute a new limit only from limits already known. That is no help for the sequence of Chapter 2 that closes in on the gap at \sqrt 2 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2), whose terms 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots visibly settle down while no rational is available to be their limit. This section names a property that can be checked from the terms alone: eventually they are all close to each other. We prove the facts about it that Chapter 5 needs: convergent sequences have it, sequences with it are bounded and closed under sums and products, and, when such a sequence does not tend to 0, its terms eventually keep one sign and stay away from 0. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), sequences are indexed by 
N (@def-sequence-ordered-field), and \varepsilon ranges over F_{>0}. We use the absolute-value rules of @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field and the halving rules of @prp-ordered-field-halves without restating them, and write 2 for 1 + 1 in F. Terms that agree with one another A limit relates a sequence to a point of F; boundedness (@def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field) is a property of the sequence alone. We want a second property of the sequence alone, saying “the terms settle down” without saying where. In 
Q the Newton terms satisfy 17/12 - 577/408 = 1/408, and the later terms are closer still to one another (Section 4.6 proves it). The way to say “settle down” without a target is to compare terms with terms: however small a tolerance is named, from some index on, any two terms differ by less than it. The terms eventually agree with one another to within any tolerance. [Cauchy Sequence] A sequence (a_n)_{n \in 
N} in F is a Cauchy sequence in F (or Cauchy) if for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there exists N \in 
N such that \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for all m, n \in 
N with m \ge N and n \ge N. In symbols:  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} In words: the first quantifier says the tolerance is arbitrary and is named first; the second says a threshold exists, and since it comes after \varepsilon, it may depend on \varepsilon and on nothing else; the last two say that every pair of indices beyond the threshold, near or far apart, gives terms within \varepsilon of each other. Compared with @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, the point a has been replaced by a second index m. The tolerances are the elements of F_{>0}, so the field is part of the definition. For F = 
Q, the tolerances are rational, and “Cauchy in 
Q” is a statement about rationals only, as Chapter 5 needs. Since \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{a_n - a_m} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), the roles of m and n are symmetric, and there is nothing else to check for the definition to make sense. Negation. Moving 
eg inward quantifier by quantifier (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication) and reading 
eg(x < \varepsilon) as x \ge \varepsilon by (O1), “(a_n) is not Cauchy” reads \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists m, n \in 
N \ \  igl( m \ge N \wedge n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_m - a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . One tolerance is beaten beyond every threshold. Examples. A constant sequence. Let a_n = c for every n. Then \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon for all m, n, so N = 0 works for every \varepsilon. This degenerate case matters: Chapter 5 represents each rational c by its constant sequence. The reciprocals in 
Q. Let a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon. Let m, n \ge N. Then m + 1 > N and n + 1 > N, so 0 < 1/(m + 1) < 1/N and 0 < 1/(n + 1) < 1/N (@prp-reciprocal-order). Two elements x, y of (0, c) satisfy x - y < x < c and y - x < y < c, so \abs{x - y} < c by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d). Hence \abs{a_m - a_n} < 1/N < \varepsilon. The threshold depends on \varepsilon only: for \varepsilon = 1/100, N = 101 works. Sequences with a limit. By the first result of the next subsection, the convergent sequences of Section 4.3 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field) are all examples. The definition earns its keep on sequences with no limit available, which Section 4.6 supplies. Non-example by a minimal change. Change the constant sequence 1 at every odd index: let a_n = 1 for even n and a_n = 0 for odd n. The sequence is still bounded, by 1, and every two terms still differ by at most 1. What fails is “for every \varepsilon”: take \varepsilon = 1. Whatever N is offered, the indices N and N + 1 are both \ge N, one even and one odd, and their terms differ by 1 
ot< 1. So the negation above holds with \varepsilon = 1, m = N, n = N + 1. Why this definition. Each clause is there for a reason. - Every pair, not only neighbors. Asking only that \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} < \varepsilon for n \ge N is too weak: the example at the end of this section has consecutive differences tending to 0 and is not Cauchy. - The threshold after the tolerance. With the quantifiers swapped, “\exists N \  orall \varepsilon \  orall m, n \ge N”, the condition forces \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon, hence a_m = a_n for all m, n \ge N (the argument of @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field): only sequences that are eventually constant would qualify. - Tolerances from the field. Changing the set of tolerances changes the notion: in the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Section 4.2 there are more tolerances than in 
Q, among them 1/t, and Exercise C2 of Section 4.6 shows a sequence of rationals that passes every rational test and fails the test 1/t. The definition asks for one N that serves every pair m, n \ge N. A proof that checks only some pairs, say each n against n + 2, proves nothing: in the non-example above, a_{n+2} = a_n for every n, so those pairs pass every test, and the sequence still fails. Payoff. The tail-change principle extends at once. If a_n = b_n for every n \ge N_0 and (a_n) is Cauchy, then for \varepsilon \in F_{>0} and its threshold N for (a_n), every m, n \ge \max\{N, N_0\} give \abs{b_m - b_n} = \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon. So (b_n) is Cauchy, with thresholds \max\{N, N_0\}, as in @prp-tail-change-ordered-field. Convergent sequences are Cauchy, and Cauchy sequences are bounded The first result says the new property is no stronger than convergence: it is a necessary condition, one we can test without knowing the limit. [Convergent Sequences Are Cauchy] If a_n 	o a in F, then (a_n) is a Cauchy sequence in F. Two terms that are each within \varepsilon/2 of a are within \varepsilon of each other: insert the point a between them with the triangle inequality, and spend half the tolerance on each side. N, (k + 1)/(k + 2) = 1 - 1/(k + 2), so \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{1/(n + 2) - 1/(m + 2)}. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and use @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon to choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, both 1/(m + 2) and 1/(n + 2) lie in (0, 1/N), since m + 2, n + 2 > N (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Two elements of (0, 1/N) differ by less than 1/N (as in the examples after the definition), so \abs{a_m - a_n} < 1/N < \varepsilon. (b) Not Cauchy. Take \varepsilon = 1. For any N, the indices N and N + 1 have a_{N+1} = -a_N and \abs{a_N} = 1, so \abs{a_N - a_{N+1}} = \abs{2 a_N} = 2 \ge 1. (c) Not Cauchy. If it were, it would be bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field): \abs{n} \le M for some M \in 
Q_{>0} and every n. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n \in 
N with M < n = \abs{n}, a contradiction. (Archimedes is used here; in the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Section 4.2 the sequence (n \cdot 1) is bounded, by t, and the boundedness argument says nothing.) [B2] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be Cauchy sequences in F. Prove directly from @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field that (a_n - b_n) is Cauchy, naming the rule behind each step. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. By @prp-ordered-field-halves (b), \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0}. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, choose N_1 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_1; since (b_n) is Cauchy, choose N_2 with \abs{b_m - b_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\} (a maximum of two natural numbers; it depends only on \varepsilon). Let m, n \ge N; then m, n \ge N_1 and m, n \ge N_2. By the ring rules (@prp-ring-algebra), (a_m - b_m) - (a_n - b_n) = (a_m - a_n) +  igl(-(b_m - b_n) igr) . By the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) and \abs{-x} = \abs{x} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), \abs{(a_m - b_m) - (a_n - b_n)} \le \abs{a_m - a_n} + \abs{b_m - b_n} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , adding strict inequalities by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) and using @prp-ordered-field-halves (b) for the equality. Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, (a_n - b_n) is Cauchy. [B3] Let a_n = 2 - 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. Show that (a_n) is Cauchy and not null, and find c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N as in @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign. Then run the proof of the theorem with \varepsilon = 1 and the least admissible N_0: which c and N does it produce? Cauchy. (a_n) is the difference of the constant sequence 2 and the Cauchy sequence (1/(n + 1)) (examples after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field), so it is Cauchy by @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b). Not null, and c, N directly. For every n, 0 < 1/(n + 1) \le 1, so a_n \ge 1. Then \abs{a_n} \ge 1 for every n, so \varepsilon = 1 witnesses “not null”, and c = 1, N = 0 satisfy the first alternative. (Any smaller positive c, for instance c = 1/2, works with N = 0 as well.) The proof run. With \varepsilon = 1, the Cauchy condition is asked for tolerance 1/2. Here \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{1/(n + 1) - 1/(m + 1)}; for m, n \ge 1 both reciprocals lie in (0, 1/2], so the difference is below 1/2, while N_0 = 0 fails (m = 0, n = 1: 1 - 1/2 = 1/2 
ot< 1/2). So N_0 = 1. Take n_0 = 1: a_1 = 3/2 \ge 1, Case 1. The proof gives c = 1/2, N = 1: a_n > 3/2 - 1/2 = 1 \ge 1/2 for every n \ge 1. C. Going deeper [C1] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in F and (b_n) a sequence in F such that (a_n - b_n) is null. Prove that (b_n) is Cauchy. Here is the beginning of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. For all m, n \in 
N, the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), applied twice, gives \abs{b_n - b_m} \le \abs{b_n - a_n} + \abs{a_n - a_m} + \abs{a_m - b_m} . …” The move is split \varepsilon, now into three parts, one for each term on the right: two come from the null difference, one from the Cauchy condition. Completion. Let 3 \coloneqq 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \cdot 1_F; then 3 > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so \varepsilon/3 \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), and \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = 3 \cdot (\varepsilon/3) = \varepsilon: by (F5)–(F9), with 3 
e 0. Since (a_n - b_n) is null, choose N_1 with \abs{a_n - b_n} < \varepsilon/3 for every n \ge N_1. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, choose N_2 with \abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/3 for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, which depends only on \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, using \abs{b_n - a_n} = \abs{a_n - b_n} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), \abs{b_n - b_m} <  rac{\varepsilon}{3} +  rac{\varepsilon}{3} +  rac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon , adding three strict inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). So (b_n) is Cauchy. The split \varepsilon/4, \varepsilon/2, \varepsilon/4, which needs only halving, works as well. [C2: Exit check: the sign theorem] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in an ordered field F that is not null. Prove that there are c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. “Null” means  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon). Its negation (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation (a), @fd1:prp-negated-implication, then (O1)) is \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . Fix such an \varepsilon; it stays fixed from here on. Apply the Cauchy condition with the tolerance \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)): there is N_0 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_0. Apply the negation at N_0: there is n_0 \ge N_0 with \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon. By the definition of \abs{\cdot}, a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon or a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon. Let n \ge N_0. As n, n_0 \ge N_0, -\varepsilon/2 < a_n - a_{n_0} < \varepsilon/2 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). If a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon, then a_n > a_{n_0} - \varepsilon/2 \ge \varepsilon/2. If a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon, then a_n < a_{n_0} + \varepsilon/2 \le -\varepsilon/2. With c \coloneqq \varepsilon/2 and N \coloneqq N_0, the first case gives a_n \ge c and the second a_n \le -c, for every n \ge N. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: negates “null” correctly, with the quantifiers in order, and fixes one \varepsilon. - 2: applies the Cauchy condition with a fixed tolerance \delta such that 0 < \delta < \varepsilon (for example \delta = \varepsilon/2) to get N_0. - 2: obtains n_0 \ge N_0 with \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon from the negation applied at N_0. - 3: derives the one-signed bound (with c = \varepsilon - \delta) for every n \ge N_0, in both sign cases. - 1: names c and N and concludes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): n_0 chosen before N_0, or from the negation at a threshold unrelated to N_0; “\abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon for all large n” asserted from “not null” alone. A complete proof by contradiction (assume neither alternative holds for any c, N, and refute it at c = \varepsilon - \delta, N = N_0) maps onto the same 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1. [C3: Find the error] Here is an argument that the product of two Cauchy sequences (a_n), (b_n) in F is Cauchy. “For all m, n, \abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} \le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{b_n - b_m} + \abs{b_m} \, \abs{a_n - a_m}. Given \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, choose N such that \abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) and \abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m}) for all m, n \ge N. Then for m, n \ge N, \abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, and repair it. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (c). The argument does not prove it. The failing line is “choose N such that \abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) … for all m, n \ge N”. The tolerances \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) and \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m}) depend on n and m, which are introduced after N. The definition of Cauchy supplies a threshold for one fixed tolerance \varepsilon' \in F_{>0}, named before the threshold; here the threshold is asked to serve a tolerance that changes with the very indices it controls. This is a witness depending on variables introduced later, entry (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step. The step gets one N for all the tolerances \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) from their being positive. In 
Q take the Cauchy sequence b_n = 1/(n + 1), the never-zero (but unbounded) a_n = n + 1, and \varepsilon = 1. For any N, n = N and m = 2N + 1 give \abs{b_n - b_m} =  rac{1}{N + 1} -  rac{1}{2N + 2} =  rac{1}{2(N + 1)} =  rac{\varepsilon}{2\abs{a_n}} , which is not smaller: no N works. Inside the exercise (a_n) is Cauchy, hence bounded, but the argument never uses that; the repair does. Repair. Fix bounds first: by @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field, choose A, B \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le A and \abs{b_n} \le B for every n, before \varepsilon is named. Then the fixed tolerances \varepsilon/(2A) \le \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) (when a_n 
e 0) and \varepsilon/(2B) give thresholds N_1, N_2, and N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\} works, as in the proof of @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (c).

title: 4.6 A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit
content:
A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit Section 4.5 proved that every convergent sequence is Cauchy (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field). In 
Q the converse fails, and the failure sits exactly at the hole Chapter 2 found at \sqrt 2: no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). This section proves that the rational sequence of Chapter 2 that closes in on that hole (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2) is Cauchy in 
Q and converges to no rational. Chapter 5 starts from this sequence and builds the number it is aiming at. The section ends by listing what the chapter has not proved, and why, in 
Q, it could not have. Throughout this section the field is F = 
Q: every tolerance \varepsilon is a positive rational, and “converges” means “converges in 
Q” (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field). The sequence again Recall the sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. For s \in 
Q_{>0} let t(s) \coloneqq (s^2 + 2)/(2s), the average of s and 2/s; let x_0 \coloneqq 2 and x_{n+1} \coloneqq t(x_n), and let e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2, the amount by which x_n^2 overshoots 2. The first terms are x_0 = 2 , \quad x_1 =  rac{3}{2} , \quad x_2 =  rac{17}{12} , \quad x_3 =  rac{577}{408} , with e_0 = 2 , \quad e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} . Chapter 2 proved, for every n \in 
N, the following facts, and we cite them from @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2 without proving them again:  egin{aligned} &x_n \in 
Q_{>0} , \qquad e_n > 0 \ \ (	ext{so } x_n^2 > 2) , \ &e_{n+1} =  rac{e_n^2}{4x_n^2} \le  rac{e_n^2}{8} , \qquad x_n - x_{n+1} =  rac{e_n}{2x_n} > 0 . \end{aligned} The second line says two things. The overshoot is roughly squared at each step, so it shrinks very fast; and the terms decrease. Section 4.5 asks for more than decrease: any two late terms must be close. The overshoot e_n measures how close, because every later term lies between 2/x_n and x_n, an interval of length e_n/x_n. For the proof we do not need the true speed of e_n. A crude bound is enough, as long as it can be pushed below every rational tolerance: e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} \le  rac{1}{8} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} \le  rac{1}{12} ; that is, e_n \le 1/(4n) for n = 1, 2, 3, and the theorem proves it for every n \ge 1. Archimedes then turns 1/(4n) into anything below a given \varepsilon. The theorem [The Newton Sequence Is Cauchy with No Rational Limit] Let (x_n)_{n \in 
N} and e_n = x_n^2 - 2 be as in @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. Then x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N, x_m \le x_n whenever m \ge n, and e_n \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1. The sequence (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in 
Q, and there is no L \in 
Q with x_n 	o L. The first three clauses are part of the statement, rather than steps hidden in the proof, so that Chapter 5 can cite them. Cauchy. For m \ge n, the later term x_m lies below x_n, since the terms decrease, and above 2/x_n, since x_m > 2/x_m \ge 2/x_n. So 0 \le x_n - x_m \le x_n - 2/x_n = e_n/x_n \le e_n. With e_n \le 1/(4n), every two terms beyond N differ by at most 1/(4N), and Archimedes makes 1/N smaller than any rational \varepsilon. No rational limit. Locate the missing limit: suppose x_n 	o L in 
Q and find out what L would have to satisfy. The limit laws turn x_n 	o L into x_n^2 	o L^2. But x_n^2 = 2 + e_n 	o 2, because e_n is squeezed between 0 and 1/(4n). Limits are unique, so L^2 = 2, and no rational satisfies that. Before reading on: which law turns x_n 	o L into x_n^2 	o L^2, and applied to which two sequences? We prove six facts, then the two claims. Induction is @fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b). (i), (ii), (iv) in part: cited. By @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, for every n \in 
N: (i) x_n \in 
Q_{>0}, e_n > 0 and x_n^2 > 2; (ii) e_{n+1} = e_n^2/(4x_n^2) \le e_n^2/8; and x_{n+1} < x_n. (iii) x_n > 1. Suppose x_n \le 1. Since x_n > 0 by (i), either x_n < 1, and then x_n^2 < 1^2 = 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), or x_n = 1 and x_n^2 = 1. Either way x_n^2 \le 1 < 2, against x_n^2 > 2 and (O1). So x_n > 1, by totality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). (iv) x_m \le x_n for m \ge n. Fix n. By induction on k, x_{n+k} \le x_n for every k \in 
N: the base P(0) is x_n \le x_n, and if x_{n+k} \le x_n, then x_{n+k+1} < x_{n+k} \le x_n. Every m \ge n in 
N is n + k for some k \in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)), so x_m \le x_n. (v) e_n \le 1/(4n) for n \ge 1. By induction on k, for P(k): e_{k+1} \le 1/(4(k + 1)). Base P(0): e_1 = 1/4. Step: assume P(k), and let n \coloneqq k + 1 \ge 1, so 0 < e_n \le 1/(4n) \le 1/4 (by (i), P(k), and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) with 4 \le 4n). Then, by (ii) and @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (with the factors 0 \le e_n/8 \le e_n/8 and 0 \le e_n \le 1/4, then 0 \le 1/32 \le 1/32 and 0 \le e_n \le 1/(4n)), e_{n+1} \le  rac{e_n \cdot e_n}{8} \le  rac{e_n}{8} \cdot  rac{1}{4} =  rac{e_n}{32} \le  rac{1}{128 n} \le  rac{1}{4(n + 1)} , where the last step is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), since 0 < 4(n + 1) = 4n + 4 \le 128 n for n \ge 1 (as 4 \le 124 n). This is P(k + 1). (vi) For m \ge n \ge 1: 0 \le x_n - x_m \le 1/(4n). By (iv), x_m \le x_n, so x_n - x_m \ge 0. By (i), x_m^2 > 2; multiplying by 1/x_m > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives x_m > 2/x_m. From 0 < x_m \le x_n, @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives 1/x_n \le 1/x_m, so 2/x_n \le 2/x_m < x_m (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), with 0 \le 2 \le 2). Hence x_n - x_m \le x_n -  rac{2}{x_n} =  rac{x_n^2 - 2}{x_n} =  rac{e_n}{x_n} \le e_n \le  rac{1}{4n} . Here e_n/x_n \le e_n because 0 < 1 < x_n by (iii), so 1/x_n < 1 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)), and e_n > 0; the last step is (v). Cauchy. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon; it depends only on \varepsilon. Let m, n \ge N, and let k \coloneqq \min\{m, n\} \ge N \ge 1 and l \coloneqq \max\{m, n\}. By (vi) with the pair l \ge k, \abs{x_m - x_n} = x_k - x_l \le  rac{1}{4k} \le  rac{1}{4N} \le  rac{1}{N} < \varepsilon , where 1/(4k) \le 1/(4N) \le 1/N is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) applied to N \le 4N \le 4k. So (x_n) is Cauchy in 
Q. No rational limit. Suppose, for a contradiction, that x_n 	o L for some L \in 
Q. By the product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c), applied with both sequences equal to (x_n), x_n^2 	o L^2. Next, (e_n) is null. We use the squeeze, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c), with N_0 = 1, the lower sequence constantly 0 (which tends to 0) and the upper sequence (1/(n + 1))_{n \in 
N}. The upper sequence is defined for every n \in 
N, and it is null in 
Q by @prp-archimedean-reciprocal, as in @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field. For n \ge 1 we have n + 1 \le 4n (as 1 \le 3n), so by (i), (v) and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), 0 < e_n \le  rac{1}{4n} \le  rac{1}{n + 1} \qquad (n \ge 1) . (At n = 0 the middle term is undefined and e_0 = 2; the squeeze needs the inequalities only from N_0 = 1 on.) So e_n 	o 0. Then x_n^2 = 2 + e_n for every n, and the sum law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a), with the constant sequence 2 gives x_n^2 	o 2 + 0 = 2. The sequence (x_n^2) therefore tends to L^2 and to 2, and by @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field, L^2 = 2. This contradicts @thm-no-rational-square-two. Hence no L \in 
Q has x_n 	o L. The answer to the prompt: the product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c), applied to a_n = b_n = x_n. It is the only step that uses the hypothesis x_n 	o L; the rest of the second half is about e_n, which we control without any limit, and then uniqueness compares the two limits of (x_n^2). Archimedes is used twice, both times in 
Q, where @thm-rationals-archimedean provides it: for the Cauchy threshold, through @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon, and for the upper sequence (1/(n + 1)) of the squeeze, through @prp-archimedean-reciprocal. The sequence is Cauchy and not null, since \abs{x_n} = x_n > 1 for every n, so @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign applies to it. Its proof, run with \varepsilon = 1, gives c = 1/2; directly, x_n \ge 1 for every n. Chapter 5 turns the class of (x_n) into a positive real number whose square is 2. “Cauchy” does not mean “convergent to a limit we have not named yet”. In 
Q there is nothing to name: by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, the statement “every Cauchy sequence of rationals converges in 
Q” is false, not merely unproved. A proof that says “(a_n) is Cauchy, so let a be its limit” is wrong in 
Q, whatever it goes on to do. Give an upper bound and a positive lower bound for the terms x_n in 
Q, with reasons. Upper bound 2: x_n \le x_0 = 2 for every n, by clause (iv) of the proof with n = 0. Lower bound 1: x_n > 1 for every n, by (iii). The upper bound is attained, at x_0; the lower bound 1 is crude (every term also exceeds 2/x_1 = 4/3, by the argument of (vi), and x_0 = 2 > 4/3), but any positive lower bound answers the question. What this chapter did not prove Looking back over the chapter, three familiar tools of real analysis are absent, and their absence is checkable. - No result asserts convergence without naming the limit. Each result of the chapter that concludes a_n 	o a has a in its hypotheses or in its statement: the examples of Section 4.3 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field), the tail-change rules (@prp-tail-change-ordered-field), the limit laws (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field) and the squeeze (@prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c)). The results of Section 4.5, about sequences whose limit is unknown, conclude “Cauchy”, “bounded”, or a sign, never “convergent”. - No supremum. No result uses the supremum of a subset of F (@fd2:def-order-supremum), so nothing here rests on a least upper bound property. - No monotone convergence theorem, and no Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem. Neither is stated or used. In 
Q each of the three would fail. A least upper bound property fails by Section 2.6: the set of rationals with square below 2 is non-empty and bounded above, with no rational supremum. A monotone convergence theorem fails by the sequence of this section: (x_n) is decreasing (clause (iv) of the proof), bounded (the Quick check above) and Cauchy, and it has no limit in 
Q. And so does Bolzano–Weierstrass, which would give the bounded sequence (x_n) a subsequence converging in 
Q. Indeed, let n_0 < n_1 < n_2 < \cdots be indices and suppose x_{n_k} 	o L \in 
Q as k 	o \infty. By induction, n_k \ge k for every k (if n_k \ge k, then n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k, so n_{k+1} \ge k + 1). So for k \ge 1, 0 < e_{n_k} \le 1/(4n_k) \le 1/(4k) \le 1/(k + 1), and the argument of the proof, run on the sequence (x_{n_k})_{k \in 
N}, gives L^2 = 2 again. The reader who knows real analysis will have met all three as theorems about 
R. They are true there because of an axiom about 
R, completeness, that no ordered field satisfies automatically, and this chapter never assumed it. Chapter 5 builds, from Cauchy sequences of rationals, a field in which every Cauchy sequence converges, and proves that in it every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum: a complete ordered field. Chapter 6 proves that any two complete ordered fields are copies of each other, by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes the axioms of a complete ordered field as its starting point, and its Chapter 2 revisits this chapter’s sequences, now in 
R. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit. 1. Which result gives x_n^2 	o L^2 from x_n 	o L, applied to which two sequences? 2. Why does the proof need the bound e_n \le 1/(4n), and not only “e_n > 0 and (e_n) is decreasing”? 3. Where is the Archimedean property used? 4. Check fact (vi) at n = 2, m = 3: compute x_2 - x_3 and compare it with e_2/x_2, e_2 and 1/(4 \cdot 2). 5. State the idea of the proof that (x_n) has no rational limit, in two sentences. (a) The product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c), with a_n = b_n = x_n and a = b = L. (b) The proof must show that (e_n) is null, that is, below every rational \varepsilon from some index on. A sequence can be positive and decreasing without being null: 1 + 1/(n + 1) decreases and stays above 1. The bound 1/(4n) \le 1/(n + 1) ties e_n to a sequence known to be null, and the same bound gives the Cauchy threshold. (c) Twice: for the Cauchy threshold, by @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon (an N with 1/N < \varepsilon); and for the upper sequence (1/(n + 1)) of the squeeze, null by @prp-archimedean-reciprocal. (d) x_2 - x_3 = 17/12 - 577/408 = (17 \cdot 34 - 577)/408 = (578 - 577)/408 = 1/408. Next, e_2/x_2 = (1/144) \cdot (12/17) = 1/204. So  rac{1}{408} \le  rac{1}{204} \le  rac{1}{144} \le  rac{1}{8} , which is the chain x_2 - x_3 \le e_2/x_2 \le e_2 \le 1/(4 \cdot 2) of (vi). (e) A rational limit L of (x_n) would make x_n^2 tend to L^2, by the product law. But x_n^2 = 2 + e_n tends to 2, since e_n is squeezed to 0, so uniqueness of limits gives L^2 = 2, which no rational satisfies. B. Practice [B1] With (x_n) as in @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, prove that the sequence (x_n - 2/x_n) is null in 
Q, that (2/x_n) is Cauchy in 
Q, and that (2/x_n) has no limit in 
Q. Null. For every n, x_n - 2/x_n = (x_n^2 - 2)/x_n = e_n/x_n, and as in step (vi) of the proof, 0 < e_n/x_n \le e_n \le 1/(4n) \le 1/(n + 1) for n \ge 1 (using x_n > 1 and e_n \le 1/(4n) from the theorem, and e_n > 0 from @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2 (i)). By the squeeze (@prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c)) with N_0 = 1, lower sequence 0 and upper sequence (1/(n + 1)), null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field), x_n - 2/x_n 	o 0. Cauchy. 2/x_n = x_n - (x_n - 2/x_n) is the difference of a Cauchy sequence (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit) and a null one, which is Cauchy by @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a); so it is Cauchy by @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b). No rational limit. Suppose 2/x_n 	o L \in 
Q. Then x_n = 2/x_n + (x_n - 2/x_n) 	o L + 0 = L by the sum law (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a)), against @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit. The terms 2/x_n approach the gap from below (2/x_n < x_m for all m, and (2/x_n)^2 = 4/x_n^2 < 2), while the x_n approach it from above; their differences are null, so in Chapter 5 the two sequences will represent the same real number. [B2] Let (H_n) be the sequence of @exm-consecutive-differences-not-cauchy: H_0 = 0 and H_{n+1} = H_n + 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. Prove that H_{2^k} \ge 1 + k/2 for every k \in 
N, and hence that (H_n) is not bounded. The powers 2^k of the natural number 2 are those of Section 1.6 (defined just before @prp-omega-powers-parity by @thm-omega-recursion), with 2^0 = 1 and 2^{k+1} = 2^k \cdot 2 = 2^k + 2^k. We use @fd1:ax-induction on k. Base P(0): H_{2^0} = H_1 = H_0 + 1/1 = 1 \ge 1 + 0/2. Step: assume H_{2^k} \ge 1 + k/2. The example shows H_{2n} - H_n \ge 1/2 for every n \ge 1; with n = 2^k \ge 1 (by induction, 2^k \ge 1) it gives H_{2^{k+1}} \ge H_{2^k} + 1/2 \ge 1 + (k + 1)/2. Not bounded. Let M \in 
Q_{>0}. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is k \in 
N with 2M < k. Then H_{2^k} \ge 1 + k/2 > M, and H_{2^k} > 0, so \abs{H_{2^k}} > M. No M bounds the sequence. So (H_n) is not Cauchy for a second reason: a Cauchy sequence is bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: a Cauchy sequence with no rational limit] Let y_0 \coloneqq 2 and y_{n+1} \coloneqq (y_n^2 + 3)/(2y_n), a sequence in 
Q_{>0}, and let d_n \coloneqq y_n^2 - 3. 1. Prove that no rational number squares to 3. 2. Prove that (y_n) is a Cauchy sequence in 
Q and that it converges to no element of 
Q. [Hint 1] For (b), copy facts (i)–(vi) of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit with 3 in place of 2. Since only the case 2 was proved in Chapter 2, prove the analogues of (i), (ii) and the decrease yourself, as @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2 does for 2. For (a), run the descent of @thm-no-rational-square-two. [Hint 2] First verify the identities d_{n+1} = d_n^2/(4y_n^2) and y_n - y_{n+1} = d_n/(2y_n) by clearing denominators. In the descent for (a), from p^2 = 3q^2 show q < p < 2q, and try p' \coloneqq 3q - p, q' \coloneqq p - q. (a) Suppose x \in 
Q with x^2 = 3. Then x 
e 0, and replacing x by -x if needed, x > 0; write x = a/b with a, b \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)), so a^2 = 3b^2. The set of q \in 
Z_{>0} for which some p \in 
Z_{>0} has p^2 = 3q^2 contains b and is bounded below by 0, so it has a least element q (@prp-integer-least-element); fix such a p. q < p: if p \le q, then p^2 \le q^2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), or equality), so 3q^2 \le q^2 and 2q^2 \le 0, against 2q^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (O4)). p < 2q: if 2q \le p, then 4q^2 \le p^2 = 3q^2, so q^2 \le 0, against q^2 > 0. By totality, q < p < 2q. Let p' \coloneqq 3q - p and q' \coloneqq p - q. Then q' > 0 since q < p; q' < q since p < 2q; and p' > 0 since p < 2q < 3q. Expanding,  egin{aligned} p'^2 - 3q'^2 &= (9q^2 - 6pq + p^2) - (3p^2 - 6pq + 3q^2) \ &= 6q^2 - 2p^2 = 2(3q^2 - p^2) = 0 . \end{aligned} So q' is an admissible denominator smaller than q, a contradiction. No rational squares to 3. (b) Positivity and the two identities. For s \in 
Q_{>0}, (s^2 + 3)/(2s) \in 
Q_{>0} (s^2 + 3 > 0, 2s > 0, @prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), so the recursion (@fd2:thm-recursion, read on \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b)) defines (y_n) in 
Q_{>0}. With u(s) \coloneqq (s^2 + 3)/(2s), clearing the non-zero denominators 4s^2 and 2s, u(s)^2 - 3 =  rac{(s^2 + 3)^2 - 12 s^2}{4s^2} =  rac{(s^2 - 3)^2}{4s^2} , \qquad s - u(s) =  rac{s^2 - 3}{2s} . So d_{n+1} = d_n^2/(4y_n^2) and y_n - y_{n+1} = d_n/(2y_n). By induction, d_n > 0: d_0 = 1, and d_n > 0 gives d_n^2 > 0, so d_{n+1} > 0. Hence y_n^2 > 3, 4y_n^2 > 12, and d_{n+1} \le d_n^2/12 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Also y_n - y_{n+1} > 0. Values. y_1 = 7/4, y_2 = 97/56; d_0 = 1, d_1 = 49/16 - 3 = 1/16, d_2 = 9409/3136 - 3 = 1/3136, and indeed d_2 = (1/16)^2/(4 \cdot 49/16) = 1/3136. Monotone, and y_n > 1. As in (iii) and (iv): y_n > 1, since 0 < y_n \le 1 would give y_n^2 \le 1 < 3; and y_m \le y_n for m \ge n, by induction from y_{n+1} < y_n. A bound on d_n. d_n \le 1/(16n) for n \ge 1, by induction: d_1 = 1/16; if 0 < d_n \le 1/(16n) \le 1/16, then d_{n+1} \le d_n \cdot d_n/12 \le d_n/192 \le 1/(3072 n) \le 1/(16(n + 1)), since 16n + 16 \le 3072 n for n \ge 1. Close terms. For m \ge n \ge 1: y_m \le y_n, and y_m > 3/y_m \ge 3/y_n, so 0 \le y_n - y_m \le y_n -  rac{3}{y_n} =  rac{d_n}{y_n} \le d_n \le  rac{1}{16 n} , using y_n > 1. Cauchy. Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, with k \coloneqq \min\{m, n\} \ge N, \abs{y_m - y_n} \le 1/(16k) \le 1/N < \varepsilon. No rational limit. If y_n 	o L \in 
Q, then y_n^2 	o L^2 (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c)). For n \ge 1, 0 < d_n \le 1/(16n) \le 1/(n + 1), so d_n 	o 0 by the squeeze (@prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c), with N_0 = 1 and the null upper sequence (1/(n + 1))), and y_n^2 = 3 + d_n 	o 3 (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a)). By @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field, L^2 = 3, against (a). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a), a descent with a least denominator (@prp-integer-least-element), with the inequalities q < p < 2q and the positivity of p', q' justified (another correct route, such as divisibility by 3 with a least denominator, earns the same). - 1: positivity of y_n and d_n, and the recursion identity for d_{n+1}. - 2: a comparison of y_n and y_m for m \ge n: monotonicity together with y_m \ge 3/y_n, or (factorization route, as in R4) \abs{y_n - y_m} = \abs{d_n - d_m}/(y_n + y_m) with y_n + y_m > 2, since y_n > 1 follows from y_n^2 > 3. - 2: an explicit bound on d_n (or on y_n - y_m) tending to 0, with Archimedes giving N for each rational \varepsilon. - 1: Cauchy concluded with the quantifiers in order. - 2: no rational limit, by the product law, uniqueness of limits and (a). Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming that \sqrt 3 exists in 
Q or in a larger field and comparing with it; invoking a monotone convergence theorem. A route by factorization as in R4 earns the next 2 for showing d_n 	o 0 (by an explicit bound with Archimedes, or by the squeeze), and the 1 for concluding that (d_n) is Cauchy by @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field and transferring this to (y_n) with the quantifiers in order. A route through the steps y_n - y_{n+1} and a geometric bound earns the middle 2 + 1 only if the sum of the steps from n to m is bounded explicitly, independently of m (the example at the end of Section 4.5 shows why). [C2: Cauchy depends on the field] In the ordered field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field, consider the sequence a_n \coloneqq 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1), whose terms are the rationals 1/(n + 1). Explain why (a_n) is not a Cauchy sequence in 
Q(t), although it is Cauchy in 
Q. In 
Q, (1/(n + 1)) is Cauchy (Section 4.5, the examples after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field). In 
Q(t), take the tolerance \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/t, which is positive (the example shows 0 < 1/t). Let N \in 
N, and take m \coloneqq N, n \coloneqq N + 1. Then \abs{a_m - a_n} =  rac{1}{N + 1} -  rac{1}{N + 2} =  rac{1}{(N + 1)(N + 2)} , by @lem-field-fraction-rules (c), a positive rational. The natural number k \coloneqq (N + 1)(N + 2) satisfies k \cdot 1 < t, because t - k \cdot 1 has leading coefficient 1 > 0 (@exm-rational-function-field). Since 0 < k \cdot 1 < t, @prp-reciprocal-order (b) gives 1/t < 1/(k \cdot 1) = \abs{a_m - a_n}. So for the tolerance 1/t no threshold N works, and (a_n) is not Cauchy in 
Q(t). The terms are the same in both fields; what changed is the set of tolerances. 
Q(t) has the positive element 1/t, below every positive rational, and the rational differences 1/((N + 1)(N + 2)) never get below it. Being Cauchy is a property of a sequence in a field, not of its terms alone. (The example 
Q(t) uses school polynomial algebra; nothing else in the book depends on this exercise.) R. Review [R1] Let \sC be the set of Cauchy sequences in 
Q, and for (a_n), (b_n) \in \sC write (a_n) \sim (b_n) if (a_n - b_n) is null. Prove that \sim is an equivalence relation on \sC, and that [(a_n)] + [(b_n)] \coloneqq [(a_n + b_n)] is a well-defined operation on the quotient set \sC/{\sim}. The tool is Chapter 3’s quotient of a commutative ring by an ideal (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal). Let \sN be the set of null sequences in 
Q. We show that \sC is a commutative ring, that \sN is an ideal of it, and that \sim is the relation \sim_{\sN}. \sC is a commutative ring (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), with termwise + and \cdot. By @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field, \sC contains the constant sequences 0 and 1 by (a), and it is closed under termwise sums and negatives by (b) and under termwise products by (c); so termwise + and \cdot are functions \sC 	imes \sC 	o \sC. Each of (F1)–(F7) and (F9), with the constant 0 as zero, the constant 1 as one and (-a_n) as the negative of (a_n), is an equation between sequences, and it holds at every index n because it holds in 
Q (@thm-rationals-ordered-field). Two sequences that agree at every index are equal, so each clause holds in \sC. \sN is an ideal of \sC (@def-ideal-commutative-ring). First, \sN \subseteq \sC by @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a). (I1): the constant sequence 0 tends to 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)). (I2): if (y_n), (z_n) \in \sN, then y_n + z_n 	o 0 + 0 = 0 by @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a). (I3): let (z_n) \in \sN and (r_n) \in \sC. By @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field there is M \in 
Q_{>0} with \abs{r_n} \le M for every n, so (z_n r_n) is null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, and r_n z_n = z_n r_n by (F6) in 
Q. So (r_n z_n) \in \sN. The relation is \sim_{\sN}. The difference (a_n) - (b_n) in \sC is the sequence (a_n - b_n), so (a_n) \sim (b_n) holds exactly when (a_n) - (b_n) \in \sN. Thus \sim is \sim_{\sN} and \sC/{\sim} is \sC/\sN. By @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (a), \sim is an equivalence relation, and by (b), [(a_n)] + [(b_n)] \coloneqq [(a_n + b_n)] is well defined; so is the product [(a_n)] \cdot [(b_n)] \coloneqq [(a_n b_n)], and by (c) \sC/\sN is a commutative ring. Chapter 3 proved (b) by Chapter 2’s lemma on operations on classes (@thm-well-defined-on-classes), the method by which 
Z and 
Q were built; here it runs on sequences. Chapter 5 builds 
R as this quotient, and nothing in this exercise is used there. [R2] Let F be an ordered field. Define r_0 \coloneqq 1 and r_{n+1} \coloneqq r_n/2 + 1 for n \in 
N. Prove that 1 \le r_n < 2 and r_n < r_{n+1} for every n \in 
N. The tools are definition by recursion and proof by induction (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd1:ax-induction), both read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b). Here 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), so 2 
e 0 and x/2 is defined for every x \in F. The recursion theorem with X = F, starting value 1 and rule g(n, x) \coloneqq x/2 + 1 gives exactly one sequence (r_n) in F satisfying the two equations. Its first terms are r_1 = 3/2 and r_2 = 7/4. The bounds. We prove P(n): “1 \le r_n < 2” by induction on n. Base P(0): r_0 = 1, and 1 = 2/2 < 2 by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b) with \varepsilon = 2. Step: assume 1 \le r_n < 2. Then r_n > 0, so r_n/2 > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). Multiplying r_n < 2 by 1/2 > 0 gives r_n/2 < 2/2 = 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). Adding 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), 1 = 0 + 1 <  rac{r_n}{2} + 1 = r_{n+1} < 1 + 1 = 2 . So 1 \le r_{n+1} < 2, which is P(n + 1). The increase. Let n \in 
N. By P(n), r_n > 0, so r_n = r_n/2 + r_n/2 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b) with \varepsilon = r_n), and r_n/2 < 1 as in the step. Hence r_{n+1} - r_n = \Bigl( rac{r_n}{2} + 1\Bigr) - \Bigl( rac{r_n}{2} +  rac{r_n}{2}\Bigr) = 1 -  rac{r_n}{2} > 0 , and r_n < r_{n+1} by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). [R3] Say that a sequence (a_n) in an ordered field F eventually keeps one sign if there are c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. Write this in symbols, and form its negation by moving 
eg inward one law at a time, naming each law. Then use the negation to show that a_n \coloneqq (-1)^n/(n + 1) in 
Q does not eventually keep one sign, and explain why this does not contradict the theorem that a Cauchy sequence that is not null eventually keeps one sign. “(a_n) eventually keeps one sign” is \exists c \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \ \Bigl(  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N 	o a_n \ge c) \ \vee \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N 	o a_n \le -c) \Bigr) . Negating, with the laws for bounded quantifiers (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation), De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan) and negated implication (@fd1:prp-negated-implication): 1.  orall c \in F_{>0} \ 
eg \exists N \in 
N \ (\dots), by (b) of the bounded law; 2.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \ 
eg  igl(  orall n \, (\dots) \vee  orall n \, (\dots)  igr), by (b) again; 3.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( 
eg  orall n \, (\dots) \wedge 
eg  orall n \, (\dots)  igr), by De Morgan (a) (and (b) for the converse); 4.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( \exists n \in 
N \ 
eg (n \ge N 	o a_n \ge c) \wedge \exists n \in 
N \ 
eg (n \ge N 	o a_n \le -c)  igr), by (a) of the bounded law, twice; 5.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( \exists n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \wedge 
eg (a_n \ge c)) \wedge \exists n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \wedge 
eg (a_n \le -c))  igr), by @fd1:prp-negated-implication, twice; 6. and 
eg (a_n \ge c) is a_n < c, 
eg (a_n \le -c) is a_n > -c, by totality (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). (The \vdash directions of steps 4 and 5 use ulename{RAA}, as @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication record.) So the negation says: for every c \in F_{>0} and every N \in 
N, some n \ge N has a_n < c, and some n \ge N has a_n > -c. The example. Here (-1)^n is the power in
