Q (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field), so (-1)^{n+1} = -(-1)^n (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), and by induction (-1)^n is 1 or -1 for every n. Let c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N. Of (-1)^N and (-1)^{N+1} = -(-1)^N, one is 1 and the other -1; call p the index among N, N + 1 with (-1)^p = 1, and q the other. Both are \ge N, and 1/(p + 1) > 0, 1/(q + 1) > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). So a_q = -1/(q + 1) < 0 < c and a_p = 1/(p + 1) > 0 > -c (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). This is the negation, so (a_n) does not eventually keep one sign. No contradiction. \abs{a_n} = \abs{(-1)^n} \cdot \abs{1/(n + 1)} = 1/(n + 1) (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), and (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). So for each \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} the threshold that serves (1/(n + 1)) gives \abs{a_n - 0} < \varepsilon: the sequence (a_n) is null. It is Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), but the theorem (@thm-cauchy-not-null-sign) assumes “not null”, so it says nothing about (a_n). The example shows that this hypothesis cannot be dropped. [R4] Let (a_n) be a sequence in 
Q with a_n > 0 for every n and a_n^2 	o 2 in 
Q. Is (a_n) a Cauchy sequence in 
Q? Prove your answer. Yes. The tool is the factorization a_n^2 - a_m^2 = (a_n - a_m)(a_n + a_m), which turns closeness of the squares into closeness of the terms once the factor a_n + a_m is bounded below by a positive constant. A lower bound. By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field applied to a_n^2 	o 2 > 0, there is N_0 with a_n^2 > 2/2 = 1 for every n \ge N_0. For such n, a_n > 1: otherwise 0 < a_n \le 1 would give a_n^2 \le 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). So a_n + a_m > 2 for m, n \ge N_0, and 1/(a_n + a_m) < 1/2 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). The estimate. For m, n \ge N_0, dividing the factorization by a_n + a_m 
e 0, \abs{a_n - a_m} =  rac{\abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2}}{a_n + a_m} \le  rac{\abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2}}{2} . The sequence (a_n^2) converges, so it is Cauchy (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field). Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, choose N_1 with \abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2} < 2\varepsilon for all m, n \ge N_1, and let N \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1\}. For m, n \ge N, \abs{a_n - a_m} < 2\varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. So (a_n) is Cauchy. Why the look-alike tools fail. The limit laws would need a limit of (a_n), and there is none in 
Q: a_n 	o L would give a_n^2 	o L^2, so L^2 = 2, against @thm-no-rational-square-two. @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign and @prp-cauchy-reciprocal-ordered-field presuppose that (a_n) is Cauchy, which is what is asked. The Newton sequence of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit is one such (a_n), so the question is not empty.

title: Constructing the Real Numbers from Cauchy Sequences
content:
Constructing the Real Numbers from Cauchy Sequences Chapter 4 ended at a hole. The Newton sequence 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots of Chapter 2 is Cauchy in 
Q, and no rational is its limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its terms crowd around a place where 
Q has no element. This chapter does not search for a number in the hole. It takes the sequence itself as the number. Many sequences crowd around the same hole: the decimal truncations 1, 7/5, 141/100, \dots approach it from below and never meet the Newton sequence. So two Cauchy sequences of rationals must count as one number when their difference dies out. That is an equivalence relation, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 knows what to do with one: take its classes. A real number is a Cauchy sequence of rationals, up to a null difference. The chapter defines the sum, product and order of these classes on representatives and proves each well defined. The sum and product come from the quotient of a ring by an ideal of Chapter 3. The order needs a new idea, because comparing terms does not compare classes. The chapter then places 
Q inside the new field, proves it Archimedean with 
Q dense in it, and finds there a positive number whose square is 2. Until the field exists, every tolerance, margin and threshold is rational, so nothing about real numbers is assumed on the way to building them. Then come the two forms of completeness. Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. The proof builds the limit from rationals by a rule, so it uses no axiom of choice, and Section 5.5 shows where choice would have entered. Every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound. This is proved by bisection in any ordered field that is Archimedean and Cauchy-complete, and one line of that proof needs Archimedes. So the constructed 
R is a complete ordered field, and this ends the construction of the number systems that began with the axioms of set theory in Chapter 1. Chapter 6 shows that any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic, and the optional Chapter 7 builds one from Dedekind cuts. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes the axioms of a complete ordered field as its starting point, and this chapter gives them a model. Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 builds the complex numbers on this 
R. Metric and Topological Spaces, Chapter 2 repeats the construction for an arbitrary metric space. What you need. Chapters 2 and 4 above all; Section 3.4 for one step of Section 5.2; a few facts about 
N from Chapter 1; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Section 2.5; and Logic and Proof, Chapters 2–5, chiefly Chapter 4. From Chapter 4, nearly all of it, applied with F = 
Q and, once Section 5.3 has made 
R an ordered field, with F = 
R. This covers the rules of an ordered field and the absolute value (@prp-ordered-field-halves, @lem-field-fraction-rules, @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), and powers and the copy of 
Q in an ordered field (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field, @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). It covers the Archimedean property, its reciprocal form, the integer part and density (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, @prp-archimedean-reciprocal, @prp-integer-part-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). It covers sequences, limits and null sequences (@def-sequence-ordered-field, @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, @def-null-sequence-ordered-field, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field, @prp-tail-change-ordered-field, @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field, @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field, @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field, @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean, @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field, @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field). It covers Cauchy sequences, with the sign theorem and its companions (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field, @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field, @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field, @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field, @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign, @prp-sign-stable-ordered-field, @prp-cauchy-reciprocal-ordered-field). And it covers the Newton sequence with no rational limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). The non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) (@exm-rational-function-field) appears only in prose, a warning and an exercise; no proof cites it. From Chapter 2: commutative rings, fields and ordered fields (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-reciprocal-order); the order from a positive set (@prp-order-from-positives), used here a third time; the lemma on rules on classes (@thm-well-defined-on-classes); least elements and discreteness in 
Z (@prp-integer-least-element, @thm-integers-ordered-ring); the copies of 
N in 
Z and of 
Z in 
Q (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals); 
Q as an Archimedean ordered field (@thm-rationals-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-archimedean, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon, @prp-rational-integer-part); and the Newton sequence and the gaps (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, @thm-no-rational-square-two, @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). Review exercise R2 returns to the fractions of Sections 2.4 and 2.5 (@def-rationals-as-classes, @def-rational-order). From Section 3.4: ideals and the quotient ring (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal), which give Section 5.2 the ring laws of 
R; exercise C2 of Section 5.2 mentions 
Z/4
Z (@def-integers-mod-n-ring). From Chapter 1: the citing rule (@cor-omega-identification), by which induction and recursion apply to 
N, and the arithmetic and order of 
N (@def-omega-arithmetic, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, @thm-omega-order, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic), in Sections 5.1 and 5.6. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5: equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition), with the two examples that showed what “well defined” means (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic, @fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map). Further from that volume: functions and their equality (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality), from its Chapter 1; the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion), from its Section 2.3; and upper bounds and suprema (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum), from its Section 2.6. From its Chapter 3, the axiom of choice (@fd2:ax-choice) is named only to mark the step that Section 5.5 avoids. Review exercise R3 uses countability (@fd2:thm-countable-characterizations, @fd2:thm-binary-sequences-uncountable, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective), and names @fd2:prp-card-le-surjection, from its Section 3.5, only as the route not taken, since its (\Leftarrow) direction uses choice. From Logic and Proof: the negation laws of its Chapter 4 (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication) and its rule ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential), which fixes one object at a time and is contrasted with choice. Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 gives the rules ulename{
eg I} and ulename{RAA} (@fd1:def-rules-negation, @fd1:def-rule-raa), used in Section 5.3, and its Chapter 3 gives induction (@fd1:ax-induction). Logic and Proof, Chapter 5’s catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue) serves exercise C2 of Section 5.3. Nothing from Analysis on the Real Line is used, and no fact about 
R is assumed. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - Sequences That Should Converge. The Newton sequence and the decimal truncations, defined inside 
Q by powers of ten and a largest-integer argument in 
Z, as two sequences aimed at one hole; the set \sC of Cauchy sequences of rationals; the relation a \sim b when a - b is null, proved an equivalence relation; the truncations equivalent to the Newton sequence; and finite changes and shifts, which never change the class. - The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic. 
R defined as the quotient set \sC/{\sim}; sum, product and negative defined on representatives and proved well defined, the product through “null times bounded is null”; the null sequences as an ideal of \sC, so that Chapter 3’s quotient theorem makes 
R a commutative ring; and inverses through the sign theorem of Chapter 4, after the failed termwise reciprocal. - Positive Classes and the Order. Why termwise comparison defines no order on classes; positive sequences, eventually above a fixed rational margin, and why the margin is named before the index; positivity as a property of the class; the positive classes satisfying Chapter 2’s recipe, which makes 
R an ordered field; termwise \le passing to classes, which strict < does not; and the absolute value computed on representatives. - The Rationals Inside the Reals. The map \kappa(q) = [(q)_n], which preserves the operations and the order and is Chapter 4’s embedding \iota_{
R}; 
R Archimedean, with a unique integer part; 
Q dense in 
R, proved from the Cauchy property alone; rational tolerances sufficing for limits in 
R; every Cauchy sequence of rationals converging in 
R to its own class; and the class of the Newton sequence, a positive real number whose square is 2. - Every Cauchy Sequence of Reals Converges. Cauchy completeness of 
R, proved through the rational approximants m_k/(k + 1), named by unique integer parts; where the axiom of choice would have entered (picking a representative of each term) and why the diagonal of arbitrary representatives does not work. - The Real Numbers Form a Complete Ordered Field. Complete and Cauchy-complete ordered fields; the bound 2^k \ge k + 1 in any ordered field; the theorem that an Archimedean, Cauchy-complete ordered field is complete, proved by bisection with the Archimedean line marked; the constructed 
R a complete ordered field; a table of what 
R has and 
Q lacks; and review exercises that return to Chapter 4’s sequences, Chapter 2’s fractions, uncountability and recursion. Named moves - Representatives, then independence. To define an operation or a property on classes, state it on representatives, then show that the class of the answer survives replacing each input by an equivalent one. It proves the sum, product and negative well defined in Section 5.2 and positivity a property of the class in Section 5.3. The termwise reciprocal of Section 5.2 and the termwise order of Section 5.3 fail it. Exercise B2 of Section 5.2 and Exercise C1 of Section 5.3 leave the last step, and then the last half, to you. - A term approximates its class. For a \in \sC, the rationals a_k converge in 
R to [a]. Estimate \abs{[a] - a_k} through the representative (a_m - a_k)_m, and aim the termwise bound below the target, since only \le passes to classes. It is proved in Section 5.4 and used in Section 5.5 to find the limit’s candidate. - \varepsilon/3 through an approximant. To compare two objects you cannot compare directly, here two rationals q_j, q_k known only through the reals x_j, x_k they approximate, pass through the approximated objects and give each of the three distances a third of the tolerance. It proves in Section 5.5 that the approximants form a Cauchy sequence of rationals. The triangle inequality is used in 
R, and the result is carried back to 
Q through \kappa. - Bisect and keep the invariant. Halve an interval by a rule that keeps its right end an upper bound and its left end not one; the ends converge to the supremum once the lengths tend to 0. Making the lengths tend to 0 is the one step that needs Archimedes. It proves in Section 5.6 that an Archimedean, Cauchy-complete ordered field is complete. The Quick check there and Exercise C2 of Section 5.6 run it by hand, and the latter runs it in 
Q, where it finds no supremum.

title: 5.1 Sequences That Should Converge
content:
Sequences That Should Converge Chapter 4 ended with a rational sequence that is Cauchy in 
Q and converges to no rational (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its terms crowd around a place where 
Q has a hole. This chapter builds the number that belongs in the hole, and the first step is to notice that many different sequences crowd around the same hole. This section sets up the raw material, the set \sC of Cauchy sequences of rationals, and the relation that will decide when two of them aim at the same number: their difference dies out. Nothing about real numbers is assumed. Every tolerance, bound and threshold in this section is a rational number. Two sequences aimed at one hole The first sequence is the Newton sequence of Chapter 2 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2): x_0 \coloneqq 2 and x_{n+1} \coloneqq  rac{x_n^2 + 2}{2 x_n} =  rac{x_n}{2} +  rac{1}{x_n} \qquad (n \in 
N) , with error e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2. Its first terms are 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408. We shall use the following facts, each proved earlier, for every n \in 
N: 1. x_n \in 
Q_{>0}, and e_n > 0, that is, x_n^2 > 2 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2); 2. x_n > 1, and e_n \le 1/(4n) when n \ge 1 (the first clauses of the statement of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit); 3. (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in 
Q, and there is no L \in 
Q with x_n 	o L (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). From (NS1) and (NS2), 0 < x_n^2 - 2 \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1. At n = 0 the expression 1/(4n) is not defined, and indeed x_0^2 - 2 = 2 is not small. The second sequence approaches the hole from below, by decimal truncation. To define it inside 
Q, without the school decimals, we need powers of ten. Powers of ten. For k \in 
N, 10^k is the power in the ordered field 
Q of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b): 10^0 = 1 and 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10. (Here 10 = 10 \cdot 1_{
Q}, by the identification 
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q of Chapter 2 and @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (d).) Two facts about it are used below, both by induction (@fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b)) with base P(0). - 10^k \in 
Z. Base: 10^0 = 1 \in 
Z. Step: if 10^k \in 
Z, then 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10 is a product of two integers, and products of integers computed in 
Q are integers (@prp-integers-embed-rationals: j(m) j(n) = j(mn)). - 10^k \ge k + 1. Base: 10^0 = 1 = 0 + 1. Step: suppose 10^k \ge y, where y \coloneqq k + 1. Then y \ge 1 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), and multiplying by 10 > 0 gives 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10 \ge 10y (by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) if 10^k > y; trivially if 10^k = y). Moreover 10y - (y + 1) = 9y - 1 \ge 9 - 1 > 0. So 10^{k+1} > y + 1 = k + 2, where (k + 1) + 1 = k + 2 is arithmetic in 
N (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws), carried into 
Q by the sum law of @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). In particular 10^k \ge 1 > 0, so 1/10^k > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), applied to 0 < k + 1 \le 10^k, gives 1/10^k \le 1/(k + 1). Together, 0 <  rac{1}{10^k} \le  rac{1}{k + 1} \qquad (k \in 
N) . {#eq-ten-power-reciprocal} The inequality is not strict at k = 0, where both sides are 1. We write 1/10^k throughout; negative powers have not been defined. The truncations. For k \in 
N, let m_k be the largest natural number m with m^2 \le 2 \cdot (10^k)^2 , and let d_k \coloneqq m_k / 10^k. In school terms, d_k is \sqrt 2 cut off after k decimal places; but the definition mentions only integers and the rational 10^k. That such a largest m exists, and is unique, is a fact about sets of integers. Let S_k \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z : m \ge 0 	ext{ and } m^2 > 2 \cdot (10^k)^2 \} . It is bounded below by 0, and it is non-empty: 2 \cdot 10^k is a non-negative integer, and (2 \cdot 10^k)^2 = 4 (10^k)^2 > 2 (10^k)^2 because (10^k)^2 > 0. By @prp-integer-least-element, S_k has a least element m^\ast. Since 0^2 = 0 \le 2 (10^k)^2, 0 
otin S_k, so m^\ast \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), hence m_k \coloneqq m^\ast - 1 \ge 0 is a natural number (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). It is not in S_k, being smaller than the least element, so m_k^2 \le 2 (10^k)^2. Every natural number m > m_k satisfies m \ge m^\ast (discreteness again), so m^2 \ge (m^\ast)^2 > 2 (10^k)^2 (by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) if m > m^\ast; trivially if m = m^\ast). So m_k is the largest natural number with m^2 \le 2 (10^k)^2, and there is exactly one. Because the description singles out one number for each k, the rule k \mapsto d_k is a function 
N 	o 
Q (@fd2:def-function), with no choices made. The first values are:  egin{array}{c|ccccccc} k & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \ \hline m_k & 1 & 14 & 141 & 1414 & 14142 & 141421 & 1414213 \end{array} For instance m_1 = 14, because 14^2 = 196 \le 200 = 2 \cdot 10^2 and 15^2 = 225 > 200. So d_0 = 1, d_1 = 7/5, d_2 = 141/100, d_3 = 707/500. Different sequences, one intended number. The two sequences never meet: x_k^2 > 2 \ge d_k^2 for every k, so x_k 
e d_k. They approach from opposite sides, and their differences x_1 - d_1 = 1/10, x_2 - d_2 = 1/150, x_3 - d_3 = 11/51000 shrink fast. Both “should” converge to the same number, and 
Q has no such number. The plan of the chapter is to make the sequences themselves into the numbers, and for that we must first say when two sequences count as one. Cauchy sequences of rationals The raw material is every sequence that behaves as if it had a limit. Cauchy Sequences of Rationals \sC is the set of all sequences a \colon 
N 	o 
Q (@def-sequence-ordered-field, F = 
Q) that are Cauchy sequences in 
Q (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field): for every \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for all m, n \ge N. In symbols, a \in \sC means  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} A sequence a of rationals is null if a_n 	o 0 in 
Q (@def-null-sequence-ordered-field, F = 
Q). We write a sequence as a single letter, a = (a_n)_{n \in 
N}, and do arithmetic on sequences termwise: a + b \coloneqq (a_n + b_n)_n, ab \coloneqq (a_n b_n)_n, -a \coloneqq (-a_n)_n and a - b \coloneqq (a_n - b_n)_n. For q \in 
Q, (q)_n is the constant sequence with every term q. Nothing is new here except the name: this is Chapter 4’s definition with F = 
Q, so every tolerance \varepsilon is rational. That is the point. The definition can be read by someone who knows only 
Q, and it will be used to build a larger field without assuming anything about it. Examples. Every constant sequence (q)_n is in \sC, with N = 0 for every \varepsilon. The sequence (1/(n + 1))_n is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), so it is in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). The Newton sequence (x_n) is in \sC, by (NS3), and is not null, since x_n > 1 for every n. The sequence (n)_n is not in \sC: a Cauchy sequence is bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field), and for every M \in 
Q_{>0} some n \in 
N has n > M (@thm-rationals-archimedean). The toolkit from Chapter 4, with F = 
Q. This chapter uses the following facts so often that we list them once. Each was proved in Chapter 4 for an arbitrary ordered field; here F = 
Q. - Constant sequences and null sequences are in \sC, and \sC is closed under +, -, \cdot and negatives (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field). - Sums, negatives and constant multiples of null sequences are null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a), (b)). - A null sequence times a bounded sequence is null (@prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field). - Every member of \sC is bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field). - Changing finitely many terms changes no limit, and so no nullity (@prp-tail-change-ordered-field (a)). - A sequence squeezed, from some index on, between two sequences with the same limit has that limit too (@prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c)); in particular one squeezed between (0)_n, or (-u_n)_n, and a null (u_n)_n is null. When two sequences name the same number The Newton sequence and the truncations should name one number, yet they share no term. “Eventually equal” is therefore too strict a test. What the two sequences do share is visible in the differences above: x_k - d_k shrinks to nothing. In 
Q we cannot compare the two sequences through a common limit, since there is none; but their difference is again a sequence of rationals, and whether it tends to 0 is a question 
Q can answer. Two Cauchy sequences are equivalent when their difference dies out. [Equivalent Cauchy Sequences] For a, b \in \sC, we write a \sim b, and say that a is equivalent to b, if the sequence a - b = (a_n - b_n)_n is null. In symbols, a \sim b means  orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - b_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . In words: whatever rational tolerance is named, from some index on, the two sequences agree to within it at the same index. The threshold N comes after \varepsilon, so it may depend on \varepsilon. The comparison is always between a_n and b_n with the same n; nothing is said about a_m against b_n. The relation is defined only on \sC: both sequences must be Cauchy before we ask whether they are equivalent. Examples. - Constant sequences (the degenerate case). For p, q \in 
Q, (p)_n \sim (q)_n if and only if p = q. The difference is the constant (p - q)_n, which converges to p - q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)); by uniqueness of limits (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field) it is null exactly when p - q = 0. So on constant sequences \sim is plain equality, as it must be if (q)_n is to stand for q. - A null sequence and zero. (1/(n + 1))_n \sim (0)_n: the difference is (1/(n + 1))_n, null by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b). No term of the first sequence is 0. - The truncations and the Newton sequence. (d_k) \sim (x_k); this is @exm-truncations-equivalent below. Non-example by a minimal change. Shift the null sequence of the second example up by one: b_n \coloneqq 1 + 1/(n + 1). It is still in \sC (a constant plus a null sequence, @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)), and b - (1)_n = (1/(n + 1))_n is still null, so b \sim (1)_n. But b 
ot\sim (0)_n: the clause that fails is “for every \varepsilon”. With \varepsilon = 1, every n has \abs{b_n - 0} = 1 + 1/(n + 1) \ge 1, so no threshold exists. Why this definition. - Why “null”, and not “same limit”. Two sequences with a common limit in 
Q have null difference (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)). Conversely, if a 	o L and b 	o L' with a - b null, then a - b tends to both L - L' and 0, so L = L' (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field). So for convergent sequences the new relation says exactly “same limit”. But it is stated without mentioning any limit, so it applies equally to (x_k) and (d_k), which have none in 
Q. - Why not “eventually equal”. Then (x_k) and (d_k) would name different numbers, and so would (1/(n + 1))_n and (0)_n. Sequences that agree ever more closely, without ever agreeing exactly, would never be identified. - Why only on \sC. On all sequences of rationals the same relation would not respect products, and Section 5.2 needs it to. For instance (1/(n + 1))_n and (0)_n have null difference, but multiplying both termwise by (n + 1)_n, which is not Cauchy, gives (1)_n and (0)_n, whose difference is not null. Inside \sC every multiplier is bounded, and that is what saves the product. It must be checked that \sim really sorts sequences into groups, that is, that it is an equivalence relation in the sense of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5. [Equivalence of Cauchy Sequences Is an Equivalence Relation] The relation \sim of @def-cauchy-equivalent is an equivalence relation on \sC (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Each of the three clauses becomes a statement about one difference sequence. Reflexivity looks at a - a, the zero sequence. Symmetry looks at b - a, the negative of a - b. Transitivity writes a - c as the sum (a - b) + (b - c) of two null sequences. Before reading on: which fact from Chapter 4 does transitivity use, and where is the triangle inequality hiding? Let a, b, c \in \sC. (Eq1) a - a = (0)_n, which is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)). So a \sim a. (Eq2) Suppose a \sim b. For every n, b_n - a_n = -(a_n - b_n) (since (a_n - b_n) + (b_n - a_n) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), and negatives are unique, @prp-ring-algebra (a)), so b - a = -(a - b), which is null by @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b) (-0 = 0). So b \sim a. (Eq3) Suppose a \sim b and b \sim c. For every n, a_n - c_n = (a_n - b_n) + (b_n - c_n) , so a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), a sum of two null sequences. By the sum rule @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a), it is null (0 + 0 = 0). So a \sim c. This proves that \sim is an equivalence relation on \sC. The answer to the prompt: transitivity uses the sum rule of the limit laws, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a), and the triangle inequality is inside its proof, where \abs{(a_n - b_n) + (b_n - c_n)} \le \abs{a_n - b_n} + \abs{b_n - c_n} splits the tolerance into two halves. Written out directly: given \varepsilon, take thresholds for a - b and b - c with tolerance \varepsilon/2, and their maximum serves a - c. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition, \sC now falls apart into disjoint classes, and two Cauchy sequences lie in the same class exactly when their difference is null. Section 5.2 takes these classes as the real numbers. The truncations and the Newton sequence The two sequences of the hook are the first test of the definition. [The Truncations and the Newton Sequence Are Equivalent] Show that (d_k) is non-decreasing, that (d_k) \in \sC, and that (d_k) \sim (x_k). Step 1: (d_k) is non-decreasing. Let k \in 
N. By the choice of m_k and the defining equation 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10, (10 m_k)^2 = 100 \, m_k^2 \le 200 \, (10^k)^2 = 2 \, (10^k \cdot 10)^2 = 2 \, (10^{k+1})^2 . So 10 m_k is a natural number whose square is at most 2 (10^{k+1})^2, and m_{k+1} is the largest such: 10 m_k \le m_{k+1}. Dividing by 10^{k+1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) if 10 m_k < m_{k+1}; trivially if they are equal), d_{k+1} =  rac{m_{k+1}}{10^{k+1}} \ge  rac{10 m_k}{10^k \cdot 10} =  rac{m_k}{10^k} = d_k . By @fd1:ax-induction on i, with base P(0) (d_k \le d_k) and the step just proved, d_k \le d_{k+i} for every i \in 
N. Every j \ge k is k + i for some i \in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)), so d_k \le d_j whenever j \ge k. In particular d_k \ge d_0 = 1 for every k (m_0 = 1, since 1^2 \le 2 < 2^2). No law of exponents was used, only the defining equation of 10^{k+1}. Step 2: d_k \le d_j < d_k + 1/10^k for j \ge k, and (d_k) \in \sC. The lower bound is Step 1. For the upper bound, m_j^2 \le 2 (10^j)^2 gives d_j^2 \le 2. Since m_k + 1 > m_k, the maximality of m_k gives (m_k + 1)^2 > 2 (10^k)^2, that is, \Bigl( d_k +  rac{1}{10^k} \Bigr)^2 =  rac{(m_k + 1)^2}{(10^k)^2} > 2 . If we had d_j \ge d_k + 1/10^k, then, both sides being non-negative, d_j^2 \ge (d_k + 1/10^k)^2 > 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)), against d_j^2 \le 2. By trichotomy, d_j < d_k + 1/10^k. With @eq-ten-power-reciprocal, 0 \le d_j - d_k <  rac{1}{10^k} \le  rac{1}{k + 1} \qquad (j \ge k) . {#eq-truncation-cauchy-bound} Now let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon there is n_\varepsilon \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for every integer m \ge n_\varepsilon. Let N \coloneqq n_\varepsilon, which depends on \varepsilon only. For j, k \ge N, say with j \ge k (the other case is symmetric, as \abs{d_j - d_k} = \abs{d_k - d_j}), @eq-truncation-cauchy-bound gives \abs{d_j - d_k} < 1/(k + 1) < \varepsilon, since k + 1 > N. So (d_k) \in \sC. Step 3: 0 \le 2 - d_k^2 < 5/10^k. The first inequality is d_k^2 \le 2. For the second, expand the display of Step 2 (@prp-ring-algebra (d)): 2 < d_k^2 +  rac{2 d_k}{10^k} +  rac{1}{10^k} \cdot  rac{1}{10^k} . Here d_k < 2, since 0 \le d_k and d_k^2 \le 2 < 4 = 2^2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)); and (1/10^k)(1/10^k) \le 1/10^k, since 0 < 1/10^k \le 1 by @eq-ten-power-reciprocal. Multiplying d_k < 2 by 2/10^k > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and adding the two bounds (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), 2 - d_k^2 < 4/10^k + 1/10^k = 5/10^k. Step 4: (d_k) \sim (x_k). Let k \ge 1. By (NS2), x_k > 1, and d_k \ge 1 by Step 1, so x_k + d_k \ge 1. Since \abs{x_k - d_k} \ge 0, @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) gives  egin{aligned} \abs{x_k - d_k} &\le \abs{x_k - d_k} (x_k + d_k) = \abs{x_k^2 - d_k^2} \ &\le \abs{x_k^2 - 2} + \abs{2 - d_k^2} \le  rac{1}{4k} +  rac{5}{10^k} , \end{aligned} by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) and (e), the bound 0 < x_k^2 - 2 \le 1/(4k) from (NS1)–(NS2), and Step 3. Since 4k - (k + 1) = 3k - 1 > 0, 1/(4k) \le 1/(k + 1) (@prp-ordered-field-halves (c)). Define, for every k \in 
N, u_k \coloneqq  rac{1}{k + 1} +  rac{5}{10^k} . Then -u_k \le x_k - d_k \le u_k for every k \ge 1 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). The sequence (u_k) is null: (1/(k + 1)) is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)); (1/10^k) is null by the squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) between (0)_k and (1/(k + 1)), using @eq-ten-power-reciprocal; (5/10^k) is null by @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b) with c = 5; and the sum of two null sequences is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a)). So (-u_k) is null too, by (b) with c = -1. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c), with N_0 = 1, lower sequence (-u_k) and upper sequence (u_k), shows that (x_k - d_k) is null. Both sequences are in \sC (by (NS3) and Step 2), so (x_k) \sim (d_k), and (d_k) \sim (x_k) by symmetry. The bound of Step 4 is crude but honest: at k = 1 it gives \abs{x_1 - d_1} \le 1/4 + 5/10 = 3/4, while in fact x_1 - d_1 = 3/2 - 7/5 = 1/10. The upper sequence (u_k) is defined for every k, including k = 0, where 1/(4k) is not; the squeeze only needs the inequality from N_0 = 1 on. One consequence is worth recording at once: (d_k) has no limit in 
Q either. If d_k 	o L \in 
Q, then x_k = d_k + (x_k - d_k) 	o L + 0 = L by the sum rule, against (NS3). So the truncations, like the Newton sequence, are Cauchy and aim at nothing in 
Q, and @exm-truncations-equivalent says they aim at the same nothing. Finite changes, and shifts A class will contain far more than the two sequences of the hook. The next example shows how loose the relation is at the start of a sequence. [Finite Changes and Shifts] 1. Let a \in \sC, let b \colon 
N 	o 
Q, and suppose there is N_0 \in 
N with a_n = b_n for every n \ge N_0. Show that b \in \sC and a \sim b. 2. Let a \in \sC, and let s \coloneqq (a_{n+1})_{n \in 
N} be the shifted sequence. Show that s \in \sC and s \sim a. (a) b \in \sC by the tail-change remark after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field (Section 4.5). For n \ge N_0, a_n - b_n = 0. So a - b agrees with the null sequence (0)_n from N_0 on, and is null by @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (a). Hence a \sim b. (b) Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and let N be a threshold for a with tolerance \varepsilon (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences). For m, n \ge N, also m + 1, n + 1 \ge N, so \abs{s_m - s_n} = \abs{a_{m+1} - a_{n+1}} < \varepsilon: s \in \sC, with the same thresholds. For n \ge N, apply the Cauchy condition to the pair (n + 1, n), both indices \ge N: \abs{s_n - a_n} = \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} < \varepsilon . So s - a is null, and s \sim a. By (a), a representative of a class may begin with any finite list of rationals: (5, -3, 7, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, \dots), which is 1/(n + 1) from n = 3 on, is equivalent to (1/(n + 1))_n, and so to (0)_n. Part (b) uses the Cauchy condition with the two indices n + 1 and n; a sequence of rationals that is not Cauchy can fail it (for ((-1)^n)_n, every \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} is 2). Equivalent is not “eventually equal”, and not “close at the start”. (1/(n + 1))_n \sim (0)_n, though no term of the first sequence is 0. And (0)_n and (1 - 1/(n + 1))_n have the same first term, 0, but are not equivalent: their difference (0)_n - (1 - 1/(n + 1))_n converges to -1 (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a), (b) with @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a), (b)), so it is not null, by uniqueness of limits (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field). Only the behavior far out counts, and it counts at every tolerance. Let a \coloneqq (1, 0, 1, 0, \dots), with a_n = 1 for even n and a_n = 0 for odd n; and let b \coloneqq (1, 0, 1/2, 0, 1/3, 0, \dots), with b_{2k} = 1/(k + 1) and b_{2k+1} = 0. Which of them lies in \sC? For the one that does, find a constant sequence equivalent to it. a 
otin \sC. The negation of the Cauchy condition (moving 
eg inward as in @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation) reads \exists \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists m, n \ge N \ \ \abs{a_m - a_n} \ge \varepsilon , and it holds with \varepsilon = 1/2: for any N, the indices m = N and n = N + 1 have one even and one odd (@prp-omega-powers-parity (d)), so \abs{a_m - a_n} = 1 \ge 1/2. b \in \sC, and b \sim (0)_n. Indeed b is null: given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives K \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for every integer m \ge K. For n \ge 2K, n is odd or of the form 2k (@prp-omega-powers-parity (d)), and in the second case k \ge K. So either n is odd and b_n = 0 < \varepsilon, or n = 2k with k \ge K and b_n = 1/(k + 1) < \varepsilon. So b is null, hence in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and b - (0)_n = b is null. The pattern “a non-zero term every other index” is the same in a and b; what differs is whether those terms die out. The relation is in place, and it is an equivalence relation. The next section takes its classes as the real numbers and gives them an arithmetic. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each sequence of rationals, decide whether it lies in \sC and whether it is null, with a one-line reason: ((-1)^n/(n + 1))_n; (n)_n; (1 + 1/(n + 1))_n; (d_k)_k; ((-1)^n)_n. 2. Write “a 
ot\sim b”, for a, b \in \sC, in symbols, with no 
eg in front of a quantifier. 3. True or false: if a \sim b, then a_n = b_n for at least one n. Give a reason. (a) - ((-1)^n/(n + 1)): in \sC and null. Its absolute value is 1/(n + 1) (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{(-1)^n} = 1), which is below any \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} from some index on (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)); null sequences are in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). - (n): neither. It is not bounded (@thm-rationals-archimedean), so it is not Cauchy (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field), and not null (a null sequence is convergent, hence bounded, @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field). - (1 + 1/(n + 1)): in \sC, not null. It converges to 1 (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a)), so it is Cauchy (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field), and its limit is not 0 (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field). - (d_k): in \sC (@exm-truncations-equivalent), not null: d_k \ge 1 for every k, so the tolerance \varepsilon = 1 has no threshold. - ((-1)^n): neither. Consecutive terms differ by 2, so \varepsilon = 1 has no Cauchy threshold; and it is not null, since every term has absolute value 1. (b) By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication, reading 
eg(x < \varepsilon) as x \ge \varepsilon: \exists \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n - b_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . One rational tolerance is beaten at indices beyond every threshold. (c) False. (1/(n + 1))_n \sim (0)_n, and 1/(n + 1) 
e 0 for every n. B. Practice [B1: Equivalent or not] 1. Show that (1/(n + 1))_n \sim (1/(n + 2))_n and that both are equivalent to (0)_n. 2. Determine which constant sequences (c)_n, c \in 
Q, are equivalent to (3 + 1/(n + 1))_n. Justify your answer. (a) Both sequences are null: the first by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b); the second is the first shifted by one, (a_{n+1})_n with a_n = 1/(n + 1), so it is null by @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b). Null sequences lie in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and a null sequence a satisfies a \sim (0)_n, since a - (0)_n = a. By symmetry and transitivity (@prp-cauchy-equivalent-relation), (1/(n + 1)) \sim (0)_n \sim (1/(n + 2)) gives (1/(n + 1)) \sim (1/(n + 2)). (b) Only c = 3. The difference (3 + 1/(n + 1)) - (c)_n = (3 - c) + 1/(n + 1) converges to 3 - c, by the sum rule (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (a)) with the constant 3 - c and the null (1/(n + 1)). By uniqueness of limits (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field) it is null if and only if 3 - c = 0. Hence (3 + 1/(n + 1)) \sim (c)_n exactly when c = 3; this is consistent with the degenerate example after @def-cauchy-equivalent, since two constants equivalent to one sequence are equivalent to each other, hence equal. [B2: Null differences preserve Cauchy] 1. Let a \in \sC, and let b \colon 
N 	o 
Q be a sequence such that a - b is null. Prove that b \in \sC and b \sim a. 2. Hence show that (2/x_n)_n \in \sC and (2/x_n)_n \sim (x_n)_n, where (x_n) is the Newton sequence. (a) For every n, b_n = a_n - (a_n - b_n), so b = a - (a - b). Here a \in \sC, and a - b is null, hence in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)); the difference of two members of \sC is in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b)). So b \in \sC. Then a \sim b by definition, and b \sim a by symmetry. (b) By (NS1), x_n > 0, so 2/x_n is defined. For every n, x_n -  rac{2}{x_n} =  rac{x_n^2 - 2}{x_n} =  rac{e_n}{x_n} . By (NS1) and (NS2), e_n > 0 and x_n > 1, so 0 < 1/x_n < 1 (@prp-reciprocal-order) and 0 < e_n/x_n < e_n (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). For n \ge 1, e_n \le 1/(4n) \le 1/(n + 1). So 0 \le x_n - 2/x_n \le 1/(n + 1) for every n \ge 1, and the squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c), with N_0 = 1 and the null sequence (1/(n + 1)) (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), shows that (x_n - 2/x_n) is null. Part (a), with a = (x_n) \in \sC (NS3) and b = (2/x_n), gives the claim. The terms 2/x_n satisfy (2/x_n)^2 = 4/x_n^2 < 2, so this sequence approaches the hole from below, as the truncations do. [B3: Every other Newton term] Show that (x_{2n})_n \sim (x_n)_n for the Newton sequence. Hint: imitate @exm-finite-change-equivalent (b). First, (x_{2n})_n \in \sC. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and let N be a threshold for (x_n) with tolerance \varepsilon (NS3). For m, n \ge N, also 2m \ge m \ge N and 2n \ge N, so \abs{x_{2m} - x_{2n}} < \varepsilon. Second, the difference is null. For n \ge N, the two indices 2n and n are both \ge N, so \abs{x_{2n} - x_n} < \varepsilon. So (x_{2n} - x_n)_n is null, with the same thresholds as (x_n), and (x_{2n}) \sim (x_n). The Cauchy condition was used with two indices that are far apart (2n and n). This is exactly where “every pair of indices beyond N” is needed, and not only neighbors. C. Going deeper [C1: Subsequences] Let a \in \sC, and let k \mapsto n_k be a function 
N 	o 
N with n_k < n_{k+1} for every k \in 
N (for instance n_k = 2k, or any sequence of indices defined by @fd2:thm-recursion with this property). 1. Prove that n_k \ge k for every k, that (a_{n_k})_{k \in 
N} \in \sC, and that (a_{n_k})_k \sim a. 2. Deduce: if a, b \in \sC and a_{n_k} = b_{n_k} for every k, then a \sim b. Compare with the warning after @exm-finite-change-equivalent: why does this not say that sequences which are “close at the start” are equivalent? [Hint 1] For (a), the indices n_k run ahead of k. Once you know n_k \ge k, the Cauchy condition applies to the pair (n_k, k). [Hint 2] For (a), prove n_k \ge k by @fd1:ax-induction on k; the step uses n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k. (a) n_k \ge k. By @fd1:ax-induction on k, base P(0): n_0 \ge 0 (@thm-omega-order (d)). Step: if n_k \ge k, then n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k, so k < n_{k+1}; by @thm-omega-order (b), n_{k+1} < k + 1 would give n_{k+1} \le k, so by trichotomy n_{k+1} \ge k + 1. In \sC. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and let N be a threshold for a with tolerance \varepsilon. For j, k \ge N, n_j \ge j \ge N and n_k \ge k \ge N, so \abs{a_{n_j} - a_{n_k}} < \varepsilon. Equivalent to a. For k \ge N, both n_k \ge N and k \ge N, so \abs{a_{n_k} - a_k} < \varepsilon. So (a_{n_k} - a_k)_k is null, with the same thresholds, and (a_{n_k})_k \sim a. (b) By (a), (a_{n_k})_k \sim a and (b_{n_k})_k \sim b. The two subsequences are the same sequence, since a_{n_k} = b_{n_k} for every k. So a \sim (a_{n_k})_k = (b_{n_k})_k \sim b, using symmetry for the first step, and transitivity (@prp-cauchy-equivalent-relation) gives a \sim b. The hypothesis of (b) is that the sequences agree at infinitely many indices, n_0 < n_1 < \cdots, arbitrarily far out. In the warning, (0)_n and (1 - 1/(n + 1))_n agree only at n = 0. Agreement far out, along a whole subsequence, forces equivalence for Cauchy sequences; agreement at finitely many places says nothing. (For sequences that are not Cauchy, (b) fails: (1, 0, 1, 0, \dots) and (1)_n agree at every even index, and their difference is not null.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves n_k \ge k for every k, justifying the passage from n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k (or, by a least counterexample, from n_k > n_{k-1} \ge k - 1) to the next whole number. - 3: shows (a_{n_k}) \in \sC, with one threshold that serves all j, k \ge N and with n_j, n_k \ge N justified from n_k \ge k. - 3: shows (a_{n_k} - a_k)_k is null by applying the Cauchy condition to the pair (n_k, k). - 2: deduces (b) by symmetry and transitivity of \sim. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a limit of a in 
Q; a threshold that depends on k.

title: 5.2 The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic
5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content:
Positive Classes and the Order Section 5.2 made 
R a field: its elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, added and multiplied through representatives. A field is not yet a number line. To compare two real numbers we need an order, and it must cooperate with the arithmetic: 
R should be an ordered field in the sense of @def-ordered-ring-and-field. Chapter 2 ordered 
Q in two steps. It first said which rationals are positive, and then let a < b mean that b - a is positive (@prp-order-from-positives). This section takes the same two steps for 
R. All the work is in the first: deciding which classes are positive, in a way that does not depend on the representative. Throughout, \sC is the set of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences), a \sim b means that a - b is null in 
Q (@def-cauchy-equivalent), and [a] is the class of a, an element of 
R (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). Until 
R has an order, every tolerance, margin and threshold is a rational or a natural number: we are still building 
R, and may not measure anything with it. The operations are those of @def-reals-operations: [a] + [b] = [a + b], [a][b] = [ab], -[a] = [-a], with 0_{
R} = [(0)_n] and 1_{
R} = [(1)_n], where (q)_n is the constant sequence with value q. In particular [a] - [b] = [a] + [-b] = [a - b] , since a + (-b) = a - b termwise. We use this without comment. Comparing terms does not compare classes The first idea is to compare two classes by comparing their terms. It fails, and the way it fails shows what the definition must contain. [Termwise Order Is Not an Order on Classes] Consider the rule [a] < [b] means that a_n < b_n for every n from some index on. Let a_n \coloneqq 0 and b_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1) for n \in 
N. Show that [a] = [b]. Then apply the rule to the classes [a] and [a] twice: once through the representatives a and a, once through a and b. Conclude that the rule does not define a relation on 
R. Both sequences are in \sC: a constant sequence and a null sequence are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). Termwise, b - a = (1/(n + 1)), which is null, so b \sim a, and [a] = [b] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). Through the representatives a and a: the rule asks whether 0 < 0 from some index on, and 0 < 0 never holds. So the rule says that [a] < [a] is false. Through the representatives a and b, which name the same two classes, since b \in [b] = [a]: for every n, a_n = 0 < 1/(n + 1) = b_n. So the rule says that [a] < [a] is true. A relation on 
R must give one answer for each pair of classes. The rule gives two answers for the pair (0_{
R}, 0_{
R}), depending on the representatives, so it defines no relation on 
R. Worse, the second answer, 0_{
R} < 0_{
R}, is excluded by trichotomy (O1) in any ordered field. The trouble is that the gap between a_n and b_n is allowed to shrink to nothing, and a gap that shrinks to nothing is exactly what \sim ignores. A class that deserves to be called positive must have terms that stay above 0 by a fixed margin. Positive sequences We look for a property of a single sequence a \in \sC that says “the number a names is greater than 0”. The example shows that “eventually a_n > 0” is too weak, because a null sequence can have it. The repair is to name the margin first. Positive means: eventually above one fixed positive rational. [Positive Cauchy Sequence] A sequence a \in \sC is positive if there exist \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N such that a_n \ge \delta for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. In symbols, \exists \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \Rightarrow a_n \ge \delta ) . In words: the first quantifier names a margin \delta, a positive rational, before anything else is named; the second names a threshold; the third says that every term from the threshold on is at least the margin. Because \delta comes first, one margin serves all the late terms at once. The word “positive” describes the sequence as a name for a number, not its terms one by one: the terms before N may be negative, and, as the warning below shows, terms that are all > 0 are not enough. Compare the definition with the weaker condition “the terms are eventually positive”: \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \Rightarrow a_n > 0 ) . Here each late term a_n is above 0 by its own amount, namely a_n itself, and these amounts may shrink as n grows. In the definition the amount is chosen before n, so it cannot depend on n. The two conditions differ only in the order of “there is a margin” and “for every late n”, and that order is the whole point. Examples. A positive constant. For q \in 
Q_{>0}, the constant sequence (q)_n is positive, with \delta = q and N = 0. This degenerate case is how Section 5.4 will see that the rational q, placed inside 
R, is greater than 0. The Newton sequence. Let (x_n) be the sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, which is in \sC by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit. The same theorem states that x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N. So (x_n) is positive, with \delta = 1 and N = 0. Late positivity. Let a_n \coloneqq 1 - 2/(n + 1). It is in \sC, as the difference of a constant sequence and a constant multiple of the null sequence (1/(n + 1)) (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). Its first terms are -1, 0, 1/3, 1/2, so it is not positive “from the start”. For n \ge 3, n + 1 \ge 4, so 1/(n + 1) \le 1/4 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (c)), hence 2/(n + 1) \le 2/4 = 1/2 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), with 0 \le 2 \le 2), and a_n \ge 1/2. So a is positive, with \delta = 1/2 and N = 3. No smaller N works with this \delta, since a_2 = 1/3 < 1/2; the definition allows any finite stretch of bad terms. Non-example by a minimal change. Keep every term positive, but let the margin shrink: a_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1). Every term is > 0, so the weaker condition above holds with N = 0. What fails is the order of the quantifiers. The negation of the definition, by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication, reads  orall \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \wedge a_n < \delta ) , and it holds: given \delta and N, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives n_0 \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \delta for every m \ge n_0. With n \coloneqq \max\{N, n_0\}, we have n \ge N, and m \coloneqq n + 1 \ge n_0, so a_n = 1/(n + 1) < \delta. Every margin is eventually undercut. Why this definition. Each clause has a job. - The margin \delta. Without it, the definition would be the weaker condition, and @exm-strict-termwise-order-fails shows the result: (1/(n + 1)) would be positive, while (0)_n, which names the same number 0_{
R}, is not. - A rational margin. The only positive numbers available are rationals. A real margin would use the order of 
R, which is what we are defining. - The threshold N. Changing finitely many terms does not change the class (@exm-finite-change-equivalent), so a definition meant for classes must ignore every finite stretch of terms. The late-positivity example needs N = 3. - \ge rather than >. Either would do: a_n \ge \delta gives a_n > \delta/2, and a_n > \delta gives a_n \ge \delta. We use \ge, the form in which @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign delivers its conclusion. “Every term of a is positive” does not make a positive. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) has every term > 0, and it is not positive (non-example above); its class is 0_{
R}. Let a \in \sC, with \delta ranging over 
Q_{>0}. Which of the two conditions 	ext{(A)} \ \exists \delta \ \exists N \  orall n \ge N \ \ a_n \ge \delta , \qquad 	ext{(B)} \ \exists N \  orall n \ge N \ \exists \delta \ \ a_n \ge \delta implies the other? Which of them says the same as “eventually a_n > 0”? (A) implies (B): the margin found once serves as the \delta for every late n. (B) does not imply (A): (1/(n + 1)) satisfies (B), with \delta \coloneqq 1/(n + 1) chosen after n, and fails (A). (B) says the same as “eventually a_n > 0”: if a_n > 0, take \delta \coloneqq a_n; if a_n \ge \delta > 0, then a_n > 0. So (A) is the definition of positive, and (B) is the weaker condition. Payoff: positivity belongs to the class. A real number is a class, and a definition about sequences says something about the class only if equivalent sequences agree on it. Chapter 4 proved the fact we need while preparing for this chapter: a margin survives a null change of the sequence, at half its size (@prp-sign-stable-ordered-field).
