The conclusion is true: it is @prp-positivity-well-defined. The middle lines are correct. With the tolerance \delta and the strict inequality \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta, we get a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge \delta - \delta = 0 for every n \ge \max\{N, N'\}. So the line “a'_n > 0 for all large n” is proved. The failing line is the last: “Therefore a' is positive.” What has been proved is \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \ge N \ \ a'_n > 0 , while “positive” (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence) is \exists \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \ge N \ \ a'_n \ge \delta . To pass from the first to the second, one would take the margin \delta \coloneqq a'_n, which depends on n, and then claim one margin for all n. That swaps a “for every n, there is a margin” for a “there is a margin for every n”. It is the analogue, for a margin depending on n, of entry (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, where a threshold depending on \varepsilon is treated as uniform. Counterexample to the step. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) has a'_n > 0 for all n, so it satisfies the premise of the last line, and it is not positive (the non-example after @def-positive-cauchy-sequence). So “eventually > 0” does not imply “positive”. The argument reached a true conclusion through a step that is not valid. Repair. Use the tolerance \delta/2 \in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)) instead of \delta. Since a' - a is null, choose N'' with \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta/2 for every n \ge N''. For n \ge \max\{N, N''\}, a'_n > a_n -  rac{\delta}{2} \ge \delta -  rac{\delta}{2} =  rac{\delta}{2} . So a'_n \ge \delta/2 for every n \ge \max\{N, N''\}: one margin, \delta/2, fixed before n, and a' is positive. This is the proof of @prp-sign-stable-ordered-field. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the conclusion is true, citing @prp-positivity-well-defined. - 3: identifies the last line as the failing one and names the quantifier swap (a margin depending on n treated as one margin for all n). - 2: a counterexample to the step: a sequence whose terms are eventually > 0 and which is not positive, such as (1/(n + 1)). - 3: a repair that produces one margin in 
Q_{>0} fixed before n (for instance the tolerance \delta/2 above; any tolerance strictly between 0 and \delta works equally well). Fatal errors (0 for the step): blaming one of the valid middle lines; a “counterexample” to the conclusion; a repair whose margin still depends on n.

title: 5.4 The Rationals Inside the Reals
content:
The Rationals Inside the Reals Section 5.3 made 
R an ordered field. We built it to enlarge 
Q, but so far 
Q is not inside it: a rational number is a class of pairs of integers, and a real number is a class of Cauchy sequences. This section places a copy of 
Q in 
R and shows how the copy sits there. It is preserved by all the operations and the order; it is spread through 
R without gaps, so that between any two real numbers there is a rational one; and every real number is the limit of rationals. Along the way we prove that 
R is Archimedean and that rational tolerances suffice for limits in 
R. At the end we meet the number that Chapter 4 promised: a positive real whose square is 2. Notation is as in Section 5.3: \sC is the set of Cauchy sequences of rationals, [a] is the class of a \in \sC, (q)_n is the constant sequence with value q, P = 
R_{>0} is the set of positive reals, and x < y means y - x \in P (@def-reals-order). By @thm-reals-ordered-field, the results of Chapters 2 and 4 for an arbitrary ordered field apply with F = 
R; we say “in 
R” where the context does not make the field clear. A copy of the rationals Section 5.2 already represented each rational q by the class of its constant sequence, as Chapter 4 said it would. We make that a map. [The Rationals in the Reals] For q \in 
Q, let \kappa(q) \coloneqq [(q)_n] \in 
R , the class of the constant sequence with value q. This defines a function \kappa \colon 
Q 	o 
R. The right side is in 
R because constant sequences are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and \kappa is a function because each q determines one constant sequence and that sequence one class. In this notation 0_{
R} = \kappa(0) and 1_{
R} = \kappa(1) (@def-reals-operations). The letter \kappa is new on purpose: Chapter 2 used \iota and j for 
N 	o 
Z 	o 
Q, and Chapter 4 wrote \iota_F for the copy of 
Q in an ordered field F. Part (d) of the next theorem shows that \kappa is \iota_{
R}. The theorem says that \kappa carries everything we know how to do with rationals into 
R without change: sums, products, negatives, reciprocals, the order and the absolute value. [The Rationals Embed in the Reals] For all q, s \in 
Q: 1. \kappa(q + s) = \kappa(q) + \kappa(s), \kappa(qs) = \kappa(q) \kappa(s), \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} and \kappa(1) = 1_{
R}; 2. q < s if and only if \kappa(q) < \kappa(s); hence \kappa is injective; 3. \kappa(-q) = -\kappa(q), \kappa(\abs{q}) = \abs{\kappa(q)}, and, if q 
e 0, \kappa(q) 
e 0_{
R} and \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q)^{-1}; 4. \kappa is the map \iota_{
R} of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field for the ordered field F = 
R; in particular \kappa(n) = n \cdot 1_{
R} for every n \in 
N (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field). Constant sequences add, multiply and negate termwise into constant sequences, so (a) and the first identity of (c) are the definitions of the operations. For (b), the difference of two constant sequences is constant, and a constant s - q > 0 is its own margin. The rest is algebra in a field: the absolute value by cases, reciprocals by uniqueness of inverses, and (d) by the uniqueness clause of Chapter 4’s embedding theorem. (a) By @def-reals-operations, \kappa(q) + \kappa(s) = [(q)_n + (s)_n] = [(q + s)_n] = \kappa(q + s), since the termwise sum of two constant sequences is the constant sequence of the sum. The product is the same with \cdot in place of +. The last two identities are the definitions of 0_{
R} and 1_{
R}. (c), first identity. By @def-reals-operations, -\kappa(q) = [-(q)_n] = [(-q)_n] = \kappa(-q). (b) (\Rightarrow) Let q < s. By (a) and the first identity of (c), \kappa(s) - \kappa(q) = \kappa(s) + \kappa(-q) = \kappa(s - q) = [(s - q)_n]. The constant s - q lies in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so the constant sequence (s - q)_n is positive, with margin \delta = s - q and threshold N = 0 (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence). Hence \kappa(s) - \kappa(q) \in P, that is, \kappa(q) < \kappa(s). (\Leftarrow) Let \kappa(q) < \kappa(s). By trichotomy in 
Q, q < s, q = s or s < q. If q = s, then \kappa(q) = \kappa(s); if s < q, then \kappa(s) < \kappa(q) by (\Rightarrow). Either contradicts \kappa(q) < \kappa(s) by (O1) in 
R (@thm-reals-ordered-field). So q < s. Injectivity: if q 
e s, then q < s or s < q, so \kappa(q) < \kappa(s) or \kappa(s) < \kappa(q), and in either case \kappa(q) 
e \kappa(s) by (O1). (c), the rest. If q > 0, then \kappa(q) > \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} by (b), so \abs{\kappa(q)} = \kappa(q) = \kappa(\abs{q}) (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field, in 
R and in 
Q). If q = 0, both sides are 0_{
R}. If q < 0, then \kappa(q) < 0_{
R} by (b), so \abs{\kappa(q)} = -\kappa(q) = \kappa(-q) = \kappa(\abs{q}). Now let q 
e 0. Then \kappa(q) 
e \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} by injectivity, and by (a), \kappa(q) \, \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q \cdot (1/q)) = \kappa(1) = 1_{
R} . In the field 
R (@thm-reals-field), the inverse of \kappa(q) is the only element with this property (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), so \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q)^{-1}. (d) By @thm-reals-ordered-field, 
R is an ordered field, so @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field gives exactly one map \iota_{
R} \colon 
Q 	o 
R with \iota_{
R}(1) = 1_{
R} that preserves sums and products. By (a), \kappa is such a map, so \kappa = \iota_{
R}. The same theorem states that \iota_{
R}(n) = n \cdot 1_{
R} for every n \in 
N. By (d), part (b) and the injectivity of \kappa are also part of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field with F = 
R, and (d) needs only (a). The direct proof of (b) is kept because it shows how a constant sequence is positive, with its own value as margin. Two more identities follow from (a) and (c):  egin{aligned} \kappa(q - s) &= \kappa(q) + \kappa(-s) = \kappa(q) - \kappa(s) , \ \kappa(q/s) &= \kappa(q) \, \kappa(1/s) = \kappa(q)/\kappa(s) \quad 	ext{for } s 
e 0 . \end{aligned} So any computation with rationals, done in 
Q and then moved into 
R by \kappa, gives the same answer as the computation done in 
R on the images. Part (b) adds that comparisons agree too. Archimedes in the reals Chapter 4 showed that an ordered field need not be Archimedean: in 
Q(t) the element t is larger than every n \cdot 1 (@exm-rational-function-field). So the Archimedean property of 
R has to be proved. It comes from 
Q, through the fact that a Cauchy sequence is bounded. [The Reals Are Archimedean] 
R is an Archimedean ordered field (@def-archimedean-ordered-field): for every x \in 
R there is n \in 
N with x < n \cdot 1_{
R}. A representative of x is a Cauchy sequence of rationals, so all its terms lie below one rational bound M. Archimedes in 
Q puts a natural number above M; one more unit gives a fixed margin above every term, and a fixed margin is what positivity asks for. Let x \in 
R, and write x = [a] with a \in \sC. By @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field with F = 
Q, there is M \in 
Q_{>0} with \abs{a_k} \le M for every k \in 
N. By @thm-rationals-archimedean, there is n \in 
N with M < n. For every k, (n + 1) - a_k \ge (n + 1) - M = (n - M) + 1 > 1 , since a_k \le \abs{a_k} \le M (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c)), so -M \le -a_k and then (n + 1) - a_k \ge (n + 1) - M (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), (b)), and n - M > 0. So the sequence ((n + 1) - a_k)_k is positive, with margin 1 and threshold 0. It represents \kappa(n + 1) - x, by @def-reals-operations. Hence x < \kappa(n + 1), and \kappa(n + 1) = (n + 1) \cdot 1_{
R} by @thm-rational-embedding (d). Since n + 1 \in 
N, this proves the theorem. Every result of Chapter 4 about Archimedean ordered fields now applies with F = 
R. Two of them are used at once. The integer part in 
R. By @prp-integer-part-ordered-field with F = 
R, and \iota_{
R} = \kappa (@thm-rational-embedding (d)), for every x \in 
R there is exactly one m \in 
Z with \kappa(m) \le x < \kappa(m + 1) . We call m the integer part of x. For a rational q, the integer part of \kappa(q) is the integer part  loor{q} of @prp-rational-integer-part, because \kappa preserves and reflects \le (@thm-rational-embedding (b)). The word “exactly” matters: Section 5.5 builds a sequence by taking integer parts, and uniqueness is what makes that a rule rather than a choice. The second consequence, @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R, turns into the statement that rational tolerances suffice; it comes after the density theorem. Between two reals there is a rational [The Rationals Are Dense in the Reals] Let x, y \in 
R with x < y. Then there is q \in 
Q with x < \kappa(q) < y. Try it first (ten minutes): write x = [a] and y = [b]. Which rational would you put between them? Build it from the terms of a and b, and say how far out you must go. The obvious attempt takes a rational between a_n and b_n, say their midpoint, and has to say which n. An early index is no good: a_0 may be larger than b_0, since early terms are irrelevant to the classes. Even where a_n < b_n, a later term a_m may climb past the midpoint, and the midpoint must sit above every late a_m by a fixed margin. So go far out, in two ways. Since y - x is positive, from some index on b_n - a_n \ge \delta, a fixed rational gap. Since a and b are Cauchy, from some index N on all their terms stay within \delta/4 of a_N and of b_N, respectively. The midpoint q of a_N and b_N is at least \delta/2 above a_N; every later a_n is less than \delta/4 above a_N; so q beats every later a_n by more than \delta/4. The same holds below b_n. Write x = [a] and y = [b] with a, b \in \sC. By @def-reals-order, y - x = [b - a] \in P, so b - a is positive (@prp-positivity-well-defined). Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N_1 \in 
N with b_n - a_n \ge \delta \quad 	ext{for every } n \ge N_1 [ulename{\exists E}] (@fd1:def-rules-existential). Then \delta/4 = (\delta/2)/2 \in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b), twice). Since a and b are Cauchy in 
Q, fix N_2 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \delta/4 for all m, n \ge N_2, and N_3 with \abs{b_m - b_n} < \delta/4 for all m, n \ge N_3 [ulename{\exists E}]. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2, N_3\} , \qquad q \coloneqq  rac{a_N + b_N}{2} \in 
Q . Let n \ge N. Expanding the right sides shows  egin{aligned} q - a_n &= (a_N - a_n) +  rac{b_N - a_N}{2} , \ b_n - q &= (b_n - b_N) +  rac{b_N - a_N}{2} . \end{aligned} Since n, N \ge N_2, a_N - a_n > -\delta/4 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)); since N \ge N_1, b_N - a_N \ge \delta, and multiplying by 1/2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b) with \varepsilon = 1) gives (b_N - a_N)/2 \ge \delta/2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed). Adding (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), q - a_n > - rac{\delta}{4} +  rac{\delta}{2} =  rac{\delta}{4} . In the same way, since n, N \ge N_3, b_n - b_N > -\delta/4, and b_n - q > \delta/4. So the sequences (q - a_n)_n and (b_n - q)_n are positive, each with margin \delta/4 and threshold N. By @def-reals-operations they represent \kappa(q) - x and y - \kappa(q). Hence x < \kappa(q) and \kappa(q) < y. The rational q depends on the representatives a, b and on the constants fixed in the proof; nothing makes it the “best” rational, and a different run of the proof may give a different q. The theorem only claims that one exists. The proof cites neither @thm-rationals-archimedean nor @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean: density came from the Cauchy property of the representatives, not from Archimedes. Chapter 4 proved density in every Archimedean ordered field (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field), so, with @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, it gives the same conclusion for 
R by another route (Exercise B1). We keep the direct proof for what it shows: in this construction, the rationals are dense because each real number is made of rationals. Rational tolerances suffice A tolerance for a limit in 
R is an element of 
R_{>0}, a class of sequences. That is awkward to work with. The next result lets us test convergence in 
R with the tolerances \kappa(1/n) only. Rational Tolerances Suffice 1. For every \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with \kappa(1/n) < \varepsilon for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. 2. Let (x_k)_{k \in 
N} be a sequence in 
R and x \in 
R. Then x_k 	o x in 
R (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field with F = 
R) if and only if, for every n \in 
Z_{>0}, there is K \in 
N with \abs{x_k - x} < \kappa(1/n) for every k \ge K. Likewise, (x_k) is Cauchy in 
R (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field with F = 
R) if and only if, for every n \in 
Z_{>0}, there is K \in 
N with \abs{x_j - x_k} < \kappa(1/n) for all j, k \ge K. (a) Let \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0}. Since 
R is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/(n \cdot 1_{
R}) < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. For such n, n 
e 0, n \cdot 1_{
R} = \kappa(n) (@thm-rational-embedding (d)) and 1/\kappa(n) = \kappa(1/n) (@thm-rational-embedding (c)). So \kappa(1/n) < \varepsilon. (b) (\Rightarrow) For n \in 
Z_{>0}, 1/n > 0 in 
Q (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), so \kappa(1/n) > \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} (@thm-rational-embedding (b)): it is one of the tolerances of the definition, which then supplies K. (\Leftarrow) Let \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0}. By (a), there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with \kappa(1/N) < \varepsilon. The hypothesis with n \coloneqq N gives K with \abs{x_k - x} < \kappa(1/N) for every k \ge K, and then \abs{x_k - x} < \varepsilon by (O2). So K serves for \varepsilon. The Cauchy version is the same argument with \abs{x_j - x_k} for j, k \ge K in place of \abs{x_k - x}. In practice: to prove a limit in 
R, fix n \in 
Z_{>0} and find a threshold for the rational tolerance 1/n. The threshold may depend on n, and on nothing chosen later. Each real number is the limit of its terms A real number [a] was introduced as a name for “what the rationals a_k are approaching”. Inside 
Q there may be nothing to approach. Inside 
R there is, and it is [a] itself. [A Cauchy Sequence Converges to Its Class] Let a \in \sC. Then the sequence (\kappa(a_k))_{k \in 
N} converges in 
R to [a]. For a fixed k, the difference [a] - \kappa(a_k) is represented by (a_m - a_k)_m: the sequence a with the single rational a_k subtracted from every term. For m and k past a Cauchy threshold, these terms are small, and @lem-termwise-order turns a termwise bound into a bound between classes. That lemma yields only \le, so we aim the termwise bound at 1/(2n), strictly below the target 1/n. Let n \in 
Z_{>0}. By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (b), it suffices to find K \in 
N with \abs{\kappa(a_k) - [a]} < \kappa(1/n) for every k \ge K. Since \kappa(a_k) - [a] = -([a] - \kappa(a_k)), @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) in 
R gives \abs{\kappa(a_k) - [a]} = \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)}, so we bound the latter. Since a \in \sC and 1/(2n) \in 
Q_{>0}, fix N \in 
N with \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) for all m, k \ge N. Let k \ge N. By @def-reals-operations, [a] - \kappa(a_k) = [a] + [(-a_k)_m] = [(a_m - a_k)_m], and (a_m - a_k)_m \in \sC as the difference of a and a constant sequence (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). By @prp-reals-absolute-value-termwise, \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)} = [(\abs{a_m - a_k})_m] . For every m \ge N, \abs{a_m - a_k} \le 1/(2n). So @lem-termwise-order, with the constant sequence (1/(2n))_m and N_0 = N, gives \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)} \le \kappa(1/(2n)) . Finally 0 < n < 2n in 
Q, so 1/(2n) < 1/n (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)), and \kappa(1/(2n)) < \kappa(1/n) by @thm-rational-embedding (b). Combining \le with < (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)} < \kappa(1/n) for every k \ge N. So K \coloneqq N works. Why 1/(2n) and not 1/n directly? The Cauchy property gives \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/n, but @lem-termwise-order passes only the non-strict inequality to classes, so we would reach \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)} \le \kappa(1/n), one symbol short of the definition. Halving the tolerance first leaves room for the strict inequality. The sequence does converge to the number it names, once that number exists. The theorem has a consequence worth stating in words: every real number is a limit of rationals, namely of the terms of any of its representatives. It also explains the slogan of the chapter. Equivalent sequences have the same class, so their terms converge in 
R to the same number; by uniqueness of limits (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field in 
R), that number is the only limit they have. A real number is what all its representatives converge to. Identification. From here on we write q for \kappa(q) when q \in 
Q, and 
Q \subseteq 
R. This is a convention about notation, of the kind Chapter 2 adopted twice, writing n for \iota(n) and m for j(m) (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals). It is safe because of @thm-rational-embedding: \kappa is injective and preserves sums, products, negatives, reciprocals, the order and the absolute value, so a statement about rationals means the same whether it is read in 
Q or, through \kappa, in 
R. It is not a set inclusion: the rational q is a class of pairs of integers, and \kappa(q) is a class of sequences of rationals, a different set. In the new notation the theorem says a_k 	o [a] in 
R, and @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices says that the tolerances 1/n, n \in 
Z_{>0}, suffice in 
R. The square root of two Chapter 4 ended with the Newton sequence (x_n) of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, Cauchy in 
Q and with no limit in 
Q (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its class is the number it was aiming at. [The Class of the Newton Sequence] Let (x_n) be the Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, and let r \coloneqq [(x_n)] \in 
R. Show that r > 0, that r^2 = 2, that r 
e q for every q \in 
Q, and that r = [(d_k)], where (d_k) is the sequence of decimal truncations of @exm-truncations-equivalent. The sequence (x_n) is in \sC by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, so r \in 
R. We use the facts x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N and e_n \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1, where e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2, stated in @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, and e_n > 0 for every n \in 
N, proved in @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. The first values are e_0 = 2 , \quad e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} , \quad e_4 =  rac{1}{221682772224} . r > 0. Since x_n > 1 for every n, the sequence (x_n) is positive, with margin 1 and threshold 0. So r \in P, that is, r > 0. By @lem-termwise-order, also r \ge 1. r^2 = 2. By @def-reals-operations, r^2 = r \cdot r = [(x_n^2)], and 2 = [(2)_n]. Termwise, (x_n^2) - (2)_n = (e_n). For n \ge 1, 0 < e_n \le  rac{1}{4n} \le  rac{1}{n + 1} , where the last step is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), since 4n - (n + 1) = 3n - 1 > 0. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) is defined for every n \in 
N and null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)); so is (0)_n. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) in 
Q, with N_0 = 1, shows that (e_n) is null. (At n = 0 the bound 1/(4n) is undefined and e_0 = 2; the threshold N_0 = 1 skips it.) Hence (x_n^2) \sim (2)_n and r^2 = 2. r is not rational. Suppose r = \kappa(q) for some q \in 
Q. Then \kappa(q^2) = \kappa(q)^2 = r^2 = \kappa(2) by @thm-rational-embedding (a), so q^2 = 2 by injectivity. This contradicts @thm-no-rational-square-two. So r 
otin \kappa(
Q). r = [(d_k)]. By @exm-truncations-equivalent, (d_k) \sim (x_k), so the classes are equal. So 
R contains a positive element whose square is 2, and 
Q contains none. It is the number Chapter 4 promised, and the decimal truncations name the same number as the Newton sequence. Section 4.6 noted that the rationals 2/x_n approach the gap from below while the x_n approach it from above. They name the same real number. The sequence (1/x_n) is in \sC by @prp-cauchy-reciprocal-ordered-field with c = 1 and N = 0, since \abs{x_n} = x_n \ge 1; so (2/x_n) \in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b)). Termwise, x_n -  rac{2}{x_n} =  rac{x_n^2 - 2}{x_n} =  rac{e_n}{x_n} , \qquad 0 <  rac{e_n}{x_n} \le e_n , using 0 < 1/x_n (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)) and 1/x_n \le 1 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (c) with a = 1, b = x_n): then e_n/x_n > 0 as a product of positives (O4), and e_n/x_n \le 1 \cdot e_n = e_n (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)). Since (e_n) is null, the squeeze makes (e_n/x_n) null, so (2/x_n) \sim (x_n) and [(2/x_n)] = r. r is not “the limit of (x_n) in 
Q”: there is no such limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit), and nothing in this section changes that. The statement x_n 	o r holds in 
R, by @thm-terms-converge-to-class; it is a statement about a different field, with different tolerances and a different set of candidate limits. Find a rational number strictly between [(d_k)] and [(d_k + 1/(k + 1))]. There is none, and @thm-constructed-rationals-dense does not apply. The two sequences differ by (1/(k + 1)), which is null, so they are equivalent and the classes are equal. The hypothesis x < y fails, and no number lies strictly between a number and itself. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Show that \kappa(q^k) = \kappa(q)^k for every q \in 
Q and k \in 
N, the powers being those of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field in 
Q and in 
R. 2. Let r be as in @exm-sqrt2-class. Find the integer parts of r and of 10r, and justify each from the terms d_k: use d_1 = 7/5, d_2 = 141/100, and the bounds of @exm-truncations-equivalent. 3. True or false: if a \in \sC, q \in 
Q and a_n < q for every n, then [a] < q. Give a reason or a counterexample. 4. Is \kappa \colon 
Q 	o 
R surjective? (a) By @fd1:ax-induction on k, with base P(0). Base: \kappa(q^0) = \kappa(1) = 1_{
R} = \kappa(q)^0, by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) in 
Q and in 
R and @thm-rational-embedding (a). Step: if \kappa(q^k) = \kappa(q)^k, then \kappa(q^{k+1}) = \kappa(q^k q) = \kappa(q^k) \, \kappa(q) = \kappa(q)^k \, \kappa(q) = \kappa(q)^{k+1} , by the defining equation of powers, @thm-rational-embedding (a), and the induction hypothesis. In particular \kappa(q^2) = \kappa(q)^2, the step used in @exm-sqrt2-class. (b) By @exm-truncations-equivalent, (d_k) is non-decreasing, and d_j < d_k + 1/10^k whenever j \ge k. With k = 2: for every j \ge 2,  rac{7}{5} = d_1 \le d_j < d_2 +  rac{1}{100} =  rac{142}{100} =  rac{71}{50} . By @lem-termwise-order with N_0 = 2, and r = [(d_k)] (@exm-sqrt2-class), 7/5 \le r \le 71/50. Since 1 \le 7/5 and 71/50 < 2, 1 \le r < 2, so the integer part of r is 1. Multiplying by 10 > 0 in 
R (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed), 14 \le 10r \le 71/5 < 15, so the integer part of 10r is 14. (c) False. Take a_n \coloneqq q - 1/(n + 1). Here a \in \sC: (q)_n is constant and (1/(n + 1)) is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), so both are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and so is their difference (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b)). Then a_n < q for every n, and a - (q)_n = (-1/(n + 1)) is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)), so [a] = \kappa(q), and [a] < \kappa(q) fails. The correct conclusion is [a] \le q (@lem-termwise-order); see the warning after it. (d) No. By @exm-sqrt2-class, r \in 
R is not \kappa(q) for any q \in 
Q. B. Practice [B1] Deduce @thm-constructed-rationals-dense from @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field and @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean. Then say which hypothesis each of the two proofs uses that the other does not. By @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, 
R is an Archimedean ordered field. So @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field applies with F = 
R: for x < y in 
R there is q \in 
Q with x < \iota_{
R}(q) < y. By @thm-rational-embedding (d), \iota_{
R}(q) = \kappa(q), which is the conclusion of @thm-constructed-rationals-dense. The general theorem of Chapter 4 uses that F is Archimedean; it knows nothing about representatives, since an element of an arbitrary ordered field is not a class of sequences. The direct proof of @thm-constructed-rationals-dense uses the Cauchy property of the representatives a and b, and positivity of b - a; it uses no Archimedean property, neither @thm-rationals-archimedean nor @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean. [B2] Let x \in 
R. For k \in 
N, let m_k be the integer part of (k + 1)x, and q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1) \in 
Q. Prove that q_k \le x < q_k + 1/(k + 1) for every k, and that q_k 	o x in 
R. Fix k \in 
N. By the definition of the integer part (after @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), m_k \le (k + 1)x < m_k + 1. Since k + 1 > 0, also 1/(k + 1) > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), and multiplying by it in 
R preserves both inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed on the left): q_k =  rac{m_k}{k + 1} \le x <  rac{m_k + 1}{k + 1} = q_k +  rac{1}{k + 1} . So 0 \le x - q_k < 1/(k + 1) for every k. In 
R, the sequence (1/(k + 1)), that is (1/((k + 1) \cdot 1_{
R})) by @thm-rational-embedding (c), (d), is null, by @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean and @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) in 
R, with lower sequence (0), gives that (x - q_k) is null. Then (q_k - x) is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)), so q_k 	o x (@prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field). Each q_k is given by a rule: the integer part of (k + 1)x is the only integer with the defining property, so nothing is chosen. Section 5.5 uses the same approximants, with a different real number x_k for each k. [B3: Put the proof in order] The lines below, after the identification paragraph (so q stands for \kappa(q)), contain the proof of @thm-terms-converge-to-class for a \in \sC, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Put the correct lines in order, and say what is wrong with each of the other two. 1. so \abs{[a] - a_k} = [(\abs{a_m - a_k})_m], by @prp-reals-absolute-value-termwise; 2. since a \in \sC, fix N with \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) for all m, k \ge N; 3. its terms are < 1/(2n) for m \ge N, so \abs{[a] - a_k} < 1/(2n); 4. 1/(2n) < 1/n; take K = N; 5. let k \ge N; 6. let n \in 
Z_{>0}; by @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (b), it suffices to find K with \abs{[a] - a_k} < 1/n for every k \ge K, since \abs{a_k - [a]} = \abs{[a] - a_k} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)); 7. [a] - a_k is represented by (a_m - a_k)_m; 8. for each k, fix N_k with \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) for every m \ge N_k; 9. its terms are \le 1/(2n) for m \ge N, so \abs{[a] - a_k} \le 1/(2n), by @lem-termwise-order. Order: (vi), (ii), (v), (vii), (i), (ix), (iv). No other order is admissible: line (ii) introduces N, which line (v) needs; line (v) fixes the k that lines (vii), (i) and (ix) are about; line (i) rewrites the class that line (vii) names; line (ix) bounds that class; and line (iv) concludes from line (ix), so it comes last. Line (iii) uses the strict version of @lem-termwise-order, which is false: termwise < passes to classes only as \le (@exm-strict-termwise-order-fails). That is why the proof aims at 1/(2n) and then uses 1/(2n) < 1/n. Line (viii) claims a threshold N_k for every k, and the Cauchy property does not supply one for an early k: a_k can be far from all later terms. For a = (5, 0, 0, \dots) \in \sC, n = 1 and k = 0, \abs{a_m - a_0} = 5 for every m \ge 1, so no N_0 exists. The Cauchy property gives \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) only when both m and k are at least one N, which is why line (v) takes k \ge N. (If line (viii) did hold for every k, the remaining lines would give the bound for every k, so it is the claim that is unjustified, not the dependence on k.) C. Going deeper [C1] 1. Let x \in 
R with \abs{x} \le 1/n for every n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that x = 0. 2. Which result used in your proof needs 
R to be Archimedean? Show that the statement of (a) fails in the ordered field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field. (a) Suppose that \abs{x} > 0. By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (a) with \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{x}, there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \abs{x} for every n \ge N; in particular 1/N < \abs{x}. The hypothesis with n = N gives \abs{x} \le 1/N. These contradict (O1). So \abs{x} > 0 is false, by ulename{
eg I}. Since \abs{x} \ge 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), trichotomy leaves \abs{x} = 0, and then x = 0 by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a). (b) @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (a) rests on @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, through @prp-archimedean-reciprocal. In 
Q(t), @exm-rational-function-field shows 0 < 1/t < 1/(n \cdot 1) for every n \ge 1. So x \coloneqq 1/t satisfies \abs{x} = x \le 1/(n \cdot 1) for every n \ge 1, and x 
e 0. The statement of (a) is a form of the Archimedean property, and it fails without it. [C2] Let r be as in @exm-sqrt2-class. Prove that the set \{ x \in 
R : x 
otin \kappa(
Q) \} of irrational real numbers is dense in 
R: for all x, y \in 
R with x < y there is an irrational z with x < z < y. [Hint 1] Use @thm-constructed-rationals-dense, and the irrational number r. [Hint 2] Let q \in 
Q with x < q < y (@thm-constructed-rationals-dense). How small must r/k be for q + r/k to stay below y? Let x < y. By @thm-constructed-rationals-dense, fix q \in 
Q with x < q < y. Then y - q > 0, and r > 0 (@exm-sqrt2-class), so \varepsilon \coloneqq (y - q)/r \in 
R_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (a), there is k \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/k < \varepsilon. Multiplying by r > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), r/k < y - q. Let z \coloneqq q + r/k. Since r/k > 0, x < q < z < q + (y - q) = y . If z were rational, z = p with p \in 
Q, then r = k(p - q) would be rational, since \kappa preserves differences and products (the identities after @thm-rational-embedding, and its part (a)); this contradicts @exm-sqrt2-class. So z is irrational, and lies strictly between x and y. The same argument works with r replaced by any positive irrational number. Between any two reals there are therefore both rationals and irrationals.

title: 5.5 Every Cauchy Sequence of Reals Converges
content:
Every Cauchy Sequence of Reals Converges We built 
R to fill the holes in 
Q: the Newton sequence is Cauchy in 
Q and has no rational limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit), and in 
R it converges to the class it represents (@thm-terms-converge-to-class, @exm-sqrt2-class). Could 
R have holes of its own, Cauchy sequences of real numbers crowding around nothing? If so, the construction would have to be repeated, with Cauchy sequences of reals in place of Cauchy sequences of rationals, and perhaps again after that. This section proves that it need not be: every Cauchy sequence in 
R converges in 
R. The proof builds the limit from rationals, by a rule, and so uses no axiom of choice. Throughout, F = 
R whenever a result of Chapter 4 is applied, which is legitimate because 
R is an ordered field (@thm-reals-ordered-field). We use the identification of Section 5.4: a rational q also denotes the real number \kappa(q) (@def-rational-embedding). Where an inequality is carried from 
R back to 
Q, we write \kappa out, because that step is where the proof must cite @thm-rational-embedding. The question A sequence (x_k)_{k \in 
N} in 
R is Cauchy in 
R (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field with F = 
R) if for every \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} there is K \in 
N with \abs{x_j - x_k} < \varepsilon for all j, k \ge K. By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (b), it is enough to test the tolerances 1/n with n \in 
Z_{>0}, and the same holds for convergence. So the tolerances may as well be rational; the terms x_k, however, are real numbers, that is, classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). We want a real number x with x_k 	o x. A real number is a class [a] with a \in \sC (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences), so we need a Cauchy sequence of rationals that “is” the limit. Where would its terms come from? The data are the classes x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, each of them an infinite set of sequences. The theorem [The Constructed Reals Are Cauchy-Complete] Every Cauchy sequence (x_k)_{k \in 
N} in 
R (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field, F = 
R) converges in 
R (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, F = 
R). Try it first (ten minutes): given a Cauchy sequence of reals, which Cauchy sequence of rationals would you build, and why would its class be the limit? The obvious candidate is a diagonal. Each x_k has representatives; take one, a^{(k)} \in \sC with [a^{(k)}] = x_k, for each k, and use the diagonal terms a^{(k)}_k. This attempt meets two separate obstacles. - No control. A representative may begin with any finite list of rationals and still represent x_k (@exm-finite-change-equivalent). Its k-th term may be far from x_k, and the diagonal terms need not settle down at all. Exercise C2 below turns this into a counterexample. - No rule. “Take one representative for each k” picks one element from each of infinitely many sets, with no rule saying which. That is an instance of the axiom of choice (@fd2:ax-choice), which the construction of 
R has not used so far. One device removes both: replace x_k by a single rational q_k within 1/(k + 1) of it, named by a formula. The plan has three steps. ① The q_k form a member of \sC. Compare q_j with q_k through the reals x_j and x_k: \abs{q_j - q_k} \le \abs{q_j - x_j} + \abs{x_j - x_k} + \abs{x_k - q_k}. The outer two are small once j, k are large, by the choice of the approximant; the middle one is small because (x_k) is Cauchy. Give each a third of \varepsilon. ② Its class is a candidate. Let x \coloneqq [(q_k)_k]. A term approximates its class (@thm-terms-converge-to-class), so q_k 	o x in 
R. ③ The candidate is the limit. x_k is near q_k, which is near x: give each half of the tolerance. The tolerance in ① must be rational, since membership of \sC is tested with \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences); the triangle inequality, however, is used in 
R, where the x_k live. Step 1 of the proof ends by carrying the inequality back to 
Q through \kappa (@thm-rational-embedding). The formula: q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1), where m_k is the integer part of (k + 1) x_k in the Archimedean field 
R. Before reading on: why must m_k be the integer part, and not just some integer with m_k \le (k + 1) x_k < m_k + 1? Let (x_k) be a Cauchy sequence in 
R. Step 0: the approximants. For k \in 
N, let m_k \in 
Z be the integer part of (k + 1) x_k in 
R (@prp-integer-part-ordered-field with F = 
R, which is Archimedean by @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean; there \iota_{
R} = \kappa by @thm-rational-embedding (d)), and let q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1) \in 
Q. Since the integer part is unique, k \mapsto q_k is a function 
N 	o 
Q (@fd2:def-function); no use of @fd2:ax-choice is made. Multiplying m_k \le (k + 1) x_k < m_k + 1 by the positive element 1/(k + 1) (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), and using \kappa(m_k)\kappa(k + 1)^{-1} = \kappa(q_k) (@thm-rational-embedding (a), (c)), we get 0 \le x_k - \kappa(q_k) < \kappa\Bigl( rac{1}{k + 1}\Bigr) \qquad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . {#eq-approximant-bound} Step 1: (q_k) \in \sC. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon there is K_1 \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon/3 for every integer m \ge K_1; for k \ge K_1, the integer k + 1 is \ge K_1, so 1/(k + 1) < \varepsilon/3. Next, \kappa(\varepsilon/3) \in 
R_{>0} by @thm-rational-embedding (b), since \varepsilon/3 > 0 and \kappa(0) = 0. As (x_k) is Cauchy in 
R, there is K_2 \in 
N with \abs{x_j - x_k} < \kappa(\varepsilon/3) for all j, k \ge K_2; fix one such K_2 [ulename{\exists E}], one object for this one \varepsilon. Let K \coloneqq \max\{K_1, K_2\}; it depends on \varepsilon (and on the sequence) only. Let j, k \ge K. By @eq-approximant-bound and @thm-rational-embedding (b), \abs{x_j - \kappa(q_j)} < \kappa(1/(j + 1)) < \kappa(\varepsilon/3), and likewise for k. The triangle inequality in 
R (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), applied twice, with \abs{-y} = \abs{y} from (b)) and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) give  egin{aligned} \abs{\kappa(q_j) - \kappa(q_k)} &\le \abs{\kappa(q_j) - x_j} + \abs{x_j - x_k} + \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} \ &< \kappa(\varepsilon/3) + \kappa(\varepsilon/3) + \kappa(\varepsilon/3) = \kappa(\varepsilon) , \end{aligned} where the last equality is @thm-rational-embedding (a). By @thm-rational-embedding (a) and (c), \abs{\kappa(q_j) - \kappa(q_k)} = \abs{\kappa(q_j - q_k)} = \kappa(\abs{q_j - q_k}). So \kappa(\abs{q_j - q_k}) < \kappa(\varepsilon), and @thm-rational-embedding (b) gives \abs{q_j - q_k} < \varepsilon in 
Q. Hence (q_k) is Cauchy in 
Q: (q_k) \in \sC. Step 2: the candidate. Let x \coloneqq [(q_k)_k] \in 
R (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). By @thm-terms-converge-to-class, \kappa(q_k) 	o x in 
R. Step 3: x_k 	o x. By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (b) it suffices to find, for each n \in 
Z_{>0}, a K \in 
N with \abs{x_k - x} < \kappa(1/n) for every k \ge K. Let n \in 
Z_{>0}. The tolerance \kappa(1/(2n)) is in 
R_{>0}, so Step 2 gives K_3 \in 
N with \abs{\kappa(q_k) - x} < \kappa(1/(2n)) for every k \ge K_3. For k \ge 2n we have k + 1 > 2n, so 1/(k + 1) < 1/(2n) (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)), and @eq-approximant-bound with @thm-rational-embedding (b) gives \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} < \kappa(1/(2n)). Let K \coloneqq \max\{K_3, 2n\}; it depends on n only. For k \ge K,  egin{aligned} \abs{x_k - x} &\le \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} + \abs{\kappa(q_k) - x} \ &< \kappa\Bigl( rac{1}{2n}\Bigr) + \kappa\Bigl( rac{1}{2n}\Bigr) = \kappa\Bigl( rac{1}{n}\Bigr) , \end{aligned} by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e) and @thm-rational-embedding (a). So x_k 	o x in 
R. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt about m_k: existence alone would give, for each k, a non-empty set of admissible integers, and taking one from each of these infinitely many sets, with no rule, is again a use of choice. Uniqueness makes each of these sets a singleton, so “the integer part of (k + 1) x_k” names one integer for each k, and Step 0 defines a function outright. Existence of an integer part would not be enough; the proof needs the uniqueness half of @prp-integer-part-ordered-field. Where is each hypothesis used? The Cauchy property of (x_k) is used once, for K_2 in Step 1; Step 3 uses only the approximants and Step 2. The Archimedean property of 
R is used in Step 0, through the integer part, and in Steps 2 and 3, through @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (b) (cited in Step 3 and in the proof of @thm-terms-converge-to-class); the Archimedean property of 
Q is used in Step 1, for K_1. Without the Cauchy hypothesis the conclusion fails: the sequence x_k = k has approximants q_k = k, which do not form a member of \sC, and it converges to nothing in 
R, being unbounded (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field, with @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean for the unboundedness). Real numbers have no holes of their own. Together with @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field (with F = 
R), the theorem says that a sequence in 
R converges in 
R if and only if it is Cauchy in 
R. In 
Q the “only if” half holds (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field, F = 
Q), and the “if” half fails (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). A second round of the construction, starting from Cauchy sequences of reals, would find every such sequence already convergent: there is no hole left for it to fill. The approximant, by a rule Step 0 is the heart of the proof, so we look at it again. By @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, 
R is an Archimedean ordered field. So @prp-integer-part-ordered-field applies with F = 
R, with \kappa in the role of \iota_{
R} (@thm-rational-embedding (d)): for every y \in 
R there is exactly one m \in 
Z with m \le y < m + 1, the integer part of y. For a real number x_k and the positive integer k + 1, Step 0 applies this to y = (k + 1) x_k and divides by k + 1:  rac{m_k}{k + 1} \le x_k <  rac{m_k}{k + 1} +  rac{1}{k + 1} . The rational q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1) is the largest multiple of 1/(k + 1) that does not exceed x_k, and it is within 1/(k + 1) of x_k. Picture the multiples of 1/(k + 1) as a ladder of rungs; q_k is the rung at or just below x_k, and the ladder gets finer as k grows. The word that matters is exactly. For each k the set of integers m with m \le (k + 1) x_k < m + 1 has one element, so the relation “q_k = m/(k + 1) for the m with m \le (k + 1) x_k < m + 1” assigns exactly one rational to each k \in 
N: it is a function 
N 	o 
Q (@fd2:def-function), given by a rule. Nothing is picked. Let r be the real number of @exm-sqrt2-class, so r > 0 and r^2 = 2, and let x_k \coloneqq r + 1/(k + 1). Compute q_0, q_1 and q_2. First locate r: (7/5)^2 = 49/25 < 2 < 9/4 = (3/2)^2. If r < 7/5, then r^2 < 49/25 < 2, and if r \ge 3/2, then r^2 \ge 9/4 > 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), with r > 0); both contradict r^2 = 2, so 7/5 \le r < 3/2. Next, (k + 1) x_k = (k + 1) r + 1. For k = 0: 12/5 \le r + 1 < 5/2, and 2 \le 12/5, 5/2 < 3, so m_0 = 2. For k = 1: 19/5 \le 2r + 1 < 4, and 3 \le 19/5, so m_1 = 3. For k = 2: 26/5 \le 3r + 1 < 11/2, and 5 \le 26/5, 11/2 < 6, so m_2 = 5. Hence q_0 = 2 , \qquad q_1 =  rac{3}{2} , \qquad q_2 =  rac{5}{3} . Each q_k is within 1/(k + 1) below x_k; for instance x_2 = r + 1/3 \in [26/15, 11/6) and q_2 = 5/3 = 25/15. Choice, and why it was not needed The proof used \existsE many times: to fix K_1, K_2, K_3. Each of those fixes one object, for one given \varepsilon or n, and is ordinary logic. The axiom of choice is something else: one pick from each of infinitely many sets at once, with no rule. The next example shows exactly where it would have entered. [Picking Representatives Is a Use of Choice] Let (x_k) be a sequence in 
R. A proof that says “for each k, pick a representative a^{(k)} \in x_k” asks for what? And does the proof of @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete ask for it? Each x_k is a class, a non-empty subset of \sC (@fd2:def-equivalence-class). The family (x_k)_{k \in 
N} is a family of non-empty sets indexed by 
N, and “pick a^{(k)} \in x_k for each k” asks for a function c \colon 
N 	o \sC with c(k) \in x_k for every k: a choice function for the family. Its existence, with no rule given, is what @fd2:ax-choice provides. A single \existsE would give one representative of one x_k; it cannot give infinitely many in one step. The proof of @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete never picks a representative of any x_k. It uses each x_k only as an element of the ordered field 
R (its arithmetic and order, in Steps 0, 1 and 3), never through a representative; the Cauchy condition on (x_k) enters only in Step 1. The only sequence it builds, (q_k), is given by a rule. So @fd2:ax-choice is not used. In fact the theorem produces a rule for representatives as a by-product. Run its construction on the constant sequence x_k = y for a fixed y \in 
R, which is Cauchy in 
R (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). Step 1 shows that the approximants q_k = m_k/(k + 1), with m_k the integer part of (k + 1) y, form a member of \sC, and Step 3 that the constant sequence y converges to [(q_k)]. It also converges to y (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)), so [(q_k)] = y by @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field. Thus (q_k) is a representative of y, named by a formula in y. Choice is not needed for representatives at all; what goes wrong is picking them without saying how. The uncontrolled diagonal. Even with representatives in hand, the diagonal term a^{(k)}_k need not be near x_k. A representative of x_k may start with any finite list of rationals (@exm-finite-change-equivalent): for x_k = 0 for every k, the sequence equal to k at the indices n \le k and to 0 afterwards represents 0, and its k-th term is k. Approximating x_k needs a bound, such as \abs{x_k - q_k} < 1/(k + 1), and a term of an arbitrary representative carries none. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete. 1. Why \varepsilon/3 in Step 1? Which three distances does it bound, and in which field is each of them measured? 2. Why 1/(2n) in Step 3, for each of the two distances there? 3. Where is the Cauchy property of (x_k) used? Is it used in Step 3? 4. Run the construction on the constant sequence x_k = r (the real number of @exm-sqrt2-class). Which class is x? 5. Write “(x_k) converges in 
R” in symbols, and its negation. (a) Step 1 bounds \abs{q_j - q_k} through x_j and x_k: the three distances are \abs{\kappa(q_j) - x_j} and \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)}, each below \kappa(1/(j + 1)) or \kappa(1/(k + 1)) by the choice of approximant, and \abs{x_j - x_k}, small because (x_k) is Cauchy. All three are measured in 
R; only the conclusion \abs{q_j - q_k} < \varepsilon is carried back to 
Q. Three thirds make one \varepsilon. (b) Two distances are added: \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} < \kappa(1/(2n)) for k \ge 2n, from the approximant bound, and \abs{\kappa(q_k) - x} < \kappa(1/(2n)) for k \ge K_3, from @thm-terms-converge-to-class. Two halves make 1/n. (c) Only in Step 1, for the threshold K_2. Step 3 uses the approximant bound and Step 2, not the Cauchy property directly: by then it has been spent on making (q_k) a member of \sC. (d) The approximants are q_k = m_k/(k + 1), with m_k the integer part of (k + 1) r, and x \coloneqq [(q_k)]. By the theorem’s proof, x_k 	o x; the constant sequence r also tends to r, so x = r by @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field. Concretely, q_0 = 1, q_1 = 1 (since 2 \le 2r < 3), q_2 = 4/3 (since 4 \le 3r < 5): a third sequence of rationals, besides the Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2 and the truncations (d_k), both in the class r by @exm-sqrt2-class. (e) Converges: \exists x \in 
R \  orall \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} \ \exists K \in 
N \  orall k \in 
N \ (k \ge K \Rightarrow \abs{x_k - x} < \varepsilon). Negation (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication, and 
eg(y < \varepsilon) read as y \ge \varepsilon by (O1)):  orall x \in 
R \ \ \exists \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} \ \  orall K \in 
N \ \ \exists k \in 
N \ \  igl( k \ge K \wedge \abs{x_k - x} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . Every candidate is beaten by some tolerance beyond every threshold. B. Practice [B1] Which results of Chapter 4, applied with F = 
R, show that in 
R every convergent sequence is Cauchy and has only one limit? Why may they be applied? Deduce that a sequence in 
R converges if and only if it is Cauchy. @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field (convergent sequences are Cauchy) and @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field (uniqueness of limits). Both are proved in Chapter 4 for an arbitrary ordered field F, and 
R is an ordered field by @thm-reals-ordered-field, so they apply with F = 
R and tolerances in 
R_{>0}. If (x_k) converges in 
R, it is Cauchy in 
R by the first; if it is Cauchy in 
R, it converges by @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete. So the two properties coincide in 
R, and the limit is unique by the second. [B2] Let (p_k) be a sequence of rationals such that (\kappa(p_k))_k converges in 
R to some x. Prove that (p_k) \in \sC and that x = [(p_k)]. Hint: a convergent sequence is Cauchy. By @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field with F = 
R, (\kappa(p_k)) is Cauchy in 
R. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. Then \kappa(\varepsilon) \in 
R_{>0} (@thm-rational-embedding (b)), so there is K with \abs{\kappa(p_j) - \kappa(p_k)} < \kappa(\varepsilon) for j, k \ge K. As in Step 1 of the proof of @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete, the left side is \kappa(\abs{p_j - p_k}) (@thm-rational-embedding (a), (c)), and @thm-rational-embedding (b) gives \abs{p_j - p_k} < \varepsilon. So (p_k) is Cauchy in 
Q, that is, (p_k) \in \sC. By @thm-terms-converge-to-class, \kappa(p_k) 	o [(p_k)]. Also \kappa(p_k) 	o x. By @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field with F = 
R, x = [(p_k)]. So the real numbers that are limits of sequences of rationals in 
R are exactly the classes of those sequences; with @thm-terms-converge-to-class, every real number is one. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: Cauchy completeness] Prove that every Cauchy sequence in 
R converges in 
R. Say where the axiom of choice could have entered your proof, and why it does not. Let (x_k) be Cauchy in 
R. Approximants by a rule. For k \in 
N let m_k be the integer part of (k + 1) x_k, unique by @prp-integer-part-ordered-field (
R is Archimedean, @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), and q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1). Then 0 \le x_k - q_k < 1/(k + 1), and k \mapsto q_k is a function because the integer part is unique. This is where choice could have entered: “for each k take some rational within 1/(k + 1) of x_k”, or “take a representative of each x_k”, makes infinitely many picks with no rule, a use of @fd2:ax-choice. The integer part names one rational for each k, so no choice is made. Cauchy in 
Q. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. Fix K_1 with 1/(k + 1) < \varepsilon/3 for k \ge K_1 (@cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon) and K_2 with \abs{x_j - x_k} < \varepsilon/3 for j, k \ge K_2 (the Cauchy property, at the positive real \kappa(\varepsilon/3)). For j, k \ge \max\{K_1, K_2\}, the triangle inequality in 
R gives \abs{q_j - q_k} < \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon in 
R; since \kappa preserves sums, absolute values and order and reflects order (@thm-rational-embedding (a)–(c)), the same inequality holds in 
Q. So (q_k) \in \sC. The limit. Let x \coloneqq [(q_k)]. By @thm-terms-converge-to-class, q_k 	o x in 
R. Let \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0}. By @cor-rational-epsilon-suffices (a) there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon. Fix K_3 with \abs{q_k - x} < 1/(2n) for k \ge K_3. For k \ge \max\{K_3, 2n\}, \abs{x_k - x} \le \abs{x_k - q_k} + \abs{q_k - x} < 1/(2n) + 1/(2n) = 1/n < \varepsilon. So x_k 	o x. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: an approximant q_k \in 
Q defined by a rule (unique integer part, or another explicit formula), with an explicit bound on \abs{x_k - q_k} tending to 0. - 3: (q_k) \in \sC by an \varepsilon/3 (or equivalent) estimate, with rational \varepsilon and the passage from 
R back to 
Q through \kappa justified. - 1: the candidate x = [(q_k)] named. - 2: q_k 	o x in 
R, by @thm-terms-converge-to-class, or directly as in its proof: \abs{x - \kappa(q_k)} = [(\abs{q_m - q_k})_m] (@prp-reals-absolute-value-termwise), bounded through @lem-termwise-order, which gives only \le. Either route earns both points. - 2: x_k 	o x, with the threshold chosen after the tolerance and depending on it only. Fatal errors (0 for the step): approximants or representatives “chosen” with no rule and no mention of choice; a real \varepsilon used to test membership of \sC; “q_k 	o x because x is the limit of (q_k)” (circular: that is what @thm-terms-converge-to-class proves). A proof that uses choice openly (representatives, with a threshold for each) and says so proves the theorem, but earns at most 1 of the 2 points of the first step, since the question asks for a construction that avoids it. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument for @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete. Is its conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the first line that fails and why. (1) Let (x_k) be a Cauchy sequence in 
R. (2) For each k \in 
N, pick a representative a^{(k)} \in \sC of x_k. (3) Let q_k \coloneqq a^{(k)}_k, the k-th term of the k-th representative. (4) The sequence (q_k) is Cauchy in 
Q, and \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} 	o 0 in 
R, since each a^{(k)} is Cauchy and (x_k) is Cauchy. (5) Let x \coloneqq [(q_k)]. Then x_k 	o x, by an \varepsilon/2 argument through the terms q_k. [Hint 1] Ask whether a^{(k)}_k has to be close to x_k at all. [Hint 2] Try the constant sequence x_k = 0 for every k, and representatives that are not 0 at their first few terms. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete. The failing line is (4). Each a^{(k)} being Cauchy says that the terms of one representative settle down eventually, past a threshold that depends on k; nothing ties the k-th term of a^{(k)} to x_k, and nothing ties different representatives to each other at index k. The Cauchy property of (x_k) is about the classes, and the line uses it as if it were about the diagonal terms. Counterexample to the step. Let x_k = 0 for every k, a Cauchy sequence in 
R. For each k, let a^{(k)}_n \coloneqq k for n \le k and a^{(k)}_n \coloneqq 0 for n > k. Each a^{(k)} is eventually equal to the zero sequence, so it is in \sC and represents 0 (@exm-finite-change-equivalent). Then q_k = a^{(k)}_k = k, and (k) is not Cauchy in 
Q: consecutive terms satisfy \abs{q_{k+1} - q_k} = 1, so the Cauchy condition fails for \varepsilon = 1. Nor does \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} = \kappa(k) tend to 0: it is \ge 1 for every k \ge 1. The premises of (4) hold and both parts of its conclusion fail. A second, separate defect: line (2). “For each k, pick” makes one pick from each of infinitely many classes with no rule: an unflagged use of @fd2:ax-choice (@exm-representatives-need-choice). Even if (4) were repaired, the argument would use choice without saying so. Line (5) is correct given (4): \kappa(q_k) 	o x in 
R by @thm-terms-converge-to-class, and \abs{x_k - x} \le \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} + \abs{\kappa(q_k) - x}. The bound on \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} is needed: knowing only that (q_k) is Cauchy would not do (with a^{(k)}_n = 1 for n \le k and 0 after, q_k = 1 for every k, yet x_k = 0 does not tend to [(1)] = 1). Repair. Either keep representatives and control the diagonal (for each k, go far enough out in a^{(k)} that its terms are within 1/(k + 1) of x_k, which @thm-terms-converge-to-class makes possible, and use that term in place of a^{(k)}_k), at the price of a choice of representatives and of thresholds, flagged; or, better, drop representatives and use the integer-part approximant q_k = m_k/(k + 1) of the text, which needs no choice at all. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the conclusion is true, and cites the theorem. - 3: identifies line (4) as the failing line, and says why: nothing ties a^{(k)}_k to a^{(j)}_j for j 
e k, or to x_k. - 3: a counterexample to the step, with every representative checked to lie in its class. - 2: names the use of choice in line (2), and a repair that replaces q_k by a rational with a bound on \abs{x_k - \kappa(q_k)} tending to 0 (a later term of a^{(k)}, or the integer-part approximant). Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the conclusion false; a “counterexample” in which the sequence (x_k) is not Cauchy.

title: 5.6 The Real Numbers Form a Complete Ordered Field
content:
The Real Numbers Form a Complete Ordered Field Section 5.5 proved one form of completeness: in 
R every Cauchy sequence converges (@thm-constructed-reals-cauchy-complete). Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 starts from another form, about sets rather than sequences: every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound. In 
Q both fail, the first by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit and the second by @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2. This section names the second property for an arbitrary ordered field, proves that an ordered field that is Archimedean and Cauchy-complete has it, and concludes that the constructed 
R is a complete ordered field. The proof bisects intervals, and one line of it, which we shall point at, cannot do without Archimedes. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field). Its order \le is a total order (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)), so the words “upper bound”, “bounded above” and “supremum” of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 apply to subsets of F (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). When F = 
R, we keep the identification of Section 5.4, writing q for \kappa(q). Complete ordered fields Section 2.6 found a gap in 
Q without any sequence: the set A = \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above in 
Q, and among its rational upper bounds there is no least one (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). The upper bounds crowd down toward a place where 
Q has no element. A field without such gaps is one in which every set that could have a least upper bound does have one. Every non-empty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound. [Complete Ordered Field] An ordered field F is complete if every non-empty subset A \subseteq F that is bounded above in (F, \le) (@fd2:def-order-bounds) has a supremum in F (@fd2:def-order-supremum). In symbols, writing \mathrm{ub}(u) for  orall a \in A \ \ a \le u,  egin{aligned} & orall A \subseteq F \ \  igl( (A 
e \emptyset \wedge \exists u \in F \ \mathrm{ub}(u)) \Rightarrow \ &\qquad \exists s \in F \  igl( \mathrm{ub}(s) \wedge  orall u \in F \ (\mathrm{ub}(u) \Rightarrow s \le u)  igr)  igr) . \end{aligned} An ordered field in which every Cauchy sequence (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field) converges is called Cauchy-complete. In words: the hypothesis asks for a set with at least one element and at least one upper bound in F; the conclusion asks for an element s of F that is an upper bound, clause (S1), and lies below every upper bound, clause (S2). The supremum need not belong to A. Well-definedness. A set has at most one supremum: if s and s' both are, then (S2) for each, with the other as the upper bound, gives s \le s' and s' \le s, so s = s' by antisymmetry. So “the supremum of A”, written \sup A, names one element when it exists. Examples. The negative elements. In every ordered field, A \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x < 0 \} has supremum 0. It is non-empty (-1 \in A). The element 0 is an upper bound. If an upper bound b had b < 0, then b < b/2 < 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), so b/2 \in A lies above b, which is impossible. So every upper bound b satisfies b \ge 0, and \sup A = 0 
otin A. No completeness was needed: some sets have suprema in every ordered field. The rationals. 
Q is not complete: @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 exhibits a non-empty subset bounded above with no supremum in 
Q. The constructed reals. 
R is complete; this is the main theorem of the section, proved at its end. A singleton. \sup \{a\} = a, in every ordered field. This degenerate case matters below: a set may be bounded above by its own element. Drop “non-empty”: the empty set is bounded above by every element of F, so its upper bounds are all of F, and F has no least element (x - 1 < x). Drop “bounded above”: F itself has no upper bound (x < x + 1), so no supremum. With either clause removed, no ordered field at all would be complete. Why this definition. It asks about suprema, not maxima: the set of negative elements has no greatest element in any ordered field, since x < x/2 < 0 for x < 0, and asking for maxima would make no field complete. It asks about sets, not sequences, the form Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes as its axiom. “Complete” alone always means this property; the sequence property of Section 5.5 is “Cauchy-complete”. The supremum of a set is an upper bound not necessarily in the set, and “complete” is not “every non-empty bounded set has a largest element”: the set of negative elements above has supremum 0 and no largest element. A proof that ends “so \sup A \in A” needs a reason, such as A being finite. So 
Q is neither complete nor Cauchy-complete. Section 5.5 removed the second gap for 
R; this section removes the first. Powers of two in an ordered field The bisection below halves an interval at each step, so after k steps its length is the first length divided by 2^k. We need 2^k to grow at least as fast as k + 1, inside the field. [A Lower Bound for Powers of Two] Let F be an ordered field, and let (2 \cdot 1_F)^k be the power in F of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). Then (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_F \qquad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . In particular (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge 1_F > 0. Induction on k. Multiplying by 2 doubles the right side, (k + 1) + (k + 1), and doubling gains at least 1, which is all the step needs. We use @fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b), for P(k): (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_F. Base P(0). (2 \cdot 1_F)^0 = 1_F by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), and (0 + 1) \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F = 0 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 1_F by (a) of that definition, since 0 + 1 = 1 (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)). Equality holds. Step. Assume P(k), and let y \coloneqq (k + 1) \cdot 1_F. By @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a) and @def-omega-arithmetic (c), 2 \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 1_F + 1_F, which is positive (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). By @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), P(k), and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (or equality, if P(k) holds with equality), (2 \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k (2 \cdot 1_F) \ge y (1_F + 1_F) = y + y , the last step by distributivity (F9) and (F7). Since k + 1 \ge 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)), @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) gives y \ge 1_F, so y + y \ge y + 1_F (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). Finally y + 1_F = ((k + 1) + 1) \cdot 1_F by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). Hence (2 \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} \ge ((k + 1) + 1) \cdot 1_F, which is P(k + 1). The last sentence of the lemma follows, since (k + 1) \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), as k + 1 \ge 1). From here on, 2^k means (2 \cdot 1_F)^k. By @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (c) it equals (2^k) \cdot 1_F, the multiple of 1_F by the natural number 2^k, so the two readings agree; the proofs below use only the power in F and the lemma. Since 2^k > 0, the quotient D/2^k is defined for every D \in F. From Cauchy-complete to complete [Archimedean and Cauchy-Complete Implies Complete] Let F be an ordered field that is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field) and Cauchy-complete (@def-complete-ordered-field). Then F is complete. Given A, we want a point s that is an upper bound and below every upper bound. Trap it. Start with an interval [l_0, u_0] whose right end is an upper bound of A and whose left end is not. Halve it: if the midpoint is an upper bound, it becomes the new right end; if not, the new left end. Bisect and keep the invariant: right end an upper bound, left end not. The right ends decrease and the left ends increase, and both stay within the current interval, whose length is D/2^k. If that length goes to 0, the right ends form a Cauchy sequence, and Cauchy-completeness gives a limit s. Then s is an upper bound because every right end is, and it is the least one because left ends, which are not upper bounds, come arbitrarily close to it. Step roadmap: ① the starting interval; ② the bisection, defined by a rule, and its invariants; ③ the lengths D/2^k tend to 0; ④ (u_k) converges to some s; ⑤ s is the supremum. Before reading on: which of these steps uses that F is Archimedean? Let A \subseteq F be non-empty and bounded above. Step 1: the starting interval. Fix a_0 \in A [ulename{\exists E}] and an upper bound M of A [ulename{\exists E}]; each is one object, fixed once, and no choice is involved. Let l_0 \coloneqq a_0 - 1, u_0 \coloneqq M and D \coloneqq u_0 - l_0. Then l_0 < a_0 \le M = u_0, so D > 0; u_0 is an upper bound of A; and l_0 is not, because a_0 \in A and a_0 > l_0. Step 2: the bisection. Define g \colon 
N 	imes (F 	imes F) 	o F 	imes F by g igl(k, (l, u) igr) \coloneqq  egin{cases} (l, c) & 	ext{if } c 	ext{ is an upper bound of } A , \ (c, u) & 	ext{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad c \coloneqq  rac{l + u}{2} . For each input exactly one case applies, so g is a function, given by a rule. By @fd2:thm-recursion (read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b)), with X = F 	imes F and starting value (l_0, u_0), there is exactly one sequence k \mapsto (l_k, u_k) with (l_{k+1}, u_{k+1}) = g(k, (l_k, u_k)) for every k. We prove by induction on k that, for every k \in 
N: 1. u_k is an upper bound of A; 2. l_k is not an upper bound of A; 3. u_k - l_k = D/2^k. The base is Step 1, with D/2^0 = D/1_F = D. Suppose (I1)–(I3) hold for k, and let c \coloneqq (l_k + u_k)/2. Then c - l_k = u_k - c = (u_k - l_k)/2 = D/(2^k \cdot 2) = D/2^{k+1}, by field arithmetic (@lem-field-fraction-rules (b)) and @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). If c is an upper bound, then (l_{k+1}, u_{k+1}) = (l_k, c): the right end c is an upper bound, the left end l_k is not, by (I2), and c - l_k = D/2^{k+1}. Otherwise (l_{k+1}, u_{k+1}) = (c, u_k): the left end c is not an upper bound, the right end u_k is, by (I1), and u_k - c = D/2^{k+1}. This proves (I1)–(I3) for k + 1. By (I3), u_k - l_k = D/2^k > 0, so l_k < c < u_k (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)); in either case l_k \le l_{k+1} and u_{k+1} \le u_k. By induction on i, l_k \le l_{k+i} and u_{k+i} \le u_k for every i \in 
N, and every j \ge k is k + i for some i (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). So for j \ge k, l_k \le l_j < u_j \le u_k, and therefore 0 \le u_k - u_j \le u_k - l_k =  rac{D}{2^k} \qquad (j \ge k) . {#eq-bisection-tail} Step 3: the lengths tend to 0. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since F is Archimedean, there is n \in 
N with  rac{D}{\varepsilon} < n \cdot 1_F . {#eq-bisection-archimedes} Let k \ge n. By @lem-power-two-bound and @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), 2^k \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_F > k \cdot 1_F \ge n \cdot 1_F > D/\varepsilon > 0. By @prp-reciprocal-order (b), 1/2^k < (D/\varepsilon)^{-1} = \varepsilon/D (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), and multiplying by D > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives D/2^k < \varepsilon. So \abs{D/2^k - 0} < \varepsilon for every k \ge n: the sequence (D/2^k)_k is null. Consequently (u_k) is Cauchy in F: for \varepsilon and n as above and j, k \ge n, say j \ge k (the other case is symmetric), @eq-bisection-tail gives \abs{u_j - u_k} = \abs{u_k - u_j} = u_k - u_j \le D/2^k < \varepsilon (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), @def-absolute-value-ordered-field). Steps 1–3 use only that F is an Archimedean ordered field. Step 4 is the only one that uses Cauchy-completeness. Step 4: the limit. Since F is Cauchy-complete, (u_k) converges; fix s \in F with u_k 	o s [ulename{\exists E}]. Since l_k = u_k - D/2^k and D/2^k 	o 0, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b) gives l_k 	o s - 0 = s. Step 5: s is the supremum. (S1): let a \in A. By (I1), a \le u_k for every k, so a \le s by @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (b). So s is an upper bound of A. (S2): let b be an upper bound of A, and suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that b < s. Then \varepsilon \coloneqq s - b > 0, and since l_k 	o s there is K with \abs{l_k - s} < \varepsilon for k \ge K; in particular l_K > s - \varepsilon = b (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). By (I2), l_K is not an upper bound: some a \in A has a 
ot\le l_K (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a)), that is, a > l_K by totality (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). Then a > l_K > b, against b being an upper bound. So b < s is false, and s \le b by (O1). By (S1) and (S2), s = \sup A (@fd2:def-order-supremum). Since A was an arbitrary non-empty subset bounded above, F is complete. The answer to the prompt: Step 3, and only the line @eq-bisection-archimedes. The rest of Step 3 is algebra in F and @lem-power-two-bound, which hold in every ordered field.
