The approximants m_k/(k + 1) of Section 5.5 are \le x but not always strictly increasing (for x = 0 they are all 0). The rational between two reals from the proof of @thm-constructed-rationals-dense is a midpoint of terms of representatives at thresholds fixed by \existsE: it is not given by a rule in the data (k, q), so it cannot serve as a recursion step. And “at each step take some rational between L and x” makes one pick for each k with no rule, an unflagged use of @fd2:ax-choice (compare @exm-representatives-need-choice).

title: The Complete Ordered Field Is Unique
content:
The Complete Ordered Field Is Unique Chapter 5 ended with one complete ordered field, whose elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals. The optional Chapter 7 builds another, whose elements are sets of rationals, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 builds none: it assumes that a complete ordered field exists and calls it 
R. Are these the same 
R? The axioms of an ordered field alone do not decide it. The field 
R(x) of rational functions, compared at large arguments, satisfies all of them and has an element above every natural number; the field 
Q(\sqrt 2) is even Archimedean, and still 3 has no square root in it. This chapter proves that completeness is the property that pins 
R down: any two complete ordered fields are linked by an order-preserving field isomorphism, and by only one. So “the” real numbers are well defined, and no theorem about them depends on how they were built. The tool is one idea. In an Archimedean ordered field an element is determined by the rationals below it, and a map that respects sums, products, 1 and the order must send each element to one with the same rationals below it. In a complete field the supremum of the copies of those rationals is such an element. So from an Archimedean field into a complete one there is exactly one order-preserving field map, and each identity it satisfies is checked by comparing rationals below the two sides, with no arithmetic of suprema. When both fields are complete, maps run both ways, and the word “exactly” makes them inverse to each other without a computation. The same uniqueness leaves a complete ordered field no symmetry: a map of it to itself that respects only sums, products and 1 is the identity, because there the positive elements are the non-zero squares. The two non-examples show what each hypothesis buys: 
Q(\sqrt 2) has a symmetry exchanging \sqrt 2 and -\sqrt 2, which breaks the order, and 
R(x) has one sending x to x + 1, which keeps it. The chapter, the last of the volume’s main line, ends by comparing the two ways to begin analysis, assuming the axioms or building a model, and by listing what Analysis on the Real Line takes from this volume. What you need. Chapters 4 and 5 above all, and Chapter 2; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Section 2.6; and Logic and Proof, Chapters 2–4. From Chapter 4: the rules of an ordered field and the absolute value (@prp-ordered-field-halves, @lem-field-fraction-rules, @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field); powers and the one copy \iota_F of 
Q in an ordered field, with its uniqueness clause (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field, @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field); the Archimedean property, density of 
Q, and the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, @prp-archimedean-reciprocal, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, @exm-rational-function-field); and limits (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean), with Cauchy sequences in the exercises of Section 6.5 (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field). From Chapter 5: complete ordered fields (@def-complete-ordered-field), the theorem that the Cauchy model 
R is one (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), the map \kappa = \iota_{
R} (@thm-rational-embedding), the class of the Newton sequence, a positive real number whose square is 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class), and, for contrast, completeness from Archimedes and Cauchy-completeness (@thm-cauchy-archimedean-lub). From Chapter 2: the axioms (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4) (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field) and their rules (@prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-reciprocal-order), 
Q Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean), least elements (@prp-integer-least-element), and no rational square equal to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two, @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). Chapter 1 supplies one analogy (@thm-peano-categoricity) and, in a review solution, the order arithmetic of \omega (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic); Chapter 3 supplies even and odd integers (@cor-integers-even-odd), used in Section 6.4, and one review exercise (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring, @thm-integers-mod-prime-field). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality: injective and bijective maps and two-sided inverses, Sections 1.4 and 1.5 (@fd2:def-injective, @fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse); finite sums, Section 2.3 (@fd2:def-sum-product); equivalence relations and quotient sets, Section 2.5 (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set); upper bounds and suprema, Section 2.6 (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum); and, for exercises of Sections 6.4 and 6.5, countable and uncountable sets, Chapter 3 (@fd2:thm-countable-characterizations, @fd2:thm-binary-sequences-uncountable). From Logic and Proof: the contrapositive, Chapter 2 (@fd1:prp-contrapositive); induction, Chapter 3 (@fd1:ax-induction); and the negation of quantifiers, unbounded and bounded, Chapter 4 (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - What Completeness Gives at Once. Order-preserving field maps, which reflect the order and fix the rationals; the theorem that a complete ordered field is Archimedean, by a supremum of the copy of 
N that cannot exist; the rationals below an element, 
Q_F(x), which determine x when F is Archimedean; and square roots in a complete ordered field, built as a supremum and unique. - Building the Map from the Rationals Below. The rationals below a sum, and below a product of positive elements, computed from those below each term; and the main theorem in its one-sided form: from an Archimedean ordered field F into a complete one L there is exactly one order-preserving field map, which sends x to the supremum in L of the copies of the rationals below x and keeps the rationals below every element. - Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism. The uniqueness theorem, with the inverse map obtained from the uniqueness clause instead of computed; the relation F \cong L, every complete ordered field a copy of the Cauchy model, and the Dedekind cut of Chapter 7 read as a set of rationals below; and the automorphisms of a complete ordered field, of which there is one, the identity, even among the maps that respect only sums, products and 1. - Two Non-Examples. Polynomial functions compared at large arguments, where the top term decides the sign; the ordered field 
R(x) of rational functions, which is not Archimedean and in which x is not a square; the field 
Q(\sqrt 2), Archimedean and not complete, with conjugation as a symmetry that breaks the order; the shift x \mapsto x + 1, a symmetry of 
R(x) that keeps it; and a table of which of 
Q, 
Q(\sqrt 2), 
R(x) and 
R are Archimedean, complete, have square roots of positive elements, and have no field automorphism except the identity. - Assume the Axioms or Build a Model. The two ways to begin analysis and the two questions, existence and uniqueness, that assuming the axioms leaves open; what an isomorphism carries from one complete ordered field to another, with limits as the worked case, and what it does not carry, shown by a model whose zero is the empty set; a table of what Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 assumes and where this series supplies it; and review exercises that return to Chapter 5’s real numbers, Chapter 3’s 
Z/5
Z, equivalence relations and suprema. Named moves - Rationals separate. To show a = b in an Archimedean ordered field, show that the same rationals lie below each; otherwise a rational would lie strictly between them. It is proved in Section 6.1 and then proves every equation between elements of the complete field in the main theorem of Section 6.2: the values of the map on the rationals, sums, products and uniqueness (Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7); the exit check C1 of Section 6.2 runs it alone. In 
R(x), where Archimedes fails, the elements 1/x and 2/x have the same rationals below them (Section 6.4). - Construct a point as a supremum. To produce an element you cannot name, take the supremum of a well-chosen set and refute the two wrong cases of trichotomy, one with an element of the set above the supremum, the other with a smaller upper bound. It builds square roots in Section 6.1 and the map of Section 6.2. Exercise B2 of Section 6.2 (cube roots) leaves the last step to you, and Exercise C3 of Section 6.4 (a bounded increasing sequence converges to the supremum of its terms) the last half. - Uniqueness gives inverses. If the only order-preserving field map F 	o F is the identity, then two maps F 	o L 	o F compose to the identity without computing anything. It proves in Section 6.3 that the map between two complete ordered fields is bijective, and the same uniqueness clause shows there that a complete ordered field has no order-preserving automorphism except the identity; once square roots recover the order, also no field automorphism.

title: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content:
What Completeness Gives at Once Chapter 5 ended with one complete ordered field, the classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). The optional Chapter 7 builds another from Dedekind cuts, and Analysis on the Real Line simply assumes that one exists. This chapter asks whether these are the same field. Before that question can be asked we need a precise meaning for “the same”: a map between ordered fields that respects everything. This section fixes that meaning, and then collects what completeness gives at once: the Archimedean property, a way to tell elements apart by the rationals below them, and square roots. Standing setting. Throughout the chapter, F and L are ordered fields (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), so \le is a total order on each (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)) and upper bounds and suprema in the sense of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 apply to their subsets (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). “Complete” is always the property of @def-complete-ordered-field: every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. We do not redefine it. Each ordered field F carries its own copy of 
Q: the map \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field, the only map with \iota_F(1) = 1_F that preserves sums and products. It is injective, strictly increasing and reflects order, and \iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F for n \in 
N. For the constructed reals, \iota_{
R} is the map \kappa of Chapter 5 (@thm-rational-embedding (d)). When only one field is in play, a proof may write q for \iota_F(q), as Chapter 4 did; statements keep \iota_F visible, and so does every argument that moves between two fields. Maps that respect everything To say that two ordered fields are “the same”, we want a dictionary between them: a map that turns sums into sums, products into products, 1 into 1, and smaller into smaller. An isomorphism of Peano systems in Chapter 1 (@thm-peano-categoricity) was such a dictionary for 0 and the successor; here the structure is larger. A map that respects addition, multiplication, the unit and the order. [Order-Preserving Field Map] Let F and L be ordered fields. A map \chi \colon F 	o L is an order-preserving field map if, for all a, b \in F, \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(ab) = \chi(a)\, \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(1_F) = 1_L , and a < b implies \chi(a) < \chi(b). An order-preserving field isomorphism is an order-preserving field map that is bijective (@fd2:def-bijective). An order-preserving field automorphism of F is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o F. In words: the first two equations say that computing in F and then translating gives the same answer as translating and then computing in L; the third pins down the unit; the last says that \chi is strictly increasing. Two consequences come free. A strictly increasing map is injective: if a 
e b, then a < b or b < a by (O1), and the images differ in the same way. And it reflects order: if \chi(a) < \chi(b), then a < b. For a = b would give \chi(a) = \chi(b), and b < a would give \chi(b) < \chi(a); both contradict \chi(a) < \chi(b) by (O1), so only a < b is left. (This is the contrapositive of “b \le a implies \chi(b) \le \chi(a)”, @fd1:prp-contrapositive, read with trichotomy.) So an order-preserving field map satisfies a < b \iff \chi(a) < \chi(b). Examples. The identity. \id_F satisfies all four clauses trivially; it is an order-preserving field automorphism of F. The copy of the rationals. For every ordered field F, \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F is an order-preserving field map, by @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field. It is injective and usually not surjective: \iota_{
R} = \kappa misses the class r of the Newton sequence, which is not \kappa(q) for any rational q (@exm-sqrt2-class). Doubling. On 
Q, \chi(x) \coloneqq 2x preserves sums and is strictly increasing, but \chi(1) = 2 
e 1, and \chi(1 \cdot 1) = 2 
e 4 = \chi(1)\chi(1). It is not a field map: the clauses about multiplication and the unit fail, the additive ones survive. The zero map \chi(a) \coloneqq 0_L preserves sums and products, since 0 + 0 = 0 and 0 \cdot 0 = 0. It fails the unit clause, because 1_L 
e 0_L in a field, and it fails strict increase. In @def-cof-order-preserving-map the unit clause in fact follows from the other three: additivity gives \chi(0) = \chi(0) + \chi(0), so \chi(0) = 0; strict increase then gives \chi(1) > \chi(0) = 0; and \chi(1) = \chi(1)^2 with \chi(1) 
e 0 forces \chi(1) = 1. It is stated anyway because @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, @thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity and the remark after its proof assume sums, products and the unit but no order. Without the unit hypothesis, the zero map would be a counterexample to each of them. Why this definition. Preserving sums, products and the unit is what makes \chi a dictionary for the field operations; strict increase makes it a dictionary for the order. Section 6.4 shows a map of 
Q(\sqrt 2) to itself that respects sums, products and the unit but sends a positive element to a negative one, so the order clause does not follow from the others in general. Section 6.3 shows that for complete ordered fields it does. Which clauses of @def-cof-order-preserving-map does the map \chi \colon 
Q 	o 
Q, \chi(x) \coloneqq -x, satisfy? Only the sum clause: -(a + b) = (-a) + (-b). The unit clause fails, \chi(1) = -1 
e 1, and so does the product clause, since \chi(1 \cdot 1) = -1 while \chi(1)\chi(1) = (-1)(-1) = 1; and the order is reversed, 0 < 1 but \chi(1) = -1 < 0 = \chi(0). The first result about these maps needs no order hypothesis at all. A map that preserves sums, products and the unit cannot move a rational number. [Field Maps Fix the Rationals] Let F and L be ordered fields, and let \chi \colon F 	o L satisfy \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b), \chi(ab) = \chi(a)\chi(b) for all a, b \in F, and \chi(1_F) = 1_L. Then \chi \circ \iota_F = \iota_L , \qquad 	ext{that is,} \qquad \chi igl(\iota_F(q) igr) = \iota_L(q) \quad 	ext{for every } q \in 
Q . The composite \chi \circ \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o L sends 1 to \chi(1_F) = 1_L, and for x, y \in 
Q, \chi igl(\iota_F(x + y) igr) = \chi igl(\iota_F(x) + \iota_F(y) igr) = \chi igl(\iota_F(x) igr) + \chi igl(\iota_F(y) igr) , by @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field for F and the hypothesis on \chi; products are the same with \cdot in place of +. So \chi \circ \iota_F has the three properties that, by the uniqueness clause of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field for L, only \iota_L has. Hence \chi \circ \iota_F = \iota_L. This is the remark after @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field, now with a label. Read with the identifications q = \iota_F(q) and q = \iota_L(q), it says \chi(q) = q: such a map fixes the rationals. If \chi is also order-preserving, more follows. For q \in 
Q and x \in F, \iota_F(q) < x holds if and only if \chi(\iota_F(q)) < \chi(x), that is, if and only if \iota_L(q) < \chi(x). The rationals below x in F are exactly the rationals below \chi(x) in L. That observation drives the whole chapter. A complete ordered field is Archimedean Chapter 4 called F Archimedean if every element lies below some n \cdot 1_F (@def-archimedean-ordered-field), and showed that this can fail: in 
Q(t) the element t lies above every n \cdot 1 (@exm-rational-function-field). Chapter 5 assumed it, together with Cauchy-completeness, to prove completeness (@thm-cauchy-archimedean-lub). For the supremum form of completeness, no assumption is needed: it implies the Archimedean property. We write \iota_F(
N) \coloneqq \{ \iota_F(n) : n \in 
N \} = \{ n \cdot 1_F : n \in 
N \}. A Complete Ordered Field Is Archimedean Let F be a complete ordered field. Then F is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field). If some element bounded \iota_F(
N) above, completeness would give a least upper bound s. Step down by 1: s - 1 is not an upper bound, so some n \cdot 1_F is above it, and one more step, (n + 1) \cdot 1_F, is above s. The set \iota_F(
N) is closed under adding 1, so it cannot have a least upper bound, and hence no upper bound at all. Suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that \iota_F(
N) is bounded above, and fix an upper bound b \in F [ulename{\exists E}], so that n \cdot 1_F \le b for every n \in 
N. The set \iota_F(
N) is non-empty, since 0 \cdot 1_F \in \iota_F(
N). Since F is complete, \iota_F(
N) has a supremum; fix s \coloneqq \sup \iota_F(
N) [ulename{\exists E}]. Since s - 1_F < s and s is the least upper bound, s - 1_F is not an upper bound of \iota_F(
N). So some n \in 
N has n \cdot 1_F 
ot\le s - 1_F (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a)), that is, n \cdot 1_F > s - 1_F by totality (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). Then, by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a) and (O3), (n + 1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F > (s - 1_F) + 1_F = s , and (n + 1) \cdot 1_F \in \iota_F(
N). This contradicts that s is an upper bound of \iota_F(
N). Hence \iota_F(
N) is not bounded above [ulename{
eg I}]. So no x \in F is an upper bound of \iota_F(
N) (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation). For x \in F, as above, some n \in 
N has n \cdot 1_F 
ot\le x (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a)), that is, x < n \cdot 1_F by totality. Hence F is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field). Both hypotheses of completeness were used: “non-empty” through 0 \cdot 1_F, “bounded above” through b. The converse fails: 
Q is Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean) and not complete (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). And dropping completeness can lose the conclusion: 
Q(t) is an ordered field that is not Archimedean. The proof never claimed that s is an element of \iota_F(
N); a supremum need not belong to its set. Exercise C2 shows how tempting that claim is. Completeness here is about subsets, not sequences. Chapter 5 proved that the constructed 
R is complete by going through Cauchy sequences, and @thm-cauchy-archimedean-lub needed the Archimedean property as a separate hypothesis to get from “every Cauchy sequence converges” to “every bounded non-empty set has a supremum”. In this chapter “complete” is the supremum property of @def-complete-ordered-field, and the theorem above shows that it brings the Archimedean property with it. Do not replace it by Cauchy-completeness in the proofs below: Chapter 5 records, without proof, that a Cauchy-complete ordered field need not be Archimedean. Every complete ordered field therefore has the consequences of the Archimedean property that Chapter 4 proved. The one we use most is density (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field): in an Archimedean ordered field F, for all x < y there is q \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(q) < y. We cite it, not reprove it; Section 6.2 uses it in two fields at once. Here is the Archimedean property at work on a specific supremum. The pattern has two halves: check the candidate is an upper bound, then show that anything smaller is not one. [A Supremum Computed by Archimedes] Let F be a complete ordered field. Show that \sup\{ \iota_F(1 - 1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = 1_F. Let A \coloneqq \{ \iota_F(1 - 1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}. Upper bound. For n \in 
Z_{>0}, 1/n > 0 in 
Q, so 1 - 1/n < 1, and \iota_F(1 - 1/n) < \iota_F(1) = 1_F because \iota_F is strictly increasing (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). So 1_F is an upper bound of A. Least. Let b be an upper bound of A, and suppose, for contradiction, that b < 1_F, so 1_F - b > 0. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, F is Archimedean, so @prp-archimedean-reciprocal (with \varepsilon \coloneqq 1_F - b, applied at n = N) gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < 1_F - b. Since \iota_F preserves products and \iota_F(N) = N \cdot 1_F, we have \iota_F(1/N) \cdot (N \cdot 1_F) = \iota_F(1) = 1_F, so \iota_F(1/N) = 1/(N \cdot 1_F) by uniqueness of inverses (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). Since \iota_F preserves sums, it preserves negatives, and adding b - 1/(N \cdot 1_F) to both sides of 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < 1_F - b (O3) gives \iota_F(1 - 1/N) = 1_F -  rac{1}{N \cdot 1_F} > b . This element of A lies above b, against b being an upper bound. So 1_F \le b by totality, for every upper bound b, and 1_F = \sup A (@fd2:def-order-supremum). The supremum 1_F is not an element of A: every element is strictly below it. Completeness entered only through the Archimedean property; in an ordered field that is Archimedean but not complete, such as 
Q (@thm-rationals-archimedean), the same two halves give the same answer. Exercises B1 and B2 follow this pattern. The rationals below an element How can we tell two elements of a field apart? In an Archimedean field, by a rational between them. That suggests recording, for each element, which rationals lie below it. An element is measured by the rationals below it. The Rationals below an Element Let F be an ordered field and x \in F. The rationals below x form the set 
Q_F(x) \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Q : \iota_F(q) < x \} \subseteq 
Q . In words: 
Q_F(x) is a set of rational numbers, not of elements of F; a rational q belongs to it when its copy \iota_F(q) lies strictly below x. Two properties hold in every ordered field and are used without comment. The set is closed downward: if q \in 
Q_F(x) and p < q, then \iota_F(p) < \iota_F(q) < x, so p \in 
Q_F(x). And if x \le y, then 
Q_F(x) \subseteq 
Q_F(y), by transitivity. Examples. A rational element. For r \in 
Q, 
Q_F(\iota_F(r)) = \{ q \in 
Q : q < r \}. Indeed \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) holds if and only if q < r, because \iota_F is strictly increasing and reflects order. In particular r 
otin 
Q_F(\iota_F(r)): the inequality is strict. [The Rationals below the Square Root of Two] Let r \in 
R be the class of the Newton sequence, so that r > 0 and r^2 = 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class). Show that 
Q_{
R}(r) = \{ q \in 
Q : q < 0 \} \cup \{ q \in 
Q : q \ge 0 	ext{ and } q^2 < 2 \} . Let q \in 
Q, and recall \iota_{
R} = \kappa (@thm-rational-embedding (d)). If q < 0, then \kappa(q) < \kappa(0) = 0 < r, so q \in 
Q_{
R}(r). Let q \ge 0, so \kappa(q) \ge 0. Since also r > 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) in 
R gives \kappa(q) < r \iff \kappa(q)^2 < r^2 = 2 . Now \kappa(q)^2 = \kappa(q^2) and 2 = \kappa(2) (@thm-rational-embedding (a)), and \kappa(q^2) < \kappa(2) if and only if q^2 < 2 (@thm-rational-embedding (b)). So for q \ge 0, q \in 
Q_{
R}(r) if and only if q^2 < 2. Together the two cases give the displayed set. The set of Section 2.6, \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2), is not 
Q_{
R}(r): it omits -2, whose square is 4. That set is not closed downward, and a rationals-below set always is. Let F be an ordered field and x \coloneqq \iota_F(3/2). Describe 
Q_F(x), and say whether 3/2 \in 
Q_F(x). By the first example, 
Q_F(x) = \{ q \in 
Q : q < 3/2 \}. It does not contain 3/2, since \iota_F(3/2) < \iota_F(3/2) is false by (O1). The point of the definition is that in an Archimedean field, these sets lose no information. [Rationals Separate] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, and let x, y \in F. Then x \le y \iff 
Q_F(x) \subseteq 
Q_F(y) . Consequently x = y \iff 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_F(y). (\Rightarrow) This is the second property after @def-cof-rationals-below: if \iota_F(q) < x and x \le y, then \iota_F(q) < y. (\Leftarrow) We prove the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive). Suppose that x \le y fails. Then y < x by totality (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is q \in 
Q with y < \iota_F(q) < x. Then q \in 
Q_F(x), and q 
otin 
Q_F(y), since \iota_F(q) < y and y < \iota_F(q) cannot both hold (O1). So 
Q_F(x) 
ot\subseteq 
Q_F(y). For the consequence: x = y holds if and only if x \le y and y \le x, by antisymmetry of the total order \le; by the equivalence just proved, that is 
Q_F(x) \subseteq 
Q_F(y) and 
Q_F(y) \subseteq 
Q_F(x), that is, 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_F(y). This is the first named move of the chapter, rationals separate: to prove two elements of an Archimedean field equal, show that the same rationals lie below each. A rational strictly between them would otherwise exist. Section 6.2 uses it in four of the seven steps of its main proof (Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7), each time to prove that two elements of the complete field are equal. The direction (\Rightarrow) and the remark that equal elements have equal sets hold in every ordered field. The direction (\Leftarrow) needs density, and density needs Archimedes. In the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field (school polynomial algebra, as flagged there; nothing below depends on it), every rational q satisfies q < n for some n \in 
N (@thm-rationals-archimedean), and n \cdot 1 < t, so \iota_{
Q(t)}(q) < t < t + 1. Hence 
Q_{
Q(t)}(t) = 
Q = 
Q_{
Q(t)}(t + 1), although t 
e t + 1. Both elements lie above all of the rationals, and the rationals cannot see the difference. Square roots Completeness lets us build elements we cannot name in advance, as the supremum of a well-chosen set. We show the method once, in full, on square roots; it is the second named move, construct a point as a supremum. Exercise B2 of Section 6.2 runs it again on cube roots. [Square Roots in a Complete Ordered Field] Let F be a complete ordered field and a \in F with a \ge 0. Then there is exactly one b \in F with b \ge 0 and b^2 = a. The square root of a should be the top of the set S of non-negative y with y^2 < a. Let s \coloneqq \sup S. Two of the three cases of trichotomy must be ruled out. If s^2 < a, there is room above s: we look for h > 0 with (s + h)^2 < a, which puts s + h in S above its supremum. Working backwards, for 0 < h \le 1 we have h^2 \le h, so (s + h)^2 = s^2 + 2sh + h^2 \le s^2 + h(2s + 1) , and it is enough that h(2s + 1) be at most half the room a - s^2. So h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^2)/(2(2s + 1))\}. If s^2 > a, then s overshoots: we look for h > 0 with (s - h)^2 \ge a still, which makes s - h a smaller upper bound. Since (s - h)^2 \ge s^2 - 2sh, it is enough that 2sh = s^2 - a, so h \coloneqq (s^2 - a)/(2s). Existence. If a = 0, then b \coloneqq 0 works. Let a > 0, and let S \coloneqq \{ y \in F : y \ge 0 	ext{ and } y^2 < a \} . Then 0 \in S, since 0^2 = 0 < a. And a + 1 is an upper bound of S: if y > a + 1, then y > 1 > 0, so y^2 = y \cdot y > y \cdot 1 = y > a (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), and y 
otin S; so every y \in S satisfies y \le a + 1 by totality. Since F is complete, fix s \coloneqq \sup S [ulename{\exists E}]. Since 0 \in S, s \ge 0. Case s^2 < a. Let h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^2)/(2(2s + 1))\}. It is defined and positive, since 2s + 1 \ge 1 > 0 and a - s^2 > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). Since 0 < h \le 1, h^2 \le h (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), so  egin{aligned} (s + h)^2 &= s^2 + 2sh + h^2 \le s^2 + h(2s + 1) \ &\le s^2 +  rac{a - s^2}{2} < a , \end{aligned} where the second inequality uses h \le (a - s^2)/(2(2s + 1)) and 2s + 1 > 0, and the last uses (a - s^2)/2 < a - s^2 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). So s + h \ge 0 lies in S, and s + h > s, against s being an upper bound of S. Case s^2 > a. Then s 
e 0, since 0^2 = 0 < a; so s > 0. Let h \coloneqq (s^2 - a)/(2s). It is positive, since s^2 - a > 0 and 2s > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). Then s - h = (s^2 + a)/(2s) > 0 by the same reasons, since s^2 + a > 0; and (s - h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 = s^2 - (s^2 - a) + h^2 = a + h^2 > a . We claim that s - h is an upper bound of S. Let y > s - h. Then y > 0, and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) gives y^2 > (s - h)^2 > a, so y 
otin S. Hence every element of S is \le s - h. But s - h < s, against s being the least upper bound. Both cases are impossible, so s^2 = a by trichotomy (O1), and b \coloneqq s \ge 0 works. Uniqueness. Let b, c \ge 0 with b^2 = c^2 = a. Then (b - c)(b + c) = b^2 - c^2 = 0, so b = c or b + c = 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)). If b + c = 0, then b = -c \le 0 \le b, so b = 0 and c = -b = 0. In either case b = c. For a \ge 0 in a complete ordered field we write \sqrt a for this b. In the constructed reals, the class r of @exm-sqrt2-class has r > 0 and r^2 = 2, so r = \sqrt 2 by the uniqueness clause, and @exm-cof-rationals-below-sqrt2 describes 
Q_{
R}(\sqrt 2). The constants follow the Idea: each h depends on s and a only, and each was found backwards and then placed first. Completeness was used once, to produce s; the rest is arithmetic in an ordered field. Without completeness the statement fails: in 
Q, the element 2 \ge 0 has no square root (@thm-no-rational-square-two). Section 6.4 meets a field that is Archimedean and still lacks some square roots. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. True or false, with a reason: in every ordered field F, if 
Q_F(x) 
e 
Q_F(y) then x 
e y. Is the converse true in every ordered field? 2. Write “F is Archimedean” in symbols, and state its negation with the quantifiers moved to the front (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation). 3. The eight lines (i)–(viii) below are about a complete ordered field F; six of them, in a suitable order, prove @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. Write an admissible order, and say why each of the other two lines is wrong. 1. Then \iota_F(n + 1) = \iota_F(n) + 1 > s, and n + 1 \in 
N. 2. For every n \in 
N, \iota_F(n) > s - 1. 3. The set \iota_F(
N) is non-empty (0 \in 
N), so s \coloneqq \sup \iota_F(
N) exists. 4. This contradicts that s is an upper bound of \iota_F(
N). 5. Suppose that \iota_F(
N) is bounded above. 6. So \iota_F(n) > s - 1 for some n \in 
N. 7. So s \in \iota_F(
N), say s = \iota_F(m). 8. Since s - 1 < s, the element s - 1 is not an upper bound of \iota_F(
N). (a) True. It is the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive) of “if x = y then 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_F(y)”, which holds because equal elements have the same rationals below them. The converse, “if x 
e y then 
Q_F(x) 
e 
Q_F(y)”, is the direction (\Leftarrow) of @lem-cof-rationals-separate, and it needs the Archimedean property: in 
Q(t), t 
e t + 1 and both have every rational below them (the second-reading note after @lem-cof-rationals-separate). (b)  orall x \in F \ \exists n \in 
N \ \ x < n \cdot 1_F. Negation: \exists x \in F \  orall n \in 
N \ \ n \cdot 1_F \le x, using 
eg(x < y) \iff y \le x (totality and (O1)). In words: some element lies above or at every n \cdot 1_F. (c) (v), (iii), (viii), (vi), (i), (iv). No other order is admissible: each line uses the one before it ((iii) needs the bound of (v) for the supremum to exist, (viii) needs s, (vi) unpacks (viii), (i) uses the n of (vi), and (iv) is the contradiction with (i)). The contradiction in (iv) refutes (v), so \iota_F(
N) is not bounded above; unpacked with the negation laws, as at the end of the proof of @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, that is the statement of (b). Line (vii) is wrong: a supremum need not belong to the set (in every ordered field, the set of negative elements has supremum 0, which is not negative: the first example after @def-complete-ordered-field). Line (ii) has the wrong quantifier: “s - 1 is not an upper bound” gives some n with \iota_F(n) > s - 1, by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, not every n (and for n = 0 it may be false). B. Practice [B1] Let F be a complete ordered field. Prove that \inf\{ \iota_F(1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = 0. Let T \coloneqq \{ \iota_F(1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}. For n \in 
Z_{>0}, 1/n > 0 in 
Q, so \iota_F(1/n) > 0: 0 is a lower bound of T. Let c be a lower bound of T, and suppose, for contradiction, that c > 0. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, F is Archimedean, so @prp-archimedean-reciprocal (with \varepsilon \coloneqq c, applied at n = N) gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < c. Since \iota_F preserves products and \iota_F(N) = N \cdot 1_F, we have \iota_F(1/N) \cdot (N \cdot 1_F) = \iota_F(1) = 1_F, so \iota_F(1/N) = 1/(N \cdot 1_F) by uniqueness of inverses (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). So the element \iota_F(1/N) of T lies below c, against c being a lower bound. Hence every lower bound c satisfies c \le 0, and 0 is the greatest lower bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum). [B2] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field and x \in F. Prove that the set \iota_F(
Q_F(x)) = \{ \iota_F(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} has supremum x in F. Upper bound. Every element \iota_F(q) of the set satisfies \iota_F(q) < x by the definition of 
Q_F(x). Least. Let u be an upper bound, and suppose u < x. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is q \in 
Q with u < \iota_F(q) < x. Then q \in 
Q_F(x), so \iota_F(q) is in the set and exceeds u, against u being an upper bound. So x \le u by totality, for every upper bound u. Hence x = \sup \iota_F(
Q_F(x)). No completeness was used: the supremum exists because we exhibited it. C. Going deeper [C1: An Archimedean field is no larger than the subsets of the rationals] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field. Prove that the map F 	o \powerset{
Q}, x \mapsto 
Q_F(x), is injective. What does this say about the size of F? Let x, y \in F with 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_F(y). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate, x = y. So the map is injective (@fd2:def-injective). An injection F 	o \powerset{
Q} says that F has at most as many elements as \powerset{
Q}, in the sense of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3. In particular every Archimedean ordered field, and so (by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean) every complete ordered field, is no larger than the set of all sets of rationals. The non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) shows that the hypothesis is needed for injectivity: t and t + 1 have the same image. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “proof” that a complete ordered field F is Archimedean. Suppose that \iota_F(
N) is bounded above, and let s be its supremum. Since s is the least upper bound of \iota_F(
N), it is the largest element of \iota_F(
N), so s = \iota_F(m) for some m \in 
N. But \iota_F(m + 1) > s, a contradiction. Is the conclusion true? Find the line that fails, give a counterexample to that line, and repair the proof. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. The illegal step is “the least upper bound of a set is its largest element”. A supremum is an upper bound that lies below every other upper bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum); nothing says it belongs to the set. Counterexample to the step: in the constructed 
R, A \coloneqq \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has supremum 1, and 1 
otin A. Indeed every element is < 1; and if b < 1, Archimedes in 
R (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, with @prp-archimedean-reciprocal) gives n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < 1 - b, so 1 - 1/n > b and b is not an upper bound. So the step fails for this set, though the theorem’s conclusion is not affected. Repair: replace the second and third sentences by the argument of the proof of @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. Since s - 1 < s, s - 1 is not an upper bound, so \iota_F(n) > s - 1 for some n; then \iota_F(n + 1) = \iota_F(n) + 1 > s, against s being an upper bound. The repair uses that s is least only through “s - 1 is not an upper bound”, which hands us an element of the set just below s, not s itself. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: says the conclusion is true, with the reason (the theorem). - 3: names the line “the supremum is the largest element” and says which property of suprema it wrongly assumes. - 2: a counterexample to that step: a set whose supremum is not an element of it, with the supremum verified. - 2: a correct repair that uses that s is least, without assuming s lies in the set: for example, s - 1 is not an upper bound, so some \iota_F(n) > s - 1 and then \iota_F(n + 1) > s; or, equivalently, if \iota_F(n + 1) \le s for all n then s - 1 is a smaller upper bound (the case n = 0 uses 1 \le s). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; a counterexample to the theorem rather than to the step.

title: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content:
Building the Map from the Rationals Below Section 6.1 gave every element x of an ordered field F a record, the set 
Q_F(x) of rationals below it, and showed that in an Archimedean field the record determines the element (@lem-cof-rationals-separate). This section turns the record into a map. Given an Archimedean field F and a complete field L, we send x \in F to the element of L with the same record. The result is the main theorem of the chapter in its one-sided form: there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o L. Section 6.3 applies it twice, in both directions, to compare two complete ordered fields. Two fields are in play throughout, so every proof here keeps \iota_F and \iota_L visible. Only the two lemmas, each about one field, write q for \iota_F(q). What the map must be Suppose \varphi \colon F 	o L is an order-preserving field map (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals it fixes the rationals, \varphi(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q), and it preserves and reflects order. So for q \in 
Q and x \in F, \iota_F(q) < x \iff \varphi igl(\iota_F(q) igr) < \varphi(x) \iff \iota_L(q) < \varphi(x) . In the notation of Section 6.1: 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x). The image of x has exactly the rationals below it that x has. That already shows there can be at most one such map when L is Archimedean: two candidates for \varphi(x) would have the same rationals below them, and rationals separate. For existence, we need an element of L with a prescribed set of rationals below it. When L is complete there is a natural candidate: the least element of L that lies above all the copies \iota_L(q), q \in 
Q_F(x), that is, their supremum. The check that this candidate respects sums and products goes through the record, not through suprema. For that we need to know how the rationals below a + b and below ab are made from those below a and b. Sums and products, measured by rationals A rational q lies below a + b exactly when it splits into a rational below a and a rational below b. [Rationals below a Sum] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F and q \in 
Q. Then \iota_F(q) < a + b if and only if there is r \in 
Q with \iota_F(r) < a \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \iota_F(q - r) < b . In other words, q \in 
Q_F(a + b) \iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(a) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_F(b)  igr). One direction is addition of inequalities. For the other, split q as r + (q - r) with r a rational just below a: we need r in the gap between q - b and a, which is non-empty exactly because q < a + b, and density supplies it. We write q for \iota_F(q); since \iota_F preserves sums, it preserves differences, so \iota_F(q - r) = q - r in F. (\Leftarrow) If r < a and q - r < b, then q = r + (q - r) < a + b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). (\Rightarrow) Let q < a + b. Then q - b < a (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q - b < r < a. Then r < a, and q - r < b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) again. For products the same idea works for positive elements and positive rationals, with q/r in place of q - r. [Rationals below a Product] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F with a > 0 and b > 0, and q \in 
Q with q > 0. Then \iota_F(q) < ab if and only if there is r \in 
Q with r > 0 , \qquad \iota_F(r) < a \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \iota_F(q/r) < b . For q \le 0, \iota_F(q) < ab holds always. In words: below a product of positives, a positive rational splits as a product of a rational below each factor. Exercise B1 asks for the proof; the fold below has it. As for sums, with division in place of subtraction: split q as r \cdot (q/r) with r a rational in the gap between q/b and a, a gap of positive elements. We write q for \iota_F(q); since \iota_F preserves products and \iota_F(r) 
e 0 for r 
e 0, it preserves quotients, so \iota_F(q/r) = q/r in F. If q \le 0, then q \le 0 < ab by (O4). Let q > 0. (\Leftarrow) Let r > 0 with r < a and q/r < b. Since q/r > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q = r \cdot (q/r) < a \cdot (q/r); since a > 0, it gives a \cdot (q/r) < ab. So q < ab. (\Rightarrow) Let q < ab. Multiplying by b^{-1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives q/b < a, and q/b > 0 by (O4). By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q/b < r < a. Then r > q/b > 0, so r > 0 in 
Q, since \iota_F reflects order. Multiplying q/b < r by b > 0 gives q < rb, and multiplying by r^{-1} > 0 gives q/r < b. In F = 
Q, with a \coloneqq 3/4, b \coloneqq 1/2 and q \coloneqq 1, find a rational r as in @lem-cof-below-sum. Which rationals r work? We need r < 3/4 and 1 - r < 1/2, that is, 1/2 < r < 3/4. For example r = 2/3: then 1 - 2/3 = 1/3 < 1/2. Exactly the rationals of the open gap between q - b = 1/2 and a = 3/4 work, as the proof predicts. The map into a complete field Here is the theorem. Its proof is the first key proof of the chapter. [Embedding an Archimedean Field in a Complete One] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field and L a complete ordered field. Then there is exactly one order-preserving field map \varphi \colon F 	o L. It is given by \varphi(x) \coloneqq \sup
olimits_L \, \{ \iota_L(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} \qquad (x \in F) , the supremum taken in L, and it satisfies 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) igr) = 
Q_F(x) \qquad 	ext{for every } x \in F . 	ag{$\star$} Try it first (ten minutes): if \varphi exists and fixes 
Q, which element of L must \varphi(x) be? The natural first attempt defines \varphi on the copy of 
Q, by \varphi(\iota_F(q)) \coloneqq \iota_L(q), and then tries to “extend”. It stalls at once: an element x \in F that is not a rational has no formula, and nothing in F names it. What we do know, from the previous subsection, is its record: \varphi(x) must have exactly the rationals 
Q_F(x) below it. So we construct a point as a supremum: \varphi(x) is the least upper bound in L of the copies of those rationals, and (\star) says the construction has the right record. After that, sums, products and uniqueness are checked the same way: compute the record of both sides (for sums and products by the two lemmas) and let rationals separate in L. Monotonicity needs only one rational between x and y. Step roadmap: ① \varphi(x) exists; ② (\star); ③ \varphi fixes the rationals; ④ \varphi is strictly increasing; ⑤ sums; ⑥ products and the unit; ⑦ uniqueness. Before reading on: where is completeness of L used, and where the Archimedean property of F? By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, L is Archimedean. So @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, @lem-cof-rationals-separate, @lem-cof-below-sum and @lem-cof-below-product apply in L as well as in F. For x \in F write A_x \coloneqq \{ \iota_L(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} \subseteq L. Step 1: \varphi(x) is defined. Let x \in F. Since F is Archimedean, there is n \in 
N with -x < n \cdot 1_F, so \iota_F(-n) = -(n \cdot 1_F) < x (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), and -n \in 
Q_F(x): the set A_x is non-empty. Applied to x, the Archimedean property gives m \in 
N with x < m \cdot 1_F = \iota_F(m). For q \in 
Q_F(x), \iota_F(q) < x < \iota_F(m), so q < m because \iota_F reflects order, and \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(m). So \iota_L(m) is an upper bound of A_x. Since L is complete, A_x has a supremum in L, and it is unique; \varphi(x) is that supremum. So \varphi \colon F 	o L is a function. Step 2: (\star). Let x \in F and q \in 
Q. (\subseteq) Let q \in 
Q_F(x). By density in F there is r \in 
Q with \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) < x. Then r \in 
Q_F(x), so \iota_L(r) \in A_x and \iota_L(r) \le \varphi(x), since \varphi(x) is an upper bound. Also q < r (reflection in F), so \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) \le \varphi(x), and q \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)). (\supseteq) Let \iota_L(q) < \varphi(x). Since \varphi(x) is the least upper bound of A_x, \iota_L(q) is not an upper bound, so there is r \in 
Q_F(x) with \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) (totality). Then q < r (reflection in L), so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) < x, and q \in 
Q_F(x). Step 3: \varphi fixes the rationals. Let r \in 
Q. By (\star) and the first example after @def-cof-rationals-below, used in F and in L, 
Q_L igl(\varphi(\iota_F(r)) igr) = 
Q_F igl(\iota_F(r) igr) = \{ q \in 
Q : q < r \} = 
Q_L igl(\iota_L(r) igr) . By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(\iota_F(r)) = \iota_L(r). In particular \varphi(0_F) = 0_L and \varphi(1_F) = 1_L. Step 4: \varphi is strictly increasing. Let x < y in F. By density in F there is r \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(r) < y. Then r 
otin 
Q_F(x) (by (O1)), so r 
otin 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) by (\star), and \varphi(x) \le \iota_L(r) by totality. And r \in 
Q_F(y) = 
Q_L(\varphi(y)), so \iota_L(r) < \varphi(y). Hence \varphi(x) \le \iota_L(r) < \varphi(y). Step 5: sums. Let x, y \in F and q \in 
Q. Then  egin{aligned} q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x + y) igr) &\iff q \in 
Q_F(x + y) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(x) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_F(y)  igr) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(y))  igr) \ &\iff q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) + \varphi(y) igr) , \end{aligned} by (\star), @lem-cof-below-sum in F, (\star) twice, and @lem-cof-below-sum in L. By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(x + y) = \varphi(x) + \varphi(y). Step 6: products and the unit. First let x > 0 and y > 0. By Steps 3 and 4, \varphi(x) > \varphi(0_F) = 0_L and \varphi(y) > 0_L; and xy > 0, \varphi(x)\varphi(y) > 0 by (O4). Let q \in 
Q. If q \le 0, then q \in 
Q_F(xy) = 
Q_L(\varphi(xy)), and q \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)\varphi(y)), by the last clause of @lem-cof-below-product in F and in L. If q > 0, then  egin{aligned} q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(xy) igr) &\iff q \in 
Q_F(xy) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(x) \wedge q/r \in 
Q_F(y)  igr) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \  igl( r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) \wedge q/r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(y))  igr) \ &\iff q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x)\varphi(y) igr) , \end{aligned} by (\star), @lem-cof-below-product in F, (\star) twice, and @lem-cof-below-product in L (with \varphi(x), \varphi(y) > 0). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) for x, y > 0. Now the signs. By Steps 5 and 3, \varphi(x) + \varphi(-x) = \varphi(0_F) = 0_L, so \varphi(-x) = -\varphi(x) (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). If x = 0 or y = 0, both sides of \varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) are 0_L (Step 3 and @prp-ring-algebra (b)). If x < 0 < y, then -x > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)) and xy = - igl((-x)y igr) (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), so \varphi(xy) = -\varphi igl((-x)y igr) = - igl(\varphi(-x)\varphi(y) igr) = - igl(-\varphi(x) igr)\varphi(y) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) . The case x > 0 > y follows by (F6), and if x, y < 0, then xy = (-x)(-y) and \varphi(xy) =  igl(-\varphi(x) igr) igl(-\varphi(y) igr) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y). Finally \varphi(1_F) = 1_L by Step 3. With Steps 4 and 5, \varphi is an order-preserving field map. Step 7: uniqueness. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be any order-preserving field map, and let x \in F, q \in 
Q. By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, \chi(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q). If \iota_F(q) < x, then \iota_L(q) = \chi(\iota_F(q)) < \chi(x). If \iota_L(q) < \chi(x), that is, \chi(\iota_F(q)) < \chi(x), then \iota_F(q) < x, because \chi reflects order (the remark after @def-cof-order-preserving-map). So 
Q_L igl(\chi(x) igr) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) igr) , the second equality by (\star). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \chi(x) = \varphi(x). Since x was arbitrary, \chi = \varphi. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Completeness of L is used in Step 1, where the supremum must exist, and in Step 2 (\supseteq), where its leastness turns “below \varphi(x)” into “below some \iota_L(r)”. The Archimedean property of F is used in Step 1 for the bounds -n and m, in Steps 2 and 4 through density in F, and in Steps 5 and 6 through the two lemmas applied in F. Completeness of L is used a third time, indirectly: it makes L Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), which Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 need for rationals to separate in L and for the lemmas in L. Step 7 is the whole of “uniqueness”. Its idea, comparing the rationals below two candidate values, needs only that L is Archimedean, not that it is complete: Exercise C1 runs it for any two order-preserving field maps F 	o L, with no appeal to (\star). Section 6.3 leans on the uniqueness clause throughout: to show that the maps between two complete fields are inverse to each other, that the isomorphism they give is the only one, and that a complete ordered field has no order-preserving field automorphism other than the identity. Neither hypothesis can be dropped from the existence half. Without completeness of L: take F = 
R, which is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), and L = 
Q. An order-preserving field map \varphi \colon 
R 	o 
Q would fix 2 (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals), so for \sqrt 2 \in 
R (the element of @exm-sqrt2-class, as in Section 6.1), \varphi(\sqrt 2)^2 = \varphi((\sqrt 2)^2) = \varphi(2) = 2 in 
Q, against @thm-no-rational-square-two. Without the Archimedean property of F: take F = 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field and any complete L. An order-preserving field map \varphi would fix each n \cdot 1 and be strictly increasing, so n \cdot 1_L = \varphi(n \cdot 1) < \varphi(t) for every n \in 
N, against the Archimedean property of L (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean). The supremum in the definition of \varphi is taken in L, of the copies \iota_L(q). It cannot be taken in 
Q, or in F. In 
Q: the set 
Q_{
R}(\sqrt 2) of @exm-cof-rationals-below-sqrt2 (with \sqrt 2 as in Section 6.1) has no supremum in 
Q. It contains the set A = \{ p \in 
Q : p^2 < 2 \} of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2, and its other elements are negative, so below 0 \in A; hence the two sets have the same upper bounds in 
Q, and A has no least one. In F: the supremum of \iota_F(
Q_F(x)) always exists and is x itself, since x is an upper bound and, by density in F (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field), every u < x lies below some \iota_F(q) < x. So it is an element of the wrong field. Take L \coloneqq F, a complete ordered field. Which map F 	o F does @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete produce, and why, without computing a single supremum? The identity. The theorem says there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o F (F is Archimedean by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean), and \id_F is one (the first example after @def-cof-order-preserving-map). So \varphi = \id_F. This is the argument Section 6.3 builds on. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. 1. Which steps use that L is complete, and which that F is Archimedean? Which steps use that L is Archimedean, and where does that come from? 2. Run the definition of \varphi with F = 
Q and L = 
R, the constructed reals. What is \varphi? 3. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. Why may Step 1 not define \varphi(x) as a supremum taken in F? (a) L complete: Step 1 (the supremum exists) and Step 2 (\supseteq) (its leastness). F Archimedean: Step 1 (the bounds -n, m), Steps 2 and 4 (density in F), and Steps 5 and 6 (@lem-cof-below-sum and @lem-cof-below-product applied in F). L Archimedean: Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7, through @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L and the two lemmas in L. It comes from the completeness of L, by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. (b) \varphi = \iota_{
R} = \kappa. By Step 3, \varphi(\iota_{
Q}(r)) = \iota_{
R}(r) for every r \in 
Q, and \iota_{
Q} is the identity (Chapter 4, after @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). So \varphi(r) = \iota_{
R}(r), which is \kappa(r) by @thm-rational-embedding (d). Concretely, \varphi(r) is the supremum in 
R of \{ \kappa(q) : q < r \}, and that supremum is \kappa(r). (c) An order-preserving map that fixes the rationals must send x to an element with the same rationals below it, and in a complete L the supremum of their copies is such an element. Every field identity for \varphi is then checked by comparing the rationals below the two sides, which the sum and product lemmas compute, and rationals separate in L. (d) In F the supremum of \iota_F(
Q_F(x)) always exists, since F is Archimedean, and it is x itself (Exercise B2 of Section 6.1): an element of F, not of L. So it does not give a map into L. The supremum must be of the copies \iota_L(q), taken in L. B. Practice [B1] Prove @lem-cof-below-product: let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F with a, b > 0, and q \in 
Q with q > 0; show that \iota_F(q) < ab if and only if some rational r > 0 has \iota_F(r) < a and \iota_F(q/r) < b. Show also that \iota_F(q) < ab for every rational q \le 0. Hint: imitate the proof of @lem-cof-below-sum, with division in place of subtraction. Write q for \iota_F(q). Since \iota_F preserves products, \iota_F(r)\,\iota_F(r^{-1}) = \iota_F(1) = 1 for r 
e 0, so \iota_F(r^{-1}) = \iota_F(r)^{-1} (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)) and \iota_F(q/r) = q/r in F. If q \le 0, then q \le 0 < ab by (O4). Let q > 0. (\Leftarrow) Let r > 0, r < a, q/r < b. Then q/r > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q = r(q/r) < a(q/r), and, as a > 0, a(q/r) < ab. Hence q < ab. (\Rightarrow) Let q < ab. Since b^{-1} > 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q/b < a, and q/b > 0. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q/b < \iota_F(r) < a. Then \iota_F(r) > 0 = \iota_F(0), so r > 0 since \iota_F reflects order. From q/b < r and b > 0, q < rb; multiplying by r^{-1} > 0, q/r < b. This r is as required. [B2: Cube roots] Let F be a complete ordered field and a \in F with a > 0. Let S \coloneqq \{ y \in F : y \ge 0 	ext{ and } y^3 < a \}. The following steps prove that some s \in F has s^3 = a. 1. S is non-empty (0 \in S) and bounded above by 1 + a: if y > 1 + a, then y > 1, so y^3 > y > a. Let s \coloneqq \sup S. Then s > 0, since m \coloneqq \min\{1, a/2\} has 0 < m \le 1, so m^3 \le m \le a/2 < a, and m \in S. 2. For y, z \in F, z^3 - y^3 = (z - y)(z^2 + zy + y^2) and z^2 + zy + y^2 = (z + y/2)^2 + (3/4)y^2, which is > 0 unless y = z = 0 (if y 
e 0, then (3/4)y^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c) and the square is \ge 0, so the sum is positive by (b); if y = 0 and z 
e 0, the expression is z^2 > 0 by (e)). Hence y < z \iff y^3 < z^3, for all y, z \in F. 3. The case s^3 < a is impossible. Let h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^3)/(2(3s^2 + 3s + 1))\} > 0. Since 0 < h \le 1 and s \ge 0, (s + h)^3 = s^3 + 3s^2h + 3sh^2 + h^3 \le s^3 + h(3s^2 + 3s + 1) \le s^3 + (a - s^3)/2 < a, so s + h \in S, against s being an upper bound. 4. The case s^3 > a is impossible. Name the move, then complete it. 5. Hence s^3 = a. Then explain how to get a cube root of a = 0 and of a < 0, and why every a \in F has exactly one cube root. The move is construct a point as a supremum: s is built as \sup S, and each of the two wrong cases of trichotomy is refuted by exhibiting a point that contradicts one clause of the supremum. In step (3) it was an element of S above s, against (S1). In step (4) it is an upper bound below s, against (S2). (4) Suppose s^3 > a. Let h \coloneqq (s^3 - a)/(3s^2); it is positive, since s > 0 by (1). Also h < s: this says s^3 - a < 3s^3, which holds because a > 0 and 2s^3 > 0. So s - h > 0, and (s - h)^3 - a = (s^3 - a) - 3s^2h + 3sh^2 - h^3 = h^2(3s - h) > 0 , since 3s^2 h = s^3 - a, h^2 > 0 and 3s - h > 2s > 0. Let y > s - h. By (2), y^3 > (s - h)^3 > a, so y 
otin S. Hence every element of S is \le s - h, and s - h is an upper bound of S smaller than s, against s being the least upper bound. (5) Steps (3) and (4) leave only s^3 = a, by trichotomy (O1). For a = 0, 0^3 = 0. For a < 0, -a > 0 has a cube root c by the above, and (-c)^3 = -c^3 = a (@prp-ring-algebra (c)). Uniqueness: if b^3 = c^3, then neither b < c nor c < b can hold, since by (2) either would make the cubes differ; so b = c. So every element of a complete ordered field has exactly one cube root. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: at most one map into an Archimedean field] Let F and L be Archimedean ordered fields, and let \chi_1, \chi_2 \colon F 	o L be order-preserving field maps. Prove that \chi_1 = \chi_2. [Hint 1] Compare the rationals below \chi_1(x) and below \chi_2(x). [Hint 2] By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, \chi_i(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q) for i = 1, 2 and every q \in 
Q. Let x \in F and i \in \{1, 2\}. By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals (which needs no order hypothesis), \chi_i(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q) for every q \in 
Q. Since \chi_i is strictly increasing and reflects order (the remark after @def-cof-order-preserving-map), \iota_F(q) < x \iff \chi_i igl(\iota_F(q) igr) < \chi_i(x) \iff \iota_L(q) < \chi_i(x) . So 
Q_L(\chi_1(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L(\chi_2(x)). Since L is Archimedean, @lem-cof-rationals-separate gives \chi_1(x) = \chi_2(x). As x was arbitrary, \chi_1 = \chi_2. (This is Step 7 of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete with \chi_2 in place of \varphi; completeness of L is not needed, and neither is the Archimedean property of F.) Why L must be Archimedean (remark, not proved here). The last step separates \chi_1(x) from \chi_2(x) by a rational strictly between them, which is density of \iota_L(
Q) in L, and density needs Archimedes (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). In the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field, the elements 1/t and 2/t are different and have the same rationals below them, namely all q \le 0: a positive rational q has q > 1/n in 
Q for some n \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-rationals-archimedean), so \iota_{
Q(t)}(q) > \iota_{
Q(t)}(1/n) = 1/(n \cdot 1) > 2/t, because t > 2n \cdot 1 (@exm-rational-function-field). So the separating step fails in such a field. For the stronger statement proved above, with F arbitrary, the hypothesis on L cannot be dropped: on 
Q(t), the substitution t \mapsto t + 1 keeps degrees and leading coefficients, so it is an order-preserving field map 
Q(t) 	o 
Q(t) different from the identity (school polynomial algebra, as flagged in @exm-rational-function-field). An example with F Archimedean needs more algebra than this volume has, and we give none. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: each \chi_i fixes 
Q, with the reason (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, or directly: induction for 
N, then negatives and quotients). - 3: links the rationals below x to those below \chi_i(x), using that \chi_i fixes 
Q and reflects order. Either gives the full equivalence \iota_F(q) < x \iff \iota_L(q) < \chi_i(x), or, for the squeeze route of the next item, applies reflection by \chi_1 and \chi_2 to a rational strictly between \chi_1(x) and \chi_2(x). - 3: concludes \chi_1(x) = \chi_2(x) by rationals separating, or by a rational strictly between the two, invoking the Archimedean property of L. - 2: states the conclusion for every x \in F. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using density in L without a hypothesis that gives it; assuming \chi_i surjective. [C2: Dense image, and when the map is onto] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, L a complete ordered field, and \varphi \colon F 	o L the map of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. 1. Prove that \varphi(F) is dense in L: for all u < v in L there is x \in F with u < \varphi(x) < v. 2. Prove that if F is complete, then \varphi is surjective. 3. Prove that if \varphi is surjective, then F is complete. [Hint 1] For (b), given y \in L, look at the set S \coloneqq 
Q_L(y) and its copy \iota_F(S) in F. [Hint 2] For (b): \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F; let x \coloneqq \sup_F \iota_F(S), and show 
Q_F(x) = S. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, L is Archimedean. (a) Let u < v in L. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field in L there is q \in 
Q with u < \iota_L(q) < v. By Step 3 of the proof of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, \iota_L(q) = \varphi(\iota_F(q)), so x \coloneqq \iota_F(q) works. (b) Let F be complete and y \in L. Let S \coloneqq 
Q_L(y). Since L is Archimedean, there are n, m \in 
N with -y < \iota_L(n) and y < \iota_L(m). So -n \in S, and every q \in S has \iota_L(q) < y < \iota_L(m), hence q < m and \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(m). So \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F, and x \coloneqq \sup_F \iota_F(S) exists. We show 
Q_F(x) = S. (\supseteq) Let q \in S. By density in L there is r \in 
Q with \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) < y; then r \in S and q < r, so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) \le x. (\subseteq) Let \iota_F(q) < x. Then \iota_F(q) is not an upper bound of \iota_F(S), so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) for some r \in S; hence q < r and \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) < y, so q \in S. By (\star), 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = S = 
Q_L(y), so \varphi(x) = y by @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L. (c) Let \varphi be surjective. It is injective (strictly increasing), so bijective, with an inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Let A \subseteq F be non-empty with an upper bound b. Then \varphi(A) is non-empty and bounded above by \varphi(b), since a \le b gives \varphi(a) \le \varphi(b). As L is complete, s \coloneqq \sup \varphi(A) exists; let c \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(s). Upper bound: for a \in A, \varphi(a) \le s = \varphi(c), so a \le c, because \varphi reflects order (and is injective, for the case of equality). Least: if u is an upper bound of A, then \varphi(u) is an upper bound of \varphi(A), so \varphi(c) = s \le \varphi(u), and c \le u as before. So c = \sup A (@fd2:def-order-supremum), and F is complete. So \varphi is an order-preserving field isomorphism exactly when F is complete. Section 6.3 reaches the “if” direction by a different route, which computes no supremum at all. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) L is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so some \iota_L(q) lies strictly between u and v, and \iota_L(q) = \varphi(\iota_F(q)) (Step 3). - 2: (b) \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F (Archimedes in L, transferred through \iota_F), so x = \sup_F \iota_F(S) exists by completeness of F. - 2: (b) 
Q_F(x) = S, both inclusions; (\supseteq) uses density in L. - 1: (b) 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L(y) by (\star), hence \varphi(x) = y by @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L. - 3: (c) for non-empty A \subseteq F bounded above by b, \varphi(A) is bounded above by \varphi(b), and \varphi^{-1}(\sup \varphi(A)) is an upper bound of A and the least one, both using that \varphi reflects order and is bijective. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using density of \iota_L(
Q) in L without the Archimedean property of L; in (b), taking a supremum in F before checking that the set is non-empty and bounded above; in (c), assuming \varphi^{-1} preserves order without justification.

title: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content:
Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism Section 6.2 measured an element of an Archimedean ordered field F by the rationals below it and used the measurement to build a map into a complete ordered field L: by @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete there is exactly one order-preserving field map \varphi \colon F 	o L, and it keeps the rationals below each element, 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) (property (\star) of that theorem). This section takes both fields complete. Then maps run in both directions, and the word “exactly” turns them into inverses of each other without a single computation. The result is the theorem the chapter is named for: any two complete ordered fields are copies of each other, by one isomorphism and no other. The section ends with automorphisms: the only map of a complete ordered field to itself that respects sums, products and 1 is the identity, even when the map is asked neither to respect the order nor to be onto. Throughout, “order-preserving field map” has the meaning of @def-cof-order-preserving-map: a map \chi \colon F 	o L between ordered fields with \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b), \chi(ab) = \chi(a) \chi(b), \chi(1) = 1, and a < b \Rightarrow \chi(a) < \chi(b) for all a, b \in F. Such a map also reflects order: if \chi(a) < \chi(b), then a < b, since a = b would give \chi(a) = \chi(b) and b < a would give \chi(b) < \chi(a), both excluded by trichotomy (O1) in L. The uniqueness theorem Section 6.2 gave us, for complete F and L, a map \varphi \colon F 	o L. It did not say that \varphi is onto. A map can preserve everything in sight and still miss most of its target: the map \iota_{
R} \colon 
Q 	o 
R preserves sums, products and order (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field), and the real number r of @exm-sqrt2-class, whose square is 2, is not in its image. What rules this out when the source is complete as well? [Uniqueness of the Complete Ordered Field] Let F and L be complete ordered fields (@def-complete-ordered-field). Then there is exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o L (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). It is the map \varphi of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. Section 6.2 runs in both directions. Since F is complete, it is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so it is a legal source; since L is complete, it is a legal target. That gives \varphi \colon F 	o L. Swapping the roles gives \psi \colon L 	o F. To show that \psi undoes \varphi, we could try to compute \psi(\varphi(x)) from the two suprema. We do not have to. The composite \psi \circ \varphi \colon F 	o F is again an order-preserving field map, and so is the identity of F. The uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, applied with F as source and as target, says there is only one such map. So the two are equal. Uniqueness gives inverses. Before reading on: self-explain why \psi \circ \varphi is order-preserving. Which of the four conditions of @def-cof-order-preserving-map needs more than one line? Let F and L be complete ordered fields. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, each of them is Archimedean. The two maps. Since F is Archimedean and L is complete, @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete gives an order-preserving field map \varphi \colon F 	o L. Since L is Archimedean and F is complete, the same theorem, with the roles of the two fields exchanged, gives an order-preserving field map \psi \colon L 	o F. The composite \psi \circ \varphi is an order-preserving field map F 	o F. For a, b \in F, additivity of \varphi and then of \psi gives \psi(\varphi(a + b)) = \psi(\varphi(a) + \varphi(b)) = \psi(\varphi(a)) + \psi(\varphi(b)) , and the same two steps with products give \psi(\varphi(ab)) = \psi(\varphi(a)) \, \psi(\varphi(b)). Also \psi(\varphi(1)) = \psi(1) = 1. If a < b, then \varphi(a) < \varphi(b), since \varphi is strictly increasing, and then \psi(\varphi(a)) < \psi(\varphi(b)), since \psi is. The composite is the identity. The identity map \id_F is an order-preserving field map F 	o F: each of the four conditions reads u = u or a < b \Rightarrow a < b. Now apply @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete with source F, which is Archimedean, and target F, which is complete: there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o F. Both \psi \circ \varphi and \id_F are such maps, so \psi \circ \varphi = \id_F. Exchanging the roles of F and L, the same argument gives \varphi \circ \psi = \id_L. Existence. So \psi is a two-sided inverse of \varphi, and \varphi is bijective by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Hence \varphi is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o L. Uniqueness. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be any order-preserving field isomorphism. Forgetting that it is bijective, \chi is an order-preserving field map F 	o L, and by the uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete there is only one such map. Hence \chi = \varphi. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: three of the four conditions are one line each, because each of \varphi, \psi satisfies it and the condition passes through a composite. The order condition is the same, in two steps: a < b gives \varphi(a) < \varphi(b), which is a strict inequality in L, the kind of hypothesis \psi accepts. Nothing harder is hiding there. The weight of the proof sits in the uniqueness clause, which the proof uses three times: once for \psi \circ \varphi, once for \varphi \circ \psi, and once for \chi. The proof never evaluates \psi(\varphi(x)). A direct proof that \varphi is onto exists: given y \in L, take the supremum in F of the rationals below y, and check that \varphi sends it to y. It needs the measuring argument of Section 6.2 once more, now from L back to F. The route above gets the same conclusion from a sentence about how many maps there are. Why could the proof not simply define \psi \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}, instead of building \psi from @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete? The inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F exists only if \varphi is bijective (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and bijectivity is what the theorem is trying to prove. Section 6.2 gives \varphi as an injective map (it is strictly increasing), with no claim that it is onto. The map \psi is built independently of \varphi, and only afterwards shown to be its inverse. Each hypothesis has a job. Completeness of L makes L a target, so that \varphi exists. Completeness of F makes F a target, so that \psi exists. The uniqueness clause with F on both sides is cited as stated, for a complete target, but by the remark after its proof in Section 6.2 it needs only that F is Archimedean. Completeness of each field also gives the Archimedean property that makes it a source. Drop the completeness of F, and the conclusion fails: 
Q is Archimedean, \iota_{
R} \colon 
Q 	o 
R is the only order-preserving field map (@thm-cof-embedding-into-complete), and it is not onto, as the opening of this section noted. One real line The theorem says that two complete ordered fields have the same shape, with a unique dictionary between them. We want a short way to write the first half of that sentence. Two ordered fields are the same up to relabeling when an order-preserving bijection respects the arithmetic. title: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
Two Non-Examples The uniqueness theorem of Section 6.3 used three hypotheses in three different ways. The Archimedean property let rationals separate elements (@lem-cof-rationals-separate). Completeness built the map as a supremum (@thm-cof-embedding-into-complete), and it supplied square roots (@prp-cof-square-roots). The order condition was either assumed of the map or, for complete fields, recovered from the square roots (@thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity). This section builds two ordered fields that are not 
R, each missing something. The field 
R(x) of rational functions obeys every axiom of an ordered field and fails the Archimedean property; it has an order-preserving symmetry that moves x. The field 
Q(\sqrt 2) is Archimedean and not complete; it has a symmetry that does not preserve the order. A table at the end compares the four fields. Throughout, 
R is the complete ordered field of Chapter 5 (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), and we write q for \iota_{
R}(q) when q \in 
Q, as Section 5.4 did. Powers t^i of a real number t are those of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field, and finite sums \sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i of real numbers are defined by recursion, as in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3 (@fd2:def-sum-product), with 
R as the set of values; the empty sum is 0. Polynomial functions Chapter 4 met a field of quotients of polynomials, 
Q(t) (@exm-rational-function-field), and stated without proof that it is an ordered field. Here proofs depend on such a field, so we build it from things we can check: functions on 
R, compared at large arguments, with no algebra of formal polynomials. For d \in 
N and a list (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_d) of real numbers, the function p \colon 
R 	o 
R , \qquad p(t) \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i t^i , is the polynomial function of the list. A polynomial function is a function 
R 	o 
R that is the polynomial function of at least one list. When a_d 
e 0, the list has top degree d and top coefficient a_d. The phrase “of at least one list” matters. Appending zeros to a list does not change its function: (1, 2) and (1, 2, 0) both give t \mapsto 1 + 2t. So degree and top coefficient belong to a list, not to a function, until we know more.
