Q(\sqrt 2). Since 
R is complete, it is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so y < n \cdot 1 for some n \in 
N. This inequality holds in 
Q(\sqrt 2), whose order is that of 
R. So 
Q(\sqrt 2) is Archimedean. Being Archimedean is inherited by every ordered subfield of 
R. Completeness is not. [The Field Generated by the Square Root of Two Is Not Complete] The element 3 of 
Q(\sqrt 2) is positive and has no square root in 
Q(\sqrt 2). Hence 
Q(\sqrt 2) is not complete. A square root a + b\sqrt 2 of 3 would, by unique representation, have 2ab = 0 and a^2 + 2b^2 = 3. So either a^2 = 3 or (2b)^2 = 6, with a, 2b rational. Neither 3 nor 6 is a rational square, by the descent that showed 2 is not (@thm-no-rational-square-two). The descent there used 1 < y < 2 for the would-be root y; for 3 we use 1 < y < 2 again, and for 6, 2 < y < 3. We isolate the descent as a claim; its proof is that of @thm-no-rational-square-two with 2 replaced by n, and it sits in the fold. Let n, k \in 
N with k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2. Then no y \in 
Q has y^2 = n. Suppose y \in 
Q and y^2 = n. Then y 
e 0, since n > k^2 \ge 0. Replacing y by -y if necessary, as in @thm-no-rational-square-two, we may take y > 0. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), y = a/b with a \in 
Z and b \in 
Z_{>0}; then a > 0 by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a), and y^2 = n says a^2 = n b^2, as in @thm-no-rational-square-two. So the set D \coloneqq \{ v \in 
Z_{>0} : u^2 = n v^2 	ext{ for some } u \in 
Z_{>0} \} contains b and is bounded below by 0. By @prp-integer-least-element it has a least element v; fix u \in 
Z_{>0} with u^2 = n v^2. kv < u. Otherwise 0 \le u \le kv, so u^2 \le k^2 v^2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), or equality), and k^2 v^2 < n v^2 since v^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), (e)). Then u^2 < n v^2, against u^2 = n v^2. u < (k + 1) v. Otherwise 0 \le (k + 1) v \le u, so (k + 1)^2 v^2 \le u^2 = n v^2 < (k + 1)^2 v^2, a contradiction. Descent. Put v' \coloneqq u - kv and u' \coloneqq nv - ku. By the two inequalities, 0 < v' < v. Multiplying kv < u by u > 0 gives v \cdot ku < u^2 = v \cdot nv, so ku < nv (if ku \ge nv, multiplying by v > 0 would give the reverse), and u' > 0. Expanding,  egin{aligned} u'^2 - n v'^2 &= (n^2 v^2 - 2nkuv + k^2 u^2) - (n u^2 - 2nkuv + n k^2 v^2) \ &= (k^2 - n)(u^2 - n v^2) = 0 . \end{aligned} So v' \in D and v' < v, against the choice of v. This proves the claim. Since 1 < 3 < 4 and 4 < 6 < 9, the claim with (n, k) = (3, 1) and (6, 2) shows that neither 3 nor 6 is the square of a rational. Now suppose c = a + b\sqrt 2 \in 
Q(\sqrt 2), with a, b \in 
Q, has c^2 = 3. By the product formula of @prp-cof-sqrt2-field-archimedean (b), (a^2 + 2b^2) + 2ab\sqrt 2 = 3 + 0\sqrt 2 , so by unique representation, 2ab = 0 and a^2 + 2b^2 = 3. Hence a = 0 or b = 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f), as 2 
e 0). If b = 0, then a^2 = 3; if a = 0, then 2b^2 = 3, so (2b)^2 = 6. Both are excluded by the claim. So 3, which is positive, has no square root in 
Q(\sqrt 2). If 
Q(\sqrt 2) were complete, @prp-cof-square-roots would give a square root of 3 in it. So 
Q(\sqrt 2) is not complete. The proof found no explicit set without a supremum; it found a missing square root and let @prp-cof-square-roots supply the set. The set is easy to name: \{ y \in 
Q(\sqrt 2) : y \ge 0, \ y^2 < 3 \} is non-empty and bounded above by 2, and in 
R its supremum is the square root \sqrt 3 of 3 given by @prp-cof-square-roots, which is not in 
Q(\sqrt 2). The element \sqrt 3 bounds the set above: y \ge 0 and y^2 < 3 = (\sqrt 3)^2 give y < \sqrt 3 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). If s < \sqrt 3, then, 
R being Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field gives a rational q with \max\{s, 0\} < q < \sqrt 3; then q \ge 0 and q^2 < 3, so q lies in the set and s is not an upper bound. Hence \sqrt 3 is the least upper bound. Why does the descent claim not show that 4 is not a rational square? Which hypothesis fails? There is no k \in 
N with k^2 < 4 < (k + 1)^2: k^2 < 4 forces k \le 1 (for k \ge 2, k^2 \ge 4), and then (k + 1)^2 \le 4. The descent needs the root y = u/v to lie strictly between k and k + 1, so that 0 < v' < v; the natural choice k = 2 (for which k^2 < n fails) gives v' = u - 2v = 0 when y = 2, and the descent stops. And indeed 4 = 2^2. The field 
Q(\sqrt 2) has a symmetry that the uniqueness theorem forbids in 
R. [Conjugation in 
Q(\sqrt 2)] Define \sigma \colon 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
Q(\sqrt 2) by \sigma(a + b\sqrt 2) \coloneqq a - b\sqrt 2 for a, b \in 
Q. Show that \sigma is a bijection that respects sums and products and has \sigma(1) = 1, that it is not the identity, and that it is not order-preserving. Then find the line of the proof of @thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity that fails for \sigma. Well defined. By unique representation (@prp-cof-sqrt2-field-archimedean (a)), each element has exactly one pair (a, b), so the formula defines a function. Sums, products, 1. \sigma respects sums, since (a - b\sqrt 2) + (c - d\sqrt 2) = (a + c) - (b + d)\sqrt 2. For products, by the product formula, \sigma igl( (ac + 2bd) + (ad + bc)\sqrt 2  igr) = (ac + 2bd) - (ad + bc)\sqrt 2 = (a - b\sqrt 2)(c - d\sqrt 2) . And \sigma(1) = \sigma(1 + 0\sqrt 2) = 1. Bijective. \sigma(\sigma(a + b\sqrt 2)) = a + b\sqrt 2, so \sigma is its own two-sided inverse (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Not the identity, not order-preserving. \sqrt 2 > 0, since it is a non-zero element with \sqrt 2 \ge 0. But \sigma(\sqrt 2) = -\sqrt 2 < 0 = \sigma(0). So \sigma(\sqrt 2) 
e \sqrt 2, and 0 < \sqrt 2 while \sigma(0) > \sigma(\sqrt 2). The failing line. Step 1 of the proof of @thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity begins: “there is b \in F with b \ge 0 and b^2 = a”. For a = \sqrt 2 there is no such b in 
Q(\sqrt 2). Indeed, if c \in 
Q(\sqrt 2) had c^2 = \sqrt 2, then \sigma(c)^2 = \sigma(c^2) = \sigma(\sqrt 2) = -\sqrt 2 < 0; but \sigma(c)^2 \ge 0, as every square in the ordered field 
R is (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So the step “\sigma(a) = \sigma(b)^2 > 0” cannot start, and \sigma indeed sends the positive element \sqrt 2 to a negative one. Step 2 works in any ordered field. Step 3 as written cites completeness of F, for the Archimedean property and for the target of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, but its conclusion still holds in 
Q(\sqrt 2): if \sigma were order-preserving, then \sigma followed by the inclusion would be an order-preserving field map 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
R, hence the inclusion by the uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete (source 
Q(\sqrt 2), Archimedean by @prp-cof-sqrt2-field-archimedean; target 
R), and \sigma would be the identity. Only Step 1 genuinely fails. Two maps into 
R. Since 
Q(\sqrt 2) is Archimedean and 
R complete, @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete gives exactly one order-preserving field map 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
R; it is the inclusion. The composite of \sigma with the inclusion is a second map 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
R that respects sums, products and 1. The uniqueness clause is not contradicted, because this second map is not order-preserving. A symmetry that keeps the order The conjugation of 
Q(\sqrt 2) escapes @thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity by breaking the order. The field 
R(x) escapes @cor-cof-order-automorphism-identity in the other way: it has a symmetry that keeps the order and still moves elements. The symmetry shifts the argument by 1. [Shifting the Argument] For a polynomial function p, write p^{+} for the function t \mapsto p(t + 1). Show that \sigma([p/q]) \coloneqq [p^{+}/q^{+}] defines an order-preserving field automorphism \sigma of 
R(x) with \sigma(x) = x + 1 
e x. (i) p^{+} is a polynomial function. By induction on the length of a list of p (@fd1:ax-induction). A list of length 1 gives a constant p, and p^{+} = p. For a list (a_0, \dots, a_d) with d \ge 1, let p' be the function of (a_1, \dots, a_d); re-indexing the sum, p(t) = a_0 + t \cdot p'(t), so p(t + 1) = a_0 + (1 + t) \cdot p'(t + 1) . By the induction hypothesis p'^{+} is a polynomial function, t \mapsto 1 + t is that of (1, 1), and @lem-cof-polynomial-closure (b), (a) make the right side a polynomial function. (ii) Fractions go to fractions. If (p, q) is a fraction, then q(t) 
e 0 for every t > T_q, so q^{+}(t) 
e 0 for every t > T_q - 1. If every entry of a list of q^{+} were 0, then q^{+} would vanish everywhere; so a list of q^{+} has a non-zero entry, and (p^{+}, q^{+}) is a fraction. Its value at t is the value of (p, q) at t + 1. (iii) Well defined, additive, multiplicative. If (p_1, q_1) and (p_2, q_2) have equal values for every t > T, the shifted fractions have equal values for every t > T - 1; so \sigma is well defined (@thm-well-defined-on-classes (a)). Since sums and products are pointwise at large t, and shifting the argument commutes with pointwise operations, \sigma(f + g) and \sigma(f) + \sigma(g) have the same values at all large t, and likewise for products. And \sigma(1) = 1, since a constant is unchanged by the shift. (iv) Order. If f \in P, with positive values for t > T, then \sigma(f) has positive values for t > T - 1, so \sigma(f) \in P. For f < g, \sigma(g) - \sigma(f) = \sigma(g - f) \in P (additivity gives \sigma(-f) = -\sigma(f), as in Step 2 of the proof of @thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity), so \sigma(f) < \sigma(g). (v) Bijective. Shifting by -1 in the same way defines 	au with 	au(\sigma(f)) = f = \sigma(	au(f)): the values are shifted by 1 and back. By @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \sigma is bijective. (vi) It moves x. \sigma(x) has value t + 1, which is the value of x + 1; so \sigma(x) = x + 1. And x + 1 
e x, since 1 
e 0. So @cor-cof-order-automorphism-identity needs its hypothesis. Its proof went through @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, whose uniqueness clause rests on @lem-cof-rationals-separate, which needs the Archimedean property. In 
R(x) that lemma fails exactly here: every rational lies below x and below x + 1, so x and x + 1 have the same rationals below them, all of 
Q, and nothing can tell them apart. An order-preserving map that fixes the rationals is free to send one to the other. No proof uses this example; only the table below cites it. What each hypothesis buys The table collects the four fields of this chapter. Each entry names where it is proved; no entry rests on an exercise. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Q is not complete: if it were, @prp-cof-square-roots would give a rational square root of 2, against @thm-no-rational-square-two. And a map \sigma \colon 
Q 	o 
Q that respects sums and products and fixes 1 is the identity, with no order hypothesis: by @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals with F = L = 
Q, \sigma = \sigma \circ \iota_{

Q} = \id_{
Q}, the last equality by the uniqueness clause of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field, since \id_{
Q} is such a map. Read across, the table shows what the uniqueness theorem used. 
Q(\sqrt 2) has the Archimedean property and lacks square roots, and its symmetry breaks the order. 
R(x) lacks the Archimedean property, and its symmetry keeps the order. Of these three, only 
R, which has both, has no symmetry at all. Read down, the column of 
Q shows that the last row does not characterize 
R: a field can be rigid for a cheaper reason, having nothing besides rationals to move. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Is x^2 - 100x positive in 
R(x)? Justify your answer. 2. Here is an argument. “
Q(\sqrt 2) is Archimedean, so by @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete it has an order-preserving field map into the complete ordered field 
R. Hence 
Q(\sqrt 2) is complete.” Is the conclusion true? Which step fails? 3. Put 1/x, 1/x^2 and 1/10^6 in increasing order in 
R(x). (a) Yes. Its value t^2 - 100t = t(t - 100) is positive for every t > 100. (Or: the list (0, -100, 1) has top coefficient 1 > 0, and @lem-cof-leading-term-sign applies with T = 101.) (b) The conclusion is false (@prp-cof-sqrt2-field-incomplete). The illegal step is the last: completeness of the target says nothing about suprema in the source. A set A \subseteq 
Q(\sqrt 2) that is bounded above has a supremum in 
R, but it may lie outside 
Q(\sqrt 2): for A = \{ y \in 
Q(\sqrt 2) : y \ge 0, \ y^2 < 3 \} it is \sqrt 3, which is not in 
Q(\sqrt 2) (the remark after @prp-cof-sqrt2-field-incomplete). (c) 0 < 1/x^2 < 1/x < 1/10^6. The value of 1/x - 1/x^2 is (t - 1)/t^2 > 0 for t > 1, and that of 1/10^6 - 1/x is 1/10^6 - 1/t > 0 for t > 10^6. B. Practice [B1] Prove that multiplication in 
R(x) is associative and that the positive set P is closed under sums. In each, choose representatives, name a threshold T beyond which every denominator involved is non-zero (and, for P, every value involved is positive), compute the values of both sides at t > T with the pointwise rule, and say which fact about 
R makes them equal or positive. Associativity. Let f = [p_1/q_1], g = [p_2/q_2], h = [p_3/q_3], and T \coloneqq \max\{T_{q_1}, T_{q_2}, T_{q_3}\}. For t > T, the denominators of all fractions involved are non-zero, and by the pointwise rule the value of (fg)h is (u(t)v(t))w(t) and that of f(gh) is u(t)(v(t)w(t)), where u, v, w are the values of the three fractions. These are equal by (F5) in 
R. So the two fractions produced by the formula have equal values for every t > T: they are equivalent, and (fg)h = f(gh). Closure of P under sums. Let f, g \in P: the value of f is positive for t > T_1 and that of g for t > T_2 (these thresholds may be taken \ge T_{q_1}, T_{q_2}). For t > \max\{T_1, T_2\}, the value of f + g is u(t) + v(t) > 0 by (O3) in 
R (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). So f + g \in P. The finiteness of the list of thresholds is what lets us take a maximum. [B2] Show that no rational number squares to 5 or to 10. Then show that 5 has no square root in 
Q(\sqrt 2). Since 2^2 = 4 < 5 < 9 = 3^2 and 3^2 = 9 < 10 < 16 = 4^2, the claim stated with @prp-cof-sqrt2-field-incomplete, with (n, k) = (5, 2) and (10, 3), shows that neither is a rational square. (The descent there checks u'^2 - n v'^2 = (k^2 - n)(u^2 - n v^2) for these values too; the identity holds for all n, k.) Now let c = a + b\sqrt 2 with a, b \in 
Q and c^2 = 5. By the product formula, (a^2 + 2b^2) + 2ab\sqrt 2 = 5 + 0\sqrt 2, so by unique representation (@prp-cof-sqrt2-field-archimedean (a)), 2ab = 0 and a^2 + 2b^2 = 5. If b = 0, then a^2 = 5; if a = 0, then 2b^2 = 5, so (2b)^2 = 10. Both are excluded. Hence 5 has no square root in 
Q(\sqrt 2). [B3] Show that x^3 + 1 is positive in 
R(x) but is not a square there. Hint: the argument of @exm-cof-x-not-square, with t^3 + 1 in place of t. Positive. t \mapsto t^3 + 1 is the function of (1, 0, 0, 1), with top coefficient 1 > 0; by @lem-cof-leading-term-sign its value is positive for all large t. Not a square. Suppose x^3 + 1 = [p/q]^2. Then h(t) \coloneqq (t^3 + 1) q(t)^2 - p(t)^2 = 0 for all large t, and h is the function of a list by @lem-cof-polynomial-closure (a), (b). Cut q after its last non-zero entry b_e. By (b), (t^3 + 1) \cdot q^2 has a list with top degree 3 + 2e = 2e + 3, odd, and top coefficient 1 \cdot b_e^2 
e 0. If a list of p is all zeros, then (t^3 + 1) q(t)^2 = 0 for all large t, and (c) contradicts b_e^2 
e 0. Otherwise cut p after its last non-zero entry a_d; then -p^2 has a list with top degree 2d, even, and top coefficient -a_d^2 
e 0. Since 2d 
e 2e + 3 (@cor-integers-even-odd (a)), the sum list for h has the non-zero entry b_e^2 or -a_d^2 at index \max\{2d, 2e + 3\}, against @lem-cof-polynomial-closure (c). So x^3 + 1 is not a square. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the supremum property fails in the rational functions] Show directly from @def-complete-ordered-field, without @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, that 
R(x) is not complete. Let A \coloneqq \{ n \cdot 1 : n \in 
N \} \subseteq 
R(x). It is non-empty (0 \cdot 1 \in A), and it is bounded above by x: the value of x - n is t - n > 0 for t > n (@prp-cof-rational-functions-not-archimedean). Suppose s \in 
R(x) is a supremum of A. For every n \in 
N, n + 1 \in 
N, so (n + 1) \cdot 1 \le s by (S1), that is, n \cdot 1 + 1 \le s (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a)), and n \cdot 1 \le s - 1. So s - 1 is an upper bound of A, and (S2) gives s \le s - 1, that is, 1 \le 0, which is false in an ordered field (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So A has no supremum, and 
R(x) is not complete. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: exhibits a non-empty set bounded above, with the bound verified (here x, by a threshold for the value of x - n, or by @lem-cof-leading-term-sign). - 3: supposes a supremum s, and uses (S1) on (n + 1) \cdot 1. - 3: plays leastness against s - 1: either shows that s - 1 is an upper bound, from (n + 1) \cdot 1 \le s \Rightarrow n \cdot 1 \le s - 1 for every n, or notes s - 1 < s so that (S2) gives n with n \cdot 1 > s - 1. - 2: reaches the contradiction (with (S2), or with (S1) via (n + 1) \cdot 1 > s), concluding that no supremum exists. Fatal errors (0 for the step): proving only “not Archimedean” and stopping; treating x as a real number (for instance, “take n > x”). [C2: A complete ordered field is uncountable] Let F be a complete ordered field. Write 3^{n} for the power (3 \cdot 1_F)^{n} of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field. For s = (s_n)_{n \in 
N} \in \{0, 1\}^{
N}, let S_k(s) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^{k}  rac{2 s_n}{3^{n+1}} \quad (k \in 
N) , \qquad \Phi(s) \coloneqq \sup_{k \in 
N} S_k(s) . 1. Show that \Phi(s) exists. 2. Show that \Phi \colon \{0, 1\}^{
N} 	o F is injective. 3. Deduce that F is uncountable (@fd2:thm-binary-sequences-uncountable). [Hint 1] Think of ternary expansions that use only the digits 0 and 2. For (a), find a single upper bound for all S_k(s) by comparing with s_n = 1 for every n. [Hint 2] For (b), let j be the least index where s and s' differ (it exists by least elements), with s_j = 1 and s'_j = 0, and put c \coloneqq S_{j-1}(s) = S_{j-1}(s') (with c \coloneqq 0 if j = 0). Tail bound. For k \le m, by induction on m (@fd1:ax-induction), exactly as in @eq-ternary-tail but in F: 0 \le S_m(s) - S_k(s) \le  rac{1}{3^{k+1}} -  rac{1}{3^{m+1}} , since passing from m to m + 1 adds 2 s_{m+1}/3^{m+2} \in [0, 2/3^{m+2}], and -1/3^{m+1} + 2/3^{m+2} = -1/3^{m+2}. In particular S_k(s) is non-decreasing in k. (a) The set \{ S_k(s) : k \in 
N \} is non-empty, and bounded above by 1: S_k(s) \le S_0(s) + 1/3 - 1/3^{k+1} \le 2/3 + 1/3 = 1 by the tail bound with k = 0. Since F is complete, \Phi(s) exists. (b) Let s 
e s'. The set of indices where they differ is a non-empty subset of 
N, so it has a least element j (@prp-integer-least-element); say s_j = 1 and s'_j = 0. Let c \coloneqq S_{j-1}(s) = S_{j-1}(s'), the sums agreeing up to j - 1 (with c \coloneqq 0 if j = 0). Then \Phi(s) \ge S_j(s) = c + 2/3^{j+1} by (S1). For k \ge j, the tail bound gives S_k(s') \le S_j(s') + 1/3^{j+1} = c + 1/3^{j+1}; for k < j, S_k(s') \le S_j(s') = c. So c + 1/3^{j+1} is an upper bound of the S_k(s'), and \Phi(s') \le c + 1/3^{j+1} by (S2). Hence \Phi(s) - \Phi(s') \ge 1/3^{j+1} > 0, and \Phi(s) 
e \Phi(s'). (c) If F were countable, there would be an injection g \colon F 	o 
N (@fd2:thm-countable-characterizations), and g \circ \Phi would be an injection \{0, 1\}^{
N} 	o 
N (@fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective), making \{0, 1\}^{
N} countable, against @fd2:thm-binary-sequences-uncountable. Alternatively, by @cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals there is a bijection F 	o 
R, and 
R is uncountable by @exr-the-least-upper-bound-property-r3. The route above shows that uncountability follows from the supremum property directly, with no construction behind it. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a), a common upper bound for the partial sums, and completeness invoked for the supremum. - 2: the tail bound, by induction, in F. - 4: (b), the first differing index j by least elements, the lower bound c + 2/3^{j+1} for \Phi(s) by (S1), and the upper bound c + 1/3^{j+1} for \Phi(s') by (S2). - 2: (c), the composite injection and the uncountability of \{0, 1\}^{
N}. The second route, by @cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals and the uncountability of 
R, also earns these 2 points; (a) and (b) are still marked as above. Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating \Phi(s) as an infinite sum computed term by term; using decimal or ternary expansions of real numbers as known facts. [C3: Increasing and bounded] Let F be a complete ordered field and (a_n)_{n \in 
N} a sequence in F with a_n \le a_{n+1} for every n, whose set of values is bounded above. Prove that a_n 	o s in F (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field), where s is the supremum of the set of values. Here is the start of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let s \coloneqq \sup \{ a_n : n \in 
N \}, which exists because the set is non-empty and bounded above and F is complete. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. …” The move is construct a point as a supremum, and use its leastness through “s - \varepsilon is not an upper bound”, which hands us a witness. It built square roots in @prp-cof-square-roots; here it builds a limit. Completion. Since s - \varepsilon < s and s is the least upper bound, s - \varepsilon is not an upper bound of the values, so a_N > s - \varepsilon for some N \in 
N. For n \ge N, a_N \le a_n, by induction on n - N from a_m \le a_{m+1}; and a_n \le s by (S1). So s - \varepsilon < a_N \le a_n \le s < s + \varepsilon , that is, \abs{a_n - s} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, a_n 	o s. Here N depends on \varepsilon.

title: 6.5 Assume the Axioms or Build a Model
content:
Assume the Axioms or Build a Model Section 6.3 showed that two complete ordered fields are always linked, and by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism (@thm-cof-uniqueness). This last section asks what that theorem means for the rest of the series. There are two honest ways to begin analysis: assume the axioms of a complete ordered field, or build a model of them. We compare the two, show what an isomorphism carries from one model to another and what it does not, and list what Analysis on the Real Line takes from this volume. In particular \Bigl( q_n +  rac{1}{2^n} \Bigr)^2 =  rac{(k_n + 1)^2}{(2^n)^2} > 2 , \qquad q_n^2 \le 2 . 	ag{$\ast$} Since k = 2^n has k^2 \le 2 (2^n)^2, k_n \ge 2^n and q_n \ge 1. So (q_n) \in \sC (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences). (c) Expanding (\ast), 2 < q_n^2 + 2q_n/2^n + 1/(2^n)^2. By the squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c), between (0)_n and (5/(n + 1)), the sequence (2 - q_n^2) is null, and so is (q_n^2 - 2) (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b), c = -1). For each two fields in different classes, name a property that one has and the other lacks, and prove that an order-preserving field isomorphism carries it across. By the remark after @cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals, \cong is an equivalence relation on \mathcal S (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Two transfer facts. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be an order-preserving field isomorphism. By the remark after @cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals, \chi^{-1} \colon L 	o F is one too, so each fact below also holds with F and L exchanged. Recall \chi(n \cdot 1_F) = \chi(\iota_F(n)) = \iota_L(n) = n \cdot 1_L for n \in

So if n \cdot 1 is a square in F, it is a square in L, and conversely. (ii) Archimedes. Let F be Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field), and let y \in L. Take n \in 
N with \chi^{-1}(y) < n \cdot 1_F. Since \chi is strictly increasing, y = \chi(\chi^{-1}(y)) < \chi(n \cdot 1_F) = n \cdot 1_L. So L is Archimedean, and conversely. The classes. The map  eta \colon 
R 	o X of this section is an order-preserving field isomorphism, so

R and X (@prp-cof-square-roots). By (i) with n = 2,

Q(\sqrt 2) 
ot\cong 
R and 
Q(\sqrt 2)

Q \}, \{

R(x) \} and \{ 
R, X \}, and the quotient set \mathcal S/{\cong} (@fd2:def-quotient-set) has four elements. The two complete fields share a class, as @thm-cof-uniqueness requires; the other three fall into three classes. [R4] Let F be a complete ordered field, and for n \in 
N write 10^{-n} for  igl((10 \cdot 1_F)^n igr)^{-1}. Prove that \sup \{ 1 - 10^{-n} : n \in 
N \} = 1 . The tool is the Archimedean property of F, which holds by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, together with a lower bound for the powers (10 \cdot 1_F)^n of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field. The bound. We show (10 \cdot 1_F)^n \ge (1 + 9n) \cdot 1_F for every n \in 
N, by @fd1:ax-induction with base P(0): (10 \cdot 1_F)^0 = 1_F = (1 + 0) \cdot 1_F. For the step, 10 \cdot 1_F > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), P(n), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (or equality), and @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a), (b),  egin{aligned} (10 \cdot 1_F)^{n+1} &= (10 \cdot 1_F)^n (10 \cdot 1_F) \ge  igl((1 + 9n) \cdot 1_F igr)(10 \cdot 1_F) \ &= (10 + 90n) \cdot 1_F \ge (10 + 9n) \cdot 1_F =  igl(1 + 9(n + 1) igr) \cdot 1_F , \end{aligned} using 10 + 9n \le 10 + 90n in 
N. In particular (10 \cdot 1_F)^n \ge 1_F > 0, so 10^{-n} is defined and positive (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Upper bound. 10^{-n} > 0 gives 1 - 10^{-n} < 1 for every n. Least. Let b \in F with b < 1. Then 1 - b > 0, and @prp-archimedean-reciprocal gives N \in 
Z_{>0}, depending on b, with 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < 1 - b. Since (10 \cdot 1_F)^N \ge (1 + 9N) \cdot 1_F \ge N \cdot 1_F > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), @prp-reciprocal-order (b) (or equality) gives 10^{-N} \le 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < 1 - b, so the element 1 - 10^{-N} of the set exceeds b, and b is not an upper bound. Reading 1 - 10^{-n} as 0.9, 0.99, \dots and summing a geometric series uses infinite decimals, which this volume never defined; and an argument by limits would need the limit of (10^{-n}), which is the same Archimedean estimate with more machinery. title: Constructing the Real Numbers by Dedekind Cuts
content:
Constructing the Real Numbers by Dedekind Cuts This chapter is optional: nothing outside it depends on it, and the volume’s main line ended with Chapter 6. Chapter 5 built a real number as a class of Cauchy sequences of rationals, many rational approximations identified when they agree in the limit. Dedekind’s idea, published in 1872, is shorter to state: a real number is the set of all rationals below it. The gap that Section 2.6 found in 
Q splits the rationals into a lower piece, those that are negative or have square below 2, and the rest, and Dedekind takes the lower piece as the square root of 2. The chapter makes this precise. It says which sets of rationals qualify (the cuts), orders them by inclusion, adds and multiplies them, and proves that they form a complete ordered field 
R_{\mathrm D} in which the rationals sit as the rational cuts and the cut of the gap squares to 2. The question behind the chapter is: if two people build the real numbers in different ways, in what sense do they have the same numbers? On this road the costs fall the other way round from Chapter 5. The least upper bound of a bounded set of cuts is its union, checked in a few lines with no arithmetic at all, while negatives need a margin and multiplication needs a detour through positive cuts and signs; on the Cauchy road the arithmetic was termwise and completeness took two sections. The last section applies the uniqueness theorem of Chapter 6 to the two models. There is exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism from Chapter 5’s field to the cuts, and it can be written down: it sends a Cauchy real to the set of rationals below it. So the two roads give the same real numbers, and Dedekind’s definition is what the Cauchy model sees when it looks at one of its elements through the rationals. What you need. Chapter 2 above all, and Chapter 4; for Sections 7.5 and 7.6, Chapters 5 and 6; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 and 2, chiefly Section 2.6; and Logic and Proof, Chapters 4 and 5. From Chapter 2: 
Q as an ordered field, with the axioms (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4) and their rules (@thm-rationals-ordered-field, @def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-reciprocal-order); 
Q Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon); least elements and discreteness of the integers, for the walk up by \varepsilon (@prp-integer-least-element, @thm-integers-ordered-ring); and the gap at \sqrt 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two, @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). From Chapter 4: halves and fractions in an ordered field and the absolute value (@prp-ordered-field-halves, @lem-field-fraction-rules, @def-absolute-value-ordered-field); the one copy \iota_F of 
Q in an ordered field, with its uniqueness clause (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field); the Archimedean property and density of 
Q (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field); and, for exercises of Section 7.6, limits and Cauchy sequences (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field). From Chapter 5: complete ordered fields (@def-complete-ordered-field), the Cauchy model and the theorem that it is one (@def-reals-cauchy-classes, @thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), its copy of 
Q (@thm-rational-embedding), and the Newton class whose square is 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class). From Chapter 6: order-preserving field maps and the rationals below an element (@def-cof-order-preserving-map, @def-cof-rationals-below, @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals), and the rationals below a sum (@lem-cof-below-sum), for the remark after the proof in Section 7.6 and Exercise B1; the uniqueness theorem (@thm-cof-uniqueness), which Section 7.6 applies; that complete ordered fields are Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), for the second proof in Section 7.5; and the embedding of an Archimedean field into a complete one, with its property (⋆) and uniqueness clause (@thm-cof-embedding-into-complete), together with the fold after @cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals on inverses of isomorphisms, for the inverse map in Section 7.6. Chapter 1 supplies the axioms that make the set of all cuts a set (@ax-zf-fragment). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality: power sets, unions of families and inclusion, Sections 1.1 and 1.2 (@fd2:def-power-set, @fd2:def-family-union-intersection, @fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric, @fd2:prp-subset-transitive); sums of sets of numbers, Section 1.6 (@fd2:exm-sets-of-numbers-as-images); partial orders, upper bounds and suprema, Section 2.6 (@fd2:def-partial-order, @fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum); and, for one review exercise, countable sets, Chapter 3 (@fd2:thm-countable-characterizations). From Logic and Proof: the quantifier rules and the negation of quantified statements, Chapter 4 (@fd1:def-rules-universal, @fd1:def-rule-existential-introduction, @fd1:def-rules-existential, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication), and the catalogue of illegal steps, Chapter 5, for the find-the-error exercises (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - Cuts. The set below the gap at \sqrt 2; the definition of a cut by three conditions, non-empty and not all of 
Q, closed downward, no largest element, and the set 
R_{\mathrm D} of all cuts; the rational cuts D_q and the cut \sigma of the gap; why each condition is there, with a set that has a largest element as the cautionary case; and the two lemmas the rest of the chapter rests on, separation of inside and outside and the walk up by \varepsilon. - Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions. Cuts ordered by inclusion, which recovers the order of 
Q on rational cuts and is total because of separation; and the theorem that a non-empty set of cuts bounded above has a supremum, its union, with each hypothesis shown to be needed. - Addition and Negatives. The sum of two cuts as the set of sums, and the zero cut D_0; the natural recipe for a negative, which fails on the rational cuts, and its repair by a positive margin; the key proof that a cut plus its negative is D_0, by walking up; and the cuts as an ordered abelian group. - Multiplication. Why the set of all products fails; the product of positive cuts, its laws and the walk up in multiplicative form; the extension to all cuts by absolute value and sign, through one lemma of sign rules; distributivity, the reciprocal, and the theorem that the cuts form an ordered field. - The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field. The rational cuts as the copy of 
Q, with its order and arithmetic; density of the rational cuts and the Archimedean property; the cut \sigma squares to D_2 and is not rational; and the cuts as a complete ordered field, by the union theorem of Section 7.2. - The Two Roads Give the Same Real Numbers. The unique order-preserving field isomorphism from Chapter 5’s field to the cuts, computed explicitly as “the rationals below”, and its inverse as a supremum; the two square roots of 2 matched; a table of what each construction pays for; and review exercises that return to separation by rationals (Chapter 6), limits and Cauchy sequences in an ordered field (Chapter 4), and countability (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3). Named moves - Walk up by \varepsilon. From a point inside a cut, add \varepsilon until you leave; the last step inside and the first step outside are \varepsilon apart (@lem-cut-step, Section 7.1). It proves the hard \supseteq halves of the chapter: in full for the additive inverse in Section 7.3, and in a multiplicative form (@lem-cut-multiplicative-step) for the reciprocal in Section 7.4 and for \sigma\sigma = D_2 in Section 7.5. Exercise B2 of Section 7.4 leaves you its last step, and Exercise C2 of Section 7.5 (a cube root of 2) its last half. - A cut is a downset with an open top. Inside is closed downward, outside is closed upward, everything inside lies below everything outside, and the inside has no largest element (@lem-cut-separation, Section 7.1). Most “is it a cut?” checks are this sentence read clause by clause; it also makes inclusion a total order in Section 7.2 and bounds sums and products from above in Sections 7.3 and 7.4. - Reduce to the positive case. Define and prove for positive cuts, then extend to all cuts by signs once, through one lemma (@lem-cut-sign-rules, Section 7.4), never axiom by axiom. It gives the product and the reciprocal of Section 7.4, distributivity by moving the negative summand to the other side, and the products of rational cuts in Section 7.5.

title: 7.1 Cuts
content:
Cuts This section opens Chapter 7, which is optional: nothing outside the chapter depends on it, and the volume’s main line ended with Chapter 6. Chapter 5 built a real number as a class of Cauchy sequences of rationals, and Chapter 6 proved that any two complete ordered fields are linked by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism. Here we begin a second construction, Dedekind’s, in which a real number is a single set of rationals: the set of all rationals below it. This section defines these sets, called cuts, tests the definition on the rationals and on the gap that Section 2.6 found, and proves two lemmas on which the rest of the chapter rests. The inside and the outside of a cut are separated, and one can walk up through a cut in steps of any fixed size until one steps out. Throughout the chapter, lower-case Latin letters such as p, q, r, s stand for rationals and m, n, k for natural numbers; Section 7.6, which brings back the field of Chapter 5, says where that changes. Nothing about real numbers is assumed: they are what is being built. The set below the gap Section 2.6 proved that the set A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above in 
Q, and has no supremum in 
Q (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (a)). Its rational upper bounds crowd down toward a place where 
Q has no element. Chapter 5 filled that place with a new object, a class of sequences. Dedekind noticed that something already present in 
Q describes the place exactly: the set of rationals that lie below it. That set is not quite A. The set A contains -1, since (-1)^2 = 1 < 2, but not -2, since (-2)^2 = 4 > 2; it is a window of rationals around 0, not “everything below” anything. Adding the non-positive rationals repairs this. Let \sigma \coloneqq \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 2 \} . This set has the same upper bounds in 
Q as A. It contains A, so every upper bound of \sigma bounds A. Conversely, let u be an upper bound of A; since 1 \in A, u \ge 1 > 0, and every element p of \sigma outside A has p \le 0 < u. The conditions (S1) and (S2) of a supremum mention only the set of upper bounds (@fd2:def-order-supremum), so \sigma, like A, has no supremum in 
Q; this is the argument of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (b). So no rational sits at the top of \sigma, yet \sigma itself is a perfectly good set of rationals. Dedekind’s move is to take the set as the number. The rest of the chapter makes this precise: it says which sets of rationals qualify, orders them, adds and multiplies them, and proves that they form a complete ordered field. Dedekind cuts Which subsets of 
Q should count as “the set of rationals below a number”? Three features of \sigma suggest the answer. It is neither empty nor all of 
Q: a number should have rationals below it and rationals above it. With any rational it contains every smaller one. And it has no largest element, as @exm-cut-sqrt2 below shows. The third feature is the least obvious, and the paragraph “Why this definition” after the examples explains it. A real number is the set of rationals below it. [Dedekind Cut] A subset \alpha \subseteq 
Q is a cut (or Dedekind cut) if 1. \alpha 
e \emptyset and \alpha 
e 
Q; 2. for every p \in \alpha and every q \in 
Q with q < p, q \in \alpha; 3. \alpha has no largest element: for every p \in \alpha there exists p' \in \alpha with p' > p. The set of all cuts is 
R_{\mathrm D} \coloneqq \{ \alpha \in \powerset{
Q} : \alpha 	ext{ satisfies (C1), (C2) and (C3)} \} , a subset of the power set \powerset{
Q} (@fd2:def-power-set). In symbols, with bounded quantifiers,  egin{aligned} &	ext{(C1)} \quad \exists p \in 
Q \ (p \in \alpha) \ \wedge \ \exists q \in 
Q \ (q 
otin \alpha) , \ &	ext{(C2)} \quad  orall p \in \alpha \  orall q \in 
Q \ (q < p \Rightarrow q \in \alpha) , \ &	ext{(C3)} \quad  orall p \in \alpha \ \exists p' \in \alpha \ (p' > p) . \end{aligned} In words, clause by clause. (C1) says that the cut is a proper, non-empty part of 
Q: some rational is in it and some rational is not. (C2) says that the cut is closed downward: whatever rational it contains, it contains every smaller one too. (C3) says that it has no top: above each of its elements it has another. The letters \alpha,  eta, \gamma, \delta are reserved for cuts in this chapter. Well-definedness. The collection 
R_{\mathrm D} is a set: it is carved out of the set \powerset{
Q} by a condition, which (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment allows, and \powerset{
Q} exists by (Z5). A real number in the sense of this chapter is therefore literally an element of \powerset{
Q}, a subset of 
Q. Negations. We shall often show that a set is not a cut, so the three negations are worth writing out once. By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication, a subset \alpha \subseteq 
Q fails - (C1) if \alpha = \emptyset or \alpha = 
Q; - (C2) if \exists p \in \alpha \ \exists q \in 
Q \ (q < p \wedge q 
otin \alpha): some element has a smaller rational missing; - (C3) if \exists p \in \alpha \  orall p' \in \alpha \ (p' \le p): \alpha has a largest element. In the last line, “not p' > p” became p' \le p by trichotomy in 
Q (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). The first examples are the rationals themselves. For a rational q, the rationals below q form a cut, and this is how the old numbers will sit among the new ones. [Rational Cut] For q \in 
Q, let D_q \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r < q \} . It is a cut (checked below), the rational cut of q. A cut \alpha is rational if \alpha = D_q for some q \in 
Q. D_q is a cut. (C1): q - 1 \in D_q, since q - (q - 1) = 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in the field 
Q, @thm-rationals-ordered-field), so q - 1 < q by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a); and q 
otin D_q, since q < q fails by (O1). (C2): if p \in D_q and r < p, then r < p < q, so r < q by (O2), and r \in D_q. (C3): if r \in D_q, the midpoint (r + q)/2 satisfies r < (r + q)/2 < q (Section 2.5, “Between two rationals”), so it lies in D_q and is larger than r. The letter D is for Dedekind. [The cut of the gap] Show that \sigma = \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 2 \} is a cut. (C1): 0 \in \sigma, since 0 \le 0. And 2 
otin \sigma: 2 > 0, and 2^2 = 4 > 2. (C2): let p \in \sigma and q \in 
Q with q < p. If q \le 0, then q \in \sigma. Otherwise 0 < q < p. Then p > 0, so p \le 0 fails and p^2 < 2. Since 0 \le q < p, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) gives q^2 < p^2, so q^2 < 2 by (O2), and q \in \sigma. (C3): let p \in \sigma. If p \le 0, then 1 \in \sigma (as 1^2 = 1 < 2) and 1 > 0 \ge p. If p > 0, then p^2 < 2. Put d \coloneqq 2 - p^2 , \qquad h \coloneqq  rac{d}{2p + 2} . Here d > 0, and d < 2 because p^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)); also 2p + 2 > 2, since p > 0. So 0 < h < 1 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a) for h > 0; d < 2p + 2 for h < 1). From 0 < h < 1, h^2 < h by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). Hence  egin{aligned} (p + h)^2 &= p^2 + 2ph + h^2 < p^2 + 2ph + h \ &< p^2 + h(2p + 2) = p^2 + d = 2 , \end{aligned} where the second inequality adds h > 0 (O3). So p + h \in \sigma, and p + h > p. The step size h depends on p: the closer p^2 is to 2, the smaller d and so h. That is unavoidable, since a fixed step would jump out of \sigma from points near the top. Section 7.5 proves that \sigma is not a rational cut, \sigma 
e D_q for every q \in 
Q, and Exercise C1 below asks for a direct proof. So \sigma is a genuinely new number: the cut that will square to 2. Which of the following subsets of 
Q are cuts? For each that is not, name a condition that fails. 1. \{ p \in 
Q : p < 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 4 \}; 2. \{ p \in 
Q : p^2 < 2 \}; 3. \{ p \in 
Q : p^3 < 5 \}; 4. \emptyset. (a) It is a cut, because it equals D_2. If p < 0, then p < 2. If p \ge 0 and p^2 < 4 = 2^2, then p < 2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). Conversely, if p < 2, either p < 0, or 0 \le p < 2 and then p^2 < 4 by (g). (b) Not a cut: (C2) fails. The set contains 1, and -2 < 1, but (-2)^2 = 4 > 2, so -2 is missing. (c) A cut. Call the set E. Cubes are monotone on non-negatives: for 0 \le q < p, p^3 - q^3 = (p - q)(p^2 + pq + q^2), where p - q > 0 and p^2 + pq + q^2 \ge p^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), with pq, q^2 \ge 0); so p^3 - q^3 > 0 by (O4). (C1): 0 \in E, and 2 
otin E, as 2^3 = 8 > 5. (C2): let q < p \in E. If q \le 0, then q^3 \le 0 < 5 (q^3 = q \cdot q^2, a non-positive times a non-negative). If q > 0, then 0 < q < p and q^3 < p^3 < 5. (C3): let p \in E. If p \le 0, then 1 \in E is larger. If p > 0, put d \coloneqq 5 - p^3 and h \coloneqq d/(3p^2 + 3p + 5). Then 0 < d < 5 < 3p^2 + 3p + 5, so 0 < h < 1, hence h^3 < h^2 < h by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), and  egin{aligned} (p + h)^3 &= p^3 + 3p^2 h + 3p h^2 + h^3 \ &< p^3 + h(3p^2 + 3p + 1) < p^3 + d = 5 . \end{aligned} So p + h \in E and p + h > p. (d) Not a cut: (C1) fails, since \emptyset has no element. Why this definition. Each clause excludes something that would spoil the arithmetic to come. - Without (C1), \emptyset and 
Q would be numbers, below and above every rational. Section 7.3 adds cuts as sets, and 
Q + D_0 = 
Q = 
Q + D_1 there would make cancellation fail. - Without (C2), \{ p : p^2 < 2 \} of the Quick check would be a number. It contains 1 but not the smaller rational -2, so it is not the set of all rationals below anything. - Without (C3), each rational q would be represented twice, by D_q and by \{ r \in 
Q : r \le q \}. The next example shows that this is more than untidy: the sum of sets cannot tell the two apart. [Two candidates for one rational] Let E_1 \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 1 \}. Show that E_1 satisfies (C1) and (C2) but not (C3), and that, with the sum of sets X + Y \coloneqq \{ x + y : x \in X, \ y \in Y \} of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.6 (@fd2:exm-sets-of-numbers-as-images), E_1 + D_1 = D_2 = D_1 + D_1 , \qquad 	ext{although } E_1 
e D_1 . The conditions. (C1): 0 \in E_1 and 2 
otin E_1. (C2): q < p \le 1 gives q < 1. (C3) fails: 1 \in E_1, and every p' \in E_1 has p' \le 1, so 1 is a largest element. And E_1 
e D_1, since 1 \in E_1 \setminus D_1. E_1 + D_1 = D_2. (\subseteq): if a \le 1 and b < 1, then a + b < 2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). (\supseteq): if s < 2, then s = 1 + (s - 1) with 1 \in E_1 and s - 1 < 1, so s - 1 \in D_1. D_1 + D_1 = D_2. (\subseteq): a < 1 and b < 1 give a + b < 2, by (b) again. (\supseteq): if s < 2, then s = s/2 + s/2, and multiplying s < 2 by 1/2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives s/2 < 1, so s/2 \in D_1. So if E_1 were admitted as a number, the equation \xi + D_1 = D_2 would have two solutions, E_1 and D_1, and addition could not be canceled, so the numbers could not form a group under addition. Condition (C3) chooses between the two sets \{ r \in 
Q : r < 1 \} and \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 1 \} that describe “the rationals up to 1”: it keeps the one that leaves 1 out. A cut is a set of rationals, not a rational. “\sigma < 2” compares a set with a number and means nothing yet. Section 7.2 orders cuts, so that \sigma < D_2 acquires a meaning, and Section 7.5 shows that D_2 plays the part of the rational 2 among the cuts. Until then, every comparison in this chapter is between rationals, or between sets by inclusion. Inside and outside The defining conditions speak about the inside of a cut. The first lemma says what they imply about the outside: everything outside lies above everything inside. [Separation] Let \alpha be a cut, p \in \alpha and q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha. Then p < q. Consequently the complement 
Q \setminus \alpha is closed upward: if q 
otin \alpha and q' \in 
Q with q' > q, then q' 
otin \alpha. Suppose p < q fails. By trichotomy (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), q \le p. If q = p, then q \in \alpha; if q < p, then q \in \alpha by (C2). Either way q \in \alpha, against q 
otin \alpha. So p < q. For the consequence, let q 
otin \alpha and q' > q, and suppose q' \in \alpha. The first part, with q' in the role of p, gives q' < q, which together with q < q' contradicts (O1). So q' 
otin \alpha. So a cut and its complement split 
Q into a lower piece and an upper piece, every element of the lower below every element of the upper. In particular every rational outside a cut is an upper bound of it. Together with (C3), this gives the picture to keep in mind, and one of the chapter’s named moves: A cut is a downset with an open top. Inside is closed downward, outside is closed upward, everything inside lies below everything outside, and the inside has no largest element. The outside may have a least element: the complement of D_q is \{ r \in 
Q : r \ge q \}, with least element q. Most “is it a cut?” checks in this chapter are this sentence, read clause by clause. The second result locates a rational relative to a cut by comparing two sets. It is the bridge between a rational q and its cut D_q. [Where a Rational Lies] Let \alpha be a cut and q \in 
Q. Then 1. q \in \alpha if and only if D_q \subsetneq \alpha; 2. q 
otin \alpha if and only if \alpha \subseteq D_q. If q is in \alpha, closure downward brings everything below q along, and q itself is the extra element. If q is outside, separation puts all of \alpha below q. The two converses come from the same two facts. (a) (\Rightarrow) Let q \in \alpha. For r \in D_q, r < q, so r \in \alpha by (C2); thus D_q \subseteq \alpha. The inclusion is proper, because q \in \alpha and q 
otin D_q (as q < q fails, (O1)). (\Leftarrow) Let D_q \subsetneq \alpha. Then some r \in \alpha has r 
otin D_q, that is, r < q fails, so q \le r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). If q = r, then q \in \alpha; if q < r, then q \in \alpha by (C2). (b) (\Rightarrow) Let q 
otin \alpha. For r \in \alpha, @lem-cut-separation gives r < q, so r \in D_q; thus \alpha \subseteq D_q. (\Leftarrow) Let \alpha \subseteq D_q. Since q 
otin D_q, also q 
otin \alpha. Since every rational is either in \alpha or not, exactly one of D_q \subsetneq \alpha and \alpha \subseteq D_q holds. Section 7.2 rewrites (a) as q \in \alpha \iff D_q < \alpha, once inclusion has become the order on cuts. Walking up through a cut Many proofs in this chapter need two rationals, one inside a cut and one outside, that are close together: within a prescribed rational distance \varepsilon > 0. Separation says that the inside lies below the outside, but not that the two come close. They do, and the reason is a walk: start inside, climb in steps of \varepsilon, and stop at the first step that leaves the cut. [The Step Lemma] Let \alpha be a cut, a \in \alpha, and \varepsilon \in 
Q with \varepsilon > 0. Then there is n \in 
N with a + n\varepsilon \in \alpha \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad a + (n + 1)\varepsilon 
otin \alpha . Picture the rungs a, a + \varepsilon, a + 2\varepsilon, \dots. The bottom rung a is inside. Some rung is outside: pick any rational b outside \alpha; the rationals are Archimedean, so finitely many steps of size \varepsilon climb past b, and everything above b is outside by separation. Among the rungs outside there is a lowest one, because a non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element. It is not the bottom rung, so the rung just below it exists and is inside. The n found depends on \alpha, a and \varepsilon. By (C1), there is b \in 
Q with b 
otin \alpha. By @thm-rationals-archimedean, applied to the rational (b - a)/\varepsilon, there is m \in 
N with (b - a)/\varepsilon < m. Multiplying by \varepsilon > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives b - a < m\varepsilon, so b < a + m\varepsilon by (O3). Since b 
otin \alpha, @lem-cut-separation gives a + m\varepsilon 
otin \alpha. Let K \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : a + k\varepsilon 
otin \alpha \} . Then m \in K, so K is a non-empty set of integers, and 0 is a lower bound of it. By @prp-integer-least-element, K has a least element k_0. Since a + 0 \cdot \varepsilon = a \in \alpha, 0 
otin K, so k_0 
e 0 and k_0 > 0. By discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), k_0 \ge 1. Put n \coloneqq k_0 - 1. Then n \ge 0 by (O3), so n \in 
N (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). Since n < k_0 and k_0 is least in K, n 
otin K, that is, a + n\varepsilon \in \alpha. And a + (n + 1)\varepsilon = a + k_0 \varepsilon 
otin \alpha, since k_0 \in K. This proves the lemma. Since n \ge 0 and \varepsilon > 0, the point p \coloneqq a + n\varepsilon found by the lemma satisfies p \ge a. So the lemma hands over a pair p \in \alpha, p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha: a point inside and a point outside, exactly \varepsilon apart, with the inside point as high as we like above a given element. This is another of the chapter’s named moves. Walk up by \varepsilon: from a point inside a cut, add \varepsilon until you leave; the last step inside and the first step outside are \varepsilon apart. It drives the hardest “\supseteq” halves to come: the additive inverse in Section 7.3 and, in its multiplicative form of Section 7.4, the multiplicative inverse in Section 7.4 and the square of \sigma in Section 7.5. Note what it needs from 
Q: the Archimedean property, to know that the walk leaves the cut at all, and least elements and discreteness of the integers, to find the first step out and the step before it. Here is one walk, through \sigma from a = 1 in steps of \varepsilon = 1/10. The rungs 1, 11/10, 12/10, \dots are positive, so a rung r lies in \sigma exactly when r^2 < 2. Now (14/10)^2 = 196/100 < 2, because 196 < 200, and the lower positive rungs have smaller squares (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)), so the rungs for k = 0, \dots, 4 are inside. But (15/10)^2 = 225/100 > 2. So the least k with 1 + k/10 
otin \sigma is k_0 = 5, the n of the lemma is 4, and the pair is 7/5 \in \sigma, 3/2 
otin \sigma. Continue the walk with a finer step: start at a = 7/5 \in \sigma and take \varepsilon = 1/100. Which pair p \in \sigma, p + \varepsilon 
otin \sigma does the lemma give? The rungs are 140/100, 141/100, 142/100, \dots. Since 141^2 = 19881 < 20000, (141/100)^2 < 2, so 141/100 \in \sigma. Since 142^2 = 20164 > 20000, 142/100 
otin \sigma. So k_0 = 2, n = 1, and the pair is p = 141/100, p + \varepsilon = 142/100 = 71/50. Each walk traps the top of \sigma between two rationals \varepsilon apart, and a smaller \varepsilon traps it more tightly. No walk ever lands on the top, since \sigma has none. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State (C1)–(C3) for a subset \alpha \subseteq 
Q, and write the negation of (C3) in symbols. 2. For each set, name every condition among (C1)–(C3) that fails: (i) \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 3 \}; (ii) \{ p \in 
Q : p > 0 \}; (iii) \{ p \in 
Q : p^2 \le 0 \}; (iv) \{ p \in 
Q : p < p + 1 \}. 3. Let q, r \in 
Q. Is D_q \cup D_r a cut? Is D_q \cap D_r? Identify each. (a) (C1) \alpha 
e \emptyset and \alpha 
e 
Q; (C2) for every p \in \alpha and every q \in 
Q with q < p, q \in \alpha; (C3) for every p \in \alpha there is p' \in \alpha with p' > p. The negation of (C3) is \exists p \in \alpha \  orall p' \in \alpha \ (p' \le p): \alpha has a largest element. (b) (i) Only (C3) fails: 3 is a largest element. (C1) holds (0 in, 4 out) and (C2) holds (q < p \le 3 gives q < 3). (ii) Only (C2) fails: 1 is in, and 0 < 1 is not. (C1) holds (1 in, 0 out), and (C3) holds (p + 1 > p > 0). (iii) The set is \{0\}, since p 
e 0 gives p^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). (C2) fails (-1 < 0, -1 missing) and (C3) fails (0 is largest); (C1) holds. (iv) The set is 
Q, since 0 < 1 gives p < p + 1 for every p (O3). (C1) fails; (C2) and (C3) hold. (c) Both are cuts. If q \le r, then D_q \subseteq D_r (s < q \le r gives s < r), so D_q \cup D_r = D_r and D_q \cap D_r = D_q; if r \le q, the roles swap. So D_q \cup D_r = D_{\max(q, r)} and D_q \cap D_r = D_{\min(q, r)}, rational cuts by @def-rational-cut. B. Practice [B1] Prove that \{ p \in 
Q : 3p < 2 \} is a cut, and that it equals D_{2/3}. For p \in 
Q, 3p < 2 implies p < 2/3, by multiplying with 1/3 > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)); and p < 2/3 implies 3p < 2, by multiplying with 3 > 0. So the set is \{ p \in 
Q : p < 2/3 \} = D_{2/3}, and it is a cut because every rational cut is one (@def-rational-cut, with the check after it). [B2] Prove that \{ p \in 
Q : p < 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 3 \} is a cut. For (C3), give an explicit larger element. Call the set  eta. (C1): 0 \in  eta, since 0^2 = 0 < 3; and 2 
otin  eta, since 2 \ge 0 and 2^2 = 4 > 3. (C2): let q < p \in  eta. If q < 0, then q \in  eta. Otherwise 0 \le q < p, so p > 0, p < 0 fails, and p^2 < 3. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), q^2 < p^2 < 3, so q \in  eta. (C3): let p \in  eta. If p < 0, then 0 \in  eta and 0 > p. If p \ge 0, then p^2 < 3. Put d \coloneqq 3 - p^2 , \qquad h \coloneqq  rac{d}{2p + 4} . Then 0 < d \le 3 < 4 \le 2p + 4, so 0 < h < 1 and h^2 < h (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). Hence  egin{aligned} (p + h)^2 &= p^2 + 2ph + h^2 < p^2 + h(2p + 1) \ &< p^2 + h(2p + 4) = p^2 + d = 3 , \end{aligned} so p + h \in  eta and p + h > p. (The denominator is chosen to exceed d, so that h < 1, and to be at least 2p + 1; any such denominator works.) C. Going deeper [C1: The cut of the gap is not rational] Prove directly from the definitions that \sigma 
e D_q for every q \in 
Q. [Hint 1] If \sigma = D_q, where would q itself sit relative to \sigma? What does that say about q and q^2? [Hint 2] You will reach q > 0 and q^2 \ge 2. If q^2 > 2, look for a smaller positive rational whose square still exceeds 2; Section 2.6 has one. Suppose \sigma = D_q for some q \in 
Q. Since q 
otin D_q, q 
otin \sigma: so q \le 0 fails, and q^2 < 2 fails. That is, q > 0 and q^2 \ge 2. Case q^2 = 2. Impossible, by @thm-no-rational-square-two. Case q^2 > 2. Let q' \coloneqq (q^2 + 2)/(2q), the rational t(q) of Section 2.6. It is positive, as a quotient of positives (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). By the identities @eq-newton-identities, q - q' =  rac{q^2 - 2}{2q} > 0 , \qquad q'^2 - 2 =  rac{(q^2 - 2)^2}{4q^2} > 0 , the first a quotient of positives, the second because q^2 - 2 
e 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So q' < q, that is, q' \in D_q = \sigma. But q' > 0 and q'^2 > 2, so q' 
otin \sigma. This contradiction shows that \sigma 
e D_q. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: from q 
otin D_q = \sigma, derives both q > 0 and q^2 \ge 2. - 2: excludes q^2 = 2, citing that no rational squares to 2. - 3: for q^2 > 2, exhibits a rational q' with 0 < q' < q and q'^2 > 2, with both inequalities verified (any such q' earns the points). - 2: concludes: q' lies in D_q but not in \sigma. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “q = \sqrt 2” or any use of a square root of 2 as a number; a candidate q' whose square is not checked to exceed 2.

title: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content:
Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions This section belongs to the optional Chapter 7; nothing outside the chapter depends on it. Section 7.1 defined a cut as a set of rationals that is non-empty and not all of 
Q, closed downward, and without a largest element (@def-dedekind-cut), and it called the set of all cuts 
R_{\mathrm D}. Before cuts can be added or multiplied, they can already be compared, and the comparison costs nothing: one cut is below another when it is contained in it. This section shows that this order is total, and then proves the property that the Cauchy road of Chapter 5 reached only at its end. Every non-empty set of cuts that is bounded above has a least upper bound, and that least upper bound is simply the union of the set. Comparing cuts For two rationals p and q, “p is at most q” says the same as “every rational below p is below q”. In the language of Section 7.1, p \le q holds exactly when D_p \subseteq D_q: if p \le q and r < p, then r < q; and if q < p, then q \in D_p \setminus D_q. So on rational cuts, inclusion is the order of 
Q in disguise. We take it as the order of all cuts. One cut is below another when every rational in the first is also in the second. [Order of Cuts] For cuts \alpha and  eta, we write \alpha \le  eta if \alpha \subseteq  eta, and \alpha <  eta if \alpha \subsetneq  eta, that is, if \alpha \subseteq  eta and \alpha 
e  eta. As usual,  eta \ge \alpha means \alpha \le  eta, and  eta > \alpha means \alpha <  eta. The relation \le is a partial order on 
R_{\mathrm D} (@fd2:def-partial-order): it is reflexive, since \alpha \subseteq \alpha; antisymmetric, since \alpha \subseteq  eta and  eta \subseteq \alpha give \alpha =  eta (@fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric); and transitive (@fd2:prp-subset-transitive). Its strict part, \alpha \le  eta and \alpha 
e  eta, is exactly <. These are the facts that make inclusion a partial order on all of \powerset{
Q} (@fd2:exm-subset-order-not-total), restricted to the cuts. Two translations. First, the order of 
Q is recovered on rational cuts: for p, q \in 
Q, p < q \iff D_p < D_q , \qquad p = q \iff D_p = D_q . Indeed, @prp-rational-in-cut (a) with \alpha = D_q says p \in D_q \iff D_p \subsetneq D_q, and p \in D_q means p < q. For the second equivalence, if p 
e q, then p < q or q < p, and either way D_p 
e D_q by the first. Second, @prp-rational-in-cut now reads, for a cut \alpha and q \in 
Q, q \in \alpha \iff D_q < \alpha , \qquad q 
otin \alpha \iff \alpha \le D_q . So “the rational q lies in the cut \alpha” and “the rational cut of q is strictly below \alpha” are the same statement. This is the precise sense in which a cut is the set of rationals below it. Show that D_1 < \sigma < D_{3/2}, where \sigma is the cut of @exm-cut-sqrt2. By the second translation, D_1 < \sigma because 1 \in \sigma (1^2 = 1 < 2), and \sigma \le D_{3/2} because 3/2 
otin \sigma (3/2 > 0 and (3/2)^2 = 9/4 > 2). The inclusion \sigma \subseteq D_{3/2} is proper: 29/20 lies in D_{3/2}, since 29 \cdot 2 = 58 < 60 = 3 \cdot 20, but not in \sigma, since 29/20 > 0 and (29/20)^2 = 841/400 > 2 (as 841 > 800). So \sigma < D_{3/2}. Inclusion is rarely a total order: in \powerset{
Q}, neither of \{0\} and \{1\} contains the other. Among cuts it is total, and the reason is separation. [Cuts Are Totally Ordered] For all cuts \alpha and  eta, \alpha \le  eta or  eta \le \alpha. Hence exactly one of \alpha <  eta, \alpha =  eta,  eta < \alpha holds. If \alpha is not inside  eta, then \alpha has a point p outside  eta. Everything in  eta lies below every outside point of  eta, so below p; and \alpha, being closed downward, contains everything below its point p. So \alpha contains all of  eta. Let \alpha,  eta be cuts. If \alpha \subseteq  eta, then \alpha \le  eta and we are done; so suppose \alpha 
ot\subseteq  eta. Then some p \in \alpha has p 
otin  eta. Let q \in  eta be arbitrary. Since q \in  eta and p 
otin  eta, @lem-cut-separation gives q < p. Since p \in \alpha and q < p, (C2) for \alpha gives q \in \alpha. As q was arbitrary,  eta \subseteq \alpha, that is,  eta \le \alpha. For the second statement: if \alpha \le  eta, then \alpha =  eta or \alpha <  eta; otherwise  eta \le \alpha and  eta 
e \alpha, that is,  eta < \alpha. So at least one of the three holds. No two hold together: \alpha <  eta and  eta < \alpha would give \alpha =  eta by antisymmetry, against \alpha 
e  eta; and \alpha <  eta excludes \alpha =  eta by definition, as  eta < \alpha does. The proof used (C2), directly and through @lem-cut-separation, whose proof uses only (C2) and trichotomy in 
Q; it never used (C1) or (C3). So any two subsets of 
Q that are closed downward are comparable by inclusion. The pair \{0\}, \{1\} fails (C2), and that is why it could be incomparable. With @thm-cut-order-total, (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le) is a totally ordered set, and the vocabulary of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 applies to it: a set A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D} is bounded above if some cut  eta has \alpha \le  eta for every \alpha \in A (@fd2:def-order-bounds), and a cut \gamma is its supremum if it is an upper bound of A, clause (S1), and \gamma \le \delta for every upper bound \delta of A, clause (S2) (@fd2:def-order-supremum). A supremum is unique when it exists (@fd2:prp-greatest-unique, applied to the set of upper bounds). Least upper bounds are unions In 
Q, the set \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above, and has no supremum (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). The cuts were built so that no such gap remains, and here is the theorem that says so. [Least Upper Bounds of Cuts] Let A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D} be non-empty and bounded above: some cut  eta has \alpha \le  eta for every \alpha \in A. Then \gamma \coloneqq  igcup A = \{ p \in 
Q : p \in \alpha 	ext{ for some } \alpha \in A \} (@fd2:def-family-union-intersection, the family indexed by A itself) is a cut, and \gamma is the supremum of A in (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le). Try it first (ten minutes): which cut would you propose as the supremum of a set of cuts? Check your proposal against (C1)–(C3), and then against (S1) and (S2). The word “bounds” invites a first guess: the intersection  igcap A, the rationals common to all members. It sits on the wrong side. The intersection lies inside every member, so it is a candidate for a lower bound, the infimum’s job, and it can even fail to be a cut (try it in Exercise C1). An upper bound must contain every member, and the smallest set that does is the union. In \powerset{
Q} the union is the supremum: it contains every member, and any set that contains every member contains the union ((S1) and (S2) in the proof below check this for cuts). So everything comes down to one question: is the union a cut? Conditions (C2) and (C3) pass from the members to the union one element at a time, and (C1) needs both hypotheses, one for each half. Before reading on: which of the three conditions will use “bounded above”? Let  eta be an upper bound of A. The set \gamma is a subset of 
Q, since every member of A is. (C1). Since A is non-empty, fix \alpha_0 \in A; since \alpha_0 
e \emptyset by (C1) for \alpha_0, fix p_0 \in \alpha_0. Then p_0 \in \gamma, so \gamma 
e \emptyset. Next, \gamma \subseteq  eta: if p \in \gamma, then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A [ulename{\exists E}], and \alpha \subseteq  eta because  eta is an upper bound, so p \in  eta. By (C1) for  eta, some b \in 
Q has b 
otin  eta; then b 
otin \gamma, so \gamma 
e 
Q. (C2). Let p \in \gamma and q \in 
Q with q < p. Then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A [ulename{\exists E}]. By (C2) for \alpha, q \in \alpha, so q \in \gamma. (C3). Let p \in \gamma, say p \in \alpha with \alpha \in A [ulename{\exists E}]. By (C3) for \alpha, some p' \in \alpha has p' > p, and p' \in \gamma. So \gamma is a cut. (S1). For each \alpha \in A, every element of \alpha lies in \gamma, so \alpha \subseteq \gamma, that is, \alpha \le \gamma. (S2). Let \delta be an upper bound of A. If p \in \gamma, then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A [ulename{\exists E}], and \alpha \subseteq \delta, so p \in \delta. Thus \gamma \subseteq \delta, that is, \gamma \le \delta. Hence \gamma is the supremum of A. The answer to the prompt: “bounded above” is used once, in the second half of (C1), to show \gamma 
e 
Q. “Non-empty” is used once too, in the first half of (C1). Conditions (C2) and (C3) of \gamma, and the clauses (S1) and (S2), hold for every set of cuts; it is only being a cut at all that needs the hypotheses. Compare the Cauchy road. There, completeness took two sections: Section 5.5 proved that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges, by building rational approximants, and Section 5.6 bisected intervals, with one line that needed the Archimedean property, to reach least upper bounds. Here it took one union and five short checks, (C1)–(C3) and (S1)–(S2). The proof above uses no arithmetic of 
Q at all, only its order, through (C2) and (C3) of the members; in particular it does not use the Archimedean property. The price is paid elsewhere: cuts have no sum or product yet, and Sections 7.3 and 7.4 build them, multiplication with some effort. Both hypotheses of @thm-dedekind-lub are needed for the union to be a cut. Drop “bounded above”: the rational cuts D_n, n \in 
N, have union 
Q, since every rational r lies below some n \in 
N (@thm-rationals-archimedean) and so in D_n; and 
Q fails (C1). Drop “non-empty”:  igcup \emptyset = \emptyset, which fails (C1) too. The warning shows that the proof breaks without each hypothesis. In fact the conclusion fails too: without either hypothesis, there is no supremum at all. The empty set. Every cut is an upper bound of \emptyset, vacuously, so a supremum of \emptyset would be a least cut. There is none: for a cut \alpha, pick a \in \alpha (C1); then D_a < \alpha by @prp-rational-in-cut (a), and D_a is a cut, so \alpha is not least. An unbounded set. A set with no upper bound has no supremum, since a supremum is an upper bound by (S1). For example \{ D_n : n \in 
N \} has none: if  eta bounded it, then 
Q =  igcup_{n \in 
N} D_n \subseteq  eta, against (C1) for  eta. Find \sup \{ D_{1 - 1/n} : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} in (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le). Is it an element of the set? The set is non-empty and bounded above by D_1, since 1/n > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), so 1 - 1/n < 1 and D_{1 - 1/n} \subseteq D_1. By @thm-dedekind-lub its supremum is the union U \coloneqq  igcup_{n \ge 1} D_{1 - 1/n}. We show U = D_1. (\subseteq): if r < 1 - 1/n for some n, then r < 1. (\supseteq): let r < 1. Then 1 - r > 0, and @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < 1 - r, that is, r < 1 - 1/n, so r \in U. Hence the supremum is D_1. It is not in the set: D_{1 - 1/n} = D_1 would force 1 - 1/n = 1 by the first translation, and 1/n 
e 0. So (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le) is a totally ordered set in which every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. Once Sections 7.3 and 7.4 have made 
R_{\mathrm D} an ordered field with this order, Section 7.5 reads @thm-dedekind-lub as the statement that it is a complete ordered field (@def-complete-ordered-field). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about @thm-dedekind-lub and its proof. 1. Let A \coloneqq \{ D_q : q \in \sigma \}, with \sigma the cut of @exm-cut-sqrt2. Check that A satisfies the hypotheses, and find the cut \gamma of the proof, arguing directly from (C2) and (C3) of \sigma. 2. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 3. Which line of the proof fails if A = \emptyset, and what is \gamma then? 4. In the check of (C3) for \gamma, which cut’s condition (C3) is used? (a) A is non-empty, since 0 \in \sigma gives D_0 \in A. It is bounded above by \sigma: for q \in \sigma, D_q < \sigma by @prp-rational-in-cut (a). The proof’s cut is \gamma =  igcup_{q \in \sigma} D_q, and \gamma = \sigma. (\subseteq): each D_q with q \in \sigma is contained in \sigma, by (C2) of \sigma. (\supseteq): let q \in \sigma; by (C3) of \sigma there is q' \in \sigma with q' > q, so q \in D_{q'} \subseteq \gamma. So \sup A = \sigma: the cut of the gap is the supremum of the rational cuts below it. (b) The union of the cuts contains each of them, and lies inside every upper bound, so it is the least upper bound once it is known to be a cut. It is one because (C2) and (C3) pass from the members to the union element by element, while (C1) comes from A 
e \emptyset (some element) and from an upper bound  eta 
e 
Q (some non-element). (c) The first line of (C1): with A = \emptyset there is no \alpha_0 \in A to fix. Then \gamma =  igcup \emptyset = \emptyset, which is not a cut. (d) Condition (C3) of the member \alpha \in A that contains the given p \in \gamma. Different points of \gamma may use different members. B. Practice [B1] Let q, r \in 
Q. Prove that \sup \{ D_q, D_r \} = D_{\max(q, r)} in (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le). Let m \coloneqq \max(q, r). Since q \le m and r \le m, D_q \subseteq D_m and D_r \subseteq D_m (if s < q \le m, then s < m); so \{ D_q, D_r \} is non-empty and bounded above by D_m. By @thm-dedekind-lub its supremum is D_q \cup D_r. This union contains D_m, because D_m is one of D_q, D_r; and it is contained in D_m, by the two inclusions above. Hence \sup \{ D_q, D_r \} = D_q \cup D_r = D_m. [B2: Put the proof in order] Here are lines of a proof that for cuts \alpha and  eta, \alpha \le  eta or  eta \le \alpha, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Without looking back, write the lines of a correct proof in a correct order, and say what is wrong with each line you leave out. (i) Let q \in  eta be arbitrary. (ii) Since q < p and p \in \alpha, q \in  eta. (iii) As q was arbitrary,  eta \subseteq \alpha. (iv) Let \alpha,  eta be cuts with \alpha 
ot\subseteq  eta (if \alpha \subseteq  eta, there is nothing to prove). (v) Since p \in \alpha and q < p, q \in \alpha, because \alpha is closed downward. (vi) Since q \in  eta and p 
otin  eta, p < q. (vii) Then some p \in \alpha has p 
otin  eta. (viii) Since q \in  eta and p 
otin  eta, q < p, by separation. An admissible order is 	ext{(iv)}, \ 	ext{(vii)}, \ 	ext{(i)}, \ 	ext{(viii)}, \ 	ext{(v)}, \ 	ext{(iii)} . Line (i) may also come before (vii), since it only introduces a name for an arbitrary element of  eta, and (vii) does not mention q. Otherwise the order is forced: (vii) unwinds the assumption of (iv); (viii) needs p from (vii) and q from (i); (v) needs q < p from (viii); and (iii) closes the argument about the arbitrary q. Line (vi) reads separation backwards. @lem-cut-separation puts a point inside a cut below a point outside it. Here q is inside  eta and p is outside, so separation gives q < p, as in (viii); line (vi) asserts the opposite, and the two together contradict (O1). Line (ii) applies closure to the wrong cut. Closure downward of \alpha turns “p \in \alpha and q < p” into q \in \alpha, not into q \in  eta; the fact that p \in \alpha says nothing about  eta. (Its conclusion q \in  eta is true, but only because it was assumed in (i).) C. Going deeper [C1: Infima] Let A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D} be non-empty and bounded below. 1. Show that  igcap A need not be a cut, by computing  igcap A_0 for A_0 \coloneqq \{ D_{1/n} : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}. 2. Prove that A nevertheless has an infimum in (
R_{\mathrm D}, \le): it is the supremum of the set of lower bounds of A. 3. Find \inf A_0. [Hint 1] For (b), the set L of lower bounds of A is non-empty by hypothesis. Find an upper bound for L among the elements of A. [Hint 2] Let \lambda_0 \coloneqq \sup L, which exists by @thm-dedekind-lub; the claim is that \lambda_0 = \inf A. (a) Here  igcap A_0 = \{ r \in 
Q : r < 1/n 	ext{ for every } n \in 
Z_{>0} \}, the intersection taken in 
Q. We claim it is \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 0 \}. If r \le 0, then r \le 0 < 1/n for every n (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). If r > 0, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives n with 1/n < r, so r 
otin D_{1/n} and r 
otin  igcap A_0. The set \{ r : r \le 0 \} has the largest element 0, so it fails (C3) and is not a cut. (The set A_0 is non-empty and bounded below, by D_0, for instance.) (b) Let L \coloneqq \{ \lambda \in 
R_{\mathrm D} : \lambda \le \alpha 	ext{ for every } \alpha \in A \}, the set of lower bounds of A. It is non-empty, since A is bounded below. It is bounded above: fix \alpha_0 \in A (A 
e \emptyset); every \lambda \in L has \lambda \le \alpha_0. By @thm-dedekind-lub, L has a supremum \lambda_0. \lambda_0 is a lower bound of A. Let \alpha \in A. Every \lambda \in L has \lambda \le \alpha, so \alpha is an upper bound of L, and (S2) for \lambda_0 = \sup L gives \lambda_0 \le \alpha. \lambda_0 is the greatest lower bound. We just showed \lambda_0 \in L. If \lambda is any lower bound of A, then \lambda \in L, so \lambda \le \lambda_0 by (S1) for \lambda_0. Hence \lambda_0 = \inf A. (c) \inf A_0 = D_0. It is a lower bound: D_0 \subseteq D_{1/n} since 0 < 1/n. Let \lambda be any lower bound. Then \lambda \subseteq  igcap A_0 = \{ r : r \le 0 \} by (a). And 0 
otin \lambda: otherwise (C3) for \lambda gives p' \in \lambda with p' > 0, but \lambda contains no positive rational. So every element of \lambda is negative, \lambda \subseteq D_0, and \lambda \le D_0. So the infimum is the intersection with its largest element removed. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) computes  igcap A_0 = \{ r : r \le 0 \}, using the Archimedean property for the positive rationals, and names (C3) as the failing condition. - 2: (b) shows that the set of lower bounds is non-empty and bounded above by a member of A. - 2: (b) shows that its supremum is a lower bound of A, through (S2). - 2: (b) shows that it is the greatest lower bound, through (S1). - 2: (c) identifies D_0, with both inequalities. Fatal errors (0 for the step): asserting that  igcap A is the infimum without checking (C3); using a supremum of L without checking that L is non-empty and bounded above. [C2: Find the error] Here is a proof. Its conclusion is the first half of @thm-dedekind-lub. Claim. Let A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D} be non-empty and bounded above. Then \gamma \coloneqq  igcup A is a cut. (1) Since A is non-empty, pick \alpha_0 \in A; since \alpha_0 
e \emptyset, pick p_0 \in \alpha_0. Then p_0 \in \gamma, so \gamma 
e \emptyset. (2) Each \alpha \in A is a cut, so \alpha 
e 
Q. Hence \gamma 
e 
Q. (3) Let p \in \gamma and q < p. Then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A, so q \in \alpha by (C2), and q \in \gamma. (4) Let p \in \gamma. Then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A; by (C3) there is p' \in \alpha with p' > p, and p' \in \gamma. (5) So \gamma satisfies (C1)–(C3). Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say what is illegal about it, and give a counterexample to that step. The conclusion is true: it is proved in @thm-dedekind-lub. The argument does not prove it, because line (2) fails. What is illegal. Line (2) passes from “for every \alpha \in A there is a rational outside \alpha” to “there is a rational outside every \alpha \in A”, which is what \gamma 
e 
Q means. The rational outside \alpha depends on \alpha, and the line uses it as if one rational served every member at once. This is the move (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue: a witness found inside the box of one \alpha is treated as uniform in \alpha. A union of proper subsets of 
Q can be all of 
Q. Counterexample to the step. Let A' \coloneqq \{ D_n : n \in 
N \}. Each D_n is a cut, so D_n 
e 
Q, and the premise of the step holds; but  igcup A' = 
Q, since every rational lies below some natural number (@thm-rationals-archimedean). So the step leads from a true premise to a false conclusion. (This A' is not bounded above, so it is not a counterexample to the claim, which is true.) The tell. The hypothesis “bounded above” is never used. A correct proof must use it, since the warning after @thm-dedekind-lub shows that the claim fails without it. Repair. Let  eta be an upper bound of A. Every \alpha \in A satisfies \alpha \subseteq  eta, so \gamma \subseteq  eta; and  eta 
e 
Q, so some b 
otin  eta, hence b 
otin \gamma and \gamma 
e 
Q. [C3: Exit check: least upper bounds of cuts] Let A be a non-empty set of cuts, bounded above in (

e \emptyset and \alpha_0 
e \emptyset; then p_0 \in \gamma. Every element of \gamma lies in some \alpha \in A, and \alpha \subseteq  eta, so \gamma \subseteq  eta. Pick b \in 
Q \setminus  eta (C1 for  eta); then b 
otin \gamma. So \emptyset 
e \gamma 
e 
Q. (C2). If q < p with p \in \gamma, then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A, so q \in \alpha \subseteq \gamma. (C3). If p \in \gamma, then p \in \alpha for some \alpha \in A, and (C3) for \alpha gives p' \in \alpha \subseteq \gamma with p' > p. Upper bound. Each \alpha \in A satisfies \alpha \subseteq \gamma. So \gamma is a cut, an upper bound of A, and below every upper bound: \gamma = \sup A. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: \gamma
