title: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content:
Addition and Negatives Like every section of this chapter, this one is optional: nothing outside Chapter 7 depends on it. Sections 7.1 and 7.2 made cuts and ordered them, and the least upper bound property came almost for free, as a union (@thm-dedekind-lub). Now the arithmetic. Adding two cuts is the obvious thing, and it works; the zero cut works too, once (C3) is used. Negatives are where the obvious recipe fails, on the simplest cuts of all, and the repair is a small positive margin. The proof that the repaired negative is right is the walk up by ε (@lem-cut-step) worked in full. The section ends with cuts forming an ordered group under addition. Throughout, 
Q is the ordered field of @thm-rationals-ordered-field, and every letter p, q, r, s, t, x stands for a rational. We use the rules of an ordered field for rationals without comment: (F1)–(F9) of @def-commutative-ring-and-field, (O1)–(O4) of @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, and the halves of @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). Adding two cuts A cut is a set of rationals, so the first candidate for a sum is the set of all sums. [Sum of Cuts] For cuts \alpha and  eta, the sum is the set \alpha +  eta \coloneqq \{ p + q : p \in \alpha, \ q \in  eta \} . In symbols, x \in \alpha +  eta \iff \exists p \in \alpha \ \exists q \in  eta \ \ x = p + q. This is the set sum A + B of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.6 (@fd2:exm-sets-of-numbers-as-images), applied to two sets of rationals: the same notation with the same meaning. For instance, if p < 1 and q < 2, then p + q < 3, so D_1 + D_2 \subseteq D_3; the Quick check later in this section shows how the reverse inclusion goes for a similar pair. The definition makes sense for any two sets of rationals. The work is to show that a sum of cuts is again a cut, and that this addition behaves. [The Sum of Two Cuts Is a Cut] For all cuts \alpha and  eta, the set \alpha +  eta is a cut. Addition of cuts is commutative and associative: for all cuts \alpha,  eta, \gamma, \alpha +  eta =  eta + \alpha \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad (\alpha +  eta) + \gamma = \alpha + ( eta + \gamma) . Each cut condition for \alpha +  eta comes from the same condition for \alpha or  eta. A rational outside a cut is above every element of it (@lem-cut-separation), so the sum of a point outside \alpha and a point outside  eta is outside the sum. To go down from p + q, go down in the first summand. To go up, go up in the first summand. The two laws are laws of 
Q, applied element by element. Let \alpha and  eta be cuts. We check (C1)–(C3) of @def-dedekind-cut for \alpha +  eta. (C1) By (C1) for \alpha and  eta, there are p_0 \in \alpha and q_0 \in  eta, so p_0 + q_0 \in \alpha +  eta, and \alpha +  eta 
e \emptyset. Also by (C1), there are a \in 
Q \setminus \alpha and b \in 
Q \setminus  eta. Let p \in \alpha and q \in  eta. By @lem-cut-separation, p < a and q < b, so p + q < a + b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). So no element of \alpha +  eta equals a + b, and a + b 
otin \alpha +  eta. Hence \alpha +  eta 
e 
Q. (C2) Let x \in \alpha +  eta and y \in 
Q with y < x. Write x = p + q with p \in \alpha, q \in  eta. Adding -q to y < p + q gives y - q < p (O3), so y - q \in \alpha by (C2) for \alpha. Hence y = (y - q) + q \in \alpha +  eta. (C3) Let x = p + q \in \alpha +  eta with p \in \alpha, q \in  eta. By (C3) for \alpha there is p' \in \alpha with p' > p. Then p' + q \in \alpha +  eta and p' + q > p + q = x (O3). So \alpha +  eta is a cut. Commutativity. If x \in \alpha +  eta, then x = p + q with p \in \alpha, q \in  eta, and x = q + p \in  eta + \alpha by (F1) in 
Q. So \alpha +  eta \subseteq  eta + \alpha; exchanging the roles of \alpha and  eta gives the reverse inclusion. Associativity. Let \gamma be a cut. (\subseteq) If x \in (\alpha +  eta) + \gamma, then x = y + s with y \in \alpha +  eta and s \in \gamma, and y = p + q with p \in \alpha, q \in  eta. By (F2) in 
Q, x = p + (q + s), and q + s \in  eta + \gamma, so x \in \alpha + ( eta + \gamma). (\supseteq) If x = p + z with p \in \alpha and z = q + s \in  eta + \gamma, then x = (p + q) + s \in (\alpha +  eta) + \gamma, by (F2) again. This proves the theorem. Only (C3) for \alpha was needed in the third step; (C3) for  eta would serve equally. The two laws used nothing about cuts at all: they hold for the set sum of arbitrary sets of rationals (commutativity for any two, associativity for any three), and Exercise B2 asks you to check associativity in this generality. The zero cut The natural zero is D_0 = \{ r \in 
Q : r < 0 \}, the rational cut of 0 (@def-rational-cut). Adding an element of D_0 pushes a rational down, so \alpha + D_0 cannot leave \alpha. The other inclusion needs a point of \alpha strictly above the given one. The Zero Cut For every cut \alpha, \alpha + D_0 = \alpha. Let \alpha be a cut. (\subseteq) Let x \in \alpha + D_0, say x = p + q with p \in \alpha and q < 0. Then p + q < p + 0 = p (O3), so x \in \alpha by (C2). (\supseteq) Let p \in \alpha. By (C3) there is p' \in \alpha with p' > p; fix one  igl[ ulename{\exists E}  igr] (@fd1:def-rules-existential). Then p - p' < 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so p - p' \in D_0, and p = p' + (p - p') \in \alpha + D_0 . As p \in \alpha was arbitrary, \alpha \subseteq \alpha + D_0  igl[ ulename{ orall I}  igr] (@fd1:def-rules-universal). The second half used (C3), and it cannot do without it. The tempting shortcut “p = p + 0” fails because 0 
otin D_0; Exercise C2 shows a proof built on that shortcut. A set with a largest element fails the proposition: A \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 1 \} satisfies (C1) and (C2), and A + D_0 = D_1, since a \le 1, q < 0 give a + q < 1, and every x < 1 is 1 + (x - 1); so adding D_0 removes 1. Section 7.1’s example of a set with a largest element makes a related point about cancellation (@exm-cut-with-largest-element). Negatives Before reading on. Find a cut  eta with D_1 +  eta = D_0. Then try to write down a recipe that produces such a  eta from any cut \alpha, so that \alpha +  eta = D_0. For D_1 the answer is  eta = D_{-1}. Indeed, p < 1 and q < -1 give p + q < 0; and for s < 0, put h \coloneqq -s/2 > 0, so that s = (1 - h) + (-1 - h) with 1 - h < 1 and -1 - h < -1. For a general \alpha, a natural recipe reads the picture of a cut as a downset: the negative of “the rationals below x” should be “the rationals below -x”, and those are the negatives of the rationals above x, that is, of the rationals outside \alpha. The example below tests that recipe. [The Negatives of the Outside] For a cut \alpha, is the set \{ -q : q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha \} a cut? Test it on \sigma = \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 2 \} (@exm-cut-sqrt2) and on D_1. Then decide in general. Is the set \{ -p : p \in \alpha \} a cut? For \sigma it works. A rational q is outside \sigma exactly when q > 0 and q^2 \ge 2; by @thm-no-rational-square-two, q^2 
e 2, so q^2 > 2. Since (-q)^2 = q^2 (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), the set is \{ -q : q \in 
Q \setminus \sigma \} = \{ x \in 
Q : x < 0 	ext{ and } x^2 > 2 \} . It is a cut. (C1): -2 is in it, 0 is not. (C2): if y < x with x < 0 and x^2 > 2, then 0 < -x < -y, so x^2 = (-x)^2 < (-y)^2 = y^2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), and y < 0, y^2 > 2. (C3): let x < 0 with x^2 > 2, put q \coloneqq -x > 0 and q' \coloneqq  rac{q^2 + 2}{2q} ; \quad 	ext{then} \quad  egin{aligned} q - q' &=  rac{q^2 - 2}{2q} > 0 , \ q'^2 - 2 &=  rac{(q^2 - 2)^2}{4q^2} > 0 . \end{aligned} Then q' > 0, and x' \coloneqq -q' has x < x' < 0 and x'^2 > 2: an element of the set above x. For D_1 it fails. The outside of D_1 is \{ q : q \ge 1 \}, so the set is \{ x \in 
Q : x \le -1 \}. It has a largest element, -1, so (C3) fails. In general. The set always satisfies (C1) and (C2). (C1): for b 
otin \alpha, -b is in it; for a \in \alpha, -a is not, since -a = -q forces q = a \in \alpha. (C2): if y < -q with q 
otin \alpha, then -y > q, so -y 
otin \alpha by @lem-cut-separation, and y = -(-y) is in the set. (C3) fails exactly when the set has a largest element -m, that is, when 
Q \setminus \alpha has a least element m. That happens exactly when \alpha is a rational cut. If \alpha = D_m, the outside \{ q : q \ge m \} has least element m. Conversely, if m is least in 
Q \setminus \alpha, then every r < m is in \alpha (else it would be a smaller element of the outside), and every r \in \alpha has r < m (@lem-cut-separation), so \alpha = D_m. So the recipe gives a cut unless \alpha is rational. The negatives of the inside. For \alpha = D_1, \{ -p : p \in D_1 \} = \{ x : x > -1 \}. It contains 0 but not -2 < 0, so (C2) fails. In general this set is closed upward, the mirror image of a cut: if p \in \alpha and y > -p, then -y < p, so -y \in \alpha by (C2), and y = -(-y) is in the set. And it is never a cut, because (C2) fails as it did for D_1. Take a \in \alpha and b 
otin \alpha (C1). Then a < b by @lem-cut-separation, so -b < -a. The set contains -a but not -b, since -b = -p forces p = b 
otin \alpha. The recipe passes the test on \sigma, the first cut one tries, and fails on the rational cuts, the simplest cuts there are. The failure is a single point: for D_1 the recipe produces D_{-1} together with the one extra point -1. The repair is to stay a positive margin away from the outside. The negative of a cut is the set of negatives of the outside, pushed down by a positive margin. [Negative of a Cut] For a cut \alpha, its negative is the set -\alpha \coloneqq \{ p \in 
Q : -p - r 
otin \alpha 	ext{ for some rational } r > 0 \} . In symbols, p \in -\alpha \iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ {-p - r} 
otin \alpha. It is a cut (checked below). A rational r with this property is a margin for p. In words: p belongs to -\alpha when -p is not merely outside \alpha but outside with room to spare, since even -p - r, a positive distance below -p, is still outside. The quantifier is “some”: one margin suffices, and it may depend on p. Equivalently, p \in -\alpha exactly when p < -q for some q 
otin \alpha (take q \coloneqq -p - r, and conversely r \coloneqq -q - p). -\alpha is a cut. Let \alpha be a cut. - (C1) By (C1) for \alpha there is b 
otin \alpha. For p \coloneqq -b - 1, the margin r \coloneqq 1 gives -p - 1 = b 
otin \alpha, so p \in -\alpha. Also there is a \in \alpha, and -a 
otin -\alpha: for every rational r > 0, -(-a) - r = a - r < a, so a - r \in \alpha by (C2), and no margin exists. - (C2) Let p \in -\alpha with margin r, and p' < p. Then -p' - r > -p - r, and -p - r 
otin \alpha, so -p' - r 
otin \alpha, because the outside of a cut is closed upward (@lem-cut-separation). So p' \in -\alpha, with the same margin. - (C3) Let p \in -\alpha with margin r. Then p + r/2 > p, and -(p + r/2) - r/2 = -p - r 
otin \alpha, so p + r/2 \in -\alpha with margin r/2. So -\alpha \in 
R_{\mathrm D}, and \alpha \mapsto -\alpha is a function 
R_{\mathrm D} 	o 
R_{\mathrm D}. Examples. The degenerate case is -D_0 = D_0. A rational p is in -D_0 when -p - r \ge 0 for some r > 0, that is, p \le -r < 0; and every p < 0 qualifies, with margin r \coloneqq -p. The case that matters is -D_1 = D_{-1}. Here p \in -D_1 when -p - r \ge 1 for some r > 0, that is, p \le -1 - r for some r > 0. That holds for every p < -1, with margin r \coloneqq -1 - p, and for no p \ge -1. The point -1 that spoiled the recipe has no margin. The same computation gives -D_q = D_{-q} for every rational q (Exercise B1; the Quick check below does q = 3). A non-example by minimal change. Allow the margin r = 0. The condition becomes -p 
otin \alpha, and the set is the recipe of @exm-naive-negative: for D_1 it contains -1 and has a largest element. Exactly (C3) breaks, and the proof of (C3) above shows why: it moves up from p by half the margin, which needs r > 0. Why the margin. The margin is what makes -\alpha satisfy (C3) when the outside of \alpha has a least element, and it changes nothing when the outside has none: then -\alpha is exactly the recipe \{ -q : q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha \} of @exm-naive-negative. For every cut, if p \in -\alpha, then p < -q for some q 
otin \alpha by the equivalence above, so -p > q is outside \alpha (@lem-cut-separation), and p = -(-p) is in the recipe. Conversely, if the outside has no least element and q 
otin \alpha, there is q' 
otin \alpha with q' < q; then -q < -q', so -q \in -\alpha by the equivalence above. The fold below works this out for \sigma. For \sigma, the definition gives -\sigma = \{ x \in 
Q : x < 0 	ext{ and } x^2 > 2 \}. (\subseteq) Let p \in -\sigma with margin r. Then -p - r 
otin \sigma, so -p - r > 0 and (-p - r)^2 \ge 2. Hence -p > -p - r > 0, so p < 0, and p^2 = (-p)^2 > (-p - r)^2 \ge 2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). (\supseteq) Let p < 0 with p^2 > 2, and put q \coloneqq -p. The rational q' \coloneqq (q^2 + 2)/(2q) satisfies 0 < q' < q and q'^2 > 2, by the identities q - q' = (q^2 - 2)/(2q) and q'^2 - 2 = (q^2 - 2)^2/(4q^2). With the margin r \coloneqq q - q' > 0, -p - r = q', which is positive with square at least 2, so q' 
otin \sigma, and p \in -\sigma. The outside of \sigma has no least element, and that is why no margin is needed. The negative of a cut is not the set \{ -p : p \in \alpha \}. The book’s notation -A for a set of numbers means that set, but for a cut -\alpha always means @def-cut-negative. The two differ even in shape: for \alpha = D_1, \{ -p : p \in D_1 \} = \{ x : x > -1 \} contains 0 but not -2, so it fails (C2), while -D_1 = D_{-1}. Compute -D_3 from @def-cut-negative, and D_{1/2} + D_{1/3} from @def-cut-sum. -D_3 = D_{-3}. A rational p is in -D_3 when -p - r \ge 3 for some r > 0, that is, p \le -3 - r. Every p < -3 qualifies, with margin r \coloneqq -3 - p > 0; no p \ge -3 does, since then -p - r \le 3 - r < 3. D_{1/2} + D_{1/3} = D_{5/6}. (\subseteq) p < 1/2 and q < 1/3 give p + q < 5/6. (\supseteq) For x < 5/6, put h \coloneqq (5/6 - x)/2 > 0. Then x = (1/2 - h) + (1/3 - h), with 1/2 - h < 1/2 and 1/3 - h < 1/3. Section 7.5 proves D_p + D_q = D_{p+q} for all rationals by the same split. A cut plus its negative Here is the theorem the margin was designed for. Its proof is a key proof of the chapter. [Additive Inverses of Cuts] For every cut \alpha, \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0. The inclusion \subseteq is separation: an element of \alpha is below every outside point, in particular below -t - r for t \in -\alpha. For \supseteq, work backwards from the goal. Given s < 0, we want p \in \alpha and t \in -\alpha with p + t = s. The second summand is forced, t = s - p, and “t \in -\alpha with margin r” unwinds to -t - r = p + (-s - r) 
otin \alpha. So we need a point inside \alpha and a point outside, at distance -s - r, a little less than -s. That is what the walk up by ε supplies (@lem-cut-step): start inside, add \varepsilon until you leave, and the last point inside and the first point outside are exactly \varepsilon apart. Take \varepsilon and the margin r both equal to -s/2; then -s - r = \varepsilon. Before reading on: why is \varepsilon = -s/2 and not -s? Let \alpha be a cut. By @def-cut-negative and @thm-cut-sum, -\alpha and \alpha + (-\alpha) are cuts. (\subseteq) Let x \in \alpha + (-\alpha), say x = p + t with p \in \alpha and t \in -\alpha, and let r > 0 be a margin for t, so -t - r 
otin \alpha. By @lem-cut-separation, p < -t - r. Adding t gives p + t < -r < 0. So x \in D_0. (\supseteq) Let s \in D_0, so s < 0, and let \varepsilon \coloneqq -s/2 ; it depends only on s, and \varepsilon > 0 by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b), since -s > 0. By (C1) there is a \in \alpha; fix one  igl[ ulename{\exists E}  igr]. By @lem-cut-step, applied to \alpha, a and \varepsilon, there is n \in 
N with a + n\varepsilon \in \alpha \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad a + (n + 1)\varepsilon 
otin \alpha ; fix one such n  igl[ ulename{\exists E}  igr] and put p \coloneqq a + n\varepsilon, so that p \in \alpha and p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha. Now let t \coloneqq s - p . Since s = -2\varepsilon, -t - \varepsilon = p - s - \varepsilon = p + 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon = p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha , so \varepsilon is a margin for t, and t \in -\alpha  igl[ ulename{\exists I}  igr] (@fd1:def-rule-existential-introduction), with witness r \coloneqq \varepsilon. Finally p + t = s, so s \in \alpha + (-\alpha)  igl[ ulename{\exists I}  igr], with witnesses p and t. As s \in D_0 was arbitrary, D_0 \subseteq \alpha + (-\alpha)  igl[ ulename{ orall I}  igr]. The two inclusions give \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0 (@fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric). The answer to the prompt. With \varepsilon = -s, the walk gives p \in \alpha with p - s 
otin \alpha, and t = s - p would need a margin r > 0 with p - s - r 
otin \alpha. Nothing guarantees one: p - s - r lies below the first outside point of the walk, and may be inside. For \alpha = D_1, s = -1 and a = 0, the walk stops at p = 0, and p - s - r = 1 - r \in D_1 for every r > 0. The margin must be strictly smaller than the gap, and halving -s leaves room for both. The proof treats rational and irrational cuts alike: it never asks whether the outside of \alpha has a least element. The margin in @def-cut-negative is exactly what absorbs the rational case; without it the \supseteq half would still go through, but for a rational cut \alpha the set it lands in would not be a cut (@exm-naive-negative). An ordered group The results so far say that cuts under + behave like the rationals under +, with the order of Section 7.2 respected. We collect them, together with the consequences that Section 7.4 uses. [Cuts Form an Ordered Group under Addition] For all cuts \alpha,  eta, \gamma: 1. \alpha +  eta =  eta + \alpha and (\alpha +  eta) + \gamma = \alpha + ( eta + \gamma); 2. \alpha + D_0 = \alpha; 3. \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0; 4. \le is a total order on 
R_{\mathrm D}; if \alpha \le  eta, then \alpha + \gamma \le  eta + \gamma; and if \alpha <  eta, then \alpha + \gamma <  eta + \gamma; 5. (cancellation and unique inverses) if \alpha + \gamma =  eta + \gamma, then \alpha =  eta; if \alpha +  eta = D_0, then  eta = -\alpha; and -(-\alpha) = \alpha, -D_0 = D_0, -(\alpha +  eta) = (-\alpha) + (- eta); 6. \alpha <  eta if and only if - eta < -\alpha, and \alpha \le  eta if and only if - eta \le -\alpha. In particular \alpha > D_0 \iff -\alpha < D_0, and \alpha < D_0 \iff -\alpha > D_0. So (
R_{\mathrm D}, +, \le) is an ordered abelian group: (a)–(c) are (F1)–(F4) for +, with zero D_0, and (d) is a total order with (O3). Clauses (e) and (f) are consequences. (a) is @thm-cut-sum, (b) is @prp-cut-sum-zero and (c) is @thm-cut-additive-inverse. (b) By the paragraph after @def-cut-order, \le is a partial order, and by @thm-cut-order-total any two cuts are comparable, so \le is a total order. If \alpha \subseteq  eta and x = p + q \in \alpha + \gamma with p \in \alpha, q \in \gamma, then p \in  eta and x \in  eta + \gamma; so \alpha + \gamma \le  eta + \gamma. The strict form follows from the cancellation law in (e): if \alpha <  eta, then \alpha + \gamma \le  eta + \gamma, and equality would give \alpha =  eta. (c) If \alpha + \gamma =  eta + \gamma, then by (b), (c) and (a),  egin{aligned} \alpha &= \alpha +  igl( \gamma + (-\gamma)  igr) = (\alpha + \gamma) + (-\gamma) \ &= ( eta + \gamma) + (-\gamma) =  eta +  igl( \gamma + (-\gamma)  igr) =  eta . \end{aligned} If \alpha +  eta = D_0, then  eta + \alpha = D_0 = (-\alpha) + \alpha by (a) and (c), and cancellation gives  eta = -\alpha. Since (-\alpha) + \alpha = D_0, the same applied to the cut -\alpha gives \alpha = -(-\alpha). Since D_0 + D_0 = D_0 by (b), it gives D_0 = -D_0. Finally, by (a), (c) and (b), (\alpha +  eta) +  igl( (-\alpha) + (- eta)  igr) =  igl( \alpha + (-\alpha)  igr) +  igl(  eta + (- eta)  igr) = D_0 + D_0 = D_0 , so (-\alpha) + (- eta) = -(\alpha +  eta). (d) Let \alpha <  eta and \delta \coloneqq (-\alpha) + (- eta). By (d), \alpha + \delta <  eta + \delta. By (a), (c) and (b), \alpha + \delta = - eta and  eta + \delta = -\alpha. So - eta < -\alpha. Conversely, if - eta < -\alpha, the same argument applied to the cuts - eta and -\alpha gives -(-\alpha) < -(- eta), which is \alpha <  eta by (e). The non-strict form adds the case of equality: \alpha =  eta if and only if -\alpha = - eta, by (e). For the last sentence, take \alpha or  eta to be D_0 and use -D_0 = D_0. Half of the field axioms now hold for cuts. The other half needs a product, and Section 7.4 builds it by reducing to positive cuts. There (f) is what turns a negative cut into a positive one, and (e) is what lets the signs be put back. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-cut-additive-inverse and the definition of -\alpha. 1. Run the \supseteq half of the proof for \alpha = D_1, s = -1/2 and the starting point a = 0. What are \varepsilon, n, p, t and the margin? Check that t \in -D_1 and p + t = s. 2. Where in the proof is @lem-cut-step used, and what does that lemma need from 
Q? 3. In the check that -\alpha is a cut, which condition uses r > 0? What goes wrong for \alpha = D_1 if the margin r = 0 is allowed? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) \varepsilon = -s/2 = 1/4. The points a + k\varepsilon = k/4 are in D_1 exactly for k < 4, so n = 3, p = 3/4 \in D_1 and p + \varepsilon = 1 
otin D_1. Then t = s - p = -1/2 - 3/4 = -5/4, with margin \varepsilon = 1/4: -t - 1/4 = 5/4 - 1/4 = 1 
otin D_1, so t \in -D_1. And p + t = 3/4 - 5/4 = -1/2 = s. (Another starting point a may give another pair, for example a = 1/8 gives p = 7/8; any p \in D_1 with p + 1/4 \ge 1, that is 3/4 \le p < 1, works with t = -1/2 - p.) (b) Once, in the \supseteq half, to produce p \in \alpha with p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha. Its proof in Section 7.1 needs the Archimedean property of 
Q (@thm-rationals-archimedean), to get some multiple of \varepsilon that leaves \alpha, and the least element of a non-empty set of natural numbers (@prp-integer-least-element), to get the first one, and discreteness of the integers (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), to step back from the first one to the one before it. (c) (C3): from p \in -\alpha with margin r we moved up to p + r/2, which is larger than p only when r > 0. With r = 0 allowed, the set for D_1 is \{ x : -x 
otin D_1 \} = \{ x : x \le -1 \}, which has the largest element -1, so it is not a cut. (d) Inside \alpha and outside it, there are points exactly \varepsilon apart, found by walking up from a point of \alpha in steps of \varepsilon. With \varepsilon = -s/2, the last point p inside and t = s - p split s, and the first point outside certifies t \in -\alpha with margin \varepsilon. B. Practice [B1] Prove that -D_q = D_{-q} for every q \in 
Q. Let q, p \in 
Q. By @def-cut-negative and @def-rational-cut, p \in -D_q if and only if -p - r \ge q for some rational r > 0. (\subseteq) Let p \in -D_q with margin r. Then -p \ge q + r > q, so p < -q (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), and p \in D_{-q}. (\supseteq) Let p < -q. Then r \coloneqq -q - p > 0, and -p - r = q \ge q, so q 
otin D_q shows that r is a margin for p. Hence p \in -D_q. So -D_q = D_{-q}. [B2: Associativity, element by element] Let A, B, C be any subsets of 
Q, and let A + B \coloneqq \{ a + b : a \in A, \ b \in B \}. Prove that (A + B) + C = A + (B + C), writing out both inclusions element by element and naming the rule of 
Q used in each. Which of the cut conditions (C1)–(C3) did you use? (\subseteq) Let x \in (A + B) + C. By the definition, x = y + c for some y \in A + B and c \in C, and y = a + b for some a \in A, b \in B. So x = (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) by (F2) in 
Q. Since b + c \in B + C, x \in A + (B + C). (\supseteq) Let x \in A + (B + C). Then x = a + z with a \in A and z \in B + C, and z = b + c with b \in B, c \in C. So x = a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c by (F2), and a + b \in A + B, so x \in (A + B) + C. The two inclusions give the equality (@fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric). None of (C1)–(C3) was used: associativity of the set sum holds for all sets of rationals, and the only fact used was (F2). For cuts, @thm-cut-sum adds that the sum is again a cut. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: a cut plus its negative] Prove that \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0 for every cut \alpha. Then explain, on the cut \alpha = D_1, why the recipe \{ -q : q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha \} does not give an additive inverse in 
R_{\mathrm D}, while @def-cut-negative does. [Hint 1] For \supseteq, given s < 0, you need a point of \alpha and a point outside \alpha that are a fixed positive distance apart. Which lemma of Section 7.1 produces such a pair? [Hint 2] Let \varepsilon \coloneqq -s/2, and apply @lem-cut-step to a point of \alpha and this \varepsilon. Let \alpha be a cut; -\alpha is a cut by @def-cut-negative. (\subseteq) Let p \in \alpha and t \in -\alpha, with a margin r > 0, so -t - r 
otin \alpha. By @lem-cut-separation, p < -t - r, so p + t < -r < 0, and p + t \in D_0. (\supseteq) Let s < 0 be arbitrary, and \varepsilon \coloneqq -s/2 > 0. Fix a \in \alpha (C1). By @lem-cut-step there is n \in 
N with p \coloneqq a + n\varepsilon \in \alpha and p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha. Let t \coloneqq s - p. Then -t - \varepsilon = p - s - \varepsilon = p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha, so t \in -\alpha with margin \varepsilon, and p + t = s. So s \in \alpha + (-\alpha). The comparison on D_1. The recipe gives \{ -q : q \ge 1 \} = \{ x : x \le -1 \}. This set has the largest element -1, so it fails (C3) and is not a cut; it is not an element of 
R_{\mathrm D} at all, whatever its sum with D_1 may be. In @def-cut-negative, -1 would need a margin r > 0 with 1 - r 
otin D_1, and there is none, since 1 - r < 1. So the margin removes exactly the point -1, and -D_1 = \{ x : x < -1 \} = D_{-1}, a cut, with D_1 + D_{-1} = D_0 by the first part. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: \subseteq, using separation against the outside point -t - r to get p + t < 0. - 1: fixes s < 0 arbitrary. - 3: produces p \in \alpha with p + \varepsilon 
otin \alpha for an \varepsilon chosen from s alone, citing the step lemma (or proving it from the Archimedean property and least elements). - 2: exhibits t \in -\alpha with its margin, and checks p + t = s. - 2: the D_1 comparison: the recipe’s set has the largest element -1, and the margin removes it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a margin equal to the whole gap (\varepsilon = -s with margin -s); \varepsilon chosen depending on p after p was found from \varepsilon. [C2: Find the error] Here is a proof that \alpha + D_0 = \alpha for every cut \alpha. Proof. (1) Let \alpha be a cut. (2) (\subseteq) Let x \in \alpha + D_0, so x = p + q with p \in \alpha and q \in D_0. (3) Then q < 0, so x = p + q < p, and x \in \alpha by (C2). (4) (\supseteq) Let p \in \alpha. (5) Then p = p + 0 with p \in \alpha and 0 \in D_0, so p \in \alpha + D_0. (6) Hence \alpha + D_0 = \alpha. 1. Is the conclusion true? 2. Which line fails, and why? 3. Give a counterexample to the step itself. 4. Repair the proof. 5. The flawed proof never uses (C3). Show that without it the conclusion can fail: compute A + D_0 for A \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 1 \}. (a) Yes: it is @prp-cut-sum-zero. (b) Line (5). It asserts 0 \in D_0, which is false: D_0 = \{ r : r < 0 \}, and 0 < 0 fails by (O1). The line cites a “fact” that is neither proved nor true, error (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Lines (1)–(4) and (6) are correct. (c) Take \alpha = D_1 and p = 1/2. The decomposition 1/2 = 1/2 + 0 of line (5) is not a decomposition into an element of D_1 and an element of D_0, because 0 
otin D_0. (The conclusion 1/2 \in D_1 + D_0 is still true, by 1/2 = 3/4 + (-1/4); the step does not show it.) (d) Replace line (5) by: “By (C3) there is p' \in \alpha with p' > p. Then p - p' < 0, so p - p' \in D_0, and p = p' + (p - p') \in \alpha + D_0.” This is the proof of @prp-cut-sum-zero. (e) Without (C3) the conclusion fails. The set A = \{ r : r \le 1 \} satisfies (C1) and (C2) but not (C3), and A + D_0 = D_1 
e A. Indeed, if a \le 1 and q < 0, then a + q < 1; and every x < 1 is 1 + (x - 1) with 1 \in A and x - 1 < 0. So A + D_0 = D_1, which does not contain 1 \in A. An argument that never uses (C3) would prove the same equation for A, where it is false; that is the tell that some line is wrong.

title: 7.4 Multiplication
content:
Multiplication Like every section of this chapter, this one is optional: nothing outside Chapter 7 depends on it. Section 7.3 made the cuts an ordered group under addition (@thm-cut-ordered-group). This section adds a product and finishes the field axioms. On the Cauchy road of Chapter 5, multiplication was termwise and cost little; on this road it is the hard part. The set of all products of elements is useless, so we define the product of two positive cuts first, prove the laws there, and then extend to all cuts by signs, once, through one lemma (@lem-cut-sign-rules). The reciprocal needs the walk up by ε again, in a multiplicative form. The section ends with the theorem that the cuts form an ordered field. As in Section 7.3, letters p, q, r, s, t, x stand for rationals, and the rules of the ordered field 
Q (@thm-rationals-ordered-field, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-reciprocal-order) are used for them without comment. Why not the set of products For sums, the set of all sums worked. The analogous set for products, \{ pq : p \in \alpha , \ q \in  eta \} , fails in two different ways. It can be everything. Suppose 0 \in \alpha and 0 \in  eta, as for \alpha =  eta = D_1. Then both cuts contain every negative rational (C2), and \alpha contains some a > 0 (C3). Every rational is a product: for x > 0, x = (-1)(-x) with -1 \in \alpha, -x \in  eta; 0 = 0 \cdot 0; and for x < 0, x = a \cdot (x/a) with x/a < 0, so x/a \in  eta. So the set is 
Q, which fails (C1). The culprit is that negatives times negatives are unbounded above. It can be upside down. For \alpha =  eta = D_{-1}, every product pq with p, q < -1 is (-p)(-q) > 1, and every x > 1 is such a product: x = p q with p \coloneqq -(1 + x)/2 < -1 and q \coloneqq -2x/(1 + x) < -1. So the set is \{ x \in 
Q : x > 1 \}. It contains 2 but not 0 < 2, so it fails (C2): it is closed upward. Both failures come from negative elements, and every cut has them. For a cut \alpha > D_0, the positive elements carry all the information, since the others are exactly the rationals p \le 0: by @prp-rational-in-cut, \alpha > D_0 means 0 \in \alpha, so every p \le 0 is in \alpha by (C2), and \alpha has a positive element by (C3). So for positive cuts we multiply positive elements only, then put back everything below. The product of two cuts is not the set of products of their elements, even for positive cuts: D_1 and D_1 give 
Q, as shown above. Every proof in this section works with the definitions below, never with that set. Positive cuts [Product of Positive Cuts] Let \alpha and  eta be cuts with \alpha > D_0 and  eta > D_0 (equivalently, 0 \in \alpha and 0 \in  eta, by @prp-rational-in-cut). Their product is  egin{aligned} \alpha eta \coloneqq \{ p \in 
Q : {}& p \le rs 	ext{ for some } r \in \alpha 	ext{ and } s \in  eta \ & 	ext{with } r > 0 	ext{ and } s > 0 \} . \end{aligned} In words: take the products of positive elements, and then every rational at or below one of them. The second step is what makes \alpha eta closed downward; it also puts every p \le 0 in \alpha eta, since positive r \in \alpha and s \in  eta exist and p \le 0 < rs. For instance, in D_2 D_3 every product rs of positive r < 2, s < 3 is below 6, so D_2 D_3 \subseteq D_6; Exercise B1 proves equality. Let \alpha,  eta > D_0. Suppose the definition said “p = rs” instead of “p \le rs”. Which set would it give, and which cut condition would that set fail? It would give the set of products rs of positive elements, a set of positive rationals. It is non-empty, but it fails (C2): it contains a positive rs and not 0 < rs. [Positive Cuts under Multiplication] Let \alpha,  eta, \gamma be cuts with \alpha,  eta, \gamma > D_0. Then: 1. \alpha eta is a cut, and \alpha eta > D_0; 2. \alpha eta =  eta\alpha; 3. (\alpha eta)\gamma = \alpha( eta\gamma); 4. \alpha D_1 = \alpha. Each cut condition for \alpha eta is inherited from \alpha or  eta, as for sums: an outside point of each factor bounds the products, and moving up in \alpha moves the product up. The laws (b) and (c) are (F6) and (F5) of 
Q, applied to positive elements. For (d), multiplying by an element of D_1 pushes down, so one inclusion is (C2); the other writes p as a larger element of \alpha times a factor below 1. Throughout, \alpha,  eta, \gamma contain 0 and a positive element (by @prp-rational-in-cut and (C3)), and every element outside one of them is positive (@lem-cut-separation, against 0). (a) (C1): 0 \in \alpha eta, as noted after the definition. By (C1) there are a 
otin \alpha and b 
otin  eta; then a, b > 0. For positive r \in \alpha, s \in  eta, separation gives r < a and s < b, so rs < as < ab by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), since s > 0 and a > 0. So every p \in \alpha eta has p \le rs < ab for suitable r, s, and ab 
otin \alpha eta. (C2): if p \le rs and q < p, then q \le rs, with the same r, s. (C3): let p \in \alpha eta, with p \le rs for positive r \in \alpha, s \in  eta. By (C3) for \alpha there is r' \in \alpha with r' > r; then r' > 0, so r's \in \alpha eta, and r's > rs \ge p by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). The table names, for each clause of @def-commutative-ring-and-field and @def-ordered-ring-and-field, the line that proves it. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Clause Statement for cuts Proved by ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------- (F1), (F2) + commutative, associative @thm-cut-sum (F3) \alpha + D_0 = \alpha @prp-cut-sum-zero (F4) \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0 @thm-cut-additive-inverse (F5) (\alpha eta)\gamma = \alpha( eta\gamma) @lem-cut-sign-rules (f) (F6) \alpha eta =  eta\alpha @lem-cut-sign-rules (e) (F7) \alpha D_1 = \alpha @lem-cut-sign-rules (g) (F8) \alpha\alpha^{-1} = D_1 for \alpha 
e D_0 @thm-cut-reciprocal (F9) \alpha( eta + \gamma) = \alpha eta + \alpha\gamma @lem-cut-distributive 1 
e 0 D_1 
e D_0 0 \in D_1 \setminus D_0 (O1) exactly one of \alpha <  eta, \alpha =  eta,  eta < \alpha @thm-cut-order-total (O2) \alpha <  eta < \gamma \Rightarrow \alpha < \gamma below (O3) \alpha <  eta \Rightarrow \alpha + \gamma <  eta + \gamma @thm-cut-ordered-group (d) (O4) D_0 < \alpha,  eta \Rightarrow D_0 < \alpha eta @prp-cut-product-positive (a) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- For (O2): if \alpha \subsetneq  eta \subsetneq \gamma, then \alpha \subseteq \gamma (@fd2:prp-subset-transitive), and \alpha = \gamma would give  eta \subseteq \gamma = \alpha \subseteq  eta, so \alpha =  eta (@fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric), against \alpha <  eta. For (O4): for \alpha,  eta > D_0 the product of @def-cut-product is that of @def-cut-product-positive, as noted after the definition. Every clause is covered, so 
R_{\mathrm D} is an ordered field. Nothing in the table is left to an exercise. Two rows are proved by walking up: (F4), through @lem-cut-step, and (F8), through @lem-cut-multiplicative-step. Several others, such as (O3), (F5)–(F7) and (F9), lean on (F4) through the cancellation law and -(-\alpha) = \alpha of @thm-cut-ordered-group (e). The order rows cost almost nothing, because the order is inclusion; on the Cauchy road of Chapter 5 the order took a section of its own. Section 7.5 puts 
Q inside 
R_{\mathrm D} and adds completeness, and Section 7.6 compares the result with Chapter 5’s field. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Why is the set \{ pq : p \in \alpha, \ q \in  eta \} useless as a product for \alpha =  eta = D_1? 2. In the table of the proof of @thm-cuts-ordered-field, which rows are proved by a lemma that walks up through a cut, @lem-cut-step or @lem-cut-multiplicative-step? Which further rows depend on such a row? 3. Compute \abs{D_{-1}}, \sgn D_{-1}, \abs{D_{1/2}}, \sgn D_{1/2} and D_{-1} D_{1/2} from the definitions. 4. True or false: if \alpha > D_0, then \alpha^{-1} contains every negative rational. Give a reason. (a) It is all of 
Q, so it fails (C1): x > 0 is (-1)(-x), 0 = 0 \cdot 0, and x < 0 is (1/2)(2x), with every factor in D_1. (b) (F4), the additive inverse: @thm-cut-additive-inverse uses @lem-cut-step. (F8), the multiplicative inverse: @thm-cut-reciprocal uses @lem-cut-multiplicative-step, whose proof uses @lem-cut-step. Further rows depend on (F4): the strict form of (O3) uses cancellation, and (F5)–(F7) and (F9) use @lem-cut-sign-rules and @lem-cut-distributive, which use -(-\alpha) = \alpha, cancellation, or both (@thm-cut-ordered-group (e)), all proved from \alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0. The rows (F1)–(F3), 1 
e 0, (O1), (O2) and (O4) use neither lemma. (c) D_{-1} < D_0: D_{-1} > D_0 fails since 0 
otin D_{-1}, and D_{-1} 
e D_0 since -1/2 \in D_0 \setminus D_{-1}. So \sgn D_{-1} = -1 and \abs{D_{-1}} = -D_{-1} = D_1 (@exr-addition-b1 with q = -1). Since 0 \in D_{1/2}, D_{1/2} > D_0, so \sgn D_{1/2} = 1 and \abs{D_{1/2}} = D_{1/2}. The signs differ, so D_{-1} D_{1/2} = - igl( D_1 D_{1/2}  igr) = - igl( D_{1/2} D_1  igr) = -D_{1/2} = D_{-1/2} , by @prp-cut-product-positive (b) and (d), and @exr-addition-b1 with q = 1/2. (d) True: by @def-cut-reciprocal, \alpha^{-1} contains every p \le 0, with no condition. B. Practice [B1] Prove from @def-cut-product-positive that D_2 D_3 = D_6. Hint: for 0 < x < 6, scale 2 and 3 down by suitable factors. D_2, D_3 > D_0, since 0 \in D_2 and 0 \in D_3. (\subseteq) Let p \le rs with 0 < r < 2, 0 < s < 3. Then rs < 2s < 6 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), twice), so p < 6. (\supseteq) Let x < 6. If x \le 0, then x \le 1 \cdot 1 with 1 \in D_2 and 1 \in D_3. Let 0 < x < 6, and put \lambda \coloneqq  rac{1}{2} \Bigl( 1 +  rac{x}{6} \Bigr) , \qquad r \coloneqq 2\lambda , \qquad s \coloneqq  rac{x}{2\lambda} . Since 0 < x/6 < 1, \lambda is the midpoint of x/6 < 1, so x/6 < \lambda < 1. Hence 0 < r < 2, so r \in D_2. Also s > 0, and s < 3 because x < 6\lambda; so s \in D_3. Finally rs = x, so x \in D_2 D_3. Hence D_2 D_3 = D_6. [B2: The last step of the reciprocal] Let \alpha be a cut with \alpha > D_0, and let p \in 
Q with 0 < p < 1. We show that p \in \alpha\alpha^{-1}. 1. Let \mu \coloneqq (1 + 1/p)/2. Since 1/p > 1, \mu is the midpoint of 1 and 1/p, so 1 < \mu < 1/p. 2. By @lem-cut-multiplicative-step there is r \in \alpha with r > 0 and \mu r 
otin \alpha. 3. Hence p \in \alpha\alpha^{-1}. Name the move, then complete it: write out step (3). The move is the walk up by ε, in its multiplicative form: step (2) walks up through \alpha until the next point is outside, which gives a point inside and a point outside whose ratio is \mu, less than 1/p. (3) Put s \coloneqq p/r; it is positive. Then s \cdot (\mu r) = p\mu < p \cdot  rac{1}{p} = 1 , using \mu < 1/p and p > 0. Since \mu r 
otin \alpha, the rational q \coloneqq \mu r witnesses s \in \alpha^{-1} (@def-cut-reciprocal). Now r \in \alpha and s \in \alpha^{-1} are positive and p = rs \le rs, so p \in \alpha\alpha^{-1} by @def-cut-product-positive. Why \mu and not 1/p itself: with \mu = 1/p, step (2) gives r with r/p 
otin \alpha, and s = p/r would need some q 
otin \alpha with (p/r) q < 1, that is, q < r/p. The point r/p itself does not qualify, and there may be no smaller one outside. The strict room between \mu and 1/p plays the part of the margin. [B3] Prove that (-\alpha)(- eta) = \alpha eta for all cuts \alpha and  eta. By @lem-cut-sign-rules (d), applied first with -\alpha in front and then to \alpha(- eta), (-\alpha)(- eta) = - igl( \alpha(- eta)  igr) = - igl( -(\alpha eta)  igr) = \alpha eta , where the last step is -(-\xi) = \xi (@thm-cut-ordered-group (e)) with \xi = \alpha eta. C. Going deeper [C1: The reciprocal without strictness] For a cut \alpha > D_0, let  egin{aligned} ho(\alpha) \coloneqq {}& \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 0 \} \ {}\cup{}& \{ p \in 
Q : p > 0 	ext{ and } pq \le 1 	ext{ for some } q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha \} . \end{aligned} Prove that ho(\alpha) is a cut if and only if \alpha is not a rational cut, that is, \alpha 
e D_a for every a \in 
Q. [Hint 1] Compute ho(D_a) first. Which element of the outside of D_a does all the work? [Hint 2] If \alpha is not rational, the outside 
Q \setminus \alpha has no least element: a least element m would force \alpha = D_m. Let \alpha > D_0. Then 0 \in \alpha, every q 
otin \alpha is positive (@lem-cut-separation), and \alpha has a positive element. If \alpha = D_a, then ho(\alpha) is not a cut. Here a > 0, since 0 \in D_a, and the outside is \{ q : q \ge a \}. For p > 0: if pq \le 1 with q \ge a, then pa \le pq \le 1; conversely pa \le 1 gives the witness q = a. So ho(D_a) = \{ p : p \le 0 \} \cup \{ p > 0 : p \le 1/a \} = \{ p : p \le 1/a \}. It has the largest element 1/a, so (C3) fails. If \alpha is not rational, then ho(\alpha) is a cut. First, 
Q \setminus \alpha has no least element. Suppose m were one. Every r < m is then in \alpha (otherwise r is a smaller element of the outside), and every r \in \alpha has r < m (@lem-cut-separation). So \alpha = D_m, against the hypothesis. (C1) 0 \in ho(\alpha). For a positive a \in \alpha, 1/a 
otin ho(\alpha): every q 
otin \alpha has q > a, so (1/a) q > 1. (C2) As for \alpha^{-1}: if 0 < p' < p and pq \le 1 with q > 0, then p'q < pq \le 1; and every p' \le 0 is in ho(\alpha). (C3) If p \le 0, then for any q 
otin \alpha, 1/(2q) is in ho(\alpha) and larger. Let p > 0 with pq \le 1, q 
otin \alpha. Since q is not least in the outside, there is q' 
otin \alpha with q' < q; then q' > 0 and pq' < pq \le 1, so p < 1/q'. The midpoint p'' \coloneqq (p + 1/q')/2 has p < p'' < 1/q', so p'' q' < 1, and p'' \in ho(\alpha) is larger than p. So ho(\alpha) is a cut exactly when \alpha is not rational. For such \alpha, ho(\alpha) = \alpha^{-1}: the argument for (C3) shows that pq \le 1 with q 
otin \alpha gives pq' < 1 with q' 
otin \alpha, and the converse is immediate. As with the negatives of the outside in Section 7.3, the non-strict recipe works for the cut \sigma of @exm-cut-sqrt2, which is not a rational cut (Exercise C1 of Section 7.1), and fails on the simplest cuts; the strict inequality in @def-cut-reciprocal is the multiplicative margin. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: shows that ho(D_a) has the largest element 1/a (1/a \in ho(D_a) and every element is \le 1/a; the full equality ho(D_a) = \{ p : p \le 1/a \} also earns this), and names (C3) as the failing condition. - 2: proves that the outside of a non-rational cut has no least element. - 1: (C1) and (C2) for ho(\alpha). - 3: (C3) for ho(\alpha), using a smaller outside point q' to make the inequality strict. - 1: states the equivalence with both directions. Second route: showing ho(\alpha) = \alpha^{-1} for non-rational \alpha (\subseteq by a smaller outside point q' making pq' < 1, \supseteq since < implies \le) and citing @thm-cut-reciprocal earns the 1 point for (C1) and (C2) and the 3 points for (C3). The 2 points for the no-least-element step still require that step. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming q > 0 without separation against 0 \in \alpha; “a smaller outside point exists” asserted for every cut.

title: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content:
The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field This section is part of the optional Chapter 7, and nothing outside the chapter depends on it. Section 7.4 finished the arithmetic: by @thm-cuts-ordered-field the cuts form an ordered field 
R_{\mathrm D}, with zero D_0 and one D_1. Three questions are left before 
R_{\mathrm D} can be called a model of the real numbers. Do the rational cuts D_q form a faithful copy of 
Q, with the arithmetic of 
Q? Is the new field complete? And does the cut \sigma of @exm-cut-sqrt2, built to sit at the gap of 
Q, really square to D_2? This section answers all three with yes. On the Cauchy road, Section 5.4 asked the first question about the map \kappa (@thm-rational-embedding), and Sections 5.5 and 5.6 together answered the second; here the second answer is already in hand, from Section 7.2. A copy of the rationals Every ordered field F contains a copy of 
Q: by @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field there is exactly one map \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F that sends 1 to 1_F and respects sums and products, and it is strictly increasing. For F = 
R_{\mathrm D} we have a candidate in hand, the map q \mapsto D_q of @def-rational-cut. It sends 1 to D_1, the one of the field. The theorem below checks the rest: sums and positive products by computing with sets, negatives and the other signs by the field rules; and the uniqueness clause then says the candidate is \iota_{
R_{\mathrm D}}. [The Rationals Inside the Cuts] The map 
Q 	o 
R_{\mathrm D}, q \mapsto D_q, is injective, and for all p, q \in 
Q: 1. p < q if and only if D_p < D_q; 2. D_p + D_q = D_{p+q}; 3. -D_q = D_{-q}; 4. D_p D_q = D_{pq}; 5. D_1 is the one of the ordered field 
R_{\mathrm D} of @thm-cuts-ordered-field. Consequently D_q = \iota_{
R_{\mathrm D}}(q) for every q \in 
Q, where \iota_{
R_{\mathrm D}} is the map of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field. The identity (b), and (d) for positive p, q, are equalities of sets of rationals, so each has two halves. The \subseteq halves are closure: if r < p and s < q, then r + s < p + q. The \supseteq halves must split a given rational x < p + q as a sum of something below p and something below q, and the obvious split x = p + (x - p) fails, because p 
otin D_p. So we take a little off both summands: half the gap p + q - x from each. For products we do the same with a factor instead of a summand. Signs other than “both positive” are reduced to that case, the chapter’s named move of reducing to the positive case (Section 7.4); since 
R_{\mathrm D} is already known to be a field, the ring rules for signs do the reduction. Throughout, 
R_{\mathrm D} is an ordered field (@thm-cuts-ordered-field), so the rules of @prp-ordered-ring-rules hold in it as well as in 
Q. (a) If p < q, then p \in D_q, so D_p \subsetneq D_q by @prp-rational-in-cut (a) applied to the cut D_q; that is, D_p < D_q (@def-cut-order). Conversely, if D_p \subsetneq D_q, then @prp-rational-in-cut (a), applied to the cut D_q and the rational p, gives p \in D_q, that is, p < q. Injectivity. If p 
e q, then p < q or q < p by trichotomy (O1) in 
Q, and (a) gives D_p 
e D_q in either case. (b) (\subseteq) An element of D_p + D_q is r + s with r < p and s < q (@def-cut-sum), and r + s < p + q by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). (\supseteq) Let x \in 
Q with x < p + q, and put \delta \coloneqq  rac{p + q - x}{2} > 0 . Then p - \delta < p and q - \delta < q, so p - \delta \in D_p and q - \delta \in D_q, and (p - \delta) + (q - \delta) = p + q - 2\delta = x. Hence x \in D_p + D_q. (c) By (b), D_q + D_{-q} = D_{q + (-q)} = D_0. By @thm-cut-additive-inverse, also D_q + (-D_q) = D_0. The negative of an element of the commutative ring 
R_{\mathrm D} is unique (@prp-ring-algebra (a)), so -D_q = D_{-q}. (d), both positive. Let p > 0 and q > 0. By (a), D_p > D_0 and D_q > D_0, so the product is that of @def-cut-product-positive: D_p D_q = \{ x \in 
Q : x \le rs 	ext{ for some } r \in D_p, \ s \in D_q 	ext{ with } r > 0, \ s > 0 \} . (\subseteq) If 0 < r < p and 0 < s < q, then rs < ps < pq by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), used twice. So x \le rs gives x < pq. (\supseteq) Let x < pq. If x \le 0, take r \coloneqq p/2 and s \coloneqq q/2: they are positive, lie in D_p and D_q, and x \le 0 < rs. If 0 < x < pq, put \lambda \coloneqq  rac{1}{2} \Bigl( 1 +  rac{x}{pq} \Bigr) , \qquad r \coloneqq \lambda p , \qquad s \coloneqq  rac{x}{\lambda p} . Since 0 < x/(pq) < 1, the midpoint \lambda satisfies x/(pq) < \lambda < 1. Hence 0 < r < p; and s > 0, with s < q because this is equivalent, after multiplying by \lambda p > 0, to x < \lambda pq, that is, to x/(pq) < \lambda. So r \in D_p, s \in D_q, both are positive, and rs = x. Hence x \in D_p D_q. (d), the other signs. If p = 0 or q = 0, then one factor is D_0, so D_p D_q = D_0 by @def-cut-product, and D_{pq} = D_0. For negative entries, (c) gives D_p = -D_{-p} for every p, since -(-\alpha) = \alpha (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). If p < 0 < q, then by the sign rule (-a)b = -(ab) of @prp-ring-algebra (c) in 
R_{\mathrm D} (in the cut model it is part of @lem-cut-sign-rules) and the positive case, D_p D_q = (-D_{-p}) D_q = -(D_{-p} D_q) = -D_{-pq} = D_{pq} , the last step by (c). The case q < 0 < p follows by commutativity of the product. If p < 0 and q < 0, then the rule (-a)(-b) = ab of @prp-ring-algebra (c) and the positive case give D_p D_q = (-D_{-p})(-D_{-q}) = D_{-p} D_{-q} = D_{(-p)(-q)} = D_{pq} . (e) This is part of @thm-cuts-ordered-field. The consequence. By (e), (b) and (d), the map q \mapsto D_q sends 1 to the one of 
R_{\mathrm D} and respects sums and products. By the uniqueness clause of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field, applied to the ordered field F = 
R_{\mathrm D}, it is \iota_{
R_{\mathrm D}}. This proves the theorem. So the rationals live inside 
R_{\mathrm D} as the rational cuts, with their order and arithmetic unchanged. From now on, a computation with rational cuts may be done in 
Q and carried over: D_{1/2} + D_{1/3} = D_{5/6}, D_{-2} D_3 = D_{-6}, D_2^{-1} = D_{1/2}. The last one holds because D_2 D_{1/2} = D_1 by (d), and in a field the inverse is the only element with that property (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). In the (\supseteq) half of (b), why not write x = p + (x - p)? It has x - p < q. Because p 
otin D_p: the cut D_p consists of the rationals strictly below p. The split must take something from p as well, and \delta > 0 is that something. The flawed proof of Exercise C2 of Section 7.3 falls into the same trap, with 0 
otin D_0. On the Cauchy road the same theorem was @thm-rational-embedding, and its proof was a computation with constant sequences. There the sum of two constant sequences is the constant sequence of the sum, termwise. Here the sum of two rational cuts is not obviously a rational cut, and the \supseteq half needs the room that \delta provides. [A Cut Is the Union of the Rational Cuts Below It] For every cut \alpha, \alpha =  igcup \{ D_q : q \in \alpha \} = \sup \{ D_q : q \in \alpha \} . (\supseteq) If q \in \alpha and r < q, then r \in \alpha by (C2) of @def-dedekind-cut; so D_q \subseteq \alpha. (\subseteq) If p \in \alpha, then (C3) gives p' \in \alpha with p' > p, and p \in D_{p'}. This proves the first equality. The set \{ D_q : q \in \alpha \} is non-empty, since \alpha 
e \emptyset, and bounded above by \alpha, by the \supseteq half; so by @thm-dedekind-lub its supremum is its union. The proposition is the cut model’s way of saying that every real number is approached from below by rationals. Nothing later in the chapter uses it. Between two cuts there is a rational cut In 
Q between two rationals lies a third, their midpoint. In an Archimedean field, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field puts a rational between any two elements. For 
R_{\mathrm D} we prove the corresponding statement directly from the cut conditions. We do not yet know that 
R_{\mathrm D} is Archimedean, and the direct proof is shorter anyway. [The Rational Cuts Are Dense] Let \alpha and  eta be cuts with \alpha <  eta. Then there is q \in 
Q with \alpha < D_q <  eta. Try it first (ten minutes): given cuts \alpha <  eta, which rational would you put between them, and why is one point of  eta \setminus \alpha not quite enough? Since \alpha \subsetneq  eta, there is a rational p in  eta but not in \alpha, and the natural guess is q = p. By @prp-rational-in-cut, p 
otin \alpha gives \alpha \subseteq D_p (part (b)), and p \in  eta gives D_p \subsetneq  eta (part (a)). So \alpha \le D_p <  eta. The first inequality need not be strict: for \alpha = D_1,  eta = D_2 and p = 1, the guess gives D_p = \alpha. The cure is to move up once more inside  eta: condition (C3) of  eta gives p' \in  eta above p, and D_{p'} is strictly above D_p, so strictly above \alpha, and still strictly below  eta. Since \alpha \subsetneq  eta (@def-cut-order), there is p \in  eta with p 
otin \alpha. By (C3) of @def-dedekind-cut for  eta, there is p' \in  eta with p' > p. Then: - \alpha \subseteq D_p, by @prp-rational-in-cut (b), since p 
otin \alpha; - D_p \subsetneq D_{p'}, by 1 (a), since p < p'; - D_{p'} \subsetneq  eta, by @prp-rational-in-cut (a), since p' \in  eta. Hence \alpha \subsetneq D_{p'} \subsetneq  eta, that is, \alpha < D_{p'} <  eta. Take q \coloneqq p'. Each hypothesis has a job. “\alpha <  eta” supplies p, and the strictness is needed: for \alpha =  eta there is nothing strictly between. Condition (C3), used for  eta, supplies the second step up; without it, D_1 and the set \{ r \in 
Q : r \le 1 \} would be two “cuts”, the first strictly inside the second, with no D_q strictly between them: D_1 \subsetneq D_q forces q > 1, and then D_q contains (1 + q)/2 > 1, which the second set lacks. “Dense” does not mean that every cut is rational. The rational cuts are dense, and still \sigma of @exm-cut-sqrt2 is not one of them, as @prp-cut-sqrt2-square below proves. Density says only that between two cuts there is a rational cut, never that a cut is one. Name a rational q with \sigma < D_q < D_{3/2}, and check both inequalities. Take q = 29/20. Then q > 0 and q^2 = 841/400 > 800/400 = 2, so q 
otin \sigma, and @prp-rational-in-cut (b) gives \sigma \subseteq D_q. The inclusion is strict: 10/7 > 0 and (10/7)^2 = 100/49 > 98/49 = 2, so 10/7 
otin \sigma, while 10/7 < 29/20 (200/140 < 203/140), so 10/7 \in D_q. Hence \sigma < D_q. And 29/20 < 30/20 = 3/2, so D_q < D_{3/2} by 1 (a). The rational q = 10/7 works the same way, with 17/12 as the witness of strictness: (17/12)^2 = 289/144 > 2 and 17/12 < 10/7 (119/84 < 120/84). Archimedes in the cuts An ordered field is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field) if no element lies above every n \cdot 1_F, n \in 
N. In 
R_{\mathrm D}, n \cdot 1 = \iota_{
R_{\mathrm D}}(n) = D_n, by @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field and 1. A cut is bounded inside 
Q by any rational it misses, and 
Q is Archimedean, so the property comes almost for free. [The Cuts Are Archimedean] For every cut \alpha there is n \in 
N with \alpha < D_n. Hence 
R_{\mathrm D} is an Archimedean ordered field. By (C1) of @def-dedekind-cut there is b \in 
Q with b 
otin \alpha, and @prp-rational-in-cut (b) gives \alpha \subseteq D_b. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n \in 
N with b < n, so D_b < D_n by 1 (a). Hence \alpha < D_n = n \cdot 1_{
R_{\mathrm D}}, which is @def-archimedean-ordered-field for 
R_{\mathrm D}. The square root of two The cut \sigma \coloneqq \{ p \in 
Q : p \le 0 	ext{ or } p^2 < 2 \} of @exm-cut-sqrt2 was introduced as “the rationals below \sqrt 2”. Now that cuts can be multiplied, that description becomes a theorem: \sigma \sigma = D_2. The proof is the chapter’s multiplicative form of walk up by \varepsilon, @lem-cut-multiplicative-step: step up by a factor \mu > 1 until you leave \sigma. [The Cut of the Square Root of Two] The cut \sigma of @exm-cut-sqrt2 satisfies \sigma > D_0 and \sigma \sigma = D_2. Consequently \sigma 
e D_q for every q \in 
Q. The \subseteq half is a bound: two positive elements of \sigma have squares below 2, so their product has square below 4. The \supseteq half must write a given x < 2 as a product rs of positive elements of \sigma. Small x are easy: x \le 1 \cdot 1. For 1 \le x < 2 we want r \in \sigma with r^2 > x, since then s \coloneqq x/r is smaller than r and so lies in \sigma. Such an r is found by walking up by a factor: if r \in \sigma and \mu r 
otin \sigma, then r^2 \ge 2/\mu^2, and this exceeds x as soon as \mu^2 < 2/x. So we need a rational \mu > 1 with \mu^2 < 2/x, written down without square roots. \sigma > D_0. Every p < 0 has p \le 0, so D_0 \subseteq \sigma; and 0 \in \sigma \setminus D_0. Hence D_0 \subsetneq \sigma. So \sigma \sigma is the product of @def-cut-product-positive. (\subseteq) Let x \in \sigma \sigma, so x \le rs with r, s \in \sigma, r > 0, s > 0. Since r > 0 and r \in \sigma, r^2 < 2; likewise s^2 < 2. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), used twice, (rs)^2 = r^2 s^2 < 2 s^2 < 4 = 2^2. Since rs \ge 0 and 2 \ge 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) gives rs < 2. So x < 2 and x \in D_2. (\supseteq), small x. title: 7.6 The Two Roads Give the Same Real Numbers

The Two Roads Give the Same Real Numbers This section is part of the optional Chapter 7, and nothing outside the chapter depends on it. We now have two complete ordered fields. Chapter 5 built one from classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), and Section 7.5 built another from cuts (@thm-cuts-complete-field). Their elements have nothing in common: a class of sequences is not a set of rationals. Chapter 6 proved that any two complete ordered fields are linked by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism (@thm-cof-uniqueness). This section applies that theorem to the two models, computes the isomorphism explicitly, and compares what each road had to pay for. Two models on one page With both models in view, one letter 
R is not enough. In this section only, 
R_{\mathrm C} denotes the field

R_{\mathrm D} that copy is q \mapsto D_q (@thm-rationals-embed-cuts). In 
R_{\mathrm C} we write \iota \coloneqq \iota_{
R_{\mathrm C}} \colon

R_{\mathrm C} , which is the map \kappa(q) = [(q)_n] of @def-rational-embedding, by @thm-rational-embedding (d). From the identification in Section 5.4 on, Chapter 5 wrote q for \kappa(q). The Cauchy road gets its arithmetic cheaply, termwise, and pays at both ends: every definition must be checked against a change of representative, the order needs a margin, and completeness takes two sections. The Dedekind road gets order and completeness almost free, because a cut is a set and inclusion is already an order, and pays in the middle: negatives need a margin, and multiplication needs a detour through positive cuts and signs. The last row looks beyond this volume. The Cauchy construction works for any metric space, with sequences whose terms get close: Metric and Topological Spaces, Chapter 2 builds the completion of a metric space that way. The Dedekind construction has an analogue for any ordered set, in which a cut is a set of elements that equals the set of lower bounds of its upper bounds; the result is called the Dedekind–MacNeille completion, and no volume of this series develops it. Each road leads somewhere the other does not. Richard Dedekind published the construction by cuts in 1872, in Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen; he says there that the idea came to him in 1858, while preparing lectures on the differential calculus. Charles Méray had built the irrational numbers from convergent sequences of rationals in 1869, and Georg Cantor and Eduard Heine gave constructions from fundamental sequences, our Cauchy sequences, in 1872. Karl Weierstrass had presented his own construction of the real numbers in his Berlin lectures of the 1860s. The two roads of this volume were thus laid out within a few years of each other. title: Axiom 1.1.1 (The Axioms (Z1)–(Z6))
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Extensionality. Sets with the same elements are equal: for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , if \(x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B\) for every \(x\) , then \(A = B\) . Empty set. There is a set with no elements. Pairing. For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) there is a set whose elements are exactly \(a\) and \(b\) . Union. For every set \(\sS\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the elements of members of \(\sS\) . Power set. For every set \(X\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the subsets of \(X\) . Separation. For every set \(A\) and every property \(P(x)\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the \(x \in A\) with \(P(x)\) .

title: Exercise (C1: What the empty-set axiom really says; intersections as greatest lower bounds)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Show that (Z2) follows from (Z6), once some set \(A\) is known to exist. Let \(\sS\) be a non-empty set. Show that \(\bigcap \sS \subseteq S\) for every \(S \in \sS\) , and that every set \(C\) with \(C \subseteq S\) for all \(S \in \sS\) satisfies \(C \subseteq \bigcap \sS\) . title: Proposition 1.1.2 (The Sets Named by the Axioms)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: There is exactly one set with no elements. It is written \(\emptyset\) . For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) the set of (Z3) is unique. It is written \(\{a, b\}\) , and \(\{a\} \coloneqq \{a, a\}\) , the set whose only element is \(a\) . For every set \(\sS\) the set of (Z4) is unique. It is written \(\bigcup \sS\) , and \(A \cup B \coloneqq \bigcup \{A, B\}\) for sets \(A\) , \(B\) , so that \(x \in A \cup B\) if and only if \(x \in A\) or \(x \in B\) . The sets \(A \cap B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x \in B \}\) and \(A \setminus B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x \notin B \}\) exist by (Z6). For a non-empty set \(\sS\) , the set \[ \bigcap \sS \coloneqq \{ x \in A_0 : x \in S \text{ for every } S \in \sS \} \] exists by (Z6) for any \(A_0 \in \sS\) , it does not depend on \(A_0\) , and \(x \in \bigcap \sS\) if and only if \(x \in S\) for every \(S \in \sS\) . For all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} \iff (a = c \wedge b = d) \vee (a = d \wedge b = c). \] In particular \(\{a\} = \{c, d\}\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(c = d\) .

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Ordered Pair as a Set)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For sets \(a\) and \(b\) , the ordered pair of \(a\) and \(b\) is the set \[ (a, b) \coloneqq \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} . \] Its first coordinate is \(a\) and its second coordinate is \(b\) .

title: Example (Three Encodings That Lose Information)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Consider the claim: any set built from \(a\) and \(b\) in which \(a\) is mentioned first is an ordered pair , that is, has the characteristic property. Test it on the three encodings \[ \text{(i) } \{a, b\}, \qquad \text{(ii) } \{\{a\}, \{b\}\}, \qquad \text{(iii) } \{a, \{b\}\} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: In the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair , where is the hypothesis \(a \ne b\) of Case 2 used, and what replaces the argument when \(a = b\) ? Run the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair on the equation \((\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) = (c, d)\) : which case applies, and what does each step give? Which axioms make \((a, b)\) a set? State the idea of the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Coordinates from unions and intersections)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Let \(p = (a, b)\) . Compute \(\bigcap p\) and \(\bigcup p\) , and show that, when \(a \ne b\) , the set \(\bigcup p \setminus \bigcap p\) has exactly one element, namely \(b\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Nested pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Write \(((a, b), c)\) for the pair whose first coordinate is the pair \((a, b)\) . Prove that \(((a, b), c) = ((a', b'), c')\) if and only if \(a = a'\) , \(b = b'\) and \(c = c'\) . Determine whether \(((\emptyset, \emptyset), \emptyset) = (\emptyset, (\emptyset, \emptyset))\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: Kuratowski pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Prove that for all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \(\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(b = d\) . You may use @prp-zf-basic-sets .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Here is an argument for @thm-kuratowski-pair , direction \((\Rightarrow)\) . Let \((a, b) = (c, d)\) . (2) Matching the members of \(\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}\) and \(\{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}\) in the order written, \(\{a\} = \{c\}\) and \(\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}\) . (3) From \(\{a\} = \{c\}\) , \(a = c\) . (4) Then \(\{a, b\} = \{a, d\}\) , and so \(b = d\) . Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and give a counterexample to that step.

title: Exercise (C3: Wiener’s encoding)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For sets \(a\) and \(b\) let \(W(a, b) \coloneqq \{\{\{a\}, \emptyset\}, \{\{b\}\}\}\) . Prove that \(W(a, b) = W(c, d)\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(b = d\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (The Product Exists)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) there is exactly one set \(A \times B\) whose elements are exactly the pairs \((a, b)\) with \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) : \[ p \in A \times B \iff \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ \ p = (a, b) . \]

title: Proposition 1.2.3 (The Working Rules from the Axioms)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: The axioms (Z1)–(Z6) give the working rules (W1)–(W5) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Section 1.1 in the following form. For every set \(A\) and every admissible property \(P(x)\) (one whose unwinding is a formula of the language, Section 1.1), \(\{ x \in A : P(x) \}\) is a set. For each list \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) written out in the text, entry by entry, there is a set \(\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}\) whose elements are exactly \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) . For sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A \cup B\) is a set. For a set \(X\) and a family \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(X\) , given as a function \(I \to \powerset{X}\) ( @fd2:def-indexed-family ), the union \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) and the intersection \(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\) of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection are sets. For every set \(X\) , \(\powerset{X}\) is a set. For sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A \times B\) is a set.

title: Theorem 1.2.1 (Characteristic Property of Pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d . \]

title: Axiom 1.3.1 (Axiom of Infinity)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: (Z7) There is an inductive set.

title: Definition 1.3.3 (The set of natural numbers)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Fix an inductive set \(I\) , which exists by (Z7). Define \[ \omega \coloneqq \{ x \in I : x \in J \text{ for every inductive set } J \subseteq I \} . \] The elements of \(\omega\) are the natural numbers .

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Successor of a set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: For every set \(x\) , the successor of \(x\) is the set \[ \mathrm{S}(x) \coloneqq x \cup \{x\} . \]

title: Definition 1.3.2 (Inductive set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: A set \(I\) is inductive if \(\emptyset \in I\) and, for every \(x \in I\) , also \(\mathrm{S}(x) \in I\) .

title: Example (The first natural numbers as sets)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Define \[ \begin{aligned} 0 &\coloneqq \emptyset , & 1 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0) , & 2 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1) , \\ 3 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2) , & 4 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(3) . \end{aligned} \] Write each of \(1, 2, 3, 4\) as a set of the earlier numerals, and then using only \(\emptyset\) and braces. Check that \(0, 1, 2, 3\) are four different sets.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: List the elements of \(3\) and of \(4\) as sets of numerals. Is \(2 \subseteq 3\) ? Is \(2 \in 3\) ? True or false, with a reason: every inductive set has \(5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4)\) as an element. Write “ \(J\) is not inductive” in symbols, with the negation moved inward until it stands only in front of a membership statement.

title: Exercise (B1: Intersections and differences)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(J\) and \(K\) be inductive sets. Prove that \(J \cap K\) is inductive. Is \(J \setminus \{\emptyset\}\) inductive? Justify your answer, and say which clause of the definition holds and which fails.

title: Exercise (B2: Zero or a successor)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that every \(n \in \omega\) is \(\emptyset\) or is \(\mathrm{S}(k)\) for some \(k \in \omega\) , by showing that the set \[ A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : n = \emptyset \text{ or } n = \mathrm{S}(k) \text{ for some } k \in \omega \} \] is inductive.

title: Exercise (C1: Two steps back)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that every \(n \in \omega\) is \(0\) , or is \(1\) , or is \(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k))\) for some \(k \in \omega\) . Let \(I\) be an arbitrary inductive set. Running the argument of (a) on \(\{ x \in I : x = 0 \text{ or } x = 1 \text{ or } x = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) \text{ for some } k \in I \}\) , what does it prove about the elements of \(I\) , and what does it not prove?

title: Theorem 1.3.3 (Induction on \omega)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: (Set form.) Let \(A \subseteq \omega\) . If \(0 \in A\) , and \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in A\) for every \(n \in A\) , then \(A = \omega\) . (Property form.) Let \(P(n)\) be a property, that is, a formula of the first-order language with \(\in\) and \(=\) , possibly with other variables as parameters. If \(P(0)\) holds and, for every \(n \in \omega\) , \(P(n)\) implies \(P(\mathrm{S}(n))\) , then \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.3.2 (The Least Inductive Set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: \(\omega\) is inductive. \(\omega \subseteq J\) for every inductive set \(J\) , whether or not \(J \subseteq I\) . \(\omega\) is the only set with properties (a) and (b). In particular, \(\omega\) does not depend on the inductive set \(I\) fixed in @def-omega .

title: Definition 1.4.2 (Peano system)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: A Peano system \((M, e, s)\) consists of a set \(M\) , an element \(e \in M\) , and a function \(s \colon M \to M\) , such that: (P3) \(s(x) \ne e\) for every \(x \in M\) ; (P4) \(s\) is injective; (P5) every subset \(A \subseteq M\) with \(e \in A\) and \(s(x) \in A\) for every \(x \in A\) is equal to \(M\) .

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Transitive set)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: A set \(x\) is transitive if every element of \(x\) is a subset of \(x\) : for every \(y \in x\) , \(y \subseteq x\) .

title: Example (Each axiom is needed)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Show that each of the following structures \((M, e, s)\) , with \(s \colon M \to M\) , satisfies two of (P3), (P4), (P5) and fails the third. \(M \coloneqq \{0\}\) , \(e \coloneqq 0\) , \(s(0) \coloneqq 0\) . \(M \coloneqq \{0, 1\}\) , \(e \coloneqq 0\) , \(s(0) \coloneqq 1\) , \(s(1) \coloneqq 1\) . ( The natural numbers beside a two-sided chain. ) \(M \coloneqq \omega \times 3\) , whose elements are the pairs \((n, i)\) with \(n \in \omega\) and \(i \in 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\) ; \(e \coloneqq (0, 0)\) ; and \[ \begin{aligned} s(n, 0) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) , & s(n, 1) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) , \\ s(0, 2) &\coloneqq (0, 1) , & s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) &\coloneqq (k, 2) , \end{aligned} \] for \(n, k \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: For each of the three structures in @exm-peano-axioms-independent , which of (P3), (P4), (P5) fails? In the proof of (P4) in @thm-omega-peano , where is @lem-omega-transitive (a) used, and where is (c)? Is \(\omega \cup \{\omega\}\) inductive? Justify your answer. Is \(\{0, 1, \{1\}\}\) a transitive set? Is it an element of \(\omega\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \(m, n \in \omega\) . The following lines contain a proof that if \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , then \(m = n\) , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. So \(m \in n \subseteq m\) , that is, \(m \in m\) . Suppose \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) . We have \(m \cup \{m\} = n \cup \{n\}\) , so \(m = n\) by canceling \({\cup}\{\cdot\}\) on both sides. Since \(n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m)\) , we have \(n \in m\) or \(n = m\) . Suppose \(m \ne n\) ; then \(m \in n\) and \(n \in m\) . This contradicts \(m \notin m\) ( @lem-omega-transitive (c)); so \(m = n\) . From \(m \in n\) and \(n \in m\) we get \(m = n\) , since \(\in\) is antisymmetric. Since \(m\) is transitive ( @lem-omega-transitive (a)) and \(n \in m\) , we have \(n \subseteq m\) . Since \(m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , we have \(m \in n\) or \(m = n\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two steps at a time)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \(d \coloneqq \mathrm{S} \circ \mathrm{S} \colon \omega \to \omega\) ( @fd2:def-composition ), so that \(d(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n))\) . Show that \((\omega, 0, d)\) satisfies (P3) and (P4) of @def-peano-system , and that it does not satisfy (P5). Hint: look at the set \(\omega \setminus \{1\}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: A Peano system with a different start)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Give an example of a Peano system \((M, e, s)\) with \(M \subseteq \omega\) and \(e \ne 0\) . Check every clause of @def-peano-system .

title: Exercise (C2: Closed subsets of the chain)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be the structure (iii) of @exm-peano-axioms-independent . Call \(A \subseteq M\) good if \(e \in A\) and \(s(x) \in A\) for every \(x \in A\) . Show that every good set contains \(\omega \times \{0\}\) . Show that each of the following sets is good, where \(m, k \in \omega\) : \[ \begin{aligned} G_0 &\coloneqq \omega \times \{0\} , \qquad G_\infty \coloneqq M , \\ R_m &\coloneqq G_0 \cup \{ (n, 1) : n \in \omega, \ m \in \mathrm{S}(n) \} , \\ L_k &\coloneqq G_0 \cup (\omega \times \{1\}) \cup \{ (j, 2) : j \in \mathrm{S}(k) \} . \end{aligned} \] Show that a good set that contains \((k, 2)\) contains \(L_k\) .

title: Lemma 1.4.1 (Natural Numbers Are Transitive Sets)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content:
Every \(n \in \omega\) is a transitive set. \(\omega\) is a transitive set: every element of a natural number is a natural number. \(n
