e 0\) is \(\mathrm{S}(k)\) for some \(k \in \omega\) . \(0 \in n\) for every \(n \in \omega\) with \(n 
e 0\) .

title: Proposition 1.4.3 (No Pair Is a Natural Number)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) , the pair \((a, b)\) is not an element of \(\omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.2 (Peano’s Axioms Hold in \omega)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: \(0 \in \omega\) . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega\) . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(\mathrm{S}(n) \ne 0\) . For all \(m, n \in \omega\) , if \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , then \(m = n\) . Every \(A \subseteq \omega\) with \(0 \in A\) and \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in A\) for every \(n \in A\) is equal to \(\omega\) . Moreover, \(\{ (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) : n \in \omega \}\) is a set, and with codomain \(\omega\) it is a function \(\mathrm{S} \colon \omega \to \omega\) , which is injective and does not take the value \(0\) .

title: Corollary 1.5.2 (Successor Cancellation)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For all \(k, l \in \omega\) : if \(k + 1 = l + 1\) , then \(k = l\) ; and \(k + 1 \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 1.5.1 (Addition and Multiplication on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For each \(m \in \omega\) , let \(A_m \colon \omega \to \omega\) be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with \(X = \omega\) , \(a = m\) and \(g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x)\) . The sum of \(m\) and \(n\) is \(m + n \coloneqq A_m(n)\) . Thus, for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \[ m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n) . \] For each \(m \in \omega\) , let \(M_m \colon \omega \to \omega\) be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with \(X = \omega\) , \(a = 0\) and \(g(n, x) = x + m\) . The product of \(m\) and \(n\) is \(m \cdot n \coloneqq M_m(n)\) , also written \(mn\) . Thus, for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \[ m \cdot 0 = 0, \qquad m \cdot \mathrm{S}(n) = m \cdot n + m . \] The numerals are \(0 \coloneqq \emptyset\) and \(1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0)\) , \(2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1)\) , \(3 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2)\) , and so on, as in @exm-von-neumann-numerals . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n)\) ; in particular \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(k + 2 = (k + 1) + 1\) for every \(k \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-omega-recursion . Where in the proof is \(\mathrm{S}(n) \notin \mathrm{S}(n)\) used, and what would fail without it? Run the construction for \(X = \omega\) , \(a = 0\) and \(g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x))\) : write the graphs of the partial solutions up to \(0\) , \(1\) and \(2\) . Why does the uniqueness half need only an induction, while existence needs partial solutions? State the idea of the proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Small products)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Compute \(3 \cdot 2\) and \(2 \cdot 3\) from the defining equations of @def-omega-arithmetic alone, without using @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws . Here \(5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4)\) and \(6 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(5)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Distributivity, last step blank)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Here is the proof of \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) for all \(m, n, k \in \omega\) , with the last step left blank. Name the move, then complete it. Fix \(m, n \in \omega\) and induct on \(k\) . Base case: \(m(n + 0) = mn = mn + 0 = mn + m \cdot 0\) . Inductive step: suppose \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) . Then \[ m\bigl(n + (k + 1)\bigr) = m\bigl((n + k) + 1\bigr) = m(n + k) + m = (mn + mk) + m = \underline{\hspace{6em}} . \] Justify each equality you add.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: addition is commutative)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: From the two defining equations of addition, \(m + 0 = m\) and \(m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1\) , and @thm-omega-induction alone, prove that \(m + n = n + m\) for all \(m, n \in \omega\) . Prove every auxiliary fact you need.

title: Exercise (C2: Associativity of multiplication, last half blank)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Prove that \((km)n = k(mn)\) for all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) . The first half is given; name the move, then complete it. Fix \(k, m \in \omega\) and induct on \(n\) . Base case: \((km) \cdot 0 = 0 = k \cdot 0 = k(m \cdot 0)\) . Inductive step: \(\underline{\hspace{10em}}\) You may use (a)–(f) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws .

title: Exercise (C3: Doubling)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Show that there is exactly one function \(D \colon \omega \to \omega\) with \(D(0) = 0\) and \(D(n + 1) = (D(n) + 1) + 1\) for every \(n \in \omega\) , and prove that \(D(n) = n + n\) for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.5.3 (Laws of Arithmetic on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) : \(0 + n = n\) , and \((m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1\) ; \(m + n = n + m\) ; \((k + m) + n = k + (m + n)\) ; \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) and \((n + k)m = nm + km\) ; \(0 \cdot n = 0\) , \((m + 1) \cdot n = mn + n\) , and \(n \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot n = n\) ; \(mn = nm\) ; \((km)n = k(mn)\) .

title: Theorem 1.5.1 (Recursion Theorem on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Let \(X\) be a set, let \(a \in X\) , and let \(g \colon \omega \times X \to X\) be a function. Then there is exactly one function \(f \colon \omega \to X\) such that \[ f(0) = a \quad \text{and} \quad f\bigl(\mathrm{S}(n)\bigr) = g\bigl(n, f(n)\bigr) \ \text{ for every } n \in \omega . \]

title: Definition 1.6.1 (Order on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: For \(m, n \in \omega\) , we write \(m < n\) if \(m \in n\) , and \(m \le n\) if \(m < n\) or \(m = n\) . As usual, \(n > m\) means \(m < n\) , and \(n \ge m\) means \(m \le n\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: List the elements of \(\{ k \in \omega : k \le 3 \}\) . Which natural number is this set? True or false: for \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m < n\) implies \(m \subseteq n\) . Justify your answer. Find the least element of \(\{ n \in \omega : n \cdot n > 10 \}\) , and say why it is least. Which clause of @thm-omega-order says that the notation \(\{0, \dots, n\}\) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Chapter 2 still means what it meant there, and what set is it on \(\omega\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Order as inclusion)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m \le n\) if and only if \(m \subseteq n\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A product is at least its factor)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that for all \(m, n \in \omega\) with \(n \ge 1\) , \(m \le mn\) . Show by an example that the hypothesis \(n \ge 1\) is needed.

title: Exercise (C1: Strong induction on ω)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(P(n)\) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that, for every \(n \in \omega\) , if \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k \in \omega\) with \(k < n\) , then \(P(n)\) holds. Prove that \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Here is an attempted proof that any two natural numbers are comparable. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, give the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and a counterexample to the step. Claim. For all \(m, n \in \omega\) : \(m \in n\) , \(m = n\) or \(n \in m\) . We use @thm-omega-induction (b) on \(n\) , for the property “for every \(m \in \omega\) : \(m \in n\) , \(m = n\) or \(n \in m\) ”. (2) For \(n = 0\) : every \(m\) is \(0\) or contains \(0\) , by @lem-omega-transitive (e). (3) Suppose the property holds for \(n\) , and let \(m \in \omega\) . (4) If \(m \in n\) or \(m = n\) , then \(m \in n \cup \{n\} = \mathrm{S}(n)\) . (5) If \(n \in m\) , then \(\mathrm{S}(n) \le m\) , because nothing lies strictly between \(n\) and \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) : no \(k \in \omega\) has \(n \in k \in \mathrm{S}(n)\) . (6) In every case \(m \in \mathrm{S}(n)\) , \(m = \mathrm{S}(n)\) or \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in m\) , which is the property for \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) . (7) By @thm-omega-induction (b), the claim holds.

title: Proposition 1.6.3 (Order and Arithmetic on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content:

title: Proposition 1.6.4 (Powers and Parity on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: For all \(b, m, n \in \omega\) : \(b^{m+n} = b^m \cdot b^n\) ; if \(b \ne 0\) , then \(b^n \ne 0\) ; if \(b > 1\) and \(m < n\) , then \(b^m < b^n\) ; there is exactly one pair \((q, r)\) with \(q \in \omega\) , \(r \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(n = 2q + r\) . In particular, no \(n \in \omega\) is both of the form \(2q\) and of the form \(2q' + 1\) .

title: Proposition 1.6.5 (Tuples and Lists as Sets)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(X\) be a set. For \(n = 2\) , an \(n\) -tuple in \(X\) is a pair \((x_1, x_2)\) with \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) ( @def-kuratowski-pair ), and \(X^2 \coloneqq X \times X\) . For \(n \in \omega\) with \(n \ge 3\) , an \(n\) -tuple in \(X\) is the graph \(G\) of a function \(x \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to X\) ; with \(x_k \coloneqq x(k)\) it is written \[ (x_1, \dots, x_n) \coloneqq \bigl\{ (k, x_k) : k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \bigr\} = G . \] For \(n \ge 2\) , there is exactly one set \(X^n\) whose elements are exactly the \(n\) -tuples in \(X\) ; for \(n = 2\) it is \(X \times X\) . For \(n \ge 2\) , two \(n\) -tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) and \((y_1, \dots, y_n)\) in \(X\) are equal if and only if \(x_k = y_k\) for every \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) . For \(n \ge 3\) , no \(n\) -tuple is a pair; and for \(n, n' \ge 3\) with \(n \ne n'\) , no \(n\) -tuple is an \(n'\) -tuple. For every \(n \in \omega\) ( \(n = 0, 1\) allowed) and every function \(x \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to X\) , the list \[ \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \coloneqq \bigl\{ y \in X : y = x_k \text{ for some } k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \bigr\} \] is a set: the image \(x(\{1, \dots, n\})\) of @fd2:def-image . For \(n \ge 3\) , no \(n\) -tuple is an element of \(\omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.1 (Order on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: \(<\) is a strict total order on \(\omega\) : for all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) , never \(n < n\) ; if \(k < m\) and \(m < n\) , then \(k < n\) ; and exactly one of \(m < n\) , \(m = n\) , \(n < m\) holds. For \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m < \mathrm{S}(n)\) if and only if \(m \le n\) . Hence no \(k \in \omega\) satisfies \(n < k < \mathrm{S}(n)\) . Every \(n \in \omega\) is the set of the natural numbers less than it: \(n = \{ m \in \omega : m < n \}\) . Hence \(\{0, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in \omega : k \le n \}\) equals \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) . \(0 \le n\) for every \(n \in \omega\) ; if \(n \ne 0\) , then \(1 \le n\) ; and \(0 < 1\) . For \(n \in \omega\) , \(\{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in \omega : 1 \le k \le n \}\) equals \(\mathrm{S}(n) \setminus \{0\}\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.2 (Well-Ordering of \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Every non-empty subset \(A \subseteq \omega\) has a least element: an \(a \in A\) with \(a \le x\) for every \(x \in A\) . The least element is unique.

title: Proposition 1.7.2 (Isomorphisms Preserve Arithmetic and Order)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be a Peano system, and let \(\oplus, \otimes \colon M \times M \to M\) be functions such that, for all \(x, y \in M\) , \[ \begin{aligned} x \oplus e &= x, & x \oplus s(y) &= s(x \oplus y), \\ x \otimes e &= e, & x \otimes s(y) &= (x \otimes y) \oplus x . \end{aligned} \] Let \(\varphi \colon \omega \to M\) be the bijection of @thm-peano-categoricity . Then for all \(m, n \in \omega\) : \(\varphi(m + n) = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(n)\) ; \(\varphi(m n) = \varphi(m) \otimes \varphi(n)\) ; \(m < n\) if and only if \(\varphi(n) = \varphi(m) \oplus z\) for some \(z \in M\) with \(z \ne e\) .

title: Theorem 1.7.1 (Categoricity of the Peano Axioms)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be a Peano system. There is exactly one function \(\varphi \colon \omega \to M\) with \(\varphi(0) = e\) and \(\varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n))\) for every \(n \in \omega\) . This \(\varphi\) is a bijection. For any two Peano systems \((M, e, s)\) and \((M', e', s')\) there is exactly one bijection \(\psi \colon M \to M'\) with \(\psi(e) = e'\) and \(\psi(s(x)) = s'(\psi(x))\) for every \(x \in M\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Functions on Classes)
page: 2.2 Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , and \(\approx\) an equivalence relation on a set \(Y\) . Classes are taken for \(\sim\) in \(X\) and for \(\approx\) in \(Y\) . Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) implies \(f(x) \approx f(x')\) . Then there is exactly one function \(F \colon X/{\sim} \to Y/{\approx}\) with \(F([x]) = [f(x)]\) for every \(x \in X\) . Let \(g \colon X \times X \to X\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x', y, y' \in X\) , \[ \begin{aligned} x \sim x' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) , \\ y \sim y' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x, y') . \end{aligned} \] Then there is exactly one function \(G \colon (X/{\sim}) \times (X/{\sim}) \to X/{\sim}\) with \(G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)]\) for all \(x, y \in X\) . Let \(S \subseteq X\) be such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) and \(x \in S\) imply \(x' \in S\) . Let \(\bar S \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in S \} \subseteq X/{\sim}\) . Then, for every \(x \in X\) , \([x] \in \bar S\) if and only if \(x \in S\) .

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Commutative Ring, Field)
page: 2.3 The Integers as an Ordered Ring
content: A commutative ring is a set \(R\) with two functions, addition \(+ \colon R \times R \to R\) and multiplication \(\cdot \colon R \times R \to R\) (written \(a \cdot b = ab\) ), such that clauses (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of the following list hold; clause (F8) is used only for fields. \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . There is an element \(0 \in R\) with \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every \(a \in R\) there is an element \(-a \in R\) with \(a + (-a) = 0\) . \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . There is an element \(1 \in R\) with \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every non-zero \(a \in R\) there is an element \(a^{-1} \in R\) with \(a a^{-1} = 1\) . \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . A field is a commutative ring in which, in addition , \(1 \ne 0\) and (F8) holds. We write \(a - b \coloneqq a + (-b)\) , and in a field \(a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1}\) for \(b \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 2.3.2 (Ordered Ring, Ordered Field)
page: 2.3 The Integers as an Ordered Ring
content: An ordered commutative ring is a commutative ring \(R\) ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ) together with a relation \(<\) on \(R\) such that, for all \(a, b, c \in R\) : (trichotomy) exactly one of \(a < b\) , \(a = b\) , \(b < a\) holds; (transitivity) if \(a < b\) and \(b < c\) , then \(a < c\) ; (addition) if \(a < b\) , then \(a + c < b + c\) ; (multiplication) if \(0 < a\) and \(0 < b\) , then \(0 < ab\) . An ordered field is a field that is an ordered commutative ring. We write \(b > a\) for \(a < b\) , and \(a \le b\) for “ \(a < b\) or \(a = b\) ” (likewise \(b \ge a\) ). An element \(a\) is positive if \(a > 0\) , negative if \(a < 0\) , and non-negative if \(a \ge 0\) .

page: 2.4 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content: The relation \(\sim\) on \(\nZ \times \nZ_{>0}\) given by \[ (p, q) \sim (r, s) \iff ps = rq \] is an equivalence relation ( @fd2:def-equivalence-relation ).

title: Theorem 2.4.3 (The Rationals Form a Field)
page: 2.4 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content: \(\nQ\) , with the operations of @def-rational-operations , is a field ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ), with zero \([(0, 1)]\) and one \([(1, 1)]\) . A rational number \([(p, q)]\) is zero if and only if \(p = 0\) . If \(p > 0\) , its inverse is \([(q, p)]\) ; if \(p < 0\) , its inverse is \([(-q, -p)]\) .

content: For every \(x \in \nQ\) there is exactly one \(m \in \nZ\) with \(m \le x < m + 1\) . It is called the integer part of \(x\) and written \(\floor{x}\) .

Set \(p' \coloneqq 2q - p\) and \(q' \coloneqq p - q\) ; both are positive integers, by the two inequalities between \(p\) and \(q\) . Write \(x = a/b\) with \(a, b \in \nZ_{>0}\) ; then \(a^2 = 2b^2\) . Since \(p^2 = 2q^2\) , we have \(p < q\) . Suppose \(x \in \nQ\) has \(x^2 = 2\) ; replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) if necessary, take \(x > 0\) . \(p < 2q\) , since \(p \ge 2q\) would give \(p^2 \ge 4q^2 > 2q^2\) . title: Theorem 2.6.1 (No Rational Squares to Two)
page: 2.6 The Gaps in the Rationals
content: There is no \(x \in \nQ\) with \(x^2 = 2\) .

title: Theorem 2.6.2 (A Bounded Set of Rationals with No Rational Supremum)
page: 2.6 The Gaps in the Rationals
content:
Let \[ A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} , \qquad A^+ \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x > 0 \} = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} . \] \(A\) is non-empty and bounded above in \((
Q, \le)\) , but \(A\) has no supremum in \(
Q\) . \(A\) and \(A^+\) have the same upper bounds in \(
Q\) . Hence \(A^+\) is also non-empty and bounded above, and has no supremum in \(

title: Corollary 3.1.3 (Even and Odd Integers)
page: 3.1 Divisibility and Division with Remainder
content:
Every \(a \in 
Z\) is even or odd, and not both . More precisely, either \(a = 2q\) for exactly one \(q \in 
Z\) and \(a\) is not of the form \(2k + 1\) , or \(a = 2q + 1\) for exactly one \(q \in 
Z\) and \(a\) is not of the form \(2k\) . If \(a \in 
Z\) and \(a^2\) is even, then \(a\) is even.

title: Corollary 3.2.2 (Coprime Means 1 Is a Combination)

page: 3.2 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Integers \(a, b \in \nZ\) are coprime if \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) .

content: Let \(a, b \in \nZ\) . If \((a, b) \ne (0, 0)\) , the greatest common divisor \(\gcd(a, b)\) is the greatest element, for \(\le\) , of the set of common divisors of \(a\) and \(b\) . We set \(\gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0\) .

title: Corollary 3.3.2 (A Prime Dividing a Product)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Let \(p\) be prime. For every \(a \in 
Z\) : \(p \mid a\) or \(\gcd(p, a) = 1\) . For all \(b, c \in 
Z\) : if \(p \mid bc\) , then \(p \mid b\) or \(p \mid c\) . If \((q_1, \dots, q_l)\) is a list of primes, with \(l \in 
N\) , and \(p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j\) , then \(p = q_j\) for some \(j \in \{1, \dots, l\}\) .

title: Definition 3.3.1 (List, Product of a List, Prime Factorization)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Let \(k \in 
N\) . A list of length \(k\) in \(
Z\) is a function \(p \colon \{1, \dots, k\} 	o 
Z\) , written \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) with \(p_i \coloneqq p(i)\) ; for \(k = 0\) it is the empty list . Its product \(\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i \in 
Z\) is given by the recursion \[ \prod_{i=1}^{0} p_i = 1 , \qquad \prod_{i=1}^{j+1} p_i = \Bigl( \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i \Bigr) p_{j+1} \quad 	ext{for } j < k , \] where \(\prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i\) is the product of the shortened list \((p_1, \dots, p_j)\) . A prime factorization of \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) is a list \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) such that every entry \(p_i\) is prime ( @fd2:def-prime ), the list is non-decreasing ( \(i \le j\) implies \(p_i \le p_j\) ), and \(\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i = n\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: These questions are about the uniqueness half of the proof of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic . Why must the empty list count as a prime factorization? Run the induction step on \((p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4) = (2, 2, 3, 5)\) and a second prime factorization \((q_1, \dots, q_l)\) of \(60\) . Which equalities does the proof derive, and to which two lists is \(P(3)\) applied? Which line of the proof uses Euclid’s lemma, and through which result? Where is “non-decreasing” used? Give the idea of the uniqueness proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: The following lines contain a proof of @thm-euclid-lemma-integers , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Suppose \(a \mid bc\) and \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) . There are \(x, y \in \nZ\) with \(ax + by = 1\) . (ii′) Since \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) and \(a \mid bc\) , we have \(a \mid b\) or \(a \mid c\) . Multiplying by \(c\) : \(c = acx + bcy\) . (iii′) Dividing \(1 = ax + by\) by \(a\) : \(1/a = x + (b/a)y\) . \(a \mid acx\) , since \(acx = a(cx)\) . Write \(bc = ak\) ; then \(bcy = a(ky)\) , so \(a \mid bcy\) . Hence \(a \mid acx + bcy\) . So \(a \mid c\) .

title: Exercise (B2: The least common multiple)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:

Z\) with \(a \mid c\) and \(b \mid c\) . The first part of a proof is given. \(ab > 0\) by (O4), and \(a \mid ab\) , \(b \mid ab\) , so \(ab \in M\) ; and \(0\) is a lower bound of \(M\) . By @prp-integer-least-element , \(M\) has a least element \(L\) . Let \(c \in 
Z\) with \(a \mid c\) and \(b \mid c\) . By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), \(c = qL + r\) with \(q, r \in 
Z\) and \(0 \le r < L\) . Since \(r = c + (-q)L\) , and \(a\) divides \(c\) and \(L\) , \(a \mid r\) ( @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)); likewise \(b \mid r\) . The last step is blank. Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B3: Two factorizations and a gcd)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Find the prime factorizations of \(1001\) and of \(2^{10} - 1\) , proving that each entry is prime. Then show that \(\gcd(1001, 1023) = 11\) in two ways. First, use the factorizations to write \(1001 = 11 \cdot 91\) and \(1023 = 11 \cdot 93\) : show \(\gcd(91, 93) = 1\) , and deduce \(\gcd(1001, 1023) = 11\) from a Bézout identity for \(91\) and \(93\) ( @cor-coprime-iff-combination ). Second, use the Euclidean algorithm. Hint: the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime shortens each primality check. Do not use the school rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”: this chapter does not prove it.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: unique factorization)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Prove that two prime factorizations of the same positive integer are equal: the uniqueness half of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic . You may cite @thm-euclid-lemma-integers and @cor-prime-divides-product .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) . If \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) , then \(mn \mid c\) . Argument. (1) Write \(c = mk\) and \(c = nl\) with \(k, l \in \nZ\) . (2) Then \(c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl\) . (3) So \(mn \mid c^2\) . (4) Hence \(mn \mid c\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step.

title: Exercise (C3: There is no last prime)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) , with \(k \in \nN\) , there is a prime that is not an entry of the list.

title: Lemma 3.3.4 (The Least Divisor Is Prime)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(n \in \nZ\) with \(n \ge 2\) . The set \(D \coloneqq \{ d \in \nZ : d \ge 2 \text{ and } d \mid n \}\) has a least element, and that element is prime. In particular, \(n\) has a prime factor.

title: Proposition 3.3.3 (Coprime Divisors of a Number)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) with \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) . Then \(mn \mid c\) .

title: Theorem 3.4.1 (Quotient Ring by an Ideal)
page: 3.4 Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(I\) an ideal of \(R\) . Setting \(a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I\) defines an equivalence relation \(\sim_I\) on \(R\) , and the class of \(a\) is \([a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}\) . The rules \([a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b]\) , \([a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab]\) and \(-[a] \coloneqq [-a]\) are well defined on \(R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}\) . \(R/I\) , with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero \([0]\) and one \([1]\) . The quotient map \(\pi \colon R \to R/I\) , \(\pi(a) \coloneqq [a]\) , satisfies \(\pi(a + b) = \pi(a) + \pi(b)\) , \(\pi(ab) = \pi(a) \pi(b)\) and \(\pi(1) = [1]\) . \([a] = [0]\) if and only if \(a \in I\) . In particular \([1] = [0]\) if and only if \(I = R\) .

title: Definition 3.5.1 (Unit of a Commutative Ring)
page: 3.5 Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ). An element \(u \in R\) is a unit of \(R\) if there exists \(v \in R\) with \(uv = 1\) . The set of units of \(R\) is written \(R^{\times}\) . For a unit \(u\) , the element \(v\) is unique ; it is written \(u^{-1}\) and called the inverse of \(u\) .

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Absolute Value in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. For \(x \in F\) , the absolute value of \(x\) is \[ \abs{x} \coloneqq \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 , \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} \] For \(x, y \in F\) , the element \(\abs{x - y}\) is the distance from \(x\) to \(y\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field

True or false in every ordered field: “if \(a < b\) , then \(a^2 < b^2\) ”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in \(
Q\) . True or false in every ordered field: “if \(\abs{a} < \abs{b}\) , then \(a < b\) ”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in \(
Q\) . True or false in every ordered field: “ \(x^2 + 1 > 0\) for every \(x\) ”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in \(

Here \(3\) , \(5\) , \(8\) and so on denote the multiples \(3 \cdot 1\) , \(5 \cdot 1\) , \(8 \cdot 1\) , … of Section 2.3 (defined before @prp-ordered-ring-rules ), and \(2 = 1 + 1 = 2 \cdot 1\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Maximum and minimum through the absolute value)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: For \(a, b\) in an ordered field \(F\) , let \(\max\{a, b\}\) be \(b\) if \(a \le b\) and \(a\) otherwise, and \(\min\{a, b\}\) be \(a\) if \(a \le b\) and \(b\) otherwise. Prove that \[ \max\{a, b\} = \frac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} , \qquad \min\{a, b\} = \frac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2} . \] Deduce that \(\abs{x} = \max\{x, -x\}\) for every \(x \in F\) .

title: Lemma 4.1.1 (Fraction Rules in a Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \(F\) be a field ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ), and let \(a, b, c, d \in F\) with \(b 
e 0\) and \(d 
e 0\) . \(b^{-1}\) is the only element \(y\) with \(b y = 1\) , and \((b^{-1})^{-1} = b\) . Moreover \(bd 
e 0\) and \((bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}\) . \(\dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad + bc}{bd}\) and \(\dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}\) . \(\dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{d - b}{bd}\) . For all \(x, y \in F\) : if \(xy = 0\) , then \(x = 0\) or \(y = 0\) .

title: Proposition 4.1.3 (Rules for the Absolute Value)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field, and let \(x, y, z, r \in F\) . \(\abs{x} \ge 0\) , and \(\abs{x} = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) . \(\abs{-x} = \abs{x}\) , \(\abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}\) and \(\abs{x}^2 = x^2\) ; if \(x \ne 0\) , then \(\abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}\) . \(-\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}\) . \(\abs{x} \le r\) if and only if \(-r \le x \le r\) ; and \(\abs{x} < r\) if and only if \(-r < x < r\) . (Triangle inequality.) \(\abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) , and \(\abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}\) . (Reverse triangle inequality.) \(\bigl| \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr| \le \abs{x - y}\) .

title: Proposition 4.1.2 (Halves and Comparisons in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. \(\le\) is a total order on \(F\) ( @fd2:def-partial-order ), and its strict part is \(<\) . \(2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 > 0\) . For every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) , \[ 0 < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . \] For all \(a, b \in F\) with \(a < b\) , \(a < \dfrac{a + b}{2} < b\) . For \(a, b \in F_{>0}\) : if \(a \le b\) , then \(\dfrac{1}{b} \le \dfrac{1}{a}\) . For \(a, b, c, d \in F\) : if \(0 \le a \le b\) and \(0 \le c \le d\) , then \(ac \le bd\) .

title: Definition 4.2.2 (Archimedean Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: An ordered field \(F\) is Archimedean if for every \(x \in F\) there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(x < n \cdot 1_F\) . In symbols, \[ \forall x \in F \ \ \exists n \in \nN \ \ x < n \cdot 1_F . \]

page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property

title: Proposition 4.2.1 (The Natural Numbers inside an Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
Let \(F\) be an ordered field, and let \(m, n, k \in 
N\) . \((m + n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F\) and \((mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)\) . If \(m < n\) , then \(m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F\) . Hence \(n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F\) is injective, and \(n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0\) whenever \(n \ge 1\) . \((n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k\) . In particular \((2^k) \cdot 1_F = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k\) , the \(k\) -th power in \(F\) of \(2 = 1 + 1\) . In \(
Q\) , \(n \cdot 1_{
Q} = j(\iota(n))\) , the image of \(n\) under the embeddings @prp-naturals-embed-integers and @prp-integers-embed-rationals . With the identifications \(
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q\) , this says \(n \cdot 1_{
Q} = n\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.5 (The Rationals Are Dense in an Archimedean Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: In an Archimedean ordered field \(F\) , for all \(x, y \in F\) with \(x < y\) there is \(q \in \nQ\) with \(x < \iota_F(q) < y\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.2 (The Rationals Embed in Every Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
Let \(F\) be an ordered field. There is exactly one map \(\iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F\) such that, for all \(x, y \in 
Q\) , \[  egin{gathered} \iota_F(1) = 1_F , \ \iota_F(x + y) = \iota_F(x) + \iota_F(y) , \qquad \iota_F(xy) = \iota_F(x)\, \iota_F(y) . \end{gathered} \] It satisfies \(\iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F\) for every \(n \in 
N\) . It is injective and strictly increasing ( \(x < y\) implies \(\iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y)\) ), and it reflects order : \(\iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y)\) implies \(x < y\) .

title: Definition 4.3.4 (Bounded Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) is bounded if there exists \(M \in F_{>0}\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . Such an \(M\) is a bound for \((a_n)\) .

title: Definition 4.3.3 (Null Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) is null if \(a_n \to 0\) .

title: Definition 4.3.2 (Limit of a Sequence in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) and \(a \in F\) . The sequence converges to \(a\) in \(F\) , written \(a_n 	o a\) , if for every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) there exists \(N \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N\) . In symbols, \[  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) . \] Then \(a\) is a limit of \((a_n)\) . The sequence is convergent if it converges to some \(a \in F\) , and divergent otherwise.

title: Definition 4.3.1 (Sequence; Eventually)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
A sequence in \(F\) is a function \(a \colon 
N 	o F\) ( @fd2:def-function ). Its value at \(n\) is written \(a_n\) and called the \(n\) -th term ; the sequence is written \((a_n)_{n \in 
N}\) , or \((a_n)\) , and \(\{ a_n : n \in 
N \}\) is its set of values. A property \(P(n)\) of natural numbers holds eventually if there is \(N_0 \in 
N\) such that \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N_0\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Here is an argument for @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field . Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. Then repair the argument. Let \(a_n \to a\) . (2) Take \(\varepsilon \coloneqq 1\) in the definition of the limit, and let \(N\) be the index it provides. (3) Then for every \(n \in \nN\) , \(\abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}\) . (4) So \(M \coloneqq 1 + \abs{a}\) is a bound for \((a_n)\) .

title: Proposition 4.3.5 (Convergent Sequences Are Bounded)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Every convergent sequence in \(F\) is bounded.

title: Proposition 4.3.3 (Limits Through Null Sequences)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: For a sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) and \(a \in F\) : \(a_n \to a\) if and only if the sequence \((a_n - a)\) is null.

title: Proposition 4.3.1 (Archimedes as a Null Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: The sequence \(\bigl( 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F) \bigr)_{n \in \nN}\) is null in \(F\) if and only if \(F\) is Archimedean.

title: Proposition 4.3.2 (Only the Tail Matters)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be sequences in \(F\) , and \(a \in F\) . If there is \(N_0 \in 
N\) with \(a_n = b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a_n 	o a\) if and only if \(b_n 	o a\) ; in particular \((a_n)\) is null if and only if \((b_n)\) is; and \((a_n)\) is bounded if and only if \((b_n)\) is. For \(k \in 
N\) , the shifted sequence \((a_{n+k})_{n \in 
N}\) converges to \(a\) if and only if \((a_n)\) does.

title: Theorem 4.3.4 (Uniqueness of Limits)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) and \(a, b \in F\) . If \(a_n \to a\) and \(a_n \to b\) , then \(a = b\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: These questions are about the proof of the product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c). Why is \(M\) fixed before \(\varepsilon\) , and what does it depend on? Which hypothesis supplies \(N_1\) , which supplies \(N_2\) , and which supplies \(M\) ? Why does the proof use \(\abs{b} + 1\) rather than \(\abs{b}\) ? State the idea of the proof in two sentences. Run the proof in \(\nQ\) on \(a_n = 1 + 1/(n + 1)\) , \(b_n = 2\) and \(\varepsilon = 1/10\) : give a valid \(M\) , the least \(N_1\) , the least \(N_2\) , and \(N\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Find the following limits in \(\nQ\) by the limit laws, naming the result used at each step. \(\dfrac{n + 2}{3n + 1}\) . \(\dfrac{n^2 + 1}{(n + 1)^2}\) . \(\Bigl( \dfrac{1}{n + 1} - 2 \Bigr) \Bigl( 3 + \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} \Bigr)\) . title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Here are lines of the proof of @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (a), shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Recall the hypotheses: \(a_n \to a\) , \(b_n \to b\) , and \(a_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) . Write the seven lines of a correct proof in a correct order, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Let \(n \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1, N_2\}\) . Let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq a - b\) , which lies in \(F_{>0}\) . Choose \(N_2\) with \(\abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(b < a\) . This contradicts \(a_n \le b_n\) ; so \(b < a\) is false, and \(a \le b\) by trichotomy. Let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq (a - b)/2\) , which lies in \(F_{>0}\) by @prp-ordered-field-halves . Let \(n \coloneqq N_1\) . Then \(a_n > a - \varepsilon = (a + b)/2 = b + \varepsilon > b_n\) . Choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Close to a convergent sequence)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) in \(F\) , and let \((b_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) such that \((b_n - a_n)\) is null. Prove that \(b_n \to a\) . Here is the start of a proof. Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . Then \(\varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0}\) . Since \(a_n \to a\) , choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) . Since \((b_n - a_n)\) is null, choose \(N_2\) with \(\abs{b_n - a_n} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . Let \(N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}\) . … Name the move, then complete it.

page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits

You may use that convergent sequences are bounded ( @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field ), the rules for the absolute value ( @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field ), @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field and @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field , but not @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field .

title: Lemma 4.4.2 (Terms Near a Non-zero Limit)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) with \(b \ne 0\) . Then there is \(N_0 \in \nN\) with \(\abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) . If \(b > 0\) , then moreover \(b_n > b/2\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) .

title: Proposition 4.4.4 (Limits Preserve Weak Inequalities)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) and \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) , and let \(N_0 \in \nN\) . If \(a_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \le b\) . In particular, for \(c \in F\) : if \(a_n \le c\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \le c\) ; and if \(a_n \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \ge c\) . (Squeeze.) Let \((c_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) . If \(a = b\) and \(a_n \le c_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(c_n \to a\) .

title: Proposition 4.4.1 (Null Times Bounded Is Null)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a null sequence in \(F\) , and let \((b_n)\) be a sequence with \(\abs{b_n} \le M\) for every \(n\) , where \(M \in F_{>0}\) . Then \((a_n b_n)\) is null.

title: Theorem 4.4.3 (Limit Laws)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) and \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F\) . Then: \(a_n + b_n \to a + b\) ; \(c a_n \to c a\) ; in particular \(-a_n \to -a\) and \(a_n - b_n \to a - b\) ; \(a_n b_n \to a b\) ; if \(b \ne 0\) and \(b_n \ne 0\) for every \(n\) , then \(a_n / b_n \to a / b\) .

title: Definition 4.5.1 (Cauchy Sequence)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content:
A sequence \((a_n)_{n \in 
N}\) in \(F\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) (or Cauchy ) if for every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) there exists \(N \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon\) for all \(m, n \in 
N\) with \(m \ge N\) and \(n \ge N\) . In symbols: \[  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} \]

title: Example (Shrinking Steps, Terms That Do Not Settle)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Here is an argument for the false claim in the warning. “Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . Since \(a_{n+1} - a_n \to 0\) , choose \(N\) with \(\abs{a_{k+1} - a_k} < \varepsilon\) for every \(k \ge N\) . Let \(m > n \ge N\) . Then \(a_m - a_n\) is the sum of the consecutive differences \(a_{k+1} - a_k\) for \(k = n, \dots, m - 1\) , and each of them is smaller than \(\varepsilon\) in absolute value. So \(\abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon\) , and \((a_n)\) is Cauchy.” In \(\nQ\) , let \(H_0 \coloneqq 0\) and \(H_{n+1} \coloneqq H_n + 1/(n + 1)\) for \(n \in \nN\) . Show that \(H_{n+1} - H_n \to 0\) , that \(H_{2n} - H_n \ge 1/2\) for every \(n \ge 1\) , and that \((H_n)\) is not Cauchy. Find the line of the argument that fails.

title: Exercise (C3: Find the error)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Here is an argument that the product of two Cauchy sequences \((a_n)\) , \((b_n)\) in \(F\) is Cauchy. “For all \(m, n\) , \(\abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} \le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{b_n - b_m} + \abs{b_m} \, \abs{a_n - a_m}\) . Given \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) , choose \(N\) such that \(\abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n})\) and \(\abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m})\) for all \(m, n \ge N\) . Then for \(m, n \ge N\) , \(\abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon\) .” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, and repair it.

title: Proposition 4.5.2 (Cauchy Sequences Are Bounded)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Every Cauchy sequence in \(F\) is bounded.

title: Proposition 4.5.6 (Reciprocals of Cauchy Sequences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F_{>0}\) and \(N \in \nN\) be such that \(\abs{a_n} \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N\) . Define \[ b_n \coloneqq \begin{cases} 1/a_n & \text{if } n \ge N , \\ 1 & \text{if } n < N . \end{cases} \] Then \((b_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) , and \(a_n b_n = 1\) for every \(n \ge N\) .

title: Proposition 4.5.1 (Convergent Sequences Are Cauchy)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: If \(a_n \to a\) in \(F\) , then \((a_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) .

title: Proposition 4.5.5 (Sign Stability under Null Differences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be sequences in \(F\) such that \((a_n - b_n)\) is null. If \(c \in F_{>0}\) , \(N \in \nN\) , and \(a_n \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N\) , then there is \(N' \in \nN\) with \(b_n \ge c/2\) for every \(n \ge N'\) .

title: Theorem 4.5.3 (Sums and Products of Cauchy Sequences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be Cauchy sequences in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F\) . Every constant sequence and every null sequence in \(F\) is Cauchy. The sequences \((a_n + b_n)\) , \((c \, a_n)\) , \((-a_n)\) and \((a_n - b_n)\) are Cauchy. The sequence \((a_n b_n)\) is Cauchy.

title: Theorem 4.5.4 (The Sign of a Non-Null Cauchy Sequence)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) that is not null. Then there are \(c \in F_{>0}\) and \(N \in \nN\) such that either \[ a_n \ge c \ \text{ for every } n \ge N , \qquad \text{or} \qquad a_n \le -c \ \text{ for every } n \ge N . \] The two alternatives do not both hold.

title: Proposition 5.1.1 (Equivalence of Cauchy Sequences Is an Equivalence Relation)
page: 5.1 Sequences That Should Converge
content: The relation \(\sim\) of @def-cauchy-equivalent is an equivalence relation on \(\sC\) ( @fd2:def-equivalence-relation ).

title: Definition 5.2.1 (The Real Numbers)
page: 5.2 The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic
content: The set of real numbers is the quotient set ( @fd2:def-quotient-set ) \[ \nR \coloneqq \sC/{\sim} \] of the set \(\sC\) of Cauchy sequences of rationals ( @def-rational-cauchy-sequences ) by the relation \(\sim\) of @def-cauchy-equivalent . Its elements are the classes \([a] = \{ b \in \sC : b \sim a \}\) for \(a \in \sC\) ( @fd2:def-equivalence-class ), and any \(b \in [a]\) is a representative of \([a]\) .

title: Definition 5.2.2 (Sum, Product and Negative of Real Numbers)
page: 5.2 The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic
content: For \(a, b \in \sC\) , let \[ [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b] , \qquad [a] \, [b] \coloneqq [ab] , \qquad -[a] \coloneqq [-a] , \] where \(a + b\) , \(ab\) and \(-a\) are the termwise sum, product and negative. Let \(0_{\nR} \coloneqq [(0)_n]\) and \(1_{\nR} \coloneqq [(1)_n]\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: Here is an argument for @prp-positivity-well-defined . “Let \(a\) be positive and \(a' \sim a\) . Fix \(\delta \in \nQ_{>0}\) and \(N\) with \(a_n \ge \delta\) for every \(n \ge N\) . Since \(a' - a\) is null, there is \(N'\) with \(\abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta\) for every \(n \ge N'\) . So, for \(n \ge \max\{N, N'\}\) , \(a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge 0\) . Hence \(a'_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) . Therefore \(a'\) is positive.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, give a counterexample to that step, and repair the argument.

page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order

page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: Let \(a \in \sC\) . Then \((\abs{a_n})_n \in \sC\) , and \[ \abs{[a]} = [(\abs{a_n})_n] , \] where the left side is the absolute value in the ordered field \(\nR\) and \(\abs{a_n}\) is the absolute value in \(\nQ\) .

title: Theorem 5.3.3 (The Reals Form an Ordered Field)
page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: With the operations of @def-reals-operations and the order of @def-reals-order , \(\nR\) is an ordered field ( @def-ordered-ring-and-field ), and its positive elements are exactly the elements of \(P\) .

title: Theorem 5.3.2 (The Positive Real Numbers)
page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: For every \(x \in \nR\) , exactly one of \(x \in P\) , \(x = 0_{\nR}\) , \(-x \in P\) holds. If \(x \in P\) and \(y \in P\) , then \(x + y \in P\) and \(xy \in P\) .

title: Definition 5.6.1 (Complete Ordered Field)
page: 5.6 The Real Numbers Form a Complete Ordered Field
content: An ordered field \(F\) is complete if every non-empty subset \(A \subseteq F\) that is bounded above in \((F, \le)\) ( @fd2:def-order-bounds ) has a supremum in \(F\) ( @fd2:def-order-supremum ). In symbols, writing \(\mathrm{ub}(u)\) for \(\forall a \in A \ \ a \le u\) , \[ \begin{aligned} &\forall A \subseteq F \ \ \bigl( (A \ne \emptyset \wedge \exists u \in F \ \mathrm{ub}(u)) \Rightarrow \\ &\qquad \exists s \in F \ \bigl( \mathrm{ub}(s) \wedge \forall u \in F \ (\mathrm{ub}(u) \Rightarrow s \le u) \bigr) \bigr) . \end{aligned} \] An ordered field in which every Cauchy sequence ( @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field ) converges is called Cauchy-complete .

title: Definition 6.1.1 (Order-Preserving Field Map)
page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be ordered fields. A map \(\chi \colon F \to L\) is an order-preserving field map if, for all \(a, b \in F\) , \[ \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(ab) = \chi(a)\, \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(1_F) = 1_L , \] and \(a < b\) implies \(\chi(a) < \chi(b)\) . An order-preserving field isomorphism is an order-preserving field map that is bijective ( @fd2:def-bijective ). An order-preserving field automorphism of \(F\) is an order-preserving field isomorphism \(F \to F\) .

page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once

title: Proposition 6.1.1 (Field Maps Fix the Rationals)
page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be ordered fields, and let \(\chi \colon F \to L\) satisfy \(\chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b)\) , \(\chi(ab) = \chi(a)\chi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in F\) , and \(\chi(1_F) = 1_L\) . Then \[ \chi \circ \iota_F = \iota_L , \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad \chi\bigl(\iota_F(q)\bigr) = \iota_L(q) \quad \text{for every } q \in \nQ . \]

title: Proposition 6.1.4 (Square Roots in a Complete Ordered Field)
page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field and \(a \in F\) with \(a \ge 0\) . Then there is exactly one \(b \in F\) with \(b \ge 0\) and \(b^2 = a\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Cube roots)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field and \(a \in F\) with \(a > 0\) . Let \(S \coloneqq \{ y \in F : y \ge 0 \text{ and } y^3 < a \}\) . The following steps prove that some \(s \in F\) has \(s^3 = a\) . \(S\) is non-empty ( \(0 \in S\) ) and bounded above by \(1 + a\) : if \(y > 1 + a\) , then \(y > 1\) , so \(y^3 > y > a\) . Let \(s \coloneqq \sup S\) . Then \(s > 0\) , since \(m \coloneqq \min\{1, a/2\}\) has \(0 < m \le 1\) , so \(m^3 \le m \le a/2 < a\) , and \(m \in S\) . For \(y, z \in F\) , \(z^3 - y^3 = (z - y)(z^2 + zy + y^2)\) and \(z^2 + zy + y^2 = (z + y/2)^2 + (3/4)y^2\) , which is \(> 0\) unless \(y = z = 0\) (if \(y \ne 0\) , then \((3/4)y^2 > 0\) by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c) and the square is \(\ge 0\) , so the sum is positive by (b); if \(y = 0\) and \(z \ne 0\) , the expression is \(z^2 > 0\) by (e)). Hence \(y < z \iff y^3 < z^3\) , for all \(y, z \in F\) . The case \(s^3 < a\) is impossible. Let \(h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^3)/(2(3s^2 + 3s + 1))\} > 0\) . Since \(0 < h \le 1\) and \(s \ge 0\) , \((s + h)^3 = s^3 + 3s^2h + 3sh^2 + h^3 \le s^3 + h(3s^2 + 3s + 1) \le s^3 + (a - s^3)/2 < a\) , so \(s + h \in S\) , against \(s\) being an upper bound. The case \(s^3 > a\) is impossible. Name the move, then complete it. Hence \(s^3 = a\) . Then explain how to get a cube root of \(a = 0\) and of \(a < 0\) , and why every \(a \in F\) has exactly one cube root.

title: Theorem 6.3.4 (Field Maps of a Complete Ordered Field to Itself)

title: Exercise (C3: Increasing and bounded)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field and \((a_n)_{n \in \nN}\) a sequence in \(F\) with \(a_n \le a_{n+1}\) for every \(n\) , whose set of values is bounded above. Prove that \(a_n \to s\) in \(F\) ( @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field ), where \(s\) is the supremum of the set of values. Here is the start of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let \(s \coloneqq \sup \{ a_n : n \in \nN \}\) , which exists because the set is non-empty and bounded above and \(F\) is complete. Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . …”

title: Lemma 6.4.1 (The Top Term Decides the Sign)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
Let \(d \in 
N\) , let \(a_0, \dots, a_d \in 
R\) with \(a_d 
e 0\) , and let \(p(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i t^i\) . Put \[ T \coloneqq 1 + \sum_{i=0}^{d-1}  rac{\abs{a_i}}{\abs{a_d}} . \] Then for every \(t > T\) , \(p(t) 
e 0\) , and \(p(t)\) has the sign of \(a_d\) : \(p(t) > 0\) if \(a_d > 0\) , and \(p(t) < 0\) if \(a_d < 0\) .

title: Lemma 6.4.2 (Sums, Products and the Identity Principle)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
Let \(p(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i t^i\) and \(r(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{e} b_j t^j\) , for arbitrary lists \((a_0, \dots, a_d)\) and \((b_0, \dots, b_e)\) of real numbers (zero entries, and lists of zeros, are allowed). The function \(p + r\) is the polynomial function of the list \((a_k + b_k)_k\) , where the shorter list is first extended by zeros to the length of the longer. The function \(p \cdot r\) is the polynomial function of a list \((c_0, \dots, c_{d+e})\) whose last entry is \(c_{d+e} = a_d b_e\) . If moreover \(a_d 
e 0\) and \(b_e 
e 0\) , then \(a_d b_e 
e 0\) : the product list has top degree \(d + e\) and top coefficient \(a_d b_e\) . (Identity principle.) If \(p(t) = 0\) for all large \(t\) , then \(a_i = 0\) for every \(i\) .

title: Proposition 6.4.4 (Rational Functions Are Not Archimedean)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
In \(
R(x)\) , \(n \cdot 1 < x\) for every \(n \in 
N\) . Hence \(
R(x)\) is not Archimedean ( @def-archimedean-ordered-field ), and it is not complete ( @def-complete-ordered-field ).

title: Proposition 6.4.3 (Rational Functions Form an Ordered Field)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
\(
R(x)\) , with the sum, product and order of @def-cof-rational-functions , is an ordered field ( @def-ordered-ring-and-field ), with zero \([0/1]\) , unit \([1/1]\) , and positive elements exactly the elements of \(P\) . The map \(
R 	o 
R(x)\) , \(c \mapsto [c/1]\) , is an order-preserving field map ( @def-cof-order-preserving-map ).

title: Proposition 6.4.5 (An Archimedean Ordered Field Inside the Reals)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
(Unique representation.) If \(a + b\sqrt 2 = a' + b'\sqrt 2\) with \(a, b, a', b' \in 
Q\) , then \(a = a'\) and \(b = b'\) . \(
Q(\sqrt 2)\) is closed under sums, negatives and products, contains \(0\) and \(1\) , and contains the inverse of each of its non-zero elements: \[ (a + b\sqrt 2)^{-1} =  rac{a}{a^2 - 2b^2} -  rac{b}{a^2 - 2b^2} \sqrt 2 , \qquad a^2 - 2b^2 
e 0 . \] With the operations and order of \(
R\) , \(
Q(\sqrt 2)\) is an Archimedean ordered field.

title: Proposition 6.4.6 (The Field Generated by the Square Root of Two Is Not Complete)
page: 6.4 Two Non-Examples
content:
The element \(3\) of \(
Q(\sqrt 2)\) is positive and has no square root in \(
Q(\sqrt 2)\) . Hence \(
Q(\sqrt 2)\) is not complete.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 6.5 Assume the Axioms or Build a Model
content:
Throughout, \(F\) and \(L\) are complete ordered fields and \(\varphi \colon F 	o L\) is the order-preserving field isomorphism. For each statement, decide whether its truth could depend on which complete ordered field is taken as \(
R\) , and justify your answer: (i) \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 > 3\) ; (ii) the rational number \(0\) is an element of the set \(\sqrt 2\) ; (iii) \(
R\) is uncountable. True or false: “The ordered-field axioms prove every statement that is true in \(
Q\) .” Which step of the example “limits are carried across” uses that \(\varphi\) is onto? Why does a model of the axioms, built inside set theory, show that the axioms of a complete ordered field cannot contradict each other unless that set theory does?

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 6.5 Assume the Axioms or Build a Model
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be complete ordered fields and \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) the order-preserving field isomorphism. title: Definition 7.1.1 (Dedekind Cut)
page: 7.1 Cuts
content:
A subset \(\alpha \subseteq 
Q\) is a cut (or Dedekind cut ) if \(\alpha 
e \emptyset\) and \(\alpha 
e 
Q\) ; for every \(p \in \alpha\) and every \(q \in 
Q\) with \(q < p\) , \(q \in \alpha\) ; \(\alpha\) has no largest element : for every \(p \in \alpha\) there exists \(p' \in \alpha\) with \(p' > p\) . The set of all cuts is \[ 
R_{\mathrm D} \coloneqq \{ \alpha \in \powerset{
Q} : \alpha 	ext{ satisfies (C1), (C2) and (C3)} \} , \] a subset of the power set \(\powerset{
Q}\) ( @fd2:def-power-set ).

title: Definition 7.1.2 (Rational Cut)
page: 7.1 Cuts
content:
For \(q \in 
Q\) , let \[ D_q \coloneqq \{ r \in 
Q : r < q \} . \] It is a cut (checked below), the rational cut of \(q\) . A cut \(\alpha\) is rational if \(\alpha = D_q\) for some \(q \in 
Q\) .

page: 7.1 Cuts
content: Show that \(\sigma = \{ p \in \nQ : p \le 0 \text{ or } p^2 < 2 \}\) is a cut.

page: 7.1 Cuts
content: Let \(E_1 \coloneqq \{ r \in \nQ : r \le 1 \}\) . Show that \(E_1\) satisfies (C1) and (C2) but not (C3), and that, with the sum of sets \(X + Y \coloneqq \{ x + y : x \in X, \ y \in Y \}\) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Section 1.6 ( @fd2:exm-sets-of-numbers-as-images ), \[ E_1 + D_1 = D_2 = D_1 + D_1 , \qquad \text{although } E_1 \ne D_1 . \]

page: 7.1 Cuts
content:
State (C1)–(C3) for a subset \(\alpha \subseteq

title: Lemma 7.1.1 (Separation)
page: 7.1 Cuts
content:
Let \(\alpha\) be a cut, \(p \in \alpha\) and \(q \in 
Q \setminus \alpha\) . Then \(p < q\) . Consequently the complement \(
Q \setminus \alpha\) is closed upward : if \(q 
otin \alpha\) and \(q' \in 
Q\) with \(q' > q\) , then \(q' 
otin \alpha\) .

title: Lemma 7.1.3 (The Step Lemma)
page: 7.1 Cuts
content:
Let \(\alpha\) be a cut, \(a \in \alpha\) , and \(\varepsilon \in 
Q\) with \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Then there is \(n \in 
N\) with \[ a + n\varepsilon \in \alpha \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad a + (n + 1)\varepsilon 
otin \alpha . \]

title: Proposition 7.1.2 (Where a Rational Lies)
page: 7.1 Cuts
content: Let \(\alpha\) be a cut and \(q \in \nQ\) . Then \(q \in \alpha\) if and only if \(D_q \subsetneq \alpha\) ; \(q \notin \alpha\) if and only if \(\alpha \subseteq D_q\) .

title: Definition 7.2.1 (Order of Cuts)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content: For cuts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , we write \(\alpha \le \beta\) if \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) , and \(\alpha < \beta\) if \(\alpha \subsetneq \beta\) , that is, if \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) and \(\alpha \ne \beta\) . As usual, \(\beta \ge \alpha\) means \(\alpha \le \beta\) , and \(\beta > \alpha\) means \(\alpha < \beta\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content: These questions are about @thm-dedekind-lub and its proof. Let \(A \coloneqq \{ D_q : q \in \sigma \}\) , with \(\sigma\) the cut of @exm-cut-sqrt2 . Check that \(A\) satisfies the hypotheses, and find the cut \(\gamma\) of the proof, arguing directly from (C2) and (C3) of \(\sigma\) . State the idea of the proof in two sentences. Which line of the proof fails if \(A = \emptyset\) , and what is \(\gamma\) then? In the check of (C3) for \(\gamma\) , which cut’s condition (C3) is used?

page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content: Let \(q, r \in \nQ\) . Prove that \(\sup \{ D_q, D_r \} = D_{\max(q, r)}\) in \((\nR_{\mathrm D}, \le)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content:
Here are lines of a proof that for cuts \(\alpha\) and \( eta\) , \(\alpha \le  eta\) or \( eta \le \alpha\) , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Without looking back, write the lines of a correct proof in a correct order, and say what is wrong with each line you leave out. Let \(q \in  eta\) be arbitrary. Since \(q < p\) and \(p \in \alpha\) , \(q \in  eta\) . As \(q\) was arbitrary, \( eta \subseteq \alpha\) . Let \(\alpha\) , \( eta\) be cuts with \(\alpha 
ot\subseteq  eta\) (if \(\alpha \subseteq  eta\) , there is nothing to prove). Since \(p \in \alpha\) and \(q < p\) , \(q \in \alpha\) , because \(\alpha\) is closed downward. Since \(q \in  eta\) and \(p 
otin  eta\) , \(p < q\) . Then some \(p \in \alpha\) has \(p 
otin  eta\) . Since \(q \in  eta\) and \(p 
otin  eta\) , \(q < p\) , by separation.

title: Exercise (C1: Infima)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content:
Let \(A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D}\) be non-empty and bounded below. Show that \( igcap A\) need not be a cut, by computing \( igcap A_0\) for \(A_0 \coloneqq \{ D_{1/n} : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}\) . Prove that \(A\) nevertheless has an infimum in \((

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content:
Here is a proof. Its conclusion is the first half of @thm-dedekind-lub . Claim. Let \(A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D}\) be non-empty and bounded above. Then \(\gamma \coloneqq  igcup A\) is a cut. Since \(A\) is non-empty, pick \(\alpha_0 \in A\) ; since \(\alpha_0 
e \emptyset\) , pick \(p_0 \in \alpha_0\) . Then \(p_0 \in \gamma\) , so \(\gamma 
e \emptyset\) . (2) Each \(\alpha \in A\) is a cut, so \(\alpha 
e 
Q\) . Hence \(\gamma 
e 
Q\) . (3) Let \(p \in \gamma\) and \(q < p\) . Then \(p \in \alpha\) for some \(\alpha \in A\) , so \(q \in \alpha\) by (C2), and \(q \in \gamma\) . (4) Let \(p \in \gamma\) . Then \(p \in \alpha\) for some \(\alpha \in A\) ; by (C3) there is \(p' \in \alpha\) with \(p' > p\) , and \(p' \in \gamma\) . (5) So \(\gamma\) satisfies (C1)–(C3). Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say what is illegal about it, and give a counterexample to that step.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: least upper bounds of cuts)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content: Let \(A\) be a non-empty set of cuts, bounded above in \((\nR_{\mathrm D}, \subseteq)\) . Prove that \(\bigcup A\) is a cut and that it is the supremum of \(A\) .

title: Theorem 7.2.1 (Cuts Are Totally Ordered)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content: For all cuts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , \(\alpha \le \beta\) or \(\beta \le \alpha\) . Hence exactly one of \(\alpha < \beta\) , \(\alpha = \beta\) , \(\beta < \alpha\) holds.

title: Theorem 7.2.2 (Least Upper Bounds of Cuts)
page: 7.2 Order by Inclusion, and Least Upper Bounds by Unions
content:
Let \(A \subseteq 
R_{\mathrm D}\) be non-empty and bounded above : some cut \( eta\) has \(\alpha \le  eta\) for every \(\alpha \in A\) . Then \[ \gamma \coloneqq  igcup A = \{ p \in 
Q : p \in \alpha 	ext{ for some } \alpha \in A \} \] ( @fd2:def-family-union-intersection , the family indexed by \(A\) itself) is a cut, and \(\gamma\) is the supremum of \(A\) in \((
R_{\mathrm D}, \le)\) .

title: Definition 7.3.2 (Negative of a Cut)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content:
For a cut \(\alpha\) , its negative is the set \[ -\alpha \coloneqq \{ p \in 
Q : -p - r 
otin \alpha 	ext{ for some rational } r > 0 \} . \] In symbols, \(p \in -\alpha \iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ {-p - r} 
otin \alpha\) . It is a cut (checked below). A rational \(r\) with this property is a margin for \(p\) .

title: Definition 7.3.1 (Sum of Cuts)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For cuts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , the sum is the set \[ \alpha + \beta \coloneqq \{ p + q : p \in \alpha, \ q \in \beta \} . \]

title: Example (The Negatives of the Outside)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For a cut \(\alpha\) , is the set \(\{ -q : q \in \nQ \setminus \alpha \}\) a cut? Test it on \(\sigma = \{ p \in \nQ : p \le 0 \text{ or } p^2 < 2 \}\) ( @exm-cut-sqrt2 ) and on \(D_1\) . Then decide in general. Is the set \(\{ -p : p \in \alpha \}\) a cut?

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-cut-additive-inverse and the definition of \(-\alpha\) . Run the \(\supseteq\) half of the proof for \(\alpha = D_1\) , \(s = -1/2\) and the starting point \(a = 0\) . What are \(\varepsilon\) , \(n\) , \(p\) , \(t\) and the margin? Check that \(t \in -D_1\) and \(p + t = s\) . Where in the proof is @lem-cut-step used, and what does that lemma need from \(\nQ\) ? In the check that \(-\alpha\) is a cut, which condition uses \(r > 0\) ? What goes wrong for \(\alpha = D_1\) if the margin \(r = 0\) is allowed? State the idea of the proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: Prove that \(-D_q = D_{-q}\) for every \(q \in \nQ\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Associativity, element by element)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) be any subsets of \(\nQ\) , and let \(A + B \coloneqq \{ a + b : a \in A, \ b \in B \}\) . Prove that \((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)\) , writing out both inclusions element by element and naming the rule of \(\nQ\) used in each. Which of the cut conditions (C1)–(C3) did you use?

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: a cut plus its negative)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: Prove that \(\alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0\) for every cut \(\alpha\) . Then explain, on the cut \(\alpha = D_1\) , why the recipe \(\{ -q : q \in \nQ \setminus \alpha \}\) does not give an additive inverse in \(\nR_{\mathrm D}\) , while @def-cut-negative does.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: Here is a proof that \(\alpha + D_0 = \alpha\) for every cut \(\alpha\) . Proof. (1) Let \(\alpha\) be a cut. (2) \((\subseteq)\) Let \(x \in \alpha + D_0\) , so \(x = p + q\) with \(p \in \alpha\) and \(q \in D_0\) . (3) Then \(q < 0\) , so \(x = p + q < p\) , and \(x \in \alpha\) by (C2). (4) \((\supseteq)\) Let \(p \in \alpha\) . (5) Then \(p = p + 0\) with \(p \in \alpha\) and \(0 \in D_0\) , so \(p \in \alpha + D_0\) . (6) Hence \(\alpha + D_0 = \alpha\) . Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why? Give a counterexample to the step itself. Repair the proof. The flawed proof never uses (C3). Show that without it the conclusion can fail: compute \(A + D_0\) for \(A \coloneqq \{ r \in \nQ : r \le 1 \}\) .

title: Proposition 7.3.2 (The Zero Cut)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For every cut \(\alpha\) , \(\alpha + D_0 = \alpha\) .

title: Theorem 7.3.3 (Additive Inverses of Cuts)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For every cut \(\alpha\) , \(\alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0\) .

title: Theorem 7.3.4 (Cuts Form an Ordered Group under Addition)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For all cuts \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) : \(\alpha + \beta = \beta + \alpha\) and \((\alpha + \beta) + \gamma = \alpha + (\beta + \gamma)\) ; \(\alpha + D_0 = \alpha\) ; \(\alpha + (-\alpha) = D_0\) ; \(\le\) is a total order on \(\nR_{\mathrm D}\) ; if \(\alpha \le \beta\) , then \(\alpha + \gamma \le \beta + \gamma\) ; and if \(\alpha < \beta\) , then \(\alpha + \gamma < \beta + \gamma\) ; (cancellation and unique inverses) if \(\alpha + \gamma = \beta + \gamma\) , then \(\alpha = \beta\) ; if \(\alpha + \beta = D_0\) , then \(\beta = -\alpha\) ; and \(-(-\alpha) = \alpha\) , \(-D_0 = D_0\) , \(-(\alpha + \beta) = (-\alpha) + (-\beta)\) ; \(\alpha < \beta\) if and only if \(-\beta < -\alpha\) , and \(\alpha \le \beta\) if and only if \(-\beta \le -\alpha\) . In particular \(\alpha > D_0 \iff -\alpha < D_0\) , and \(\alpha < D_0 \iff -\alpha > D_0\) . So \((\nR_{\mathrm D}, +, \le)\) is an ordered abelian group : (a)–(c) are (F1)–(F4) for \(+\) , with zero \(D_0\) , and (d) is a total order with (O3). Clauses (e) and (f) are consequences.

title: Theorem 7.3.1 (The Sum of Two Cuts Is a Cut)
page: 7.3 Addition and Negatives
content: For all cuts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , the set \(\alpha + \beta\) is a cut. Addition of cuts is commutative and associative: for all cuts \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) , \[ \alpha + \beta = \beta + \alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\alpha + \beta) + \gamma = \alpha + (\beta + \gamma) . \]

title: Definition 7.4.2 (Absolute Value, Sign and Product of Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: For a cut \(\alpha\) , its absolute value and sign are \[ \abs{\alpha} \coloneqq \begin{cases} \alpha & \text{if } \alpha \ge D_0 , \\ -\alpha & \text{if } \alpha < D_0 , \end{cases} \qquad \sgn \alpha \coloneqq \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha > D_0 , \\ 0 & \text{if } \alpha = D_0 , \\ -1 & \text{if } \alpha < D_0 . \end{cases} \] For cuts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , their product is \[ \alpha\beta \coloneqq \begin{cases} D_0 & \text{if } \alpha = D_0 \text{ or } \beta = D_0 , \\ \abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta} & \text{if } \sgn \alpha = \sgn \beta \ne 0 , \\ -\bigl( \abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta} \bigr) & \text{if } \sgn \alpha \ne \sgn \beta \text{ and neither is } 0 , \end{cases} \] where \(\abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\) is the product of positive cuts of @def-cut-product-positive .

title: Definition 7.4.1 (Product of Positive Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be cuts with \(\alpha > D_0\) and \(\beta > D_0\) (equivalently, \(0 \in \alpha\) and \(0 \in \beta\) , by @prp-rational-in-cut ). Their product is \[ \begin{aligned} \alpha\beta \coloneqq \{ p \in \nQ : {}& p \le rs \text{ for some } r \in \alpha \text{ and } s \in \beta \\ & \text{with } r > 0 \text{ and } s > 0 \} . \end{aligned} \]

title: Definition 7.4.3 (Reciprocal of a Cut)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content:

content: Why is the set \(\{ pq : p \in \alpha, \ q \in \beta \}\) useless as a product for \(\alpha = \beta = D_1\) ? Which further rows depend on such a row? Compute \(\abs{D_{-1}}\) , \(\sgn D_{-1}\) , \(\abs{D_{1/2}}\) , \(\sgn D_{1/2}\) and \(D_{-1} D_{1/2}\) from the definitions. page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: Let \(\alpha\) be a cut with \(\alpha > D_0\) , and let \(p \in \nQ\) with \(0 < p < 1\) . We show that \(p \in \alpha\alpha^{-1}\) . Let \(\mu \coloneqq (1 + 1/p)/2\) . Since \(1/p > 1\) , \(\mu\) is the midpoint of \(1\) and \(1/p\) , so \(1 < \mu < 1/p\) . By @lem-cut-multiplicative-step there is \(r \in \alpha\) with \(r > 0\) and \(\mu r \notin \alpha\) . Hence \(p \in \alpha\alpha^{-1}\) . Name the move, then complete it: write out step (3).

title: Lemma 7.4.5 (Distributivity for All Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: For all cuts \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) , \(\alpha(\beta + \gamma) = \alpha\beta + \alpha\gamma\) .

title: Lemma 7.4.3 (Distributivity for Positive Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: For all cuts \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma > D_0\) , \(\alpha(\beta + \gamma) = \alpha\beta + \alpha\gamma\) .

title: Lemma 7.4.2 (The Walk Up, Multiplicatively)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: Let \(\alpha\) be a cut with \(\alpha > D_0\) , and let \(\mu \in \nQ\) with \(\mu > 1\) . Then there is \(r \in \alpha\) with \(r > 0\) and \(\mu r \notin \alpha\) .

title: Lemma 7.4.4 (Sign Rules for Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: For all cuts \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) : \(\alpha = \sgn(\alpha)\abs{\alpha}\) , reading \(1 \cdot \xi \coloneqq \xi\) , \(0 \cdot \xi \coloneqq D_0\) and \((-1) \cdot \xi \coloneqq -\xi\) ; so two cuts with the same sign and the same absolute value are equal; \(\abs{\alpha\beta} = \abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\) and \(\sgn(\alpha\beta) = \sgn\alpha \, \sgn\beta\) ; \(\abs{-\alpha} = \abs{\alpha}\) and \(\sgn(-\alpha) = -\sgn\alpha\) ; \((-\alpha)\beta = -(\alpha\beta) = \alpha(-\beta)\) ; \(\alpha\beta = \beta\alpha\) ; \((\alpha\beta)\gamma = \alpha(\beta\gamma)\) ; \(\alpha D_1 = \alpha\) .

title: Proposition 7.4.1 (Positive Cuts under Multiplication)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: Let \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) be cuts with \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma > D_0\) . Then: \(\alpha\beta\) is a cut, and \(\alpha\beta > D_0\) ; \(\alpha\beta = \beta\alpha\) ; \((\alpha\beta)\gamma = \alpha(\beta\gamma)\) ; \(\alpha D_1 = \alpha\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.6 (Reciprocals of Cuts)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: Let \(\alpha\) be a cut with \(\alpha \ne D_0\) . Then \(\alpha^{-1}\) is a cut, \(\alpha^{-1} > D_0\) if \(\alpha > D_0\) , \(\alpha^{-1} < D_0\) if \(\alpha < D_0\) , and \[ \alpha \alpha^{-1} = D_1 . \]

title: Theorem 7.4.7 (The Cuts Form an Ordered Field)
page: 7.4 Multiplication
content: With the addition of @def-cut-sum , the multiplication of @def-cut-product and the order of @def-cut-order , \(\nR_{\mathrm D}\) is an ordered field ( @def-ordered-ring-and-field ), with zero \(D_0\) and one \(D_1\) .

content: Let \(\rho \coloneqq \{ p \in \nQ : p \le 0 \text{ or } p^2 < 3 \}\) . page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: Prove that between any two cuts \(\alpha < \beta\) lies a cut that is not rational: there is a cut \(\gamma\) with \(\alpha < \gamma < \beta\) and \(\gamma \ne D_r\) for every \(r \in \nQ\) .

title: Exercise (C2: A cube root of two)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field

Let \(	au \coloneqq \{ p \in

Monotone cubing. For rationals \(0 \le a < b\) , \(b^3 - a^3 = (b - a)(b^2 + ab + a^2) > 0\) , since \(b - a > 0\) , \(b^2 > 0\) ( @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), \(ab \ge 0\) , \(a^2 \ge 0\) , and a product of positives is positive ( @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). Only non-negative \(a, b\) are needed, because of the clause “ \(p \le 0\) or”. \(	au\) is a cut and \(	au > D_0\) . (C1) \(0 \in 	au\) , and \(2 
otin 	au\) since \(2^3 = 8 \ge 2\) . (C2) Let \(q < p \in 	au\) . If \(q \le 0\) , then \(q \in 	au\) . If \(0 < q < p\) , then \(p > 0\) , so \(p^3 < 2\) , and monotone cubing gives \(q^3 < p^3 < 2\) . (C3) If \(p \le 0\) , then \(1 \in 	au\) is larger. If \(p > 0\) and \(p^3 < 2\) , put \(d \coloneqq 2 - p^3\) , so \(0 < d \le 2\) , and \[ h \coloneqq  rac{d}{3p^2 + 3p + 2} . \] Then \(0 < h < 1\) , because \(d \le 2 < 3p^2 + 3p + 2\) . So \(h^2 < h\) and \(h^3 < h\) , and since \(p > 0\) , \[  egin{aligned} (p + h)^3 &= p^3 + 3p^2 h + 3p h^2 + h^3 \ &< p^3 + h (3p^2 + 3p + 1) \ &< p^3 + h (3p^2 + 3p + 2) = p^3 + d = 2 , \end{aligned} \] so \(p + h \in 	au\) and \(p + h > p\) . Finally \(D_0 \subseteq 	au\) and \(1 \in 	au \setminus D_0\) , so \(	au > D_0\) . The \(\subseteq\) half of \(	au	au	au = D_2\) . Since \(	au > D_0\) , the proof of @prp-cut-product-positive (c), with \(\alpha =  eta = \gamma = 	au\) , shows that \((	au	au)	au = 	au(	au	au)\) (so we write \(	au	au	au\) ) is the set of \(x \in 
Q\) with \(x \le rst\) for some positive \(r, s, t \in 	au\) . For such \(r, s, t\) , let \(m\) be the largest. Then \(rst \le m^3 < 2\) , by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) and monotone cubing. So \(	au	au	au \subseteq D_2\) . The \(\supseteq\) half, easy cases. Let \(x < 1\) . Then \(1 \in 	au\) ( \(1^3 < 2\) ) and \(x \le 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1\) , so \(x \in 	au	au	au\) . This covers \(x \le 0\) and \(0 < x < 1\) together. The \(\supseteq\) half, the case \(1 \le x < 2\) . Let \(1 \le x < 2\) . Find \(r \in 	au\) , \(r > 0\) , with \(r^3 > x\) , and then write \(x\) as a product of three positive elements of \(	au\) . Name the move, then complete it.

title: Proposition 7.5.5 (The Cut of the Square Root of Two)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: The cut \(\sigma\) of @exm-cut-sqrt2 satisfies \(\sigma > D_0\) and \(\sigma \sigma = D_2\) . Consequently \(\sigma \ne D_q\) for every \(q \in \nQ\) .

title: Proposition 7.5.2 (A Cut Is the Union of the Rational Cuts Below It)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: For every cut \(\alpha\) , \[ \alpha = \bigcup \{ D_q : q \in \alpha \} = \sup \{ D_q : q \in \alpha \} . \]

title: Proposition 7.5.4 (The Cuts Are Archimedean)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: For every cut \(\alpha\) there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(\alpha < D_n\) . Hence \(\nR_{\mathrm D}\) is an Archimedean ordered field.

title: Theorem 7.5.3 (The Rational Cuts Are Dense)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be cuts with \(\alpha < \beta\) . Then there is \(q \in \nQ\) with \(\alpha < D_q < \beta\) .

title: Theorem 7.5.6 (The Cuts Form a Complete Ordered Field)
page: 7.5 The Rationals Inside the Cuts, and a Complete Ordered Field
content: \(\nR_{\mathrm D}\) , with the sum of @def-cut-sum , the product of @def-cut-product and the order of @def-cut-order , is a complete ordered field ( @def-complete-ordered-field ).
